Sports.title: Merson: Arsenal didn't make X factor signing to win Champions League
Sports.content:
Arsenal's record last year was amazing in the Champions League and they're going to be there or thereabouts again – but I don't think they bought that X factor signing to take them to that next level.

They have enough to win the Premier League with their squad. I just think the forward line against the big boys, they're missing that little ingredient.

If they'd had a Vinicius Junior or a Julian Alvarez, that would have given them the edge to go on and win the Champions League.

I think they might just fall short.

I'm a big fan of Kai Havertz. He does a lot of work and he's what I call a good footballer. He works hard and makes the right decisions. I just think he's not going to score 20 goals in a season. To take them to the Premier League title, there's no doubt about it, he's a top-drawer player.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at some of Kai Havertz's best goals in the Premier League.

The other thing I look at is when Arsenal go and play against Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain, teams like that in the Champions League latter stages, the centre-halves and the full-backs, getting up in the morning and going to their team talk and saying to one of the other players, "Didn't sleep very well last night, a bit worried about who I'm playing against".

I don't see that for Arsenal. Maybe Bukayo Saka for the left-back, but they haven't got that X factor.

I think that's what they found out in the final last year. Arsenal had no pace getting forward, and PSG just squeezed the game up and didn't let Arsenal out of their half. That would be the worry.

They had been so close to winning the Premier League and then they got over the line, I wouldn't say comfortably, but they've kicked on again.

They've got some good players. I think they could have gone on again and bought a real, real superstar. But their squad is immense. It's so solid.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Arsenal head coach Mikel Arteta says they are prepared for the start of their Champions League campaign against Napoli.

It's so hard just to get a shot off against them, let alone score a goal. Chelsea went there with one of the best, if not the best, front threes in the Premier League.

They scored after 77 seconds, but I can't remember them ever looking like they'd score another goal after that. So that just shows you how dominant Arsenal are at the moment.

It's important you start well in the Champions League. When the tournament changed to this format, teams struggled. They had eight games, they thought they'd win enough and get through. Manchester City and Paris Saint-Germain struggled at times to get through.

And then last year, everybody tried to get their wins under their belt very, very quickly. This is an important game tonight. They'll want to keep the momentum going.

If you'd said to me a year or two ago, Napoli away, I'd have said it was a hard game. But Chelsea went there in Europe and beat them and they hadn't been beaten for a long time at home. So they're beatable and I don't expect Arsenal to lose.

Sports.title: Chandhok: Not driving for Ferrari has taken pressure off Antonelli
Sports.content:
Sky Sports F1's Karun Chandhok believes Kimi Antonelli driving for Mercedes, rather than Ferrari, has taken some pressure off the Italian.

Antonelli joined the Mercedes junior programme as an 11-year-old after some remarkable results in karting and quickly rose up the motorsport ranks to Formula 1 and replaced Lewis Hamilton at the Silver Arrows only last year.

He currently leads the Drivers' Championship by 66 points from team-mate George Russell ahead of this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid and is on course to become the youngest world champion in F1 history at 20 years old.

His father, Marco Antonelli, has previously revealed he held discussions with Ferrari but the Scuderia did not want to sign someone so young whereas Mercedes were willing to take the risk.

On the latest episode of The F1 Show, Chandhok said: "I actually think by not making him a Ferrari junior, not putting him in front of Ferrari, not trying to make him a Ferrari young driver, and going down the Mercedes path, is actually the best thing that Marco Antonelli has done for his son. It's taken the pressure off in so many ways.

"Could you imagine if he was there as a Ferrari Italian driver? The pressure would be unbelievable. And Mercedes have done a fantastic job of nurturing him and bringing him here.

"I saw Kimi's parents and his sister afterwards by the Mercedes motorhome. They looked so delighted with the fact that obviously he'd won the home Grand Prix. I couldn't help but think they've managed to take away some pressure by not having him as a Ferrari driver."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli wins the Italian Grand Prix from 19th on the grid

Last week, Antonelli played down suggestions that he could drive for Ferrari in the future as he claimed he could spend his entire career with Mercedes.

He said "as much as Ferrari is massive, incredible brand, I am very happy where I am" but Chandhok hopes he does drive in red one day.

"For the sake of the sport and the sake of Ferrari, I hope, a bit like Lewis, in 10, 15 years' time when Kimi's achieved a whole lot of things, maybe he will become a Ferrari driver. It'll be great for Ferrari to have him one day," he said.

'A total breath of fresh air for F1'

Antonelli has stunned most of the F1 paddock this year with his speed and performances so far, but his most recent in Monza where he won from 19th on the grid made headlines around the world.

Sky Sports F1's David Croft says Antonelli is a "generational talent" but is still "keeping his feet on the ground".

"At the start of the weekend he was getting pranked in the paddock, getting cream pies flung at him from his team as they got him back with a birthday surprise. I'm not sure the majority of F1 drivers on the grid would have stood for that," said Croft.

"Kimi absolutely revelled in it and there is a driver who is so at ease and so comfortable in the team that he's in. Long may that continue on track and off it as well. He is a total breath of fresh air for Formula 1."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli reflects on his sensational 19th to first Monza victory, catching teammate George Russell to claim a landmark home win and strengthen his championship lead

Chandhok added: "He's been prepared from a much younger age as a professional, all-rounded driver - how to work with a team, how to work with a bigger structure.

"These kids now who are being signed to driver programmes from the ages of 10, 11, 12 in junior karting, they're being moulded from a younger age.

"You compare and contrast to the generation above, a Fernando Alonso or a Michael Schumacher, they only signed to professional contracts by the time they were already in F3.

"So I think, in some ways, it's not a surprise, I guess, that he is arriving as a more finished package because he's had 10 years of being as part of a professional structure, which the generation above wasn't."

Sports.title: Shelton beats Alcaraz at 3.33am in New York epic
Sports.content:
Ben Shelton clinched the biggest win of his career as he defeated defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set epic stretching deep into the New York night to reach the semi-finals of the US Open.

The American prevailed 6-7 (5-7) 6-1 6-3 1-6 7-6 (10-7) over four hours and 28 minutes to reward a raucous Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd gripped until 3.33am in what was the latest-ever finish to a US Open match.

It marked Shelton's first career win over a top-three player, against which he had been 0-17 coming into the match.

Shelton will now play Frances Tiafoe in the final four after his fellow countryman's thrilling five-set victory over Alex Michelsen earlier in the evening.

"For me it's always about the people in the crowd, whether it's my coaches, team or friends and family, or the city of New York that showed up tonight until 3am with the USA chants, that's what kept me going and what got me this win," Shelton said on-court.

"It's incredible. This is the greatest sports city and greatest stadium in the world. I'm hoping my best friend and sister don't have to be at work at 6am.

"I'm so grateful, so blessed to be in front of you guys and share the court with Carlos is an absolute honour."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Trinity Rodman was left shocked after her boyfriend Ben Shelton thanked his best friend and sister but appeared to forget his partner.

Shelton's victory means the United States is guaranteed representation in Sunday's men's final, with Andy Roddick the last American man to win a major title back in 2003.

It also spelled the end of Alcaraz's courageous return to the court having been out for more than four months with a wrist injury and initially been a doubt to compete in New York.

The seven-time major champion, playing his first tournament since April, was seen vomiting before the beginning of the final set, which culminated in a 10-point match-deciding tie-break.

"As I said before the tournament began, the expectation was to go there, compete... playing these kind of matches, for me being healthy," said Alcaraz. "It was close, it really was close. So I'm just a little bit disappointed, about, (not) getting the win at the end.

"But, I'm just happy, I'm just proud about myself, about how I fought. After the third set, physically I was really tired, but I found a way to push myself up, physically give an extra. In the fifth set,

"I just started to feel better and better. I was playing against one of the... he is a beast. He's an unbelievable player. Powerful. He just managed how to play really, really well in every situation, so credit to him. I leave the court happy, I leave the court with a smile, healthy, and this is what I needed."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch this insane point from the match between Shelton and Alcaraz

Shelton heads into his third Grand Slam semi-final having previously reached the final four of the 2023 US Open and the 2025 Australian Open.

Having lost the opening tie-break, the 23-year-old stormed to nine straight games on his way to dominant second and third sets. Back came Alcaraz to send it to a decider, where he would win four successive points to lead 5-3 in the tie-break before inviting Shelton to turn things around.

In true Shelton fashion, he iced the game with a serve of 146mph that Alcaraz failed to tame, bringing the New York crowd to their feet.

"I remember, the last tiebreak that I played was in Paris," recalled Alcaraz. "It was an unbelievable game that I played in that moment. This time, when you are trying to fight and trying to overcome all the problems you might have - physically, tired a lot, obviously when he's serving, he puts a lot of pressure on you.

"You're thinking about, trying to put the return in, and it's unknown if you're going to play the point or he's going to get a free point with the serve. I think in these moments he takes a lot of advantage with serve, but not any excuse, but I would say it's an important weapon in these moments."

Image: Shelton celebrates his US Open victory over Alcaraz

Tiafoe reaches US Open semis in thrilling fightback

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the US Open quarter-final match between Frances Tiafoe and Alex Michelsen

Frances Tiafoe recovered from two sets down and ‌erased a 0-3 deficit in the fifth set to beat American compatriot Alex Michelsen 5-7 3-6 7-5 6-3 7-6 (10-6), reaching the semi-finals for a third time.

The 11th seed ​appeared to have lost all the magic of his early campaign before claiming the momentum in the third set and clinching ​it with a forehand winner to the deafening cheers of ‌the fans on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Michelsen had flown under the radar in his deepest major run but ​earned respect on the biggest stage of American tennis with 21 aces, and Tiafoe cut his own celebration short to comfort the 22-year-old in an emotional ​embrace.

"I hope he gets tight," Tiafoe said of his mindset at 4-5 down in the third set. "He gave me some gifts, a couple of double faults there.

"But then I slowly started to get my rhythm there, snuck out the third set and slowly started playing better and better.

"He is a hell of a player. He should've easily won today, so shout out Alex Michelsen."

Sports.title: F1's toughest street track ever? Why new Madring could cause Spanish GP chaos
Sports.content:
Formula 1 has a brand-new track to look forward to this weekend and the expectation is there will be carnage and the drivers will be seriously tested at the Madring.

The Spanish Grand Prix has moved from its traditional circuit in Barcelona to a high-speed street track in Madrid and has been described as "Jeddah on steroids" by Formula 3 drivers who tested there last month - the Jeddah track itself is one of the most challenging circuits in F1.

So why is the Madring so difficult and how will it impact the racing we see this weekend, live on Sky Sports F1?

A lap around the Madring

There are 22 official corners on the 3.365-mile Madring circuit, although unusually the track layout has Turns 5A and 20A - so maybe there are 24.

Whatever the number, after the start/finish straight the driver will almost always be turning the steering wheel at some point as there are few straights.

The left-right chicane of Turns 1 and 2 is one of just a few overtaking spots thanks to its heavy braking zone before a long blast through Turns 3 and 4 towards arguably the most awkward chicane in F1 since the old 'Singapore Sling' chicane which was used at the Singapore Grand Prix between 2008 and 2012.

Just how much speed and how much kerb the drivers can use at Turn 5 will be a critical point of the circuit. If cars go side by side approaching Turn 5, hold your breath, because you cannot fit two cars through there alongside each other. However, the long flat-out zone before the chicane means drivers will be keen to make an overtake here...

Image: The Madring F1 track layout (Credit: F1)

After that, the track goes up and down into a really tricky uphill braking zone of Turn 7 where we may see drivers glancing the barriers on the outside.

The track then veers left, right and left, which may be flat out come qualifying when the track is clean after plenty of rubber has gone down from the practice sessions.

Then comes, what could become iconic, Turn 12, known as La Monumental. A huge banked corner that turns 180 degrees at 24 per cent gradient (13.5 degrees) where the drivers will try to stay hard on the throttle as much as possible while experiencing massive G-forces.

Image: The banked Turn 12 known as La Monumental will be a big test for the drivers to stay on the throttle (Photo by Aaron Heredia/NurPhoto)

After a left-hand flick at Turn 13, the next few corners should be flat out until you arrive at a 90-degree right hander of Turn 17 before the drivers dance through Turns 18 and 19 at high speed, then hit the brakes into a sharp left hander at Turn 20.

The last corner of Turn 22 is a 90-degree right hander where the inside barriers jut out, so the drivers will need to be careful not to cut the apex too much as they arrive on the main straight to complete a rollercoaster lap which should be around 90 seconds in qualifying.

New F1 tracks from last 10 years 2026: Madring

2023: Las Vegas Strip Circuit

2022: Miami International Autodrome

2021: Lusail International Circuit

2021: Jeddah Corniche Circuit

2020: Portimao

2020: Mugello

2016: Baku City Circuit

What have the drivers said?

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, plus Williams' Carlos Sainz are the only drivers to have any experience of driving the circuit.

Sainz is a Madring ambassador and gave input on the Turn 12 La Monumental banking so track designers could ensure it is safe, while still being unique.

Leclerc said: "It's a very, very special corner. It's a corner where I feel in qualifying, we'll have to, I will say it in a polite way, but we'll have to be very brave because it's going to be on the limit.

"And so that's going to be really cool, I think. It's going to be a really cool corner. I do believe it can become one of the most iconic corners of the season, especially once the grandstand will be built. I think that will add also to the experience of that corner."

Image: Madrid has a contract to host F1 races until at least 2035

Leclerc and Hamilton conducted a filming day in July when the track had only just finished its completion, so it was extremely hot and dusty.

"As you would expect, there was no grip. So your tyres were basically just covered in dust, and that's the whole time," said Hamilton.

"It looks like it will be a qualifying lap sort of circuit, and there's not really any straights. So it looks like a difficult place to overtake."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A first look at F1's newest circuit - the Madring

For much of the track, if the drivers are slightly off the racing line by turning at the wrong time or carrying a little too much speed, they could easily find themselves in the barriers at high speed.

The risk-versus-reward stakes will be very high and the bravest drivers, who get it right, will come out on top.

"I think definitely with the way they've put the barriers and the design of the track it's going to be one of the biggest challenges in Formula 1 recently," said Sainz.

"The track reminds me a lot of Jeddah, it reminds me a lot of Baku, even reminds me a bit of Macau in some ways. So having that in an F1 [car] with 1,000 horsepower is going to be quite an interesting challenge, so let's see how it goes."

Image: F1 Drivers' Championship ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix

So we are going to get safety cars and red flags?

In short, almost certainly. Such is the difficulty of the track, it is a question of how many red flags will we see across practice, qualifying and the race. As we saw at the Italian Grand Prix, if any barriers need to be repaired for crashes, that will definitely require a red flag.

In the two-day F3 test, there were 19 red flags - albeit not all of them were for crashes.

"Looking at the track and hearing of what happened in the F3 test, I think we are all expecting safety cars, red flags and yellow flags in qualy and things like this," said Sainz.

"It has been a fashion or a tendency of Formula 1 to go to these kind of tracks like Jeddah, Baku recently that are closer to the city - and Miami - but they have more walls and we haven't had any issues with it. The races actually seem to be going quite well to every place we've gone, so it's that similar trend we're going towards."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch F3 drivers complete in-season testing at the Madring for the first time

Predicting the pecking order is anyone's guess but the track layout will suit cars that are strong in the corners - akin to what we saw at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort when McLaren's Lando Norris won.

McLaren and Ferrari will hope to wrestle some momentum back off Mercedes and Kimi Antonelli following the Italian's stunning victory at Monza.

Avoiding a qualifying or race-ending crash for the title contenders this weekend will be pivotal. But we all know F1 drivers will push the limits, but they must all be careful when attacking the new Madring because this track will bite you, and bite hard.

Sports.title: ‘A dream come true’: behind the scenes with Wolves Women as they enter new era
Sports.content:
Suddenly the bustling classroom at the back of the Guru Nanak Satsang Sikh Gurdwara falls almost silent and all eyes are on Dan McNamara. The Wolves head coach, experiencing a wrestling lesson, is engaged in a tense tussle. He twists, panting and heaving, eventually ends up on top of his opponent, and the room erupts. Compared with some of the challenges McNamara and Wolves have grappled with during his eight and a half years coaching the team, this exercise was child’s play.

Wolves, promoted to Women’s Super League Two in May, are visiting the gurdwara – which became Wolverhampton’s first in 1966 – as part of an afternoon city tour which has also included a trip to the historic The Halls music venue and a walk in the centre, as some of their new signings acquaint themselves with the area before the club’s first season as a fully professional women’s team, and their first WSL2 home match, against Sheffield United, on Sunday.

View image in fullscreen The Wolves head coach, Dan McNamara, in his new office at the Sir Jack Haywood training ground. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

Victory against Plymouth in the third-tier promotion playoff was the culmination of years of hard graft in the amateur game, and McNamara pauses for reflection as he chats from his office overlooking the Sir Jack Hayward training ground in Compton.

“Initially, I think my ‘office’ was me sitting in the driver’s seat of an old Ford Focus,” he says. “I first walked on to an Astroturf with about seven bibs, three footballs and 58 players and probably thought: ‘What the hell have I done?’ Now I’m in my own office. We’ve got a fantastic setup here, we’ve got our own spaces for the women, changing facilities, which have been added over the summer. It’s night and day.

View image in fullscreen The Wolves captain, Anna Morphet, leads players during a session at the Sir Jack Haywood training ground. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

“Everybody grows up and dreams of being a professional footballer. I was no different. My claim to fame was I was in the same youth team as Wayne Rooney for a few years at Everton – our tactics were: ‘Pass the ball to Wayne and he will score.’ And [when I left Everton] I probably fell out of love with the game for a little bit. To be here now working professionally in football is a dream come true.

“People always talk about what success looks like. And I think: ‘Leave the place in a better place than what you got it.’ I don’t think anyone could argue that we’re going to leave this place in a better place than when we first picked it up. It’s not been me; the girls have gone on the pitch and they’ve achieved it. But to have inputted a small bit into making dreams come true gets me quite emotional.”

View image in fullscreen The Wolves squad are put through their paces at the Sir Jack Haywood training ground. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

Promotion was a long time coming for Wolves, who won tier three’s northern division in 2022 but – with only one team promoted then – lost the playoff decider against the southern champions, Southampton. McNamara missed that because he was overseas with the Royal Air Force, and watched from the Falkland Islands. Since 2024, he has coached Wolves full-time as part of the RAF’s elite athlete scheme – “they have extended me for an additional year to continue at WSL2; hopefully I can do them proud and represent the air force in a good way over the next 12 months,” he says – and his team lost two league games across the next two seasons.

In 2025, they finished second but were heartbroken to find the club had not applied for a licence for promotion. A year later, with a new executive chair in Nathan Shi, the club’s approach to the women’s team has changed, and McNamara’s team have cabins at the training ground as private changing areas, a meeting/analysis room and places to relax together. Some of the squad engage in a tense round of the card game Dobble after having breakfast together, before heading out for training. Further new training pitches will follow soon.

View image in fullscreen The England youth international goalkeeper Emily Orman has arrived on loan from London City Lionesses. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

This summer the club also hired a new head of women’s and girls football, Russ Fraser, who worked in the WSL at Reading, West Ham, Leicester and Liverpool over the past decade, before a spell with Al-Qadsiah in Saudi Arabia. Many of last season’s squad left their day jobs and turned professional but there has also been a big recruitment drive. Signings include former WSL players such as Mel Lawley, Jasmine Matthews, Yana Daniëls and Mel Filis.

“We don’t want to just be a team that goes up and then straight back down, so the work was almost immediately after the playoff,” McNamara says. “It’s been non-stop since. We were quite careful at what we went after. We wanted to bring in the right technical players, but also players that represent this great club and the city. And that’s hard work, ethics, having the right morals on the pitch, being quite energetic.”

Another new signing the England youth goalkeeper Emily Orman, on loan from London City Lionesses, enjoyed taking part in the wrestling demonstration. “I’ve never wrestled before,” she says. “That was really tough. I got a real bead on doing that!” It is not the squad’s only team-building experience. They also went bouldering in the Lake District, and the midfielder Tammi George – who first joined Wolves aged 13, before a spell at Sunday’s opponents – says: “That brought the group together so much because people were put through difficult situations and needed an arm around them at times. Everybody really saw the benefit.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen The Wolves squad take a walking tour through the city. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

On the city walk the players learn about everything from the AD910 battle of Tettenhall to the origins of the Prince Albert statue, and are informed of the iconic sets played by bands such as Queen and Nirvana at The Halls. There is also an important stop at Molineux, first so the players can help out at a session run by the club’s foundation during the school holidays for youngsters, through Premier League Kicks, in partnership with West Midlands police. The squad play pool and help with arts and crafts before touring the club’s museum, where the women’s football writer and Wolves fan Tony Leighton has written the latest part of an exhibition charting the women’s team’s rise.

View image in fullscreen The Wolves players Mel Lawley (left) and Chloe Williams play table football with attendees during a summer youth club organised by the Wolves Foundation at Molineux. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

The former BBC WM presenter Jenny Wilkes has been the chair of Wolves Women since 1999 and is full of pride. She knows how much the efforts of volunteers have helped the club. “I remember Rachael Heyhoe Flint, who had been such an amazing support for us in the days when it literally was one woman and a dog watching the game and she was one woman who brought her dog and walked her dog around the pitch,” she says. “We’re come a long way since then.

“It’s incredible, being fully professional, which we never thought we’d manage to do. In the long history of the club, we have played in the top flight before but it was when the top flight wasn’t professional. Now to see professional footballers at Wolves Women for the first time really is incredible.”

View image in fullscreen The squad take part in wrestling at Wolverhampton Wrestling Club. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

The captain, Anna Morphet, who handed in her notice for her day job as a physio a week after Wolves’ promotion, says: “We used to collect the kit out the back of Macca’s car boot. Those 90 minutes [against Plymouth] were the opportunity to change our lives. The work that’s gone on over the summer and in pre-season has been immense and I think now it’s about believing that we are ready for this level.”

Wolves opened with a defeat, albeit a respectable one, 2-0 at one of the favourites for promotion, Newcastle. Fraser says: “Wherever we finish in the league, I want other teams to go: ‘Wow, Wolves were so much better than I thought they were,’ because I think a lot of teams will probably think: ‘Oh, Wolves have just come up, they’ll go straight back down.’ I think we’re better than that. I think we’ve got a good group here.”

Sports.title: Dani Olmo: ‘Winning the World Cup changes you, it changes your life’
Sports.content:
Dani Olmo nods towards his right arm. “Look: goosebumps,” he says. The Spain midfielder is sitting in a back room at Barcelona’s Joan Gamper training ground trying to pinpoint the moment he knew he was a world champion. “There’s an image in my mind with Ferran [Torres]’s mum: hugging her, the two of us in tears,” he says. “‘What your son just did … what we all did … this is historic.’ And that’s when you start to feel it. In those final minutes of the game it’s impossible, impossible, but when the referee blows, the thought enters your head: ‘Have we done it?’ ‘Are we …?’ There, you feel it a little bit. When you lift the cup, a little bit more. And then when you see the families, when I see the reaction from my brother, my partner, my dad. I’m not one to cry, but …”

But then Olmo knew, felt it: Spain were world champions. It was 19 July in New Jersey and it was real: Spain had beaten Argentina and nothing would be the same again.

“It changes you, changes your life,” Olmo says. “I’m not sure we grasp it still. You realise when you’re [applauded] at other grounds, but we’ll truly realise with time. It’s like you’ve entered another dimension, a very select group. As a kid, I held 2010 up there. [Andrés] Iniesta, Xavi, [Sergio] Busquets, Xabi Alonso, [David] Villa … legends. We held on to the past, longed for that generation, how happy they made us. Now it’s like, ‘You’re there, too.’”

So now it’s time to, well, to get back to work, another generation to emulate. Twenty-three days after victory in the US, Olmo was back where he sits now, another session complete, another European season about to start. His club coach was waiting.

What did Hansi Flick say? “‘You’re a champion of the world, Dani.’” “‘I know, mister.’” Olmo laughs at what came next. “And now [we have to do it] with Barcelona,” he says.

Eight of Spain’s 26-man squad were Barcelona players and although Maria’s son Ferran has departed for Paris Saint German, Rodri has joined from Manchester City. What they have done with their country can infuse club success, Olmo believes, just as what they do with their club infused success with the country. Winning the World Cup changes your life; it can also reinforce an idea, and while Olmo analyses the differences between Spain and Barcelona, Flick and Luis de la Fuente, this is the triumph of an idea, continuity and commitment.

“We came from a very successful year; winning the league, the Super Cup … the World Cup was the finishing touch,” Olmo says. “Having that Barcelona base, players with a great level, competitive and ambitious, that know how to win and also good people – and I think we are – helps the national team. Whether you play a lot or a little, you’re a team. This is a winning generation at Barcelona, too. We’ve shown that in Spain; in Europe, we’re competing for the highest prize.”

View image in fullscreen ‘You’re a champion of the world, Dani,’ was the comment from the head coach, Hansi Flick, on Olmo’s return to Barcelona. Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters

That’s what drives them: for 11 years the Champions League has evaded them, an entire generation gone. No one is left from when Barcelona last lifted the trophy in June 2015; Olmo had just turned 17. Having departed the academy he first joined at nine and set out alone the previous summer, he had made five substitute appearances for Dynamo Zagreb’s first team – the determined, bold beginning of a journey that would eventually bring him back, via RB Leipzig, in 2024.

In his first season back, he helped Barcelona to a domestic treble. Last year, they were champions again. In Europe, though, they were defeated by Inter and Atlético Madrid in the semi-finals and quarter-finals respectively. On Wednesday night another campaign begins against Feyenoord at Camp Nou. It ends, they hope, at the Metropolitano in Madrid on 5 June. Lessons have been learned, in success and failure. The World Cup can bring them ever closer, Olmo believes. “You can feel that extra confidence,” he says. “The Champions League is decided by small details that haven’t gone our way but the last two years were experiences for the future. We were a young team.”

Were? “Still are,” Olmo concedes. Against Athletic Bilbao last month, Barcelona fielded their youngest starting XI at Camp Nou, with an average age of 23.18 years. This is a special generation; it is also one given opportunities Olmo wasn’t sure would be open when he set off at 16. “I’m still young … I think,” says the 28-year-old. “But I feel like a veteran. La Masia is more alive than ever. Exceptional players have always emerged but it can be hard to find space. Thiago [Alcântara] had incredible quality and had to go to Bayern to play at the highest level.”

“In my opinion, Barcelona have the best academy in the world; [Marc] Bernal, Lamine [Yamal] and now Xavi Espart. Pedri is still young and he’s been at the highest level for six, seven years. We have that experience now. What was lacking? The first year against Inter was, pfff, it was hard [to take]. We could see ourselves in the final. Last year against Atlético … the first game weighed too heavily on us; there were moments when we let it slip from us. We’re a young team, maybe you think there’s no problem, nothing can go wrong. I think we’ve learned that every detail, every minute, every sprint, every run is important. ‘Hey, 90 minutes, 120, do or die.’ We have to minimise the risk.”

Yet Barcelona live with risk, embrace it. It is here, in fact, where they most differ from Spain. If there’s a shared idea, transferable lessons, it’s not exactly the same, Olmo explains. He also insists that “risk” should come in speech marks: it’s been successful after all, critical talk of high lines and defensive weakness too simplistic at times. “Flick gives us confidence, always,” he says. “We believe in the idea and we will keep doing that because it has brought titles and shown us we can compete in the Champions League.

“In the seleccion we don’t have the line so high, that’s true. De la Fuente demands pressure and intensity from us, but it is also true that we can live more in a mid block or a mid-low block when we have to grit our teeth. Here we always try to step forward without the ball, look for fast transitions. They’re similar coaches, close to the players, their doors open if there’s anything you need. They’re both motivators; maybe Luis a little bit more. Hansi can look a bit more serious but sometimes lets go, cracks a joke. And the ideas are similar: attacking, possession.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In regards to lessons being learned, certainly from the semi-final against Inter where Barcelona scored six and didn’t go through, Olmo says: “Every year there are nuances, tweaks, adaptations. We’re doing good work to ensure opponents don’t do us damage. We want to go forward but if someone’s late to close, we can keep calm. We can’t leave ourselves exposed because one player doesn’t get there. I think we have that experience now.”

They also have Rodri, who perhaps embodies that control, that understanding, better than anyone, a Barcelona player without having been there. While they have lost Robert Lewandowski as well as Torres and been unable to sign Julián Alvarez, this is not, Olmo insists, an insurmountable problem. “There’s no one like Robert in history,” he says. “But we’re playing with Raphinha at No 9. Gabriel Jesus has come. Hamza [Abdelkarim] is doing really well. The manager knows he also has that wildcard of putting me or Fermin [López] there, which is a position I feel comfortable in. So he has solutions.”

View image in fullscreen Dani Olmo (centre) and Rodri during training before Barcelona’s Champions League match against Feyenoord. Photograph: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press/Getty Images

“The club has done an incredible job,” Olmo adds. “Rodri, Gabriel Jesus, Karim [Adeyemi], [Anthony] Gordon give us so much. Anthony and Karim are so fast which helps our idea in attack, but most important is without the ball, which the manager really values: pressing, defending as one. And Rodri is the player who is most like Busquets.”

Did Olmo spend the summer encouraging him to come? There’s a grin. “Erm, it was all very fast,” he says. “It’s not like we wanted to talk about signings during the World Cup. But when the rumours started, we might have sent a little message or something. He decided and we’re so happy. . He fits perfectly in our play, our system, our idea, which is similar to the seleccion. He’s positional, brings balance, which will give me more freedom to interpret where the spaces are. He sustains the structure. We know the system is risky at times but we have the experience and knowledge to judge when to go and when not to, when to cover our backs. Rodri gives us that too.”

When Barcelona won the league in 2025, four players celebrated by taking out city bikes and cycling up the Diagonal. It started with Torres, who they visited in hospital where he was recovering from an appendicitis and, although Olmo says it was just the easiest way to get there, something had started. In New York they again set off in the saddle: he, Torres and Eric García pedalling away to the sound of sirens, which sounds a little risky in the final days before the game of their lives. Olmo laughs. “We would have waited until after to post the images,” he says. “But we were very careful and it was fine.”

The tradition was maintained and another trophy lifted; just one to go. From Barcelona to New York. And Madrid? Olmo smiles. Incognito in a mask and helmet, perhaps. “Maybe we’ll have to download the app just in case,” he says.

Sports.title: Revitalised Ødegaard’s forward thinking gives Arsenal new lines of attack
Sports.content:
As Christos Tzolis cut in from the left flank and drove towards the penalty area, Kai Havertz could see history repeating itself.

Tzolis had done just the same on his competitive debut for Arsenal against Manchester City in the Community Shield a few weeks earlier, running at his opposition full-back, cutting inside and driving at goal, before fizzing a ball towards the penalty spot.

Martin Ødegaard was the grateful recipient, arriving just behind Havertz to take the ball smoothly into his path. He then faked a shot to send Gianluigi Donnarumma the wrong way before passing into the empty net.

With the scores level early in the second half of Arsenal’s win against Chelsea on Sunday, Tzolis did something very similar.

This time, his pass was intended for Havertz, but it was played ever so slightly behind the German. But Havertz had watched this before. He knew that Ødegaard, upon seeing Tzolis cut in, would have tiptoed into the penalty area.

View image in fullscreen Martin Ødegaard enjoyed a successful World Cup with Norway. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/Sportsphoto

Havertz produced a moment of genius to turn Tzolis’s slightly misplaced pass into a perfect assist, lifting his foot over the ball to leave it for his captain. Ødegaard again took the ball under his control with one touch, before this time lifting it over Emiliano Martínez to put Arsenal into a lead they would not surrender.

Ødegaard getting into more advanced positions has been an early theme of this season. He has three goals in four appearances, after scoring once in 36 outings last season.

There has clearly been an effort from Mikel Arteta and his staff to get their fit-again midfielder into attacking areas more consistently. In Premier League games this season, Ødegaard is making 3.2 high-intensity runs per 90 minutes into the opposition’s box while Arsenal have possession, up from 1.4 per 90 last term.

It’s only a small sample size from this season, but the fact that his numbers have more than doubled makes it significant nonetheless. And most important, his goal threat has clearly skyrocketed.

View image in fullscreen Photograph: Opta

Similarly, he has made seven off-ball runs to make himself a cross option for a teammate in three Premier League games, almost matching his tally from last season (10). On a per-90 basis, that’s 0.65 to 2.8, or more than a fourfold increase. One of those runs led to his goal in the season opener against Coventry.

After an injury-disrupted couple of years, it appears the far-from-linear rise of the 27-year-old has taken a steep, upward turn for the better. And, for an Arsenal team looking imperious this season, that is a very positive sign.

Their captain played his part in their 2025-26 title triumph, but he probably feels more driven than most at the club to repeat the trick. He missed a big chunk of the season with a series of recurring knee injuries, and when he was available he was used sparingly.

He played 1,371 of a possible 3,420 minutes in the league – a scratch over 40.0% – and although he was available for the run-in, playing in key games and in Arsenal’s run to the Champions League final, he was a long way from the key man he has been since his permanent move to the club in the summer of 2021.

Back then Arsenal were signing a hugely talented No 10, but Ødegaard has developed into more of a No 8, a rounded midfielder who drops deep to get on the ball in front of the opposition’s midfield and moves it around the pitch.

The evidence this season suggests that we should expect to see him getting closer to Havertz more often (while also continuing to do the job of a No 8). Havertz isn’t the most reliable goalscorer, but he is an excellent and intelligent centre-forward who performs more of a false 9 role, and he needs more runners ahead of him than Viktor Gyökeres.

View image in fullscreen Photograph: Opta

It appears this season that Arteta is going to prefer using Havertz up front, which will increase the need for Ødegaard to score more consistently. After the Norwegian’s start, he should at the very least challenge his season-best 15 goals in all competitions from 2022-23. He is averaging 5.6 high-intensity runs ahead of the ball per 90 this season, up from 3.9 last term.

He seems to have benefited from this summer’s World Cup, where he played a key role in his team’s run to the quarter-finals. Only Michael Olise (seven) got more assists at the tournament than Ødegaard (four).

There is pressure on him at club level, though. Eberechi Eze is breathing down his neck after standing in for him for large swathes of last season, though Arteta clearly prefers Ødegaard in the middle, perhaps for his defensive work, positioning and ability to coach Arsenal’s press on the pitch.

But there is just as much pressure on him to stay fit. He started 32, 37 and 35 of a possible 38 Premier League games in his first three full seasons, but has managed 26 then 16 in the past two.

He needs to prove he can stay fit, because not only are Arsenal better with him, but he is more likely to maintain his best form that way.

View image in fullscreen Illustration: Opta

Ødegaard is showing his best in the early part of 2026-27. He is, along with Chelsea’s Morgan Rogers, one of only two players with at least 1.0 expected goals and 1.0 expected assists in the Premier League, highlighting his all-round attacking game.

Only seven players have played a role in more open-play shot-ending sequences than him (20), and he leads the Premier League for the number of such sequences where he took the shot and was involved in the buildup (four).

It helps that Arsenal look a very functional team, and have benefited from limited changes in personnel over the summer. But how much is that functionality a cause of Ødegaard’s form and how much is it a result? During his time at the club Arsenal have mounted sustained challenges for the Premier League title, and that is surely no coincidence.

Ødegaard is looking back to his best and then some, and that is ominous news for the rest of the Premier League.

This is an article by Opta Analyst

Sports.title: Football’s most damaging red cards: a brief history of collapses and turnarounds | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“The Saturday before last, Clyde were winning 3-0 at The Spartans after an hour when Logan Dunachie was sent off. Twenty-eight minutes later, the score was 3-3. What is the biggest turnaround in a game following a red card/most quantitative blame that can be thrown at a player for getting sent off?” asks Jamie Wills.

At Knowledge Towers, we usually receive questions about the greatest comebacks with 10 men. We covered that in 2021, so it’s a nice change to look at teams who went to seed after having a player sent off.

Before we get to the meat of the question, a quick detour to cover some teams who were already losing and then fell apart completely after losing a player. There are examples dotted throughout the Premier League era. At the Etihad in 2017-18, Liverpool were a goal down to Manchester City when Sadio Mané was sent off in the 37th minute for a high challenge on Ederson. They lost 5-0.

Two seasons later, Southampton were 1-0 down at home to Leicester when Ryan Bertrand was sent off in the 12th minute. They were eventually humiliated 9-0. VVV-Venlo went one worse against Ajax the following season. They were 4-0 down at home when Christian Kum was sent off in the 52nd minute. By the hour mark it was 8-0; Ajax eventually won 13-0.

View image in fullscreen Oriol Romeu (left) and James Ward-Prowse don’t know where to look after Southampton’s 9-0 home defeat by Leicester in 2019. Photograph: Robin Jones/Getty Images

In the same season, 2020-21, Southampton lost another Premier League game 9-0, this time to Manchester United at Old Trafford. The score was goalless when the Swiss midfielder Alexandre Jankewitz walked in the second minute. Opta doesn’t keep records of how much eye contact Jankewitz made with his teammates over the next few days, but we imagine it wasn’t much.

The most costly red cards, literally and figuratively, are those that precipitate a team losing a lead. Zdenek Zeman’s joyfully reckless Foggia were 4-1 up at Atalanta during the 1991-92 Serie A season when Dan Petrescu was given a second yellow card in the 72nd minute. Chaos ensued, Atalanta’s Carlo Cornacchia scored a 14-minute hat-trick and the match finished 4-4.

An even more dramatic 4-4 draw took place in the Premier League 15 years ago. “While there might be bigger turnarounds, my thoughts immediately went to Newcastle v Arsenal at St James’ Park in 2010-11,” writes Rein. “I had just moved to the city and being Dutch, this game really hit home the highs and lows of supporting the Toon and tied me to the club. And that Cheick Tioté goal ….”

We’re sure you remember the game, but if not, here’s a quick precis. Arsenal strolled to a 4-0 half-time lead, then things started to change when Abou Diaby was sent off in the 50th minute for manhandling Joey Barton. Arsenal collapsed in the final quarter of the game. Barton scored twice, Leon Best chipped in with another – and then, in the 87th minute, the late Tioté volleyed a glorious equaliser.

At least Arsenal took a point back to London. Venezia had no such solace after the Derby del Veneto in December 2021. They were 3-1 up at home to Verona in Serie A when Pietro Ceccaroni was sent off in the 62nd minute for handling on the goalline. Gianluca Caprari scored the resulting penalty before Giovanni Simeone struck twice to give Verona a famous win.

And finally, we shouldn’t forget Emmanuel Adebayor’s scene-stealing cameo on his return to the Emirates in November 2012. He gave Spurs an early lead before being given a straight red card in the 17th minute for a dangerous challenge on Santi Cazorla. Arsenal, who had beaten Spurs 5-2 at the Emirates earlier in the year, enjoyed a bit of deja 5-2.

The million dollar question

“Are Liverpool the first club to have three £100m+ players on their books? And which clubs were first to have three £10m+ and three £1m+ players?” wonders Owen Powell.

It’s tricky to answer this question definitively, mainly because reported transfer fees can vary wildly. With that caveat, these are the best answers we could find – if you can find earlier examples, send them to knowledge@theguardian.com. Turns out Real Madrid aren’t the only Spanish club partial to a galactico or three.

£1m: Nottingham Forest (1981)

Trevor Francis (Birmingham City, 1979)

Ian Wallace (Coventry City, 1980)

Justin Fashanu (Norwich City, 1981)

Fashanu joined Forest in August 1981, precipitating the sale of Francis to Manchester City a few weeks later. He became City’s third £1m+ player after Steve Daley and Kevin Reeves. Francis, Wallace and Fashanu were on Forest’s books together for a few weeks.

£10m: Lazio (1998)

Marcelo Salas (River Plate, 1998)

Christian Vieri (Atletico Madrid, 1998)

Ivan de la Pena (Barcelona, 1998)

We think Barcelona were the first team to sign three players for £10m or more – Ronaldo in 1996, Sonny Anderson and Rivaldo in 1997 – but they weren’t on the books at the same time.

£100m: Barcelona (2019)

Ousmane Dembélé (Borussia Dortmund, 2017)

Philippe Coutinho (Liverpool, 2018)

Antoine Griezmann (Atletico Madrid, 2019)

Dembélé joined Barcelona for a reported fee of £96.8m, potentially rising to £135.5m with add-ons. We’re quietly confident they paid at least £3.2m in add-ons. The first club to sign three players for an upfront fee of £100m+ appears to be Chelsea: Enzo Fernández, Moisés Caicedo and Morgan Rogers. They were briefly on the same wage bill this summer until Fernández moved to Manchester City.

View image in fullscreen The shirts of Moisés Caicedo and Enzo Fernández are displayed inside the Chelsea dressing room in March this year. Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

Trophy-laden players (part two)

Last week, we looked at whether any footballer has won more trophies than Marquinhos (41 and counting). Our answer at the time was no. Since then, we’ve had a few follow-ups in our inbox putting forward the name of Gibraltar legend Lee Casciaro.

Given that the question did not specify whether the trophies needed to have been won in a major league, we should mention Casciaro’s honours. Here’s Sean DeLoughry with the details. “According to Wikipedia (so there’s a 3% chance it’s accurate) Gibraltar’s Lee Casciaro won 23 league titles, 15 Rock Cups, 13 Pepe Reyes Cups and 11 Gibraltar Premier Cups with Lincoln Red Imps for a total of 62 trophies.” Even if Wiki’s a little bit out, Casciaro’s trophy haul is still going to be heavier than that of Marquinhos. He isn’t a full-time professional, however, working as a police officer alomgside his football career, so maybe that counts againt him. Sean points us in the direction of Linfield’s Noel Bailie, another former semi-pro, as a member of the 40-trophy club, winning all his silverware during 22 years with the Blues.

View image in fullscreen Lee Casciaro must have one hell of a trophy cabinet. Photograph: DeFodi Images/Getty Images

Knowledge archive

“Against Wolves this week, West Ham’s Konstantinos Mavropanos scored a goal and then, just five minutes later, scored an own goal. Either way round, what’s the fastest such an unlikely double has been achieved?” wonders Sam Coare.

We had this question in 2022, when Ajax’s Sébastien Haller scored at both ends in the space of four minutes. Here’s what we said back then:

There are many members of the “scored at both ends” club but finding a player who has done it quicker than the Ajax striker did is tricky. Robert Davies wrote in with a player who matched Haller’s three minutes, but we can’t confirm whether he was faster or slower. Either way, it was an eventful match for Walsall’s Conor Wilkinson in the 3-3 draw with Newport on 1 January this year. Here’s the rundown:

52 min: Came on as sub

53 min: Scored with first touch

56 min: Scored own goal

90+5min: Scored equaliser

We also remember Troy Deeney going from hero to villain within three minutes when he equalised for Watford against Manchester United in the 87th minute in November 2015, before putting through his own net in the 90th. And a doff of the cap to Tammy Abraham, who scored a hat-trick for Chelsea before adding an own goal 14 minutes later during their 5-2 win over Wolves in 2019.

Can you help?

“In their draw at Forest, Spurs managed an xG of 1.6 despite not having a single shot on target,” writes Chris. “What is the highest single-game xG a team has achieved without ever putting one on frame?”

“When did fans wearing replica kits become a thing?” asks Alex Ecob. “Older footage shows people in regular clothes and a few scarves/flags in the team colours. What kickstarted the trend? Did one club get there first?”

View image in fullscreen Arsenal fans weren’t shy of wearing replica kits in the match against Chelsea. Photograph: Ryan Pierse/Getty Images

“From 2007-08 to 2017-18, Newcastle United’s player of the year award was won by nine defenders and two goalkeepers,” begins Matt Cowan. “From 2002-03 to 2018-19, no forward won the award. Has any club had a longer streak without a forward or midfielder winning the award?”

Sports.title: Men’s Ballon d’Or 2026 power rankings: will there be an English winner for the first time in 25 years?
Sports.content:
1) Harry Kane (England/Bayern Munich)

Even adjusting for the goal-drunken Bundesliga, his 61 goals in 51 matches for Bayern last season undersells his all-around impact, considering his playmaking and hold-up skills. Kane was gameplanned out of England’s later games at the World Cup, but he was unstoppable through the last-16 to close out the finest year of his career to date. If not now, when?

2) Rodri (Spain/Manchester City – now at Barcelona)

He boasts a comparable case to when he won this prize in 2024 – Rodri remains the epicenter of an incredibly effective Spanish collective. This time around, there’s no Premier League glory to bolster his hopes, as City’s late challenge fizzled out with the club “only” winning domestic cups in his final season at the Etihad. Back to his best en route to Spain’s second World Cup title, though only one of the four previous World Cup champions had the corresponding Ballon d’Or winner (Lionel Messi, 2023).

3) Kylian Mbappé (France/Real Madrid)

Mbappé and José Mourinho have launched an aggressive campaign for the Frenchman to win his first Ballon d’Or. He was even more difficult to slow in his second Spanish season, with 40 goals in 42 matches across La Liga and the Champions League; the less said about his pressing, the better. Few players captivated and dominated like Mbappé at the World Cup, as he won the Golden Boot. But a lack of team accomplishments could set back his candidacy, made even more glaring given Madrid’s chronic success.

4) Lamine Yamal (Spain/Barcelona)

Another member of the World Cup champions, although injuries limited his impact in North America – the master of suspense was not as involved as he’d have liked. Then again, he managed greater consistency in his third season as a regular for Barcelona, with 41 goal contributions in all competitions across 45 appearances. He only just turned 19 in July.

5) Lionel Messi (Argentina/Inter Miami)

Messi could well have ranked higher if Argentina had won the World Cup this summer, as the 39-year-old was the heart and soul of their campaign. Alas, a putrid final showing (by his teammates, more than Messi) dulls the sheen on his hopes for a ninth Ballon d’Or, and he is also hit by the fact that he doesn’t play for one of Europe’s elite clubs, even though Inter Miami won the MLS title. His remarkable 17th appearance on a Ballon d’Or shortlist is well deserved.

6) Michael Olise (France/Bayern Munich)

Who knew Bayern’s most thrilling attack in recent memory would be spearheaded by signings from Tottenham and Crystal Palace? An elite secondary attacker, and one who has come to relish operating as the string-puller in transition and at the edge of the final third. Spain masterfully closed his passing lines and took him out of the semi-final, but a pair of assists in the third-place match left him tops in that category at the World Cup. A career year, or evidence he’s set a new standard for himself?

7) Erling Haaland (Norway/Manchester City)

Even as City stumbled down the stretch, this was another season to pad his growing legacy as one of the game’s great strikers of any era. He made the most of Norway’s return to the World Cup, finishing as the tournament’s joint-third top goalscorer (seven) despite exiting in the quarter-final.

8) Jude Bellingham (England/Real Madrid)

A man for the biggest moments, Birmingham City’s decision to retire his number when his career had barely started has aged well. He forged a rare tandem with Kane at the World Cup, alternating headline hero shifts en route to another semi-final heartbreaker. His goals and assists plummeted in his third season with Madrid, though most of his teammates saw diminishing returns in a forgettable campaign.

9) Ousmane Dembélé (France/Paris Saint-Germain)

Lacking some of the bombast that typifies his rivals, Dembélé remains a silky threat for club and country. His stats for PSG dipped from last year’s award-winning campaign, from 35 goals in 53 games to 20 in 40. His partnership with Mbappé and Olise for France was as dangerous as the international game has seen. If nothing else, Dembélé has made certain that he is no one-year wonder.

10) Khvicha Kvaratskhelia (Georgia/Paris Saint-Germain)

On a per-minute basis, few players are more effective in the biggest games. Unfortunately, his club’s domestic dominance means he can take more shifts off than most of his gilded peers, logging a measly 1,479 Ligue 1 minutes in 28 appearances. Georgia’s absence from this summer’s World Cup also limits the evidence available to bolster his case. Nonetheless, his barnstorming exploits in the Champions League knockouts saw the 25-year-old hit rare form.

11) Declan Rice (England/Arsenal)

The most vital cog in Mikel Arteta’s meticulous machine, and a key all-around impact in England’s run to the semi-final, even if he at times understandably looked tired after a long domestic campaign.

12) Bruno Fernandes (Portugal/Manchester United)

One of a few Portuguese players whose cases for this prize were scuppered by this summer’s underwhelming showing under the stubborn Roberto Martínez. Truly sensational to restore the Red Devils to prouder days.

13) Pau Cubarsí (Spain/Barcelona)

Looked every part the lead center-back that his club and country need to play in a possession-dominant way. Then again, these prizes seldom skew towards defenders.

14) Fabián Ruiz (Spain/Paris Saint-Germain)

Success in the Champions League and World Cup has seen this fine facilitator get his due at age 30.

15) Vitinha (Portugal/Paris Saint-Germain)

Involved in PSG’s best stuff no matter the competition, with six of his seven club goals coming in the Champions League last season. Unable to shed the stench of Portugal’s World Cup, but he is the world’s finest deep-lying playmaker all the same.

16) Luis Díaz (Colombia/Bayern Munich)

Took to Germany with glee, bagging 26 goals and 19 assists in 51 appearances dwarfed his output at Liverpool. Struggled for most of the World Cup, however, as Colombia crashed out sooner than expected.

17) Gabriel (Brazil/Arsenal)

Always close to any fracas, Gabriel was steady as ever as Arsenal enjoyed a long-awaited Premier League title. Some great summer showings at the World Cup, especially against Japan, but struggled – like the rest of his team – against Norway.

18) Nuno Mendes (Portugal/Paris Saint-Germain)

Few opponents have found how to best neutralize Mendes, save for hoping that PSG give him another domestic day off between Champions League games.

19) Lautaro Martínez (Argentina/Inter)

Another dependable goalscoring campaign in Italy, and excelled in a super-sub role during Argentina’s knockout run. One of this era’s great strikers, and already off to a hot start this season.

20) William Saliba (France/Arsenal)

Especially steady in the Premier League and Champions League, helping Arsenal to their most successful year in decades. His injury hurt France’s chances against Spain in the World Cup semi-final, perhaps bolstering his reputation in absentia.

And the rest of the field …

21) Achraf Hakimi (Morocco/Paris Saint-Germain)

22) Vinícius Júnior (Brazil/Real Madrid)

23) Dayot Upamecano (France/Bayern Munich)

24) Marc Cucurella (Spain/Chelsea – now at Real Madrid)

25) João Neves (Portugal/Paris Saint-Germain)

26) Willian Pacho (Ecuador/Paris Saint-Germain)

27) Ferran Torres (Spain/Barcelona – now at Paris Saint-Germain)

28) Marquinhos (Brazil/Paris Saint-Germain)

29) Julián Quiñones (Mexico/Al Qadsiah)

30) Sadio Mané (Senegal/Al Nassr)

Sports.title: Real Madrid somehow cling on to beat Inter on José Mourinho’s big night
Sports.content:
Sometimes football is silly, sometimes it doesn’t make much sense, and sometimes it’s fun for it. On a night when there were 37 shots and the goalkeepers shared 13 occasionally absurd saves between them, José Mourinho’s current side beat his former team Inter on his Champions League return to Real Madrid. Just don’t ask exactly how. Except perhaps to cite Thibaut Courtois, whose astonishing 89th-minute stop from Henrikh Mkhitaryan explained much and allowed them, just, to hold on to the first-half lead they had been given by goals from Kylian Mbappé and Fede Valverde.

By Mbappé, Valverde, and Inter themselves, that is. You might be tempted to say the Italians had shot themselves in the foot, only if they tried Courtois would probably save that too. “If he wasn’t voted man of the match tonight, he never will be,” Mourinho said. It took 77 minutes for him to be beaten, Carlos Augusto’s goal giving this match a frantic last 15 minutes and Inter hope of justice, but it didn’t happen again. So a game that could have had any scoreline – “5-1 to us, 6-6, I don’t want to say they could have won,” Mourinho suggested – actually ended 2-1. Madrid’s manager called it “mad, and not a madness I like.”

This wasn’t always good from Madrid, in fact at times it was terrible. There was a void where the midfield should be, Mourinho thanking Trent Alexander-Arnold for filling in a “specific” midfield role that’s not for him. The intensity in the press high up was matched by a passivity elsewhere. Inter played through and round them, clocking up twice as many attacks and passes. At the end the Santiago Bernabéu whistled; Vinícius Júnior in particular felt their frustration. Yet their team, who also could have won by more – Jude Bellingham said he had missed “two sitters” – have started with a win.

View image in fullscreen José Mourinho makes his point against the team with whom he won the treble. Photograph: Diego Souto/Getty Images

The irritation had grown. When Madrid scored the first, this placed cheered but they might have laughed too. That Madrid led didn’t make sense; not when it came to the goal, not when it came to the game either. It had taken Madrid four minutes to get a meaningful touch, and by then Courtois had already made a superb save from Marcus Thuram. But this is Madrid in the Champions League and now somehow they led. Ninety minutes later, they still did, which didn’t compute either.

Quick Guide Dortmund's Karetsas taken to hospital Show Borussia Dortmund's Konstantinos Karetsas was taken to hospital after slumping to the turf 25 minutes into his Champions League debut against Villarreal. “Konstantinos Karetsas had to leave the field due to circulatory problems,” Dortmund said in a statement. “Kosta is doing well under the circumstances and is on his way to the hospital for further tests.” The 18-year-old Greece international passed the ball to a teammate then signaled his distress to the referee before sitting on the grass. Karetsas was treated laying down then taken away on a stretcher. The score was 0-0 at the time. Dortmund went on to win 3-2 at home. Renato Veiga’s 53rd-minute own goal put the Bundesliga side ahead before Santiago Mouriño equalised in the 66th. Serhou Guirassy restored the lead in the 80th minute and scored the third with an 84th-minute penalty, before scoring an own goal in added time while trying to help in defence. Real Betis twice came from behind to beat Lille 3-2 away, ⁠with Marc Bartra scoring in the 34th and 49th minutes before Troy Parrott’s 54th-minute winner. Lille ​scored their opener in the 12th minute ‌and regained the lead through ‌Alexsandro in the 37th. The hosts later had Ethan Mbappé sent off for an elbow to ‌the face of an opponent. AEK Athens ​made a winning start, beating the Austrian side LASK 1-0 in Greece thanks to Romanian midfielder Razvan Marin’s curling free-kick midway through the first half. Agencies Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Inter had been playing with what looked like ease until suddenly even the simplest things looked complicated. Hakan Calhanoglu and Lautaro Martínez had just fired off the third and fourth shots without reward when it happened. Inter had enjoyed 65% of possession so far but gave it up in a way that was comic. Curtis Jones struggled with the first ball, playing to Yann Bisseck who fatally lost his bearing and his footing. Stumbling like someone attached his legs the wrong way round, he gave it to Brahím Diaz who sent Mbappé away to score.

It was Madrid’s first shot and the opening goal. If that was silly, what came next was even more ridiculous. What is it Madrid do to goalkeepers in this competition? Receiving on his line, Josep Martínez saw Valverde steaming in and tried a drag back, which failed. A flick of the ankle and the Uruguayan had scored. Twenty-three minutes, two shots, 2-0. “That was not chance,” Mourinho said and the lead might have grown when another robbery saw Vinícius dashing away. Bissek, this time, made a fantastic saving challenge. For all the fortune this felt like a plan now: force the mistake, punish it. Madrid forced more too, which they didn’t punish.

View image in fullscreen Kylian Mbappé opens the scoring for Real Madrid in the 14th minute. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters

Inter recovered and reasserted themselves, a calmness in possession at one end that contrasted with the calamitousness further back. Curtis Jones, Lautaro Martínez and Augusto virtually walked into the area, where Jones’ effort smashed the crossbar. Then another gift, from Benjamin Pavard, saw Madrid escape just before the break. Bellingham was denied by a wonderful stop from Josep Martínez and Díaz hit the post. Inter led 12-3 in shots, boasted 70% possession and had completed 125 final third passes to Madrid’s 13. Madrid, though, led.

Those numbers evened as the game opened, the second half beginning with Josep Martínez coming out to stop Mbappé before Inter came back at them. Courtois saved from Jones, Nicolò Barella shot wide and Thuram scooped over. The roar that then greeted an outrageous Courtois double stop spoke of disbelief, although the flag was up. The feeling was similar when Josep Martínez scrambled across his line to stop Bellingham after Díaz’s glorious scoop over him and into the Englishman.

A competition built between the keepers. Madrid could have killed this, many times. Inter could have revived it. Courtois saved from Alessandro Bastoni. Josep Martínez saved from Mbappé with his legs. That was 6-5 to Courtois. There were whistles, frustration, but chances too: the 20 seconds or so between Lautaro Martínez being blocked at one end and Díaz slotting wide at the other told a tale. Inter finally scored when another incisive exchange saw Lautaro Martínez pull back for Augusto to score. There were f15 minutes left and a game on, but that, somehow, was that. Which didn’t make sense either.

Sports.title: Haaland double gives Manchester City ideal Champions League start in Porto
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca admitted a liking for the “boom-boom” of house music in the buildup to this match, then enjoyed the sweet notes of victory having overseen a gritty performance from his Manchester City side in incessant rain.

City had lost six of their past nine away games in the competition, and been beaten in the 2021 Champions League final at this venue, so to beat Porto and claim three points is a fillip for the manager’s nascent project.

A bust-up at half-time as the players and staff neared the tunnel may bring Uefa scrutiny, though. Images showed Rúben Dias placing a hand on what appeared to be Francesco Farioli, the Porto head coach. The defender did so as tempers frayed after a clash between Marc Guéhi and Gabriel Veiga that left the latter with a head injury, though he continued.

Informed of Dias’s act, Maresca was visibly angered when asked if his captain will be spoken to, as it could cost City. “Probably, anyway you can ask what you want but how many times you see me or my bench or the guys that work with me stand up on the bench. Zero, for 95 minutes. How many times you see their bench?” he said.

Overall, the Italian should feel exuberant. All four of his opening games have been won – maybe more than even the 46-year-old could have hoped for, Erling Haaland’s double maintaining the perfect start. The goalscoring phenomenon is now third on City’s all-time chart with 167 goals after only four years, with 59 in 59 Champions League matches.

Haaland said: “Amazing game, against the champions of Portugal. We have to deliver on the biggest stage and we did that tonight.”

Maresca gave Ayyoub Bouaddi a full debut, alongside Enzo Fernández in midfield, and the 18-year-old Moroccan impressed, though a failure to find Haaland brought a reprimand. “I told the chairman [Khaldoon al-Mubarak] we’ve got a gem there,” said Haaland. “But he should’ve played me through in the second half, I was all alone. I was a bit angry so I’ll tell him right now – but he played a good game, except that pass.”

Initially, Porto could allow City to pitter-patter passes about as there was no quickness or penetration. Farioli’s men offered an example of how when Guéhi’s ball short-changed Bouaddi, possession was nabbed, and suddenly William Gomes had to be stopped on the edge of City’s area. Earlier, Veiga sliced through and had Gianluigi Donnarumma saving: the offside flag went up but here were two warnings.

Karetsas was treated laying down then taken away on a stretcher. The score was 0-0 at the time. Dortmund went on to win 3-2 at home. Thank you for your feedback.

Discard the ponderous pace might have been Maresca’s message because when Phil Foden switched flanks from the right and accelerated, Porto were splayed, and Haaland’s header from the cross required Diogo Costa to keep the contest goalless.

A near-carbon copy arrived when Antoine Semenyo popped the ball over from the left but, this time, Haaland’s header sailed over. City were warming up: Foden, Rayan Cherki and Haaland all being denied, as Porto were caught in a chokehold around their area.

At Leicester and then Chelsea Maresca drew criticism for a quasi-sideways style. Yet tonight’s XI had become direct and a threat, as when Bouaddi chipped the ball left from near halfway, it went forward at speed, and a panicked Porto cleared.

Now, when Veiga went down after the challenge with Guéhi, the match was halted and the discord that continued to the tunnel area started up.

Yet following the seemingly de rigueur fireworks before every Champions League game, Porto had begun with sky-high confidence after winning all of their five Primeira Liga outings, so when wandering off they remained content.

The mood changed instantaneously on their return. City, at last, showed the ruthlessness needed at this level. Cherki, broke into the area, swerved left, leaving Costa stranded. He fed Fernández and Haaland headed the delivery into the turf and home and the visitors had a priceless lead.

What would be Porto’s response? To rove upfield and go close to the equaliser, was the answer, a corollary of City’s openness, as when André Silva had an age to dip right and let fly, the former Portugal forward’s attempt hitting the side netting.

View image in fullscreen Erling Haaland outjumps Jakub Kiwior to head City into the lead. Photograph: Clive Brunskill/Getty Images

The lead was slender, as it was in Saturday’s 1-0 win over Coventry. Maresca acted when the hour passed, removing Cherki and Semenyo for Elliot Anderson and Iliman Ndiaye: two attackers for one forward and a holding player in Anderson whose role was to exert control and aid Bouaddi in snuffing out any Porto threat.

A second goal would also stymie the hosts, so Ndiaye skipped across the grass and unloaded, but the effort went straight into Costa’s clutches. Foden, too, tried to break in behind, but the ball was shepherded back to the Porto keeper.

Whenever Farioli’s team moved forward City remained vulnerable, despite Anderson’s presence. At the death, though, Haaland’s right-footed finish made sure of victory and meant that even when tempers flared again it was of zero import to Maresca’s team, who had emerged victorious on a difficult evening.

Sports.title: First-half treble powers Aston Villa to Champions League win at Club Brugge
Sports.content:
Aston Villa were 3-1 up after 43 minutes but were made to sweat for their first win of the season, emerging victorious from an entertaining Champions League opener with Club Brugge. John McGinn, who struck the only goal when Villa belatedly got their season up and running last September against Bologna, opened the scoring before Emi Buendía and a first goal for Nicolas Jackson in claret and blue appeared to put Villa out of sight at half-time.

The Belgian side have become familiar foes since Villa returned to the big time, the glitziest club competition of them all; a freakish Tyrone Mings handball gifted the hosts a penalty, and subsequently victory, in 2024-25 and on this occasion Aaron Wan-Bissaka conceded a second-half penalty to plunge a seesawing contest back into the balance.

“Today was a very important step forward, being resilient when we were struggling,” said Unai Emery. “It is very important to start with three points. Hopefully it gives us confidence for the next matches, in the Premier League this Saturday against Nottingham Forest.”

Emery had been at pains to radiate positivity despite another slow start – Villa picked up their first point of the Premier League season at the weekend and these goals represented their first of the campaign – but he was typically animated on the touchline in Brugge. He was particularly agitated midway through the second half when he felt, not for the first time this season, his substitutes were not ready for action. At Hull last weekend, it was Tammy Abraham and Wan-Bissaka, and a few days earlier Alejandro Garnacho against Arsenal.

This time the culprits were Alysson, Ross Barkley and Lamare Bogarde. “In the dressing room at half-time we were speaking about some players who were tired, [Boubacar] Kamara, Wan-Bissaka,” Villa’s manager said. “I tried to keep [them on for] 15 minutes, but when I asked the players to replace [them] they were talking through the set pieces, sorting individual issues, but I needed quickly their impact on the field, and they did afterwards.”

Karetsas was treated laying down then taken away on a stretcher. The score was 0-0 at the time. Dortmund went on to win 3-2 at home. Renato Veiga’s 53rd-minute own goal put the Bundesliga side ahead before Santiago Mouriño equalised in the 66th. Serhou Guirassy restored the lead in the 80th minute and scored the third with an 84th-minute penalty, before scoring an own goal in added time while trying to help in defence. Real Betis twice came from behind to beat Lille 3-2 away, ⁠with Marc Bartra scoring in the 34th and 49th minutes before Troy Parrott’s 54th-minute winner. Lille ​scored their opener in the 12th minute ‌and regained the lead through ‌Alexsandro in the 37th. The hosts later had Ethan Mbappé sent off for an elbow to ‌the face of an opponent.
