World.title: Egypt, Dubai chambers discuss boosting joint investments
World.content:
CEO of the General Authority for Investment and Free Zones (GAFI) Mohamed Awad, and CEO of Dubai Chambers Mohamed Ali Rashed Lootah discussed on Tuesday, September 8, 2026, ways to enhance economic and investment cooperation and support partnerships between Egypt and the UAE.

The meeting, attended by Head of the Egyptian Trade Representation Office in the UAE Manal Abdel Tawab, came as part of efforts to strengthen economic and investment ties between the two countries and expand cooperation between their business communities.

Awad highlighted the role of Dubai Chambers in connecting businesses with global markets, referring to the potential to activate its Cairo office to promote investment opportunities in Egypt among Emirati companies and support those seeking to expand in the Egyptian market.

He pointed to opportunities for new projects and partnerships in manufacturing, logistics, renewable energy, technology, tourism, real estate development, and supply-chain-related manufacturing and re-export.

Lootah stressed the importance of continued coordination between Dubai Chambers and GAFI to promote investment opportunities and create new avenues for Egyptian-Emirati partnerships and joint projects.

World.title: Liberia: Senior Leadership Team Fully Formed as President Boakai Commissions Three Deputies
World.content:
The appointments strengthen an institution the government is counting on to turn the country’s cultural, historical and natural assets into a larger source of jobs, investment and economic growth.

By Patience Jones

Monrovia — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai on Tuesday commissioned three deputy directors-general of the Liberia National Tourism Authority, completing the senior leadership structure of the relatively new agency as Liberia seeks to give tourism a more prominent role in its economic development.

The officials are Atty. Jani Kadiyatu Kollie, Deputy Director-General for Marketing and Promotions; Steveson Tweh Seidi, Deputy Director-General for Culture and Heritage; and Melvin Nye, Deputy Director-General for Finance and Corporate Services.

Their commissioning formally places senior officials over three areas that will be central to whether Liberia can translate its tourism ambitions into measurable results: promoting the country to domestic and international travelers, protecting and developing its cultural and heritage assets, and building the financial and administrative systems required to support the sector.

The appointments come at an important stage for the Liberia National Tourism Authority, which was established as the country moves to consolidate tourism governance and strengthen the institutional framework for an industry that has historically remained underdeveloped despite Liberia’s considerable natural and cultural resources.

Liberia has an extensive Atlantic coastline, biodiversity and protected areas, historic sites connected to the country’s founding, distinctive cultural traditions and an emerging creative economy.

Ms. Kollie will oversee the Authority’s marketing and promotional portfolio, including national destination branding, international and domestic tourism promotion, communications, digital engagement and efforts to strengthen Liberia’s visibility in regional and global travel markets.

Mr. Seidi will lead the Culture and Heritage portfolio, placing him at the center of efforts to preserve, promote and economically integrate Liberia’s culture, heritage sites and related creative economy into the country’s broader tourism offering.

Mr. Nye will oversee Finance and Corporate Services, with responsibility for the financial, administrative and institutional systems needed to sustain the Authority’s operations and implement its programs.

Together, the three deputies join the Authority’s senior leadership at a time when expectations for the institution are rising.

Liberia is seeking to compete for a larger share of Africa’s expanding tourism market while addressing longstanding constraints, including limited destination infrastructure, weak international visibility, gaps in tourism data, service standards and investment, and the need for stronger preservation and management of cultural and heritage assets.

The commissioning therefore represents more than the filling of senior government posts. It gives the Tourism Authority a complete executive structure at a point when the institution is expected to demonstrate whether Liberia can move from promoting its tourism potential to building a functioning and competitive tourism economy.

World.title: UNDP Warns Liberia: Build Resilience Now or Risk Losing Hard-Won Development Gains
World.content:
MONROVIA — Liberia must rethink its development strategy and build stronger systems capable of withstanding economic, climate, health and geopolitical shocks, participants at a high-level development dialogue convened by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) have warned.

The September 3, 2026 dialogue, held under the theme “Navigating Development in a World of Crisis: Resilience, Equity and Planetary Stewardship,” brought together senior government officials, United Nations agencies, international financial institutions, civil society organizations, academia and private-sector representatives to examine how Liberia can protect development gains while preparing for an increasingly uncertain global environment.

The discussions centered on a fundamental question: How can Liberia safeguard its development gains and build a future that is resilient, inclusive and sustainable?

UNDP Resident Representative Aliou Mamadou Dia called for resilience to become a central pillar of Liberia’s national development planning.

“The world may be becoming more uncertain, but our response can be more coordinated, more innovative and more resilient,” Dia said.

The dialogue emphasized that resilience should go beyond recovering from crises. It should involve anticipating risks, strengthening institutions, empowering communities and building systems capable of absorbing future shocks without sacrificing hard-won development gains.

A New Development Approach

Participants said Liberia can no longer afford fragmented approaches to development, particularly as climate-related disasters, disruptions to food systems, global supply-chain challenges and other cross-border shocks increasingly threaten developing economies.

They argued that Liberia’s development strategy must better connect governance, economic growth, social cohesion, environmental protection and climate resilience.

The discussions also highlighted the need for stronger coordination among government institutions, development partners, communities and the private sector.

Financing Liberia’s Future

Financing sustainable development emerged as one of the central challenges confronting Liberia.

Finance and Development Planning Minister Augustine K. Ngafuan acknowledged that while Liberia cannot completely insulate itself from global crises, the country can improve its preparedness through strategic investments, stronger institutions and more effective management of national resources.

Participants called for increased domestic resource mobilization, improved public financial management and greater accountability in ensuring that public resources translate into measurable improvements in citizens’ lives.

The dialogue also examined alternative financing mechanisms, including blended finance, concessional funding and responsible private-sector investment.

The broader message was that Liberia’s development cannot depend indefinitely on external assistance. Sustainable progress, participants said, must increasingly be anchored in strong national systems, effective governance and a vibrant private sector capable of creating jobs, attracting investment and expanding economic opportunities.

Youth at the Center of Liberia’s Future

Beyond infrastructure and economic growth, participants stressed that Liberia’s most important development asset remains its people.

Women, young people, persons with disabilities and other marginalized groups often face the greatest hardships during periods of crisis, making inclusion a critical component of national resilience.

With one of Africa’s youngest populations, Liberia has significant untapped human potential, participants noted.

They called for greater investment in education, skills development, entrepreneurship, digital innovation and green employment opportunities to enable young Liberians to contribute more meaningfully to the country’s economic transformation.

Participants emphasized that youth empowerment should not be viewed solely as a social obligation, but as an economic strategy capable of driving innovation, productivity and long-term prosperity.

Liberia’s Natural Wealth as an Economic Asset

Liberia’s forests, biodiversity, wetlands and coastal ecosystems also featured prominently in the discussions.

Participants challenged the notion that environmental protection and economic development are competing priorities, arguing instead that responsible management of Liberia’s natural resources can strengthen livelihoods, improve food security, increase climate resilience and create sustainable economic opportunities.

With global demand growing for climate and biodiversity solutions, Liberia could potentially access new sources of environmental financing while protecting the ecological resources on which communities and future generations depend.

Participants therefore called for environmental stewardship to be fully integrated into national development planning and investment decisions.

Trust and Strong Institutions

Another recurring concern was public trust.

Speakers stressed that development requires more than policies and financing. It also depends on institutions that citizens trust and that consistently deliver services and results.

UN Resident Coordinator a.i. Dr. Olushayo Olu highlighted the importance of multilateral cooperation in addressing interconnected global challenges, while emphasizing the need for strong institutions capable of delivering services, maintaining social stability and creating an environment conducive to investment.

Deputy Foreign Minister for International Cooperation and Economic Integration Dr. Ibrahim Nyei similarly underscored the importance of trust in strengthening governance, social cohesion and partnerships.

Their interventions reflected a broader consensus that development is more likely to succeed when citizens have confidence in public institutions, governments operate transparently and partnerships are built around shared responsibility and accountability.

Three Shifts for a Resilient Liberia

At the conclusion of the dialogue, participants identified three major shifts they believe could help Liberia navigate an increasingly unpredictable development environment:

From fragmented interventions to integrated solutions;

From reacting to crises to investing in resilience before shocks occur; and

From externally driven development models to stronger national ownership and leadership.

The proposed shifts, participants said, represent more than policy recommendations. They offer a framework for building a Liberia capable of adapting to uncertainty while continuing to pursue inclusive and sustainable development.

A Shared Responsibility

The dialogue ended with a recognition that no single institution can address Liberia’s development challenges alone.

Government, development partners, the United Nations, civil society, communities and the private sector must work together to strengthen the country’s resilience and expand opportunities, participants said.

As Liberia confronts increasingly complex global challenges, the discussions produced an optimistic message: resilience can be built, opportunities can be expanded and sustainable development remains achievable when national leadership, innovation and partnerships converge around a common purpose.

Minister Ngafuan captured the challenge in a closing observation:

“Development is not measured only by how fast a country moves when the road is smooth. It is also measured by how firmly a country stands when the road becomes rough.”

For Liberia, the road ahead remains challenging. But the UNDP dialogue underscored a growing determination among policymakers and development partners to ensure that the country does more than survive its next crisis—it builds the institutions, systems and human capacity needed to emerge stronger from it.

World.title: An Open Letter to CBL Governor Henry F. Saamoi
World.content:
September 8, 2026

Hon. Henry F. Saamoi

Executive Governor

Central Bank of Liberia (CBL)

Ashmun & Lynch Streets

Monrovia, Liberia

Subject: Urgent Request for Panel Configuration Rebalance at the National NPL Resolution Conference

Dear Governor Saamoi,

As the Central Bank of Liberia prepares to host the National Non-Performing Loan (NPL) Resolution Conference from September 9–11, 2026, I address you on a matter of vital importance to our nation’s macroeconomic trajectory and financial sector stability.

The public unveiling of the speaker and panelist profiles reveals a structural imbalance. The conference roster is heavily weighted toward commercial bank executives, central bank regulators, and traditional institutional operators—the very architects and managers of the financial architecture under which Liberia’s NPL ratio has reached unsustainable levels.

While the technical expertise of supply-side operators is essential, a conference composed exclusively of system insiders risks becoming a one-directional monologue. It threatens to produce a singular, predictable outcome: advocating for harsher supply-side penalties, aggressive collateral foreclosures, and punitive judicial enforcement.

Decades of economic evidence in Liberia demonstrate that relying solely on supply-side coercion is counterproductive:

●Facing predatory credit terms, rigid non-negotiable contracts, and draconian court collection, micro-entrepreneurs and formal MSMEs intentionally migrate to cash-led informal operations, deepening unbanked cash circulation.

●Exponential late fees, double-digit penalty margins, and short loan tenors push distressed borrowers into mathematical insolvency, inflating NPL balances rather than recovering principal.

●Small-scale borrowers and market vendors face aggressive collection tactics without functional consumer protection frameworks, leaving zero room for restructuring or a “fresh start.”

To achieve sustainable financial stability, supply-side discipline must be matched with demand-side rehabilitative solutions—including consumer protection frameworks, realistic debt restructuring, penalty caps, and statutory debt-discharge mechanisms for honest, insolvent entities.

I respectfully submit an urgent call to rebalance the conference panel configuration by immediately inviting representatives from the demand side of the economy:

1.Representatives from the Liberia Business Association (LIBA), domestic contractor associations, and agricultural producer unions.

2.Legal practitioners specializing in corporate restructuring, insolvency law, and financial consumer protection.

3.Representatives from micro-enterprise networks and informal sector associations who navigate daily credit friction.

Resolving Liberia’s NPL crisis requires a genuine dialogue between both sides of the aisle—creditors and debtors. I trust your leadership will ensure that this milestone conference serves as a platform for balanced national reform rather than an echo chamber of punishment.

Respectfully yours,

Paul Columbus Collins

Public Financial Commentary & Macroeconomic Analyst

World.title: Liberia: Prince Johnson’s Shadow: Kogar’s War On Boakai, Koung Exposes Nimba’s Deepening Political Fault Line
World.content:
Monrovia — Senator Samuel Kogar’s latest attack on President Joseph Boakai and Vice President Jeremiah Koung is bigger than a quarrel over Liberia’s proposed War and Economic Crimes Court.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected] , Gerald C. Koinyeneh, gerald. [email protected]

It is a warning shot over the political future of Nimba County.

Fresh from his expulsion from the Movement for Democracy and Reconstruction (MDR), Kogar has chosen one of the most politically sensitive issues in Liberia—the prosecution of those accused of atrocities during the civil war—to challenge the very administration that his former political family helped install.

And by invoking the late Senator Prince Y. Johnson, Kogar is deliberately touching a nerve that runs deep through Nimba politics.

His argument is blunt: Boakai and Koung benefited from Prince Johnson’s political machinery, but, in his view, have now abandoned the understanding that secured that support.

That accusation, whether politically sustainable or not, has the potential to resonate far beyond Kogar’s personal political dispute with the MDR.

The accusation carries particular weight because Johnson’s opposition to a war crimes tribunal was not a position he adopted late in his political career. It was a recurring feature of his political messaging and one of the issues around which he built relationships, negotiated political alliances and expressed concerns about his own political future.

Johnson had consistently complained that the proposed accountability process would disproportionately target him because of his role during Liberia’s civil conflict. His position placed him at odds with those demanding prosecution for alleged wartime atrocities, but it also became part of the political identity that helped him maintain a strong following in Nimba County.

For Johnson, politics was never simply about party labels. His alliances shifted over the years as political circumstances changed. He supported Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, later backed George Weah, and eventually became politically aligned with the Unity Party and President Boakai. Those relationships demonstrated the late senator’s ability to work with administrations across Liberia’s political spectrum while maintaining his own positions on issues he considered fundamental.

The War and Economic Crimes Court remained one of those issues. That history is important because Senator Kogar is now attempting to place himself inside that political narrative. His argument is essentially that Johnson supported political actors and administrations at different points in the country’s recent history, but ultimately felt betrayed when the issue he considered most threatening to his political legacy remained alive.

Whether that interpretation is accepted by Nimba voters is uncertain. But Kogar’s decision to raise it at a time when his relationship with the governing political establishment has sharply deteriorated gives the issue a new political dimension.

It also allows Senator Kogar to transform what might otherwise have been viewed as a party disciplinary dispute into a larger question of political loyalty.

That effort comes against the backdrop of his recent expulsion from the MDR. MDR National Chairman Cooper Kruah said the party’s decision followed complaints against Senator Kogar and a disciplinary process in which, according to him, the senator was allowed to respond. Kruah alleged that Kogar repeatedly sought excuses and ultimately failed to appear for a subsequent hearing, along with his lawyer, leading the disciplinary committee to recommend his expulsion.

But Kruah’s explanation also revealed the political dimension of the dispute. The MDR chairman said the party is working with the Unity Party and supports President Boakai, arguing that Kogar could not simultaneously benefit from membership in the governing political arrangement while publicly taking positions that appeared to undermine it.

The party therefore presented Senator Kogar’s expulsion not simply as punishment for a violation of its internal rules, but as a defense of its political relationship with the Unity Party. Senator Kogar has offered a different response, returning to Nimba and telling supporters that he was not the first politician to be expelled from a political party.

That response may be an indication that he intends to make political independence the centerpiece of his next chapter. His subsequent appearance last week at a political roundtable convened under the leadership of former President George Weah has only intensified speculation.

The meeting brought together prominent opposition figures, including several former officials of the George Weah administration and leading members of the Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC). Senator Kogar’s presence did not, by itself, amount to a formal declaration that he had joined the CDC. But politically, it was difficult to ignore the timing.

A senator expelled from a party aligned with the Unity Party was now sitting alongside some of the country’s most recognizable opposition politicians. That development inevitably raises the question of whether Senator Kogar is preparing for a political realignment.

More importantly, it raises the question of what such a realignment could mean in Nimba. For decades, Nimba’s electoral politics has demonstrated that political influence can be transferred, shared and contested — but rarely permanently owned.

Johnson’s electoral history is perhaps the clearest illustration. In the first round of the 2017 presidential election, Johnson secured 107,430 votes in Nimba, representing 53.50 percent of the county’s vote. Joseph Boakai followed with 39,964 votes, or 19.90 percent, while George Weah received 16,002 votes, equivalent to 7.97 percent.

Johnson’s influence became even more politically significant in the runoff. After supporting Weah, the former football star’s Nimba vote rose to 73,434, or 57.14 percent, while Boakai received 55,083 votes, or 42.86 percent.

Those figures helped establish the perception that Johnson could move a substantial portion of Nimba’s electorate behind a candidate he supported. But the numbers also tell a more complicated story. Johnson’s endorsement did not produce unanimous support. The same pattern appeared in the 2020 senatorial election, when Koung won the race with 37,899 votes, representing 36.12 percent. Edith Gongloe-Weh received 34,153 votes, or 32.55 percent, while Garrison Yealue secured 15,607 votes, or 14.87 percent. Other candidates divided the remaining votes.

Koung won the election, but nearly two-thirds of the electorate had voted for someone else. That election remains important to the current political debate because it demonstrates that even in a county known for powerful political personalities, voters retain the ability to make independent choices.

Three years later, however, Nimba produced a dramatically different result. In the 2023 presidential election, the ticket of Boakai and Koung received 138,070 votes, representing 59.53 percent of the county’s first-round vote. Weah received 50,427 votes, or 21.74 percent, while Tiawan Gongloe received 17,024 votes, or 7.34 percent.

The runoff was even more decisive. Boakai and Koung received 144,646 votes, representing 74.14 percent of Nimba’s valid vote, while Weah received 50,453 votes, or 25.86 percent. The figures demonstrated the enormous advantage that can be created when a national ticket contains a prominent Nimba political figure.

But once again, the numbers stopped short of suggesting complete political unanimity. Approximately one-quarter of Nimba’s voters still chose the opposing candidate. That historical pattern is now central to understanding the Kogar question.

The late Johnson’s death in November 2024 created an unusual political vacuum. Nimba had lost a politician who, regardless of one’s opinion of him, had occupied an extraordinary place in the county’s political hierarchy.

The subsequent senatorial by-election became an early test of who could command the electorate after Johnson. Kogar emerged as the winner. He received 62,136 votes, representing 52.08 percent of the vote, while Edith Gongloe-Weh received 40,506 votes, or 33.95 percent. Mack Gblinwon finished with 7,489 votes, equivalent to 6.28 percent. Unlike Koung’s 2020 victory, Kogar’s result crossed the 50-percent threshold.

That fact cannot be ignored. It provides Kogar with a legitimate electoral argument that whatever portion of the Johnson political structure may have contributed to his victory, he also demonstrated an ability to win a countywide contest decisively.

The political significance becomes greater because Kogar has subsequently been identified by chiefs and elders of Nimba as the ‘political heir’ to Johnson. That designation is more than ceremonial in a county where traditional leadership, family networks, community relationships and political organization frequently intersect.

But being named a political heir and actually inheriting a predecessor’s votes are two different things. This is where the 2029 question becomes complicated. If Kogar remains aligned with the opposition and eventually supports the CDC or another opposition presidential arrangement, can he move a meaningful portion of Nimba’s electorate away from the Unity Party?

The 2017, 2020, 2023 and 2025 elections provide evidence for both sides of the argument. They demonstrate that prominent political figures can influence large numbers of Nimba voters. But they also demonstrate that no political figure has ever achieved complete control of the county’s electorate.

Kogar therefore does not need to reproduce Johnson’s 2017 performance to become politically consequential. He would not necessarily need to win Nimba for an opposition presidential candidate.

Suppose the Unity Party enters 2029 expecting Nimba to provide another overwhelming margin because Koung remains a central figure in the administration. If Kogar succeeds in creating a substantial opposition constituency within the county, the governing ticket could still win Nimba but by a considerably smaller margin.

In a tight national contest, that difference could have consequences beyond Nimba. Conversely, if Kogar’s political influence is overstated and the majority of Nimba voters continue to identify with Koung, Boakai or the governing coalition, his opposition alignment could produce considerable political noise without significantly changing the electoral result.

The War and Economic Crimes Court could therefore become one of the issues through which those changes are expressed. For Johnson’s supporters who believed the late senator was being targeted, Kogar’s

accusation that Boakai and Koung betrayed Johnson could resonate as an emotional political grievance. For others, however, the issue may not be enough to override their support for the Unity Party or their confidence in Koung.

The political battle will therefore not necessarily be about whether Kogar can convince Nimba that Johnson was betrayed. And if Kogar can turn Johnson’s old grievance into a new political narrative, the next election in Nimba may reveal whether the late senator left behind merely a Senate seat — or a political constituency still waiting for someone to speak in its name.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-VP Howard-Taylor Camp Fires Back, TAKES CASE TO THE PUBLIC As Client Battles Illness, Prosecution Over Drug Trafficking Allegation
World.content:
As Jewel Howard-Taylor’s criminal case advances through Liberia’s justice system, her family and supporters are mounting a parallel battle in the court of public opinion—launching a “Justice for Jewel” campaign that seeks to challenge misinformation, spotlight her constitutional rights and pressure authorities for a fair and speedy process, while prosecutors continue efforts to prove allegations that could carry far-reaching political and legal consequences.

MONROVIA — As former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor faces prosecution over allegations including drug trafficking, criminal conspiracy and money laundering, her family and political supporters are taking the battle beyond the courtroom, launching a public campaign aimed at shaping the narrative surrounding one of Liberia’s most politically charged criminal cases.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The campaign, branded “Justice for Jewel,” is anchored by a new website, www.justiceforjewel.com, which presents the former vice president’s account of events, provides a timeline of the case, and calls on Liberians to rally around what supporters describe as her constitutional rights to due process, a fair hearing and the presumption of innocence.

The campaign does not claim to constitute a judicial determination of Howard-Taylor’s innocence. Instead, it repeatedly emphasizes that the allegations remain allegations and that she has not been convicted by a court.

At the heart of the campaign is a straightforward message: an accusation is not a conviction.

A Political Figure Under Prosecution

Howard-Taylor, a former vice president, senator and first lady, has been thrust into an extraordinary legal and political controversy following Liberia’s record-breaking cocaine seizures earlier this year.

Prosecutors have accused her of involvement in an alleged transnational narcotics operation, with charges relating to the importation and trafficking of controlled substances, criminal conspiracy and money laundering.

The allegations are serious. But her supporters argue that the gravity of the accusations should not override the legal principle that guilt must be established through evidence and judicial proceedings.

The “Justice for Jewel” campaign therefore seeks to shift public attention toward the conduct of the prosecution, the evidence against her and the constitutional safeguards available to an accused person.

‘Stopped at the Airport’

A major feature of the campaign is its reconstruction of the circumstances surrounding Howard-Taylor’s arrest.

According to the website, Howard-Taylor was stopped at Roberts International Airport on August 19 while preparing to leave Liberia.

Her legal team maintains that she had already agreed to report voluntarily to police and was on her way to meet her lawyers when she was stopped.

She was subsequently taken for questioning and charged.

The case later moved before the Monrovia City Court, where the defense challenged aspects of her detention and sought humanitarian consideration.

Howard-Taylor was eventually transferred to Monrovia Central Prison after the court rejected a request for home confinement.

Her detention was complicated by her health. She was hospitalized after reportedly experiencing elevated blood pressure while in custody, making her medical condition an increasingly important issue in the proceedings.

From Prison to House Arrest

The case took another turn as proceedings moved toward Criminal Court “C.”

The defense raised concerns about Howard-Taylor’s health and sought medical documentation and specialist input concerning her condition.

On September 4, Judge Ousman F. Feika granted the former vice president compassionate release on medical grounds and placed her under strict house arrest.

According to the campaign, the conditions include continuous police presence, a court-approved caregiver, a visitor log and restrictions on her movement.

She cannot travel except with court authorization for medical treatment.

The ruling effectively shifted Howard-Taylor from prison custody to a tightly controlled home detention arrangement while the criminal proceedings continue.

Defense Abandons Preliminary Examination

Another important development came Monday when Howard-Taylor’s lawyers withdrew their request for a preliminary examination of the State’s evidence.

The decision followed the defense’s complaint that the court had declined to provide access to materials it considered necessary to meaningfully challenge the prosecution’s case.

Magistrate L. Ben Barco granted the withdrawal and instructed the Clerk of Court to communicate the development to the appropriate criminal court, potentially clearing the way for prosecutors to pursue the next procedural stage, including a possible grand jury indictment.

The decision raises a critical question: Why would the defense abandon a proceeding it had initially requested to test the State’s evidence?

The defense insists that the withdrawal should not be interpreted as an admission of guilt.

“As of this statement, Madam Howard-Taylor has not been indicted by a grand jury,” her lawyers said, stressing that a criminal complaint is not an indictment and that an indictment, if returned, would not constitute a conviction.

‘Hearsay and They-Say’

Atty. Gbawou Kowou, a member of Howard-Taylor’s legal team, has mounted a strong attack on the evidentiary foundation of the government’s case.

Speaking during a live interview on Spoon FM and podcast, Kowou described the case as being built largely on what he called “hearsay and they-say.”

He specifically questioned the prosecution’s reported reliance on text messages and audio recordings allegedly retrieved from a cellphone surrendered by detained businessman Sheikh Bashiru Kante.

Investigators reportedly contend that the recordings contain discussions involving money and alleged political protection connected to a drug cartel.

Kowou, however, argued that investigators’ claims about what is contained on the cellphone should not be confused with authenticated evidence tested in court.

“The whole case is about hearsay and they-say,” he said, arguing that rumors and explosive allegations cannot substitute for proof.

His comments reflect the defense’s broader strategy: challenge not only the allegations but the quality, authenticity and admissibility of the evidence the State intends to rely upon.

Family Takes the Fight Public

The launch of “Justice for Jewel” demonstrates that Howard-Taylor’s family and supporters are not leaving the battle exclusively to her lawyers.

The campaign provides what supporters describe as a centralized source of information about the case and seeks to counter what they characterize as misinformation and premature conclusions about Howard-Taylor’s guilt.

Supporters are being encouraged to use the hashtag #JusticeForJewel and circulate information about developments in the proceedings.

The campaign also calls for judicial and civic institutions to ensure what it describes as a transparent, impartial, and speedy resolution of the case.

Health Becomes a Central Issue

Howard-Taylor’s health has emerged as another major component of the defense’s public campaign.

On Monday, she was reportedly taken again to the Gomez Institute of Medical Science for medical treatment, with family sources citing pneumonia and thyroid-related complications.

The campaign describes her as suffering from an ongoing health condition and argues that her medical circumstances must be taken into consideration throughout the proceedings.

Her supporters say her years of public service should not deprive her of humane treatment or due process.

The court’s decision to grant compassionate release and place her under house arrest has now given that argument added legal significance.

Grand Jury Next?

Despite the increasingly public nature of the battle, the ultimate fate of the case remains in the hands of Liberia’s justice system.

With the preliminary examination withdrawn, attention could now shift toward the grand jury process and whether prosecutors will secure an indictment that moves the matter further toward trial.

For Howard-Taylor’s supporters, that stage will be another opportunity to insist that the former vice president be judged on evidence rather than public accusations.

For prosecutors, it will be a test of whether the allegations against one of Liberia’s most prominent political figures can withstand formal judicial scrutiny.

The case has therefore evolved beyond a conventional criminal prosecution. It is increasingly a battle over evidence, due process, public perception and confidence in Liberia’s justice system.

For now, the message from Howard-Taylor’s camp is clear: she may be accused, but she has not been convicted.

And with the “Justice for Jewel” campaign now taking the fight directly to the public, the courtroom is no longer the only arena in which the battle over her fate is being fought.

World.title: Liberia: Civil Society Coalition Presses Boakai on War Crimes, Anti-Corruption Courts Ahead of UN Security Council Presidency
World.content:
Monrovia — A coalition of Liberian civil society organizations has accused the Joseph Nyuma Boakai administration of dragging its feet on the establishment of Liberia’s proposed War and Economic Crimes Court and Specialized National Anti-Corruption Court, warning that continued delays could undermine the country’s credibility as it prepares to assume the presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December 2026.

By Francis Boayue

In a strongly worded statement issued Tuesday, the National Civil Society Consortium for Transitional Justice said nearly three years into the Boakai administration, the government has yet to secure enactment of the legislation required to establish and operationalize the two courts.

The consortium said Liberia’s international leadership must be matched by concrete action at home, arguing that the country cannot credibly champion justice, human rights, accountability, peacebuilding and the rule of law internationally while leaving major justice reforms unfinished domestically.

“Accountability Delayed — Liberia Must Match Global Leadership with Domestic Accountability and Justice,” the group said in the statement.

Liberia was elected to a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for the 2026–2027 term, a development the consortium said reflected international confidence in the country’s transition from conflict to peace and its emerging role in international peace and security.

With Liberia scheduled to hold the Council’s rotating presidency in December, civil society leaders said the government faces a critical test of whether its international commitments are reflected in its domestic governance.

‘Justice Cannot Wait’

The consortium acknowledged steps already taken by the government, including the 55th Legislature’s passage of a joint resolution in April 2024 supporting the establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court.

It also credited President Boakai with creating the Office for the Establishment of War and Economic Crimes Court for Liberia (OWECC) and submitting draft legislation aimed at establishing the proposed courts.

But the coalition said those measures are insufficient without final legislative action, adequate funding and full operationalization.

“Government must decisively act to complete the process,” the consortium said, calling for the enactment of the enabling statutes needed to establish and fund both institutions.

The civil society organizations said victims and survivors of Liberia’s civil wars, particularly women and children, have waited for decades for justice.

They argued that the absence of a specialized war crimes court continues to perpetuate impunity, deny victims closure and undermine national reconciliation more than two decades after Liberia’s civil conflicts.

The group specifically highlighted conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence, displacement, loss of livelihoods and other serious human rights violations suffered during the wars.

Women’s Rights at Stake

According to the consortium, establishing the War and Economic Crimes Court is also critical to Liberia’s implementation of the Women, Peace and Security agenda under United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 and subsequent resolutions.

The coalition said a credible, victim-centered and gender-responsive court would help transform Liberia’s international commitments on women, peace and security into tangible justice for survivors.

It said women, children and other victims must be treated not merely as symbols of Liberia’s peace narrative, but as rights-holders entitled to truth, justice, remedies and guarantees that abuses will not recur.

Corruption Court Also Critical

The coalition also linked the proposed National Anti-Corruption Court to Liberia’s broader governance and development challenges.

It warned that entrenched corruption and the abuse of public resources continue to undermine democratic governance, erode public trust and contribute to poverty and inequality.

According to the group, corruption also has a direct impact on citizens’ access to essential services, including healthcare, education and electricity.

A specialized anti-corruption court, once established and adequately resourced, would therefore help strengthen accountability, protect public resources and support inclusive and sustainable economic development, the consortium argued.

‘Non-Negotiable’

The civil society coalition described the establishment of both courts as “non-negotiable,” saying they are consistent with Liberia’s obligations under international human rights law, international humanitarian law and broader UN rule-of-law principles.

It called for the courts to operate according to international standards, including judicial independence, equality before the law, due process, fair-trial guarantees, protection of victims and witnesses and meaningful participation by victims.

The consortium argued that the two institutions could collectively strengthen the rule of law, increase public confidence in government, advance economic and social justice, deter future abuses, reinforce reconciliation and demonstrate that no individual is above the law.

Warning to Legislature

The group also directed its criticism toward the National Legislature, urging lawmakers to act without further delay on the proposed legislation.

It cautioned against using constituency consultations as a justification for prolonged legislative inaction, recalling what it described as previous delays surrounding implementation of the recommendations of Liberia’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

While acknowledging the importance of lawmakers engaging their constituents, the coalition said such engagement should not become an excuse for delaying action on the court legislation.

Seven-Point Demand

The consortium outlined seven recommendations, calling on President Boakai to urgently engage the Senate and House of Representatives to ensure timely passage of the two bills.

It further urged the President to ensure that the 2027 National Budget includes dedicated funding for both courts while mobilizing international support for their establishment and sustainability.

The Legislature, the group said, must prioritize passage of the bills, while the Executive and lawmakers must ensure that both courts are adequately resourced and operationally independent, impartial, transparent, victim-centered and gender-responsive.

The coalition also called for Liberia’s domestic justice and anti-corruption agenda to be aligned with its international commitments on human rights, peace and security, transitional justice and Women, Peace and Security.

It urged the government to use its December 2026 UN Security Council presidency as an opportunity to demonstrate leadership by example—promoting accountability internationally while institutionalizing justice at home.

The group also called on the United Nations, European Union, United States and other international partners to continue supporting Liberians’ demands for accountability and to press for the establishment and financing of both courts.

Finally, it urged the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court to deepen collaboration with the Executive, Legislature, Judiciary and other stakeholders to move the process forward.

‘The Boakai Administration Must Act Now’

The National Civil Society Consortium said it remains prepared to work with national institutions and international partners to ensure the timely establishment and sustainability of the two courts.

But it issued a blunt closing warning to the government:

“Justice delayed is justice denied. And justice denied is a recipe for human rights violations, impunity, violence, poverty and underdevelopment.”

The coalition concluded: “The Boakai administration must act now!”

The statement was signed by representatives of the Press Union of Liberia (PUL), Center for Transparency and Accountability (CENTAL), Women’s NGO Secretariat of Liberia (WONGOSOL), Association of Female Lawyers of Liberia (AFELL), National Muslim Council of Liberia (NMCL), and Liberia Council of Churches (LCC).

World.title: Liberia- Former Police Crime Commissioner Johnny Dean Freed on US$15K Property Bond After Bribery, Criminal Conspiracy Charges
World.content:
Monrovia— Former Liberia National Police Commissioner for Crime Services Johnny Bolar Dean has been released from custody on a US$15,000 property valuation bond after being arrested and forwarded to court on allegations that he accepted US$10,000 while police were investigating a major drug-trafficking case.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Dean, a former Unit 106 commander and senior figure within Liberia’s criminal investigation structure, faces charges of criminal conspiracy, bribery, tampering with a criminal investigation, and obstruction of government functions by a public servant.

Despite the seriousness of the allegations, the offenses charged are bailable, allowing Dean to remain out of custody pending further proceedings, subject to the conditions imposed by the court.

His release does not amount to an acquittal or a judicial finding that the allegations are without merit. The property bond is intended to secure his appearance before the court as the case proceeds.

Why US$15,000 for an Alleged US$10,000 Bribe?

The value of the bond has prompted questions because the property presented to secure Dean’s release was valued at US$15,000, while the alleged bribe at the center of the case is US$10,000. The two amounts, however, serve different purposes.

The US$10,000 is the subject of the prosecution’s allegations. Police contend that the money was connected to an effort to influence or compromise an ongoing criminal investigation.

The US$15,000 property valuation, on the other hand, is a bail-security mechanism. It is not a determination of the value of the alleged bribe and does not constitute a fine or punishment.

A property bond generally requires the accused or a surety to demonstrate sufficient interest in real property to secure the defendant’s appearance in court.

At the bail stage, the court’s primary concern is whether the accused will comply with the judicial process—not whether he is guilty.

The US$10,000 That Triggered the Case

According to a police charge sheet dated September 1, Dean is accused of accepting US$10,000 from Stephanie Fefe Mensah while authorities were investigating individuals identified in the case as Edison Brown and Alpha Bah.

The investigation is linked to Liberia’s broader cocaine-trafficking case involving a shipment authority have valued at approximately US$317 million.

Police allege that Dean used his position within the security apparatus to interfere with the investigation, disclose confidential information and frustrate efforts to investigate individuals connected to the alleged drug operation.

Dean, however, has reportedly provided investigators with a different explanation for the money.

According to the charge sheet, he admitted receiving the US$10,000 but told investigators that Mensah gave him the money for safekeeping. He also reportedly described Mensah as his lover.

Police rejected that explanation and alleged that the payment was connected to the criminal investigation and intended to influence the handling of the case. Investigators subsequently recovered the money.

The circumstances surrounding the payment are therefore expected to become a central factual dispute at trial: whether the money was simply entrusted to Dean, as he reportedly claims, or whether it constituted an illicit payment intended to influence a police investigation.

From Police Commander to Criminal Defendant

The allegations carry particular significance because of Dean’s former position. As Commissioner of Crime Services, he occupied a senior role within the Liberia National Police, with responsibilities connected to the investigation of serious criminal offenses.

His previous service as a Unit 106 commander also places the case against him within the context of a career spent in Liberia’s security and criminal-investigation apparatus. Prosecutors are essentially alleging that a senior police official abused the authority of his office while a major criminal investigation was underway.

If proven, such allegations could raise broader questions about professional ethics, internal controls and the ability of law-enforcement agencies to protect sensitive investigations from interference.

An Investigation Inside the Police

The case reportedly emerged from an administrative inquiry conducted by the Professional Standards Division of the Liberia National Police.

Dean and Mensah were reportedly turned over to the Crime Services Department on August 18 following that administrative process.

A Special Investigative Team headed by Assistant Commissioner of Police Harold T. Jones subsequently conducted the criminal investigation.

That inquiry ultimately resulted in Dean being charged and forwarded to court.

The sequence places the allegations within an internal police process that escalated into a criminal case.

The court will now have to determine whether the evidence gathered by investigators is sufficient to sustain the charges.

Dean: “I Am Not Connected to Any Drug Cartel”

Dean has rejected allegations linking him to any drug-trafficking organization.

The former police commissioner has maintained that he is not connected to a drug cartel and has challenged claims portraying him as a participant in criminal activity.

His explanation concerning the US$10,000 is also central to his defense.

Rather than acknowledging the payment as a bribe, Dean reportedly told investigators that the money was given to him for safekeeping.

That distinction could prove critical.

For the prosecution, the challenge will be to establish not simply that Dean received the money, but that it was connected to a criminal purpose and intended to influence or interfere with an ongoing investigation.

The defense, meanwhile, is expected to challenge the prosecution’s interpretation of the transaction and the evidence supporting the charges.

What the Court Will Have to Determine

As the case progresses, several issues are likely to come under judicial scrutiny.

The court may examine the circumstances under which the US$10,000 was delivered, communications between Dean and Mensah, the relationship between the two parties, and the nature of the investigation involving Brown and Bah.

Prosecutors may also seek to establish whether Dean disclosed confidential information, improperly used his official position or took actions intended to frustrate police efforts.

The defense is expected to challenge those allegations and the evidentiary basis for the charges.

The US$15,000 property bond does not resolve any of these questions. It simply permits Dean to remain outside custody while the judicial process continues.

A Larger Test for Liberia’s Drug Fight

The Dean case comes at a sensitive moment for Liberia’s law-enforcement institutions. The country’s investigation into a massive cocaine-trafficking operation has already brought suspected traffickers, security personnel and other actors under scrutiny.

The allegation that a former senior police commander may have accepted money and interfered with an investigation adds an institutional dimension to the case.

It raises a difficult question for Liberia’s fight against organized crime: If criminal networks can allegedly reach into institutions responsible for investigating them, how secure are those investigations?

At the same time, the case raises an equally important legal question: whether criminal liability can be established from a disputed financial transaction without prosecutors proving its criminal purpose beyond a reasonable doubt. Those questions cannot be settled by allegations alone. They must ultimately be determined through evidence presented before a court.

Road Ahead

Dean’s release on a US$15,000 property valuation bond means he will face the case from outside detention unless the court later orders otherwise. His release should not be interpreted as a declaration of innocence, just as his arrest and charging should not be treated as proof of guilt.

The prosecution retains the burden of proving the allegations.

At trial, the court will ultimately be asked to determine whether the US$10,000 was an innocent transaction or an illicit payment; whether Dean used his official authority to interfere with an investigation; whether confidential information was disclosed; and whether his conduct amounted to the offenses contained in the charge sheet.

For a former commander entrusted with fighting serious crime, the stakes are considerable.

For Liberia, the case could become an important test of accountability within the security sector—and of whether institutions tasked with combating organized crime can withstand the criminal influences they are expected to confront.

For now, Johnny Bolar Dean remains a defendant, not a convicted criminal. The allegations against him remain unproven, and he is presumed innocent unless and until a court of competent jurisdiction determines otherwise.

World.title: Liberia: In Monrovia’s Slums, Boys Are Learning to Talk About Periods Too
World.content:
Monrovia, – Maxine Lussine didn’t expect two men to run her group session that day. Her usual facilitator, Ms. Juwa, was gone. In her place stood Jerome Naa Wlalee and a colleague.

By Patience M. Jones, [email protected]

“They started talking about how boys also have a part to play in menstruation,” said the 17-year-old from Old Road, a member of a peer support group under Healing Bridge Liberia. “For our setting, where I grew up, I’ve never seen my dad really taking part in menstruation and all that. So it was really confusing to me, because those are things I’ve seen in movies.”

That confusion is the wall Healing Bridge is trying to knock down. In Liberia, periods, sex, and reproductive health have long been treated as women’s business; fathers, brothers, and boyfriends stay out of. Healing Bridge’s leadership believes that silence helps explain why teenage pregnancy has stayed stubbornly high for decades. Liberia’s 2029/2020 demographic and health survey found 32 percent of girls aged 15 to 19 are already pregnant or mothers, and adolescent girls make up 60 percent of the country’s obstetric fistula cases.

The day it happened, Maxine Lussine remembers being caught off guard. Their usual facilitator, a woman the girls called Ms. Juwa, wasn’t there. In her place stood two men, Jerome Naa Wlalee and a colleague, ready to lead the session anyway. What came next stayed with her.

“They started talking about how boys also have a part to play in menstruation,” said the 17-year-old from Old Road community, who is part of a peer support group under Healing Bridge Liberia. “For our setting, where I grew up, I’ve never seen my dad really taking part in menstruation and all that. So it was really confusing to me, because those are things I’ve seen in movies.”

That confusion is exactly the barrier Healing Bridge is trying to break down. In Liberia, conversations about periods, sex, and reproductive health have long been treated as women’s business, something fathers, brothers, and boyfriends stay out of. Healing Bridge’s leadership argues that silence is part of why teenage pregnancy has stayed stubbornly high for decades. According toLiberia’s 2029/2020 demographic and health survey , 32 percent of girls between 15 and 19 are already pregnant, or mothers, and adolescent girls account for 60 percent of the country’s obstetric fistula cases.

The program is part of the Nurture, Empower, and Protect (NEP) project, a five-year, €7 million initiative funded by the Embassy of Ireland and jointly run by UNICEF and UNFPA, targeting more than 107,000 adolescent girls across Montserrado, Grand Gedeh, and Rivercess counties by 2030. Healing Bridge is one of the community organizations selected by the Clinton Health Access Initiative to carry that work into five communities: Old Road, Clara Town, Slipway, PHP Community, and West Point.

But unlike many reproductive health programs that focus only on girls, Healing Bridge built men and boys into the design from the start. Niagulali, the organization’s executive director, said trained male volunteers don’t wait for people to come to them. They go out looking for conversation. “They met people at the attire shop, at the market, the seaside, the fishermen, all of those different places,” he said, describing informal dialogue sessions the volunteers hold in daily gathering spots around the five communities. “They did everything. It was very, very good.”

The goal, Wlalee said, is to shift what he calls a generational habit of silence, one where fathers avoid the subject entirely and mothers are left to explain everything alone, often too late or too vaguely to matter. “We also engage men and boys because they too need to get involved with this entire empowerment stuff as well,” he said.

Members of Healing Bridge Liberia’s peer support groups gather for a group photo at a graduation event under the Nurture, Empower, and Protect (NEP) project, which brings boys and men into conversations once treated as women-only.

For Maxine, the lesson went further than menstruation. It reshaped how she understood her own authority over her body. “They told me that I have the final say concerning my body,” she said, describing a separate session on consent. “My yes, me yes. My no, me no.” She said she now feels she can turn to her own mother with questions she once would have kept to herself, something she credits partly to watching men in the program speak openly about a subject she’d always been taught was off-limits to them.

Wlalee is candid that shifting an entire community’s habits doesn’t happen in one workshop, or even one graduating class of 25 girls. Healing Bridge is now restructuring its model into shorter, rolling cohorts so it can reach more communities faster, aware that the wider NEP project’s targets are enormous compared to what one organization can do alone. But he points to the male volunteers’ reports and the testimonies coming back from caregivers as early proof that something is moving. “Some participants gave testimonies that they now can talk to their parents about certain things,” he said. “It’s not more like a taboo anymore.”

He said for a program built on the idea that girls should not be treated only as beneficiaries but as agents of change in their own communities, getting boys and men into that same conversation may be one of the quieter, but more lasting, shifts underway in Monrovia’s slums.

World.title: FAZ urges corporates to help fund National Teams
World.content:
The Football Association of Zambia has appealed to the corporate sector to urgently support Zambian football, saying government cannot carry the burden alone with 11 national teams to run.

The call came today as 1xBet Zambia handed over assorted football and refereeing equipment valued about K120, 000 to FAZ in a bid to ease pressure on resources for teams and match officials countrywide.

The donation included more than 1,300 pieces – match balls, training bibs, cones, discs, whistles, referee flags, referee card sets and equipment bags – aimed at improving training and officiating standards.

Receiving the donation, FAZ General Secretary Charles Chakatazya said while government support remains valuable, the Association’s responsibilities have grown too big.

“The items being handed over today are practical resources that will make a meaningful contribution to football activities and the work of our match officials,” Chakatazya said.

“FAZ has enormous responsibilities, with eleven national teams requiring resources for training, competitions, travel, equipment and technical preparations. This is why we are appealing to the corporate world to come on board and support Zambian football. Government cannot shoulder this responsibility alone.”

1xBet Zambia representative Kafupi Muwana said the company’s gesture reflects its commitment to grassroots and elite football development.

“Football plays an important role in bringing communities together, creating opportunities and inspiring young people,” Muwana said.

“We are hopeful that this equipment will improve training conditions, support the development of young talent and contribute to the continued growth of the game. We encourage coaches, referees and players to make good use of this equipment as we continue working together to create more opportunities for football stakeholders across Zambia.”

The equipment is expected to be distributed to FAZ provincial offices, youth teams, and referees’ associations to support ongoing league and national team programs.

World.title: Tonse Alliance Suspends Secretary General Zimba Pending Disciplinary Process
World.content:
Tonse Alliance Suspends Secretary General Zimba Pending Disciplinary Process

The Tonse Alliance has suspended its Secretary General, Dr Chris Zumani Zimba, pending investigation and possible disciplinary proceedings over a series of unauthorised press statements and social media postings issued in his name.

Alliance President Brian Mundubile invoked Article 13(6) of the Tonse Constitution to effect the suspension, according to a statement issued by the Office of the Spokesperson in Lusaka. The Alliance Chairman and National Legal Affairs Chairperson have been directed to activate disciplinary provisions under Article 16.

During the suspension, Dr Zimba is barred from reporting to the Secretariat, issuing statements in the Alliance’s name, or using the title of Secretary General or Advisor to the President. He has been directed to hand over Alliance property and documents to First Vice President Chifumu Kingdom Banda, SC.

The Alliance said the suspension is an administrative measure pending due process and does not amount to a finding of guilt, with formal allegations still to be put to Dr Zimba for his response.

The full statement:

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

TONSE ALLIANCE CONFIRMS SUSPENSION OF SECRETARY GENERAL PENDING DISCIPLINARY PROCESS

Lusaka, 9 September 2026 — The Tonse Alliance wishes to inform its members, supporters, stakeholders, and the general public that Dr. Chris Zumani Zimba has been suspended from his duties as Secretary General pending investigations and possible disciplinary proceedings.

The suspension follows concerns regarding a series of unauthorised press statements, social media postings, and public releases attributed to Dr. Zimba, which the Alliance leadership considers to have brought the organisation into disrepute.

The President of the Tonse Alliance, Mr. Brian Mundubile, invoked Article 13(6) of the Tonse Constitution in effecting the suspension. The relevant Alliance structures, including the Chairman and the National Legal Affairs Chairperson, have also been directed to activate the disciplinary provisions under Article 16.

During the period of suspension, Dr. Zimba is not authorised to report to the Secretariat, issue statements in the name of the Tonse Alliance, or use the title of Tonse Secretary General or Advisor to the President or organisation. He has further been directed to hand over Alliance property and documents in his possession to First Vice President Chifumu Kingdom Banda, SC.

The Alliance wishes to emphasise that suspension is an administrative measure pending due process and should not be interpreted as a final determination of guilt. Formal allegations will be presented to Dr. Zimba for his response and explanation in accordance with the procedures outlined in the Alliance Constitution.

The Tonse Alliance remains committed to internal democracy, discipline, collective responsibility, fairness, and respect for established constitutional procedures. Members are therefore urged to remain calm and avoid speculation or statements that may prejudice the disciplinary process.

The Alliance leadership will communicate further developments through authorised channels when necessary.

Issued by:

Office of the Spokesperson

Tonse Alliance

Lusaka, Zambia

World.title: FRA to expedite purchase of maize
World.content:
North-Western Province Permanent Secretary Grandson Katambi has assured farmers that the government is putting measures in place to expedite the purchase of maize at the Food Reserve Agency (FRA).

Speaking when he made a spot check at the Solwezi Main FRA depot in Solwezi, Colonel Katambi (Retired) said his office has received reports on the challenges being faced at the depot.

ZANIS reports that Col. Katambi said his office was working with FRA to find ways of addressing the challenges to help facilitate the floor buying process.

“I have taken time to interact with you here because I want to see how things are going and see what we can do about it,” Col Katambi stated.

The Permanent Secretary has since urged the officers to increase the pace at which people are being attended to and put in extra effort.

“We will increase manpower and bring in more scales and other tools to expedite the workflow,” he added.

Meanwhile, Col Katambi has directed FRA officers to prioritise attending to people with special needs adding that they should not be subjected to spending days at the depot.

“People with disabilities, the aged and pregnant women should not be made to stand in queues, attend to them as fast as possible,” he emphasised.

The Permanent Secretary also took advantage of the opportunity to advise the farmers to take responsibility for securing the maize they take to FRA as they wait to be attended to.

Meanwhile, Solwezi Main FRA depot officers assured the Permanent Secretary of working hard and surpassing daily targets, while also appealing to farmers to follow the buying procedure.

Speaking on behalf of the farmers, Edward Sakuwaha stated the need for increased manpower at the depot to help expedite the work before the rains destroy the maize.

World.title: Body of drowned boy retrieved
World.content:
The body of 13-year-old Justine Siame, who drowned in Blue Water Dam in Mkushi District, has been retrieved seven days after the incident happened.

The body was retrieved on Monday night after community members spotted it, prompting the Fire Brigade to action.

Justine, a Grade Four pupil at Mkushi Boma Primary School, drowned while swimming with friends at the dam in the Farmers Training Centre area on, September1st, 2026.

ZANIS reports that the body has since been buried.

Meanwhile, members of the community have renewed calls for authorities to either close, bury or fence off the dam, which they say has claimed several lives over the years.

Abigail Kunda of Mkushi said the dam is extremely deep, making it difficult for people who drown there to escape.

“The dam is very deep and when someone drowns, they cannot come out. A lot of lives have been lost there,” Ms Kaunda said.

She appealed to Government to take urgent measures to prevent further deaths.

“We are calling on the Government to either bury the dam or have it fenced and locked so that people, especially children, cannot easily access it,” she added.

Another community member, Lydia Tembo, said children in the surrounding community continue to lose their lives in the dam.

“Children in this community are dying a lot in this dam. Sometimes, we also hear of people being thrown into the dam. Let it either be buried or fenced because we have lost a lot of lives,” she said.

However, Mkushi Town Council Secretary Moffat Mwanza said completely getting rid of the dam may not be feasible because of its size and the benefits it provides to some members of the community.

Mr Mwanza said the local authority has taken note of the concerns raised by residents and will engage relevant stakeholders to find a lasting solution.

“There has been a lot of talk, with people suggesting that we should get rid of the dam. However, looking at the vastness of the dam, getting rid of it may not be feasible,” Mr Mwanza said.

He indicated that fencing the dam could be considered, although the exercise would require significant financial resources and the involvement of various stakeholders.

“Fencing may also not be done easily because of the cost, and we need to involve a lot of stakeholders. At the same time, getting rid of the dam may disadvantage members of the community who use the water for irrigation and gardening,” he added.

Mr Mwanza said the council will engage key stakeholders to explore measures that can prevent further loss of life.

“As a local authority, we have taken note of the concerns and we will engage the key stakeholders so that we can avoid the loss of lives in the future,” he said.

World.title: Runner Samukonga criticises ZA over athlete welfare
World.content:
Commonwealth Games gold medalist Muzala Samukonga has publicly criticised the current Zambia Athletics administration, accusing it of failing athletes and forcing them to fund their own trips to represent the country.

The sprinter, 23, who won gold for Zambia at the 2022 Birmingham Commonwealth Games and African Championships at age 19, said the situation under Major Bernard Bwalya’s executive has led to frustration and wasted talent.

In a strongly worded statement posted on his face-book page, Samukonga said athletes should not be burdened with costs that government and the association are supposed to cover.

“It is deeply disappointing that under the current presidency and executive of Zambia Athletics led by Major Bernard Bwalya, athletes continue to represent the country at their own expense on national duties,” Samukonga said.

“How can we expect to grow the sport and win medals when athletes are being asked to pay for their own air tickets to represent the nation? Representing Zambia is a national duty, and it should come with national support especially from the ministry of sport through Zambia athletics.”

He added that since the current administration came into office, “there have been no major achievements, no proper athlete welfare, and no clear development plan for athletics in Zambia.”

“Instead, we have seen frustration, withdrawal, and athletes funding their own trips and expenses,” he said.

Samukonga acknowledged that the previous administration under Elias Mpondela “didn’t do much, but the effort was seen especially on national duties and other issues regarding Zambian athletics.”

“Us as athletes deserve better. The Ministry of Sport and relevant stakeholders must intervene and ensure that Zambia Athletics is run by leaders who can mobilize resources, account for them, and prioritize athletes first. Until then, talent will continue to go to waste,” he said.

In response, Zambia Athletics General Secretary Teddy Shimishi has issued a statement assuring members that the federation will investigate the matter.

“Zambia Athletics has taken note of the various media reports and social media posts currently circulating in relation to a post made on one of our athletes’ social media platforms,” Mr. Shimishi said.

“We wish to assure our members, athletes, coaches, officials and the general public that Zambia Athletics will thoroughly investigate the matter in accordance with the established procedures of the Federation and its safeguarding policies. A comprehensive report will be issued once the investigation has been concluded.”

Shimishi said the federation has established channels through which concerns should be raised to “avoid actions or statements that may bring the name of Zambia Athletics into disrepute.”

He explained that most international programs receive support from Government through the Ministry of Sport, NSCZ, and NOCZ for events like the Olympic Games and Commonwealth Games.

However, he noted that for “international and individual competitions where athletes participate in their professional capacity,” logistical arrangements may be handled with support from athletes’ agents or representatives.

“Zambia Athletics remains fully committed to the welfare, protection and development of all our athletes. The leadership of the Federation has continued to work tirelessly to move the sport forward,” he added.

Zambia Athletics said it will issue a comprehensive statement once investigations are concluded.
