World.title: Mwamba Alleges Military And Courts Used To Secure Election Result
World.content:
Emmanuel Mwamba, a former Zambian ambassador who now serves as spokesperson for the opposition Tonse Pamozi Alliance, has accused President Hakainde Hichilema of deploying the military, closing the courts and installing loyalists on the electoral commission to secure his re-election, in one of the most detailed public accounts the opposition has given since the vote.

Mr Mwamba made the allegations in a nearly hour-long interview on Around the World with Dane Waters, a podcast that reaches listeners in more than 100 countries, giving Zambia’s post-election crisis its widest international airing yet.

“Severely so,” he said, asked whether democracy in Zambia was under attack.

The claims add detail to a dispute that has already drawn scrutiny from Washington, the United Nations and the European Union, though none of the specific allegations in the interview has been independently verified, and the government has not addressed them directly.

Mr Mwamba traced the crisis to well before the election, arguing that Mr Hichilema’s conduct in office mirrored his rise inside his own party.

Mr Hichilema spent 23 years in opposition and lost six elections before finally winning power, Mr Mwamba said, and after inheriting the party from its founder, Anderson Mazoka, he pushed out senior co-founders and avoided a general party conference for close to 15 years.

“He turned a party that was vibrant, democratic, that had upheld freedom of expression inside into an autocratic rule, unquestionable,” Mr Mwamba said.

He did not dispute the conditions that carried Mr Hichilema to power in 2021: a pandemic-battered economy, heavy debt and a cost-of-living crisis under a governing party he described as arrogant and tolerant of violence by its own supporters.

Mr Hichilema, an economist and businessman, ran as “Mr Fix It.” “He was the only man standing,” Mr Mwamba said.

What followed, in Mr Mwamba’s telling, was a rapid consolidation of power.

The government criminalised speech and assembly through cyber-crime laws, he said, and amended the constitution without following the process set out by the Constitutional Court.

Anti-corruption enforcement became a weapon against rivals, he said, with “nearly every opposition party leader” arrested on what he described as speech or corruption charges.

Those claims track a paper trail of international criticism that predates this year’s election.

A 2023 United States State Department report found Zambia had “quickly slid into authoritarianism,” citing abuses of human rights and restrictions on media and political space, Mr Mwamba said.

The International Monetary Fund flagged similar concerns over political tension even as it approved a 1.3 billion US dollar loan for the country, he said, and by 2024, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the United Nations Human Rights Council had issued their own warnings, including from a special rapporteur who cited political repression and arbitrary arrests.

Zambia responded with image management rather than reform, according to Mr Mwamba, retaining the Brenthurst Foundation, led by Dr Greg Mills, and the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change to help shore up the government’s standing in London, Paris, New York and Washington.

The sharpest allegations concern the vote itself.

Ahead of polling day, Mr Mwamba said, authorities banned the largest opposition party and disqualified a string of candidates, forcing Brian Mundubile and running mate Makebi Zulu onto a hastily assembled ballot line with little time to organise.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia was chaired, for the first time since 1991, by someone other than a sitting or retired judge, he said, naming the chairperson as the president’s own former personal lawyer and identifying three other commissioners as ruling-party affiliates.

Once early tallies began to favour Mr Mundubile, Mr Mwamba alleged, soldiers entered counting centres, disrupted the process and confiscated Gen 20 forms, the polling-station sheets used to verify results.

Monitors were pushed out of counting centres in major towns, he said, naming the European Union, the Southern African Development Community, the Law Association of Zambia and church “mother bodies” among those forced to withdraw.

Counting was then suspended for six to 12 hours, a delay Mr Mwamba blamed on violence by ruling-party supporters in Lusaka and Kabwe.

Mr Hichilema’s numbers surged once the count resumed, he said, which he linked to a break in the chain of custody over ballots during the suspension. The European Union’s own election monitoring mission, he said, documented gross irregularities affecting the result.

The most serious allegation concerns a raid the night Mr Mundubile addressed the state of the count in remarks the government characterised as a premature claim of victory.

Mr Mundubile was returning from a meeting with African Union officials at a Lusaka hotel when, Mr Mwamba said, a military unit of more than 100 broke down the gate at his residence.

“There was a raid on his house that resulted in the killing of one of our former cabinet ministers,” he said.

Eleven people, including Mr Mundubile, were detained that night, according to Mr Mwamba, who said international pressure secured Mr Mundubile’s release within roughly two hours while others remained held. “It took five days for them to admit that they had killed our minister,” he said.

Mr Mundubile sought shelter at United Nations premises, where a special envoy attempted to broker a resolution, before he was handed to police, Mr Mwamba said.

He and Mr Zulu are now held on treason charges Mr Mwamba dismissed as “threadbare,” tied to three men from the campaign’s protection detail who were sent for defensive-driving training in June and whom the state now casts as militia recruits.

“It is again typical of a man that had decided he was entitled to a second term at all costs,” he said.

As many as 300 people linked to the alliance have been detained since the election, Mr Mwamba said, a scale he said drew two interventions from the UN Human Rights Council within two weeks, including a demand from a special rapporteur for detainees’ immediate release.

Courts, meanwhile, were closed for what he called effectively four days, though officially two, long enough, he argued, to block Mr Mundubile from filing an election petition within the constitutional deadline.

“We are civil,” Mr Mwamba said. “We will not go in the bush. We will not raise a rebellion. We said the election is stolen. We have wide-ranging evidence.”

Asked whether his account amounted to the kind of unsubstantiated fraud claim opposition parties elsewhere in Africa have made after losing, he rejected the comparison outright: “This is not one of those examples. This is a methodic process over years about retaining power.”

He set Zambia’s crisis against a continental backdrop, arguing that the democratic gains of the 1990s have given way to a decade of regression, marked by coups in Niger and Chad and mounting pressure on presidential term limits, with Senegal and Ghana among the few holdouts.

Western governments, alongside China and Russia, have prioritised access to Africa’s critical minerals over democratic standards, he argued, pointing to foreign delegations that attended Mr Hichilema’s inauguration despite adverse findings from their own election monitors, and linking the pattern to migration pressures that push young Africans toward the Mediterranean.

His closing charge targeted the mining sector underpinning Zambia’s economy.

He named First Quantum Minerals, which operates the Trident and Kansanshi mines in North-Western Province, citing an unnamed Global Witness report describing what he called a pervasive relationship between the company and Mr Hichilema.

Tax incentives passed under the president have benefited multinational miners even as copper prices hit historic highs of 13,000 to 14,000 US dollars a tonne, up from a historical range of 3,000 to 5,000 dollars, he said, with no windfall tax in place to capture the gain for Zambia.

“There are mine houses and multinationals that are walking out with billions of dollars from our country,” Mr Mwamba said.

Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu remain in custody on treason charges. No election petition has been filed before Zambia’s courts, and the government has yet to respond to the allegations made in the interview.

World.title: Al Merrikh in Ndola as Power chase CAF comeback
World.content:
Zambian champions Power Dynamos and Sudanese giants Al Merrikh have stepped up preparations for Saturday’s crucial return leg tie of the CAF Champions League First Preliminary Round at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium.

Al Merrikh hold a 1-0 advantage from the first leg played at Amahoro Stadium in Kigali, Rwanda last Saturday night.

Power Dynamos have continued with training in Kitwe since arriving there on Monday morning.

Power Media Officer Faith Kaira said the team’s desire is to overturn the deficit on home soil.

“The general expectation is to turn the result around. We have to be aggressive and ensure we score, utilize chances and win,” Kaira told Lusaka Times Sports.

Aba Yellow will be banking on home support in Ndola to overturn the narrow loss and keep Zambian hopes alive in Africa’s premier club competition.

Meanwhile, Al Merrikh arrived in Ndola on Tuesday afternoon via Simon Mwansa Kapwepwe International Airport and went straight into their first training session.

Two days before the team’s arrival, the club had sent its Public Relations Manager Khaled Aziz as part of an advance party.

“PR Manager, Bashm Engineer Khaled Aziz, has arrived in Ndola, Zambia, as part of the club’s early arrangements to receive the team delegation and prepare all the requirements for its residence before facing Power Dynamos,” the club wrote on its official Facebook page.

The winners on aggregate will advance to the Second Preliminary Round scheduled for 16-18 October and 23-25 October.

The 16 winners from that round will progress to the group stage at the end of November.

The losing teams from the First Preliminary Round drop into the CAF Confederation Cup.

Kickoff for Saturday’s match at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium is 15h00.

World.title: HoDs sensitised on access to Information law
World.content:
The Ministry of Information and Media (MIM) has successfully sensitised Heads of Government Departments (HoDs) in Chipata on the Access to Information law, which was enacted in December 2023.

The sensitisation exercise was aimed at equipping officers who serve as information officers in different departments with adequate knowledge on public expectations, as well as the dos and don’ts required to effectively carry out their information‑sharing mandate.

Eastern Province Permanent Secretary (PS) Paul Thole, who was represented by Deputy Permanent Secretary Lewis Mwape at the meeting, highlighted that access to information is a human right, and that administrative penalties will apply on individuals failing in their duties of providing information.

“Government has mandated the Human Rights Commission as the statutory body that puts administrative penalties on you HODs who may deliberately fail to comply,” he said.

Mr Thole further warned that no government officer will be allowed to use public resources to pay penalties, but their own funds, to serve as a warning to would-be offenders.

He reiterated that the government enacted the law to promote transparency in the running of public affairs.

“President Hakainde Hichilema signed this law to ensure the public service works according to the expectations of the people it serves by ensuring transparency in the system,” he indicated.

And in his presentation, MIM Director in Charge of Press and Media Development, Modern Mayembe disclosed that the law allows for institutions to appoint information officers responsible to give out information to the public.

He called on Departments to quicken this process that is key to the implementation of the Access to Information Act, adding that the law enhances service delivery and reduces corrupt practices in public offices.

“In an event where you fail to appoint an Information Officer, Heads of Departments will act as Information Officers until someone is put in place, ” the Director guided.

The meeting availed the HoDs with a number of guidelines on information sharing as provided for by the law, while indicating exceptions where information can be withheld, including matters bordering on state security and personal information in instances that compromise the safety and well-being of concerned individuals.

It was also disclosed during the meeting that requests and responses on information sharing need to be in written form, for records keeping.

World.title: Gambia: Gambian President Declares Power Emergency Amid Protests
World.content:
President Adama Barrow has declared the country's prolonged electricity crisis a national emergency and promised to increase power generation as protests over rolling blackouts intensify ahead of the December presidential election.

Barrow urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts. He said that the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa.

Demonstrators in Banjul and surrounding areas burned tyres, erected roadblocks and called for Barrow to resign after some communities experienced outages lasting up to 48 hours during the hot season.

Police used tear gas to disperse protesters gathering near Barrow's residence and the headquarters of the National Water and Electricity Corporation.

Barrow has promised a 24-megawatt generation machine by the end of October. He announced plans for a further 50-megawatt solar power plant. The electricity provider has blamed soaring temperatures, climate change and wider geopolitical disruptions for the crisis.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Kenya Launches Crackdown on Foreign Informal Traders

Kenyan officials have started to crack down on foreign nationals running small businesses in the informal economy. This comes after President William Ruto backed measures reserving activities such as hawking and petty retail primarily for Kenyan citizens. Ruto said that foreign investors should focus on bringing capital, creating jobs and supporting local production rather than competing with citizens in businesses requiring little capital. Kenyans have reacted with mixed feelings to the move, with some welcoming it as a way of protecting jobs amid high unemployment. Others fear it could fuel xenophobia and discourage foreign investment. Political economist Sheila Owigo Olang questioned whether removing foreign traders would create more opportunities for Kenyans, describing the policy as potentially populist ahead of elections. The government has insisted that foreign nationals who comply with immigration, work permit and licensing requirements remain legally protected. Questions remain over who will ultimately be affected and how the policy will be enforced.

Gambia Declares Power Crisis a National Emergency



Gambian President Adama Barrow has declared the country's prolonged electricity crisis a national emergency and promised to increase power generation as protests over rolling blackouts intensify ahead of the December presidential election. Demonstrators in Banjul and surrounding areas burned tyres, erected roadblocks and called for Barrow to resign after some communities experienced outages lasting up to 48 hours during the hot season. Police used tear gas to disperse protesters gathering near Barrow's residence and the headquarters of the National Water and Electricity Corporation. Barrow has promised a 24-megawatt generation machine by the end of October. He announced plans for a further 50-megawatt solar power plant. The electricity provider has blamed soaring temperatures, climate change and wider geopolitical disruptions for the crisis.

Funding Cuts Push Sudan's Health System to the Brink

Sudan's already fragile health system is nearing collapse as international funding cuts force healthcare facilities to close amid the country's devastating civil war, said Médecins Sans Frontières. More than 33 million people now require medical assistance following the conflict between the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces. The loss of USAID funding and reductions in European aid have left many humanitarian organisations unable to sustain their operations. MSF reported a sharp increase in patient admissions at facilities it supports and said the closure of dozens of healthcare centres is placing enormous pressure on the hospitals that remain open. In some displacement camps, maternity and surgical services have shut down, forcing patients to travel long distances for treatment. The crisis is compounded by attacks on healthcare facilities, widespread hunger and continuing violence, prompting MSF to urge world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly to increase support.

WFP Says Food Aid Key to Fighting DR Congo Ebola Outbreak

The World Food Programme has warned that food assistance must form a central part of the response to the rapidly spreading Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, where conflict, displacement and severe hunger are making it harder to contain the disease. The outbreak, declared in May and caused by the rare Bundibugyo species, has become the fastest on record, with more than 5,500 cases and 2,642 deaths reported in its first 100 days. WFP said that people struggling to feed their families cannot easily comply with the health measures needed to prevent transmission, particularly in remote areas far from treatment centres. More than 500,000 people in the affected Ituri province are facing severe food insecurity, while poor infrastructure and ongoing conflict complicate efforts to deliver assistance. The WFP is calling for more international funding to expand both food assistance and Ebola treatment services, noting that adequate nutrition in addition to medical treatment can greatly increase a patient's chances of survival.

Nurses' Strike Deepens Pressure on Kenya's Health System

Kenya's prolonged nurses' strike is placing increasing pressure on the country's public health system, with essential services disrupted as nurses demand the implementation of long-standing labour agreements. Hundreds of nurses have demonstrated in Nairobi, calling on the national and county governments to address salary arrears, allowances, staffing shortages, promotions and career progression. At the heart of the dispute is the 2017 Collective Bargaining Agreement, which the Kenya National Union of Nurses and Midwives says remains largely unimplemented despite provisions for nursing service allowances and improved working conditions. The union has said negotiations alone are no longer sufficient and insists that signed agreements must be honoured before members return to work. The government and county authorities continue engaging with the union, including on the permanent employment of UHC workers. Nurses argue that years of unfulfilled promises and poor working conditions have damaged morale and undermined their ability to provide safe and effective patient care.

Close 

Zimbabwean Vendors Vow to Defy Harare Street Clearance Order



Zimbabwean authorities have intensified efforts to remove illegal vendors from Harare's Central Business District. They declared that uncontrolled street trading is no longer acceptable and ordered traders to use designated markets and vending bays. Local Government Minister Daniel Garwe said illegal vending was contributing to congestion, blocked pavements, litter, poor sanitation and public health risks, including the potential spread of water-borne diseases such as cholera. The government insists that the crackdown is not a war against informal traders. It argued that significant investment has already been made in designated vending infrastructure that remains underused. The move has, however, been met with strong resistance from vendors, who say informal trading is their only means of survival in an economy with limited formal employment opportunities. The order is a seven-day ultimatum to vacate the streets, and vendors have vowed to resist. Traders' representatives have urged the government to implement reforms guided by the National Informal Economy Formalization Strategy of Zimbabwe, rather than just chasing traders off the streets.

World.title: South Africa: Fake Toys Raise Safety and Job Concerns - South African News Briefs - September 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Fake Toys Raise Safety and Job Concerns

Concerns are mounting over counterfeit toys flooding the South African market, reports EWN. Fake products are now estimated to account for 25% of sales. Farrel Frank, managing director of the South African Toys and Games Association, warned that counterfeit toys can pose serious health and safety risks and cost jobs. He said the growth of online sales platforms has contributed to the problem. Some major platforms are working with the industry to remove suspicious listings. Consumers are also being urged to remain vigilant after a recent complaint involving a toy with a strong chemical smell that allegedly caused burning and tingling when it touched a consumer’s face.

More Witnesses to Testify in Anele Tembe Inquest



More witnesses are set to testify in the inquest into the death of Anele Tembe, who fell from the 10th floor of a Cape Town hotel in April 2021, reports SABC News. Lawyers representing Tembe's family questioned witnesses about whether her fiancé, the late rapper Kiernan "AKA" Forbes, had asked for her family to be informed of her death. Two police officers told the court they had no knowledge of whether the family had been contacted. One officer said Forbes did not ask police to contact them. The inquest has also heard from a nearby resident who reported hearing an argument between a man and a woman shortly before Tembe’s death.

Tshuma Extradition Hinges on Plea Deal

Extradition proceedings against UK fugitive Ndodana Tshuma could depend on whether the Johannesburg Magistrates Court accepts a plea agreement between him and the State, reports EWN. Tshuma, who is accused of murdering his wife and two young daughters in the UK before fleeing to South Africa, pleaded guilty to firearm and immigration-related charges following his arrest in Johannesburg. Details of the proposed plea deal and sentence have not been disclosed. The magistrate must still decide whether the agreement is just and appropriate. A custodial sentence could further complicate his extradition to the UK, where he is expected to face the murder allegations.

World.title: Mali: Malian Women Resist Renewed Support for Female Genital Mutilation
World.content:
analysis

An online campaign defending cutting, which is still legal in Mali, recasts the practice as a means of protecting girls.

A coordinated social media campaign defending female genital mutilation (FGM) emerged in Mali this August, reigniting societal debates not just about women's bodily integrity, but also about tradition and national sovereignty.

Days after a national non-governmental organisation displayed posters in Bamako denouncing the practice, anonymous online accounts began posting images that reversed the 'no more' campaign's message. Men of various backgrounds are portrayed smiling or with thumbs up, surrounded by the national colours and the message: 'In Mali, yes to excision! Let's protect girls and build their future.'

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The slogan turns the protection argument on its head in a country where cutting out parts of young girls' genitals, often without anaesthesia and at the risk of deadly complications, remains commonplace. A 2023 study estimated that FGM caused roughly 44 000 excess deaths a year across 15 African countries, including Mali. This makes it a leading cause of death for girls and young women where it is practised.

For those who survive, the consequences are dire and both immediate and long-term. They include severe pain and bleeding, infection and emotional shock at the time of cutting. Throughout life, they manifest through chronic pain, urinary and menstrual complications, a greater risk of difficult childbirth, and lasting psychological trauma.

Local women's rights advocates have opposed the practice for decades. Soon after Mali's 1960 independence, midwife and lawmaker Aoua Kéita and fellow activists pushed for reforms to advance women's rights in the 1962 Marriage Code. They achieved a ban on forced marriage and a minimum age for matrimony. But they failed to secure a prohibition on excision and polygamy.

Powerful conservatives went on to defeat draft laws in 2009 on advancing women's rights in the household, and in 2019 on violence against women. Mali's 2024 Penal Code condemns violence generally, but stops short of naming FGM.

This legal gap has been costly for Malian women and girls. Mali's latest Demographic and Health Survey reveals that 89% of those aged 15 to 49 have been cut - one of the highest rates globally. Among girls aged 0 to 14 - the age range when cutting usually occurs - the prevalence is lower, at 70%, and down from 74% in 2018. This suggests the practice may be slowly receding.

But the decline is modest, and potentially reversible. Many in Mali, both women and men, still support FGM, believing it is a religious obligation or a tradition worth keeping. Both claims are disputed, but the lack of consensus threatens thousands of infant girls every year.

FGM supporters minimise its physical harms, presenting it as necessary to control women's sexuality - a long-standing feature of patriarchal control. Societal norms across much of Mali's southern and central regions have long glorified suffering as a badge of honour for women, essentially normalising women's pain. The stigma of bad morality that community expectations could attach to an uncut woman is presented as the greater harm she needs protection from.

'Yes' campaigners also try to portray opposition to FGM as a foreign agenda. This erases Mali's long history of home-grown opposition, from Kéita to today's human rights defenders. But it resonates with broader sovereignty narratives that recast women's rights as a foreign import and traditional gender norms as a societal strength.

But this logic replaces one domination with another. It allows men, families and communities to police women's bodies and maim girls too young to consent and call it resisting imperialism. It denies half the population sovereignty over their own bodies in the name of national sovereignty.

It is hard to determine who is behind the 'yes' campaign supporting FGM. Journalists and Malian feminist organisations have traced much of it to accounts sharing artificial intelligence-generated posters, apparently designed to manufacture the appearance of a mass movement. This makes it difficult to assess the campaign's true scope.

While most men whose portraits are used in the campaign have defended it, some have cited unauthorised use of their image or retracted their support under public pressure.

By mirroring the communication style of the 'no' advocacy, FGM supporters have sought to normalise their position, creating a false equivalence between 'yes' and 'no'. Once the two are placed on an equal footing, inaction can be presented as balance rather than a choice to condone violence. Apparent neutrality works in favour of the status quo.

But in the course of Mali's 'refoundation' - a process aimed at resetting societal norms and values, and the basis for political governance - women will not accept a more rigidly gendered social contract without a fight. The pro-excision campaign has met a strong response from women's rights advocates, health professionals and other public voices challenging the notion that defending FGM equals defending Malian values.

Women - and some men - have also been mobilised beyond national borders. In Côte d'Ivoire and Togo, the 'yes' campaign triggered its own swift backlash. Malian and West African diaspora have organised anti-FGM protests in Paris, Montreal and beyond, indicating that FGM can no longer count on silence.

On 26 August, Mali's National Human Rights Commission called on the authorities to criminalise FGM. Other countries where the practice is entrenched - including Burkina Faso, Senegal, Guinea, Niger, Egypt and Sudan - have passed such laws. It has not ended the practice, but it has made it riskier for perpetrators and handed women's rights groups a legal basis to challenge it.

Close 

But legislating may not be the end of the story. In 2024, traditional and religious leaders attempted to have The Gambia's Parliament repeal the 2015 Women's (Amendment) Act criminalising FGM. The case is still pending before the Supreme Court.

Beyond parliaments and courtrooms, significant shifts in community norms are needed to protect women's bodily integrity. Religious leaders should clarify that FGM is neither required nor consensually accepted in Islam. They should work with women's rights organisations, who have long been committed to ending the practice, and health professionals who can best explain its consequences.

International partners should support that effort without becoming its face, a move that risks feeding the campaign's own claim that reform is foreign-imposed.

Ornella Moderan, Regional Director for West Africa, the Sahel, the Lake Chad Basin and Central Africa, ISS

World.title: Ethiopia: Rising Tigray Tensions Test African Union
World.content:
AU Should Act Before Conflict Escalates

Barely a week after African leaders met in Luanda, Angola to strengthen the African Union's conflict prevention capacity, escalating tensions in northern Ethiopia are testing whether the AU can turn early warning into action.

Tensions between Ethiopia's federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the Tigray region's main political party, have grown for over a year amid increasing disputes around the implementation of the AU-brokered November 2022 Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. Both parties have accused the other of military mobilization, while unresolved questions over contested territories, the safe return of displaced people, and disarmament threaten the agreement. In August heavy fighting erupted between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan forces near Ethiopia's border with Sudan with reports of artillery and drone strikes.

The AU has expressed concern about rising tensions in Tigray as far back as March 2025 and Human Rights Watch has repeatedly highlighted concerns for the safety of civilians. In April, we documented continuing abuses against Tigrayans by authorities and security forces in Western Tigray. More recently, we documented TPLF forcibly recruiting civilians in Tigray, including children as young as 15.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The political mechanisms intended to manage growing tensions are under strain. However, efforts to revive the mediation dialogue have raised concerns about whether the existing mediation channel retains both parties' confidence.

The AU Peace and Security Council, of which Ethiopia is a member, called on August 12 for strengthening the Continental Early Warning System to bridge the gap between early warning and early action. The Council validated on August 24 a new Trigger Model for Early Warning and Response, intended to connect identifiable risks with timely preventive action. Days later, at their extraordinary summit in Luanda, African leaders emphasized strengthening conflict prevention, mediation, and early warning and early action.

Developments in northern Ethiopia now present a concrete opportunity to put those commitments into practice.

The AU should intensify engagement with Ethiopia's federal government and the TPLF to address the disputes threatening the Pretoria agreement. It should assess whether the existing mediation arrangement needs strengthening and call for public reporting by its Monitoring, Verification and Compliance Mechanism on compliance with the agreement, including allegations of remobilization and abuses against civilians.

The 2020-2022 conflict brought devastating abuses and civilian suffering. The AU should act before escalating tensions spiral out of control.

World.title: Zimbabwe: 'Order Must Be Maintained' - Govt Orders Crackdown On Illegal Harare Vendors Defying Eviction
World.content:
THE government has declared that illegal vending in Harare's Central Business District (CBD) "is no longer acceptable" and "no longer business as usual", with authorities moving to enforce the use of designated markets and vending bays.

Local Government minister Daniel Garwe issued the warning on Monday, saying the deterioration of urban order in the capital was undermining Zimbabwe's Vision 2030 goal of becoming an Upper-Middle Income economy.

"This is not a declaration of war against vendors and informal traders, but a desire to bring back orderliness and cleanliness in the City," Garwe said.

He cited public health risks, congestion, blocked pedestrian walkways, and drug and substance abuse as some of the consequences of uncontrolled vending.



The minister specifically warned of the risk of water-borne diseases such as cholera as a result of trading in areas without adequate sanitation and access to clean water.

Garwe said Harare's identity as the "Sunshine City" was under threat, pointing to "littered streets, open defaecation in service lanes, blocked pavements, makeshift trading spaces and a general erosion of civic discipline."

He warned that trading in areas without sanitation facilities and proper waste management posed a serious risk to public health.

Garwe noted that government had already invested in infrastructure, including designated vending bays in Mbare, Mabvuku, Borrowdale and around the Coca-Cola area.

However, he said many of the facilities remained underutilised "white elephants" while traders continued to occupy pavements and road reserves.

The minister placed responsibility on both the City Council and vendors' associations to ensure the facilities were made functional.

He also flagged the Trabablas Interchange as a new congestion point resulting from illegal trading.

"Every pavement occupied illegally is a pedestrian displaced. Every blocked road is a business disrupted," he said.

"Order must be maintained, not periodically restored."

Garwe called for a "whole of society approach" involving government, the private sector, residents and traders to restore Harare's status as the "Sunshine City".

The government's crackdown has, however, been met with resistance from street vendors, who have vowed to defy the order to vacate the streets.

The vendors have described the seven-day ultimatum issued last week, which ends September 9, as insensitive and out of touch with the harsh economic realities forcing thousands of Zimbabweans into informal trading.

Close 

Some vendors said they would not leave the streets, insisting informal trading was their only means of survival in an economy where formal employment opportunities remain scarce.

The Vendors Initiative for Social and Economic Transformation (VISET) said it recognised the government's responsibility to maintain clean and orderly urban environments, but urged authorities to implement any measures in line with the National Informal Economy Formalisation Strategy adopted by the government in April 2026.

World.title: Trump’s pressure campaign has Iran reeling. America can’t hesitate now
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Iranian officials claim the regime is "confident" and are considering escalation against the United States. Iran may indeed lash out, but it would be coming from a place of desperation, not strength. On Saturday, Sept. 5, U.S. Central Command struck three Iranian tankers. "Let ‌the message to the IRGC be clear: ‌If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — ⁠taking out⁠ three of yours," said Admiral Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command. Three days later, U.S. Central Command said it destroyed five more tankers, after the IRGC "targeted a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days."

President Donald Trump has chosen to crush the Iranian regime economically, but U.S. military strikes (that are hitting their intended targets at an astoundingly near-perfect success rate) continue to play a major role. The combination of the blockade, sanctions and periodic punishing strikes has crippled the Iranian regime’s ability to impose much harm to the United States or its allies. The current course is not a permanent solution to the Iranian regime problem, but the United States is winning, and the public narrative should reflect that.

The U.S. strikes were in response to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) failed attempts to hit U.S. Navy ships. U.S. officials told reporters last week that half of the 25 ballistic missiles Iran fired toward Jordan failed to so much as enter Jordanian airspace.

TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS

What should we make of this? The regime has always been bad at targeting, but all of its challenges have been exacerbated by the U.S. and Israeli campaigns, and whatever help it continues to receive from the Russians or Chinese does appear to be limited in its effectiveness. This shouldn’t get these other Iranian backers off the hook for supporting our enemies in a hot war, but it does give credence to the Trump administration’s contention that so far, the help the Iranian regime is receiving hasn’t had a meaningful impact in the IRGC’s favor.

We don't know much more about what the United States is doing to prevent other nations from assisting Iran, but Russian and Chinese support for the Iranian regime continues to be my No. 1 concern about the possible duration and expansion of the war and something to track closely.

BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY

And as for diplomacy? Trump has concluded correctly that those in power in Tehran are not ready to make a deal. "I couldn’t care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement. I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing. They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?" Trump wrote on social media.

This is good news, as the short-lived so-called Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) permitted the Iranians to sell oil and gave the regime temporary economic reprieve even though the IRGC never intended to stop trying to toll the Strait of Hormuz or shooting at commercial shipping.

TRUMP REVIVES IRAN REGIME CHANGE SPECULATION WITH CRYPTIC CALL FOR PEOPLE TO 'RISE UP'

Just a few weeks ago, critics of Trump and his decision to launch Operation Epic Fury, were insisting that Trump needed to simply leave the Middle East and accept that he led the United States to failure against the Islamic Republic. The popular narrative is that the regime is now "more hardlined" and "more determined" to get a nuclear weapon and now has significant leverage over the United States through its terrorist behavior against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The critics get it wrong and are recycling some of the erroneous assumptions used to prop up President Barack Obama’s "Iran deal." There are no moderates within the Islamic Republic of Iran. The regime has been in dogged pursuit of a nuclear weapon for years, and it was only thwarted through sanctions and now, finally, Trump’s decision to engage militarily. It is a myth that the regime was so formidable that the only course was to accept that the Iranians will have a latent nuclear program, and it is best to simply accept it and try to buy off or appease the regime.

IRAN IS NOT A NORMAL NATION YOU CAN MAKE DEALS WITH; IT’S A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT

U.S. military operations have demonstrated military competency and credibility and have degraded or eliminated entire categories of Iran’s military, significant regime leadership and key industries the regime used to support its military. Now the United States is seeking to cut off the regime’s resources through a very effective naval blockade, sanctions and selective secondary sanctions.

But the use of military strikes also continues in bursts. Trump said Tuesday, Sept. 8, that he is prepared to authorize additional strikes against Iran "any time we want." According to a Wall Street Journal report, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has extended the deployment of approximately 50,000 U.S. troops and 19 warships in the Middle East.

TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME

Independent sources have now confirmed what the Trump administration has claimed: U.S. Central Command is effectively guiding dozens of commercial ships through the strait carrying millions of barrels of oil, even amid strikes to take out Iranian launchers and radar. The United States successfully eliminated many of its targets during the most violent strikes of Operation Epic Fury, and the regime is dramatically weakened, perhaps irredeemably structurally so.

World.title: ‘You’re Fired’: Nearly 40 pro-life groups urge Trump admin to cut off Planned Parenthood funds

FIRST ON FOX — Nearly 40 pro-life and faith groups are calling on the Trump administration to cut off Planned Parenthood from all federal funding by stripping the nation's largest abortion provider of its qualified vendor status, arguing there is mounting evidence that Planned Parenthood has "allegedly defrauded taxpayers, violated federal laws, and abused public trust."

The letter, spearheaded by Students for Life President Kristan Hawkins, is addressed to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Small Business Administration (SBA) Administrator Kelly Loeffler and was announced Wednesday at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas.

In it, 39 group leaders urge Cabinet officials to finalize and expand on an audit launched in January by the SBA into whether Planned Parenthood fraudulently collected tens of millions in COVID Paycheck Protection Program funds despite being ineligible.

If the administration finds fraud occurred, it could issue a sweeping nationwide ban on Planned Parenthood doing business with any federal agency or program for up to three years, Students for Life Action Vice President of Media and Policy Kristi Hamrick told Fox News Digital.

EXCLUSIVE: PENCE WARNS GOP 'MUST DELIVER,' OR PLANNED PARENTHOOD GETS TAXPAYER CASH ON FOURTH OF JULY DEADLINE

Unlike defunding through Congress, debarment is an administrative action that would ban Planned Parenthood from receiving federal funds, usually for up to three years.

"You are delisted, and no federal agency can do any business with you whatsoever," Hamrick said.

Hamrick said it would include Title X funds, Medicaid and sex education programs.

"It would make them persona non grata for every federal agency," she added.

The groups say the administrative route would not need congressional approval and is a more tailored and effective approach to addressing what they believe is taxpayer fraud by the organization.

The letter notes that there is already Democratic precedent for the use of administrative debarment, citing a 2022 letter to the DOJ from Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., demanding the federal government make greater use of debarment against "corporate criminals" seeking government contracts.

The letter also notes that this kind of review "is not uncommon," citing the SBA's actions suspending nearly 7,000 Minnesota borrowers over suspected COVID relief loan fraud in January.

MAN PLEADS GUILTY TO STEALING OVER $1M IN PPP LOANS FOR SUPPOSED AMATEUR BASKETBALL LEAGUE

"This is about whether or not Planned Parenthood is a qualified vendor and whether or not we need to stay in business with them," Hamrick said. "And we would argue that it's time for them to be fired for the failure to offer the very thing they claim to sell."

In January, Loeffler announced the SBA was auditing 38 Planned Parenthood centers regarding their eligibility for the $88 million in Paycheck Protection Program loans they received during the pandemic.

Planned Parenthood released a statement at the time, slamming the investigation as "politically motivated."

The coalition letter referenced a bombshell New York Times report published last year that cited dozens of current and former Planned Parenthood staff who alleged poor working conditions and "rock-bottom" salaries.

It also pointed to a recent American College of Pediatricians report finding that nearly 80 percent of Planned Parenthood vendors sell cross-sex procedures — including to minors — and outlined broader allegations against the organization, including Medicaid fraud, illegal trafficking of aborted fetal body parts, health and safety violations, and failure to report sex crimes against minors.

NEW FEDERAL PROBE EXAMINES WHETHER TAXPAYER DOLLARS FUND CHILD GENDER TRANSITIONS, LEGAL DEFENSES

"It’s long overdue for the examination of an organization that has received more than $10.35 billion in taxpayer dollars, according to a 2022 report," the letter states. "In light of so many serious allegations against Planned Parenthood, we ask that a debarment investigation of Planned Parenthood be prioritized to debar and delist them, stripping them of qualified vendor status and making them ineligible for any federal taxpayer support."

Hamrick said the issue boils down to vendor standards and an alleged misuse of taxpayer funds.

"The allegations of fraud ... the racist work environment, the shoddy location of business, not following health and safety standards, all of the above," Hamrick said. "So what we are saying is Planned Parenthood goes to court again and again and says, 'You can't cut our funds because we are a qualified vendor,' and qualified is the word. We are saying they are a nonqualified vendor."

Hamrick also addressed concerns that Planned Parenthood provides vital services to low-income women, pointing out that Federally Qualified Health Centers, which are federally-funded community-based clinics, vastly outnumber Planned Parenthood facilities, with roughly 5,500 sites specifically providing women's health services compared to under 600 Planned Parenthood vendors nationwide.

"FQHCs served 32.5 million patients in 2024, compared to Planned Parenthood's 2.08 million, as reported in their most recent annual report. Women have choices in where to go," the letter states.

Besides Students for Life, other pro-life and Christian organizations that signed onto the letter include Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, Family Research Council, Faith & Freedom, National Right to Life, Concerned Women for America, American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians and Gynecologists, Americans United for Life, American Principles Project, Family Policy Alliance, CatholicVote, and the National Association of Christian Lawmakers.

World.title: Innocent woman says police use of Flock camera led to 13 days in jail
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Lindsey Brooke Isaacs was asleep at home when police arrived and told the 23-year-old that her car had been involved in a crash that killed three people. She knew they had the wrong person. Her black Dodge Durango showed no obvious collision damage, and she had a receipt showing where she had been.

Still, the investigation eventually led to her being arrested and 13 days in jail. "My heart was in my stomach," Lindsey told me on The CyberGuy Report Podcast at Cyberguy.com/podcast/. "I didn't know what was going on."

Months later, prosecutors dropped all eight felony charges against her and investigators arrested another woman in connection with the crash. Her case now raises a bigger question about how much weight investigators should give license plate camera data when a person's freedom is on the line.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE

How a Flock camera became a major lead

The deadly crash happened on Oct. 4, 2025, along eastbound Interstate 4 near DeBary, Florida. Motorcyclist Joaquin Deno died. Flagler County Deputy Administrator Jorge Salinas and his wife, Nancy Salinas, also died. Witnesses reported that a Dodge Durango was involved.

Investigators found Lindsey's black Dodge Durango through a Flock automated license plate reader. The camera recorded her vehicle traveling eastbound near the Seminole and Volusia county line at 9:51 p.m. That camera was about three miles west of the crash scene. The crash happened around 9:53 p.m. That timing became especially important later.

Lindsey's attorney, Patrick McGeehan, said his team performed a time-distance analysis and concluded Lindsey was already beyond the crash location when the collision occurred. So the camera really did capture Lindsey's vehicle. The problem came from what investigators concluded from that sighting. Lindsey put it more bluntly during our conversation. "They just picked up my car off a camera and called it the end of the day. We got her."

Other evidence pointed toward a different Dodge Durango

The Flock camera hit was far from the only information investigators had. A 911 caller described a maroon Dodge Durango and provided part of its license plate number. Later, investigators also found red or maroon paint transfer on a Ford Focus involved in the crash.

Meanwhile, Lindsey drove a black Dodge Durango. A specialized Florida Highway Patrol team later inspected Lindsey's vehicle and reported finding no damage suggesting it had been involved in a collision with another vehicle.

That finding lined up with something Lindsey said she had been telling investigators from the beginning. "Where is the damage on the vehicle?" she recalled asking police. "Because I'm standing right in front of it and I don't see any damage." Still, authorities impounded her SUV. Months passed.

Lindsey Isaacs is arrested on charges seven months later

On April 17, 2026, Lindsey got a call from her attorney. She had to surrender that day. "They are arresting you for this crime," Lindsey recalled him telling her. She faced eight felony charges: three counts of vehicular homicide, three counts of leaving the scene of a crash involving death, leaving the scene involving serious bodily injury and reckless driving causing serious bodily injury. Lindsey spent 13 days in jail.

During our podcast conversation, she described spending her first several days in solitary confinement. She said she had a toilet, a sink and a metal sleeping slab covered by a thin mat. Her charges were so serious, she said, that jail officials initially kept her separated from other people.

Later, Lindsey was transferred to other sections of the jail. After her first bond hearing, she remained behind bars. "I was devastated, I was scared," she told me. "I thought my life was over."

HOW SURVEILLANCE TECH LED POLICE TO ACCUSE THE WRONG PERSON

A new investigation changes the case

The case finally began moving in a very different direction after prosecutors and a specialized Florida Highway Patrol team took another look. That team found no meaningful crash damage on Lindsey's Durango. Investigators revisited witness information and followed evidence pointing toward another vehicle.

On May 22, the State Attorney's Office formally declined to prosecute Lindsey on all eight charges. Authorities then arrested Alisa Lee Montalvo on charges connected to the crash. Prosecutors allege Montalvo was driving a maroon Dodge Durango. She faces nine charges, including three counts of vehicular homicide and tampering with physical evidence. She has not been convicted, and the charges remain allegations.

For Lindsey, the news brought enormous relief. "I felt like a new woman," she told me. "I felt free." Lindsey told me she later received an apology from the head of the Florida Highway Patrol. "It felt like a miracle," she said. "Another miracle from God that I was hearing it in person, face to face."

However, she also said the experience left lasting emotional and physical effects. "This took and is going to take maybe years to get better mentally, physically, emotionally," Lindsey said. Lindsey has since filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against two Florida Highway Patrol troopers involved in the investigation, alleging false arrest, wrongful imprisonment and malicious prosecution. Those claims have not been proven in court.

Flock Safety responds

We reached out to Flock Safety and the Florida Highway Patrol for comment. Flock Safety responded with the following statement:

"Flock cameras provide investigative leads; they do not identify perpetrators, determine guilt, or make arrest decisions. In fact, the complaint itself calls the Flock evidence 'exculpatory, not inculpatory,' meaning the evidence pointed away from Ms. Isaacs rather than implicating her: it accurately placed her vehicle three miles from the crash scene just two minutes before the crash. Characterizing her arrest as the result of Flock technology fundamentally misrepresents both the allegations and the role our technology played in this case."

The Florida Highway Patrol did not respond to our request for comment.

What a Flock camera can record

Flock cameras are automated license plate readers, often called ALPRs. They capture images of passing vehicles and use software to identify license plates. Flock systems can also capture vehicle characteristics including make, model and color. Each camera sighting can create a record linking a vehicle with a particular place and time.

For police, that can become an extremely useful investigative tool. A stolen car can appear on a camera. A vehicle connected to a missing person case could produce a lead. However, Lindsey's experience raises another question. What happens when investigators put too much confidence in one search result? We previously explored that concern after surveillance technology helped police accuse a Colorado woman of stealing a package. Her own phone location history eventually helped show where she had really been.

Lindsey blames how investigators used the Flock data

One of the most interesting moments in my conversation with Lindsey came when I asked whether she blamed the Flock technology or the way police interpreted its data. Her answer was clear. "I 100% think the second one you said, how police interpret the camera footage," she told me. That gets to the heart of this story.

The Flock camera captured Lindsey's vehicle traveling on I-4. The machine did what it was designed to do. Human judgment came next. Investigators had to decide what that sighting meant. They also had to weigh it against witness accounts, physical evidence and the condition of Lindsey's car.

According to Lindsey's federal complaint, the Flock hit three miles from the crash two minutes beforehand, ultimately helped her legal team argue that she was already beyond the crash location when the collision occurred. Technology can surface a lead. People still have to prove what that lead actually means.

FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES

Florida orders license plate readers off state highways

The debate over these cameras has now taken a major turn in Florida. On Aug. 31, the Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for license plate reader systems within rights-of-way on Florida's state highway system.

FDOT cited the rapid growth of the systems along with reports of misuse and concerns involving data privacy and surveillance. Cameras covered by the order must be removed within 30 days. The agency also said it will stop issuing future permits for license plate readers within its jurisdiction.

However, that order does not eliminate every Flock camera in Florida. It applies to cameras within FDOT-controlled state highway rights of way. Local governments can take different approaches to cameras on city or county property. Several agencies have chosen to pull back further. Miami-Dade County, for example, announced that it would suspend its entire license plate reader program. Other Florida agencies plan to continue using cameras away from state highways.

Flock is adding new safeguards

Flock Safety has also announced significant changes to how its system operates. In August, the company announced that it was changing its recommended and default license plate data retention period from 30 days to seven days.

Flock also plans to require law enforcement customers to use its Audit Assistance tool by the end of 2026. The technology flags unusual search activity for review.

Case codes will also become mandatory for law enforcement searches by the end of the year. Flock says emergency searches can bypass that requirement, although those searches will be flagged for review. Those changes add oversight. Still, safeguards inside the software cannot determine whether an investigator has drawn the right conclusion from the information on the screen.

Your license plate can create a trail

Most of us probably drive past license plate readers without noticing them. A single plate scan may seem harmless. After all, anyone standing beside the road can see your license plate.

A searchable network changes the equation. Instead of someone seeing your vehicle once, a network of cameras can record when that vehicle passed particular locations.

We have already reported on Flock license plate cameras appearing at some Home Depot and Lowe's parking lots . We also reported on a Washington court ruling that found Flock license plate reader images can qualify as public records under that state's Public Records Act.

Lindsey told me she knew Flock cameras existed before her ordeal. She simply had no idea how much could ride on the information they collected. "I just thought it was like a traffic camera," she said. Today, her opinion has changed. "I feel very different about those cameras now."

POWERFUL CRIME-FIGHTING SURVEILLANCE GROWTH SPURS LAWMAKERS TO ISSUE WARNING: 'ORWELLIAN'

What to do if police connect your vehicle to an investigation

If police tell you that your vehicle appeared in a license plate reader search tied to a serious crime, your own records could become important.

1) Preserve your location records

Save receipts and toll records that can help establish where you were. If your phone already stores location history, preserve that information too. Avoid changing or deleting anything related to the period investigators are asking about.

2) Save camera footage quickly

Doorbell cameras and security systems often overwrite older recordings. If footage could show your vehicle at home or somewhere else, preserve a copy as soon as possible. The same goes for dashcam video.

3) Photograph and video your vehicle

If authorities claim your car was involved in a collision, take detailed pictures and video showing its condition. Photograph and record each side of the vehicle and keep the original files with their date information intact.

4) Consider contacting an attorney

A serious criminal accusation can escalate quickly. An attorney can help preserve evidence and communicate with investigators. Legal counsel can also examine whether the available data actually supports what police believe happened.

Kurt's key takeaways

I'm torn on Flock cameras. If somebody burglarizes my home, I want police to have technology that can help identify the vehicle that drove away. If investigators are trying to locate a missing person, a license plate reader could provide a valuable lead. But Lindsey's story shows what can happen when a lead begins driving the investigation instead of helping investigators test what really happened. Her black Dodge Durango had no crash damage. Other evidence pointed toward a maroon Durango. The timing of the Flock hit ultimately helped her attorney argue that she could not have caused the crash. Yet she still spent 13 days in jail. As I told Lindsey during our conversation, "I can't stand when technology is used in ways that it was never intended for." That is where I land on this. The technology can be incredibly useful. The people using it still need to challenge what they think they know before someone loses their freedom. For more of Lindsey's remarkable firsthand account, listen to or watch my full conversation with her on The CyberGuy Report Podcast at Cyberguy.com/podcast/.

After hearing what happened to Lindsey, would you want Flock cameras in your community, or has this case changed how you feel about police tracking license plates? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

World.title: Conflicting court rulings leave Missouri’s congressional map in limbo
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A fast-moving fight over whether Missouri Republicans can use a redrawn congressional map for this fall’s midterm elections was cast into chaos on Tuesday with two different courts issuing conflicting rulings.

In one, the U.S. Supreme Court, in an order issued by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, left in place a Missouri Supreme Court ruling from last week that said the map could not be used while a ballot initiative that could lead to voters rejecting the newly drawn district lines moves forward. Kavanaugh handles emergency requests that arise from Missouri.

But soon after, a federal judge in Missouri ruled in favor of two GOP congressional candidates who argue that the new map, which was in place for the August primaries, must be used in November in order to avoid federal constitutional violations. That case could also quickly face U.S. Supreme Court scrutiny with time running out for the map to be finalized. The state’s deadline to finalize ballots was 5 p.m local time, and first ballots are set to go out Sept. 19.

Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe and Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, both Republicans, said on X Tuesday evening that the redrawn map would be used for the November election.

The two cases raise different legal issues, with the Missouri Supreme Court focused only on state law while the federal case raises questions under the U.S. Constitution.

The 2025 Republican redistricting plan, part of a wave prompted by President Donald Trump, was designed to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic-held seats, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

If the Missouri Supreme Court ruling remains in effect, a map drawn in 2022, with six Republican-held seats and two Democratic-held seats, would be in place for the general election.

The new lawsuit was filed by Rick Brattin, the Republican nominee in the district currently held by Cleaver, as well as Rep. Bob Onder, R-Mo. and two voters.

The legal clash erupted after the 2025 redistricting plan was enacted.

A group called People Not Politicians Missouri, led by Richard von Glahn, gathered signatures in support of a state referendum that would veto the Legislature’s map and put it on hold for the 2026 election.

But Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, refused to put the measure on the ballot, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to being overturned by voters.

The Missouri Supreme Court found that Hoskins should not have rejected the plan, unanimously concluding there is nothing in state law that says redistricting plans are exempt from the referendum process.

The referendum petition was “legal, sufficient and timely,” the court found.

Under state law, whenever a proposed ballot initiative that overrides the Legislature is deemed valid, the law is automatically put on hold until after the people vote on it.

The court also said any confusion caused by its ruling was a result of Hoskins’ delay in deciding whether the referendum could move forward. Hoskins waited until the last minute to reject the proposal ahead of an Aug. 4 deadline and broke with the state’s typical process of putting a law facing a veto referendum on hold when enough signatures are submitted.

In the separate federal case, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, ruled that the state must use the map that people voted in during the primary. Using the old map would violate the rights of candidates under the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause and the provision of the Constitution that outlines how members of the House are elected, he found.

Hoskins argued at the Supreme Court that the state court ruling violated the U.S. Constitution’s elections clause, which he said delegates significant powers to state legislatures in overseeing elections. The Supreme Court rejected a similar argument in a redistricting case from North Carolina in 2023.

Hoskins’ lawyers told the justices that the state court ruling had created chaos because the new map was used in this year’s primary election. If the state has to revert to the old map, “hundreds of thousands of Missourians will see their votes in the primary election rendered pointless,” they wrote.

Lawyers for the referendum supporters said in court filings that Hoskins was seeking at the Supreme Court a “political victory to which he was never entitled under the Missouri Constitution.”

In May, the Supreme Court rejected a similar attempt by Democrats in Virginia who sought to revive their own congressional map that had been approved by voters. The Virginia Supreme Court had found legal flaws in the process that led to the referendum.

World.title: Iran attacks American warships and base after U.S. sinks five Iranian tankers
World.content:
The U.S. military struck five Iranian tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in response to attempted attacks by the IRGC on an American warship, according to U.S. Central Command.

“The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed.” CENTCOM said in a post on X.

Four of the tankers were attacked in the Gulf of Oman and one was hit near Kharg Island, according to CENTCOM.

“American forces directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck and rendered inoperable,” it said in a statement.

Two American warships were attacked and damaged by ballistic missiles, the IRGC said in a statement, according to the semi-official Fars news agency.

The IRGC also said in a statement Tuesday that it had retaliated by launching missiles at American forces on the Al Azraq military base in Jordan, according to Fars.

A U.S. official said that Iran fired a series of missiles toward Jordan but the Iranian response was considered ineffective, and the integrated air and missile defense systems were able to thwart the Iranian strikes. All American forces in Jordan are accounted for, the official said.

Jordanian air defense systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles and two missiles fell in unpopulated areas, a spokesperson for that country’s armed forces said Tuesday, according to Jordanian state media.

The strikes on the Iranian tankers Tuesday come after the IRGC attempted to hit an American aircraft carrier and a destroyer over the weekend, resulting in a U.S. response in which the U.S. sank one tanker and permanently disabled two more.

Iran also threatened to target oil tankers in Kuwait and Bahrain in retaliation for the U.S. strikes Tuesday.

“Following the actions of the American military in targeting several Iranian oil tankers, we warn all oil tanker crews in the areas around the ports of Kuwait and Bahrain, which are hosting these forces and are complicit in their actions, to immediately evacuate their vessels, whether they are at anchor or docked as they will be targeted,” the IRGC’s navy said in a statement posted by Fars.

The Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the war, has become the key battleground in the conflict as both the U.S. and Iran have attacked tankers.

The Trump administration on Tuesday also imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran’s aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines, as well as foreign cargo service providers, in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.

A U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has squeezed the country’s economy by limiting its oil exports, while the American military has been helping a limited number of ships transit on a route through the Strait of Hormuz off Oman. Tehran wants ships to follow a route that it chooses through the strait, which was considered an international waterway before the war.

World.title: American Ben Shelton outduels defending champ Alcaraz in latest-ever U.S. Open finish
World.content:
There’s leaving it late, and then there’s what Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz just served up at the U.S. Open.

The American star ultimately outdueled the defending champion in the latest ever finish at the tournament, a thriller that didn’t finish until 3:33 a.m. in front of a raucous New York crowd.

The five-set victory takes Shelton to the semifinals, where he will face fellow American Frances Tiafoe.

That means there is guaranteed to be an American in Sunday’s final, hoping to end a drought that has seen no U.S. men’s player win a Grand Slam since Andy Roddick in New York in 2003.

Shelton, the No. 8 seed, ended Alcaraz’ 18-match winning streak in Grand Slam tournaments in a clash that lasted 4 hours, 28 minutes. At one point, the Spaniard could be seen vomiting into a towel.

The grueling quarterfinal was played under the lights after a day of marathon contests at Flushing Meadows.

The highlight-filled match swung back and forth, with Shelton winning the second and third sets after losing the first on a tie break.

No. 2 seed Alcaraz, who missed most of the season with a wrist injury, won the fourth set 6-1 to set up a grueling final set.

World.title: Oil hits $100 a barrel for first since July as Middle East conflict intensifies again
World.content:
The price of oil breached the $100 threshold Wednesday for the first time since July, as new flare-ups in the United States’ war with Iran stoked fresh concern for global energy markets.

The spike came a day after the U.S. military said it destroyed five Iranian tankers in response to attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship. Tehran responded with attacks on U.S. ships and a base in Jordan, the latest bout of fighting in a conflict that remains unresolved after months of global economic disruption.

Elsewhere new attacks by a Tehran-backed rebel group set oil facilities ablaze in Saudi Arabia and threatened a significant new escalation in that conflict.

The international benchmark, Brent crude, rose above the symbolic $100 mark at a little after 3 a.m. ET, before pushing higher to nearly $101 later in the morning.

While about 40% higher than prewar levels, Brent was still below the peak of $120 in the early days of the war. Since the start of the year, the benchmark is up by more than 65%.

U.S. crude oil is also up by similar levels and just before 8 a.m. ET, it rose above $95 per barrel for the first time since June.

Those prices are of significant concern to the White House and Republicans ahead of the midterm elections, with consumers facing higher prices as a result.

Gas prices rose to $4.22 Wednesday, the highest since early June.

Oil exports from the Middle East have dwindled since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran in February. A fifth of the world’s oil supply had flowed through the Strait of Hormuz, the key waterway that has been throttled by Tehran in response.

While the U.S. military has managed to restore some shipping traffic through Hormuz, other key trade routes have also faced disruption.

Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have attacked tankers in the Red Sea. This week, the group launched attacks on Saudi energy facilities that set oil sites ablaze and threatened a significant expansion of its conflict with the key U.S. ally.

President Donald Trump claimed on social media Monday that “oil prices will drop precipitously, like everything else is dropping (but more!), when we WIN the war with Iran.”

He said that prices could fall to as low as “two dollars a gallon.”

There was little sign of that, or of a resolution to the war.

Earlier in the week, commodities experts warned that oil prices as measured by Brent could rise to $120 or even as high as $150 per barrel if the stalemate with Iran continues to drag on.

Trump has shifted to a strategy of squeezing the Iranian economy with the U.S. maritime blockade, but recent days have seen a number of violent flare-ups.

World.title: Does it feel like your hair is always greasy? Here’s why it could be happening
World.content:
If your hair always seems to look and feel greasy no matter how much you wash it, you’re not alone. It’s a common struggle with plenty of potential culprits, including your hair and scalp type, hormones and genetics. “Oily hair is often misunderstood as a hygiene issue, when it’s really about scalp biology,” says board-certified trichologist Aga Tompkins. “Oil itself isn’t bad, it’s actually essential for a healthy scalp.”

To learn more, I spoke to three trichologists and dermatologists about common causes, treatments and misconceptions around greasy hair (more on these below). I also rounded up their product recommendations that can help clean your hair without stripping it, plus NBC Selected staff-favorite treatments.

How I picked the best greasy hair treatments

To choose the best products that’ll help keep your hair less oily (and potentially reduce the time between washes), the trichologists I spoke to recommend considering the following factors:

Ingredients: Look for a shampoo that has niacinamide and tea tree oil to regulate sebum, as well as beta hydroxy acids (like salicylic acid) or alpha hydroxy acids (glycolic and lactic acid) to gently exfoliate your scalp, regulate oil and keep follicles clear without triggering rebound oil production, says Tompkins. Surfactants like sulfates might be good for those with oily hair because they grab onto and whisk away dirt and oil, experts say. Surfactants like sulfates might be good for those with oily hair because they grab onto and whisk away dirt and oil, experts say. However, they do strip your scalp of natural oils and can cause dryness and irritation, so use in moderation, Product type: Those with oily hair should use an exfoliating, scalp-balancing shampoo and a lightweight, volume-enhancing conditioner. (Only apply the conditioner to your ends to avoid weighing down your hair.) Once a week, use a clarifying shampoo to remove product and oil buildup, and a dry shampoo in between washes to prevent greasy, limp hair. If volume is a concern, separate scalp needs from strand needs. “The shampoo you choose should always be based on your scalp type to properly regulate oil and maintain balance, while the conditioner should be chosen based on what the hair strands need,” says Tompkins.

What causes greasy hair?

The most common cause is overactive sebaceous glands on the scalp, which produce excess oil (called sebum) to protect your hair and skin, according to the experts I spoke to. What triggers overactive sebaceous glands? Genetics can play a major role: Some people have a skin condition called seborrhea dermatitis, which means they are predisposed to higher oil production than others, says Tompkins. Hormonal fluctuations, stress and lifestyle habits (like frequent touching or brushing your hair) can also have a part in how fast oil spreads from your scalp down the hair shaft, says Sara Hallajian, a trichologist and founder of Ame Salon in Santa Monica, California.

If you notice that your hair gets greasier more quickly than others, your hair type may be the culprit. “Those with fine hair tend to show oil more quickly because there’s less surface area and cuticle layer to absorb it,” says Hallajian.

Can over-washing make greasy hair worse?

Yes, if you use harsh or stripping formulas. “The issue isn’t washing itself, but the ingredients,” says Tompkins. When you over-wash, you strip your scalp of its natural oils, and the scalp may respond by producing more oil to protect itself, she says. Harsh ingredients include drying alcohols (like isopropyl alcohol, which is common in many hair care products) and parabens (preservatives that can throw off your scalp’s oil production). Frequent washing with gentle products, on the other hand, helps regulate oil rather than stimulate excess production, says Tompkins.

How do you treat and prevent greasy hair?

The goal is to not over-cleanse and instead use products that gently remove buildup, says Tompkins. “Treating oily hair is less about ‘drying it out’ and more about balancing and regulating scalp function,” says Hallajian. In addition to ingredients that reduce oil production like niacinamide, glycolic acid and lactic acid, consider the following expert-recommended tips:

Avoid heavy conditioners or oils. Using styling products that are too heavy for your hair type and texture will make your hair look more oily. That includes conditioning hair masks, which can weigh down your hair.

Using styling products that are too heavy for your hair type and texture will make your hair look more oily. That includes conditioning hair masks, which can weigh down your hair. Use a clarifying shampoo once a week to remove buildup. Clarifying shampoos have heavier surfactants (cleansing agents that create a lather), which help remove oils from the scalp that normal shampoos aren’t strong enough to remove, experts say. But keep in mind that overusing a clarifying shampoo can strip too much oil from your hair and leave it dry and brittle.
