World.title: 'Hunted,' 'shattered,' 'scared': How victims say Canada's most prolific voyeur has altered their lives
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The 15-year-old wore her school uniform, unaware a stranger followed as she walked with her mother and brother through Victoria's Mayfair Shopping Centre.

A cellphone video would later show a voyeur trailing the family, before getting close enough to slip a camera beneath the girl's pleated skirt.

When police told the girl's mother, she faced a dilemma: tell her daughter, or keep it to herself?

"Learning my daughter's image had been taken and posted on child pornography websites was devastating," she wrote in a victim impact statement read in court earlier this year.

"I have carried significant stress over how I want to tell her and how she will cope with the information once she learns the truth."

The teen is one of 652 women and children filmed in what officials claim is the largest case of voyeurism ever reported in Canada.

Yin Yeung Derek Chan spent six years secretly recording victims throughout communities on southern Vancouver Island, filming through house windows and prowling malls and well-known stores in the heart of downtown Victoria.

In the year prior to Chan's 2024 arrest, the voyeur was creating more than a video a day, uploading footage and photos of victims to social media, porn sites and a personal website that had over a million views before it was taken down.

Chan was sentenced to four-and-a-half years in prison in May — but many of the photos and videos remain online. Only a fraction of the victims have been identified.

Despite wide reporting of the sentencing, many questions remain about the police investigation and the impact of Chan's crimes.

CBC News has spent months gathering court records, listening to audio of courtroom proceedings and reaching out to Chan's victims.

In her victim impact statement, one woman said watching the video Chan took of her "shattered" her sense of safety.

"Seeing myself through the eyes of someone who had been hiding, watching, deliberately capturing me without my knowledge or consent — it made me feel hunted," she said.

"This crime did not end when the recording stopped."

Chan used delivery job to access victims' homes

Chan came to Canada from Hong Kong as a child. Although Chan's lawyer said the 39-year-old identifies as gender fluid, police referred to Chan using male pronouns and some victims say they saw a man hovering nearby, phone in hand.

Crown prosecutor Paul Cheeseman said Chan worked as an Uber Eats delivery driver, using the job to access apartment building laundry rooms.

"[Police] found thousands of pairs of women's underwear in his house and a number of them were used," Cheeseman told the court.

"So it appears he was stealing women's underwear while he was doing these videos and deliveries."

Chan has a history of secretly recording women; in 2019, Chan was caught filming a woman in a changing room at a Forever 21.

During Chan's recent sentencing, the voyeur apologized to victims but offered little insight into a pattern of prolific offending. The judge said Chan compared it to the rush of "stealing a chocolate bar from a store" and attributed the crimes to "warm weather” in an earlier proceeding.

WATCH | Victims speak out about Saanich voyeur: Victims in Canada's largest voyeurism case felt 'hunted' | Duration 2:41

Saanich police have repeatedly declined to specify where Chan filmed victims, in spite of calls from B.C.'s attorney general to help potential victims know if they could be affected.

According to the court records, more than 400 victims were targeted at Value Village in Victoria, while about 80 were filmed at local Walmart locations. Others were recorded at Greater Victoria businesses, including Indigo Books, Munro's Books, Shoppers Drug Mart, Michaels, Mayfair Shopping Centre, Hillside Centre, and the Bay Centre mall.

A few were sunbathing at what is believed by police to be Willows Beach in Oak Bay.

Five people were recorded through the windows of their homes and apartments, at addresses in the James Bay, Fairfield, and Hillside neighbourhoods of Victoria.

Police also found about 100 hours of other videos Chan recorded of other women at gyms and malls that "don't rise to the level of criminal voyeurism," Cheeseman said.

'A part of my innocence was taken from me'

One victim told CBC News that Saanich police contacted her in January 2025 after an officer she knew recognized her in a video seized from Chan's home.

Until she saw the video, she didn’t know Chan had snuck up behind her in an Indigo Books to film up her dress — though she remembers seeing the voyeur.

"Him being so close to me was like the most icky feeling and thing to think about, like, how did I let someone get so close to me without noticing?" said the woman, whose identity is protected by a publication ban.

"It made me scared to think of, like someone could get that close to me without realizing, like what else could they have done to me?"

A woman who was unknowingly videoed by the Victoria voyeur is pictured in a park. Her identity cannot be divulged due to a court publication ban. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

For a time after she found out, the woman says she was too afraid to go out alone in public, even to the grocery store.

Just weeks ago, a man in line at a dollar store started talking to her.

"I just like, shut down in my body," said the woman.

In victim impact statements, other women told the judge who sentenced Chan that they have difficulty holding down a job, struggle with mental health, and have changed the clothes they wear.

Some spend money on Ubers to avoid public transit. One victim said she got off a bus and walked almost an hour, because another passenger had a phone camera pointed her way.

The women said Chan's crimes have affected relationships, eroded their ability to trust others, and left them feeling powerless.

"I feel as though a part of my innocence was taken from me," wrote one victim, who was 17 and days out from her high school graduation when Chan filmed her.

The Victoria Law Courts on Blanshard Street in Victoria, B.C., where Chan was sentenced in May. (Emily Fagan/CBC)

Another victim was underage when Chan recorded her working as an employee at a mall. The incident triggered past trauma and she began to isolate herself. Her grades at a local college suffered, and she had to withdraw.

She said she was unable to maintain a job due to intense anxiety and fear in public spaces.

The woman said she gets counselling and financial support from WorkSafeBC, but the $4,900 she receives a year isn't enough to make ends meet.

"My life has been delayed and derailed, and my future seems uncertain," she said in her statement to the court.

"This offence did not just take away my sense of safety, it took away my independence, my ability to support myself, and my financial stability."

Some recordings still online

Cheeseman said Chan was well known in the online voyeurism community for posting videos, which were downloaded and reposted by other users.

"Mr. Chan has made it available for the entire world to revictimize these people," he said.

While police have gotten some recordings removed from Chan's personal website and Flickr, the prosecutor said officials have faced challenges in getting others taken down.

A search of the username Chan used to upload many videos and images of the victims shows many are still easily found online on social media and porn websites.

One of these posts, on Reddit, is tagged "NSFW" — the site's label for explicit content.

Comments on this post, shown in court, ask Chan where to find the videos.

The Mayfair Shopping Centre in Saanich, B.C., where some of Chan's victims were filmed. (Roszan Holmen/CBC)

"We're all eager and ready to pay or something man you gotta bless us you got the finest bitches on camera," writes one user.

"Will u sponsor me?" Chan writes back to another, telling a third user the videos are "only open to payers."

Reddit did not respond to questions from CBC News about the post.

Saanich police did not answer questions from CBC News, but Deputy Chief Const. Damian Kowalewich said in a statement that "the scale of this case was unprecedented and the impact on victims cannot be overstated."

"We recognize that once material has been distributed online it may not be possible to remove every copy, which remains an ongoing concern for many victims and represents an additional layer of victimization."

'None of it was your fault,' woman tells other victims

On May 21, the day of Chan's sentencing, Saanich police published a notice announcing the case publicly for the first time.

The victim who spoke to CBC News says it felt strange to see everyone discussing something she'd only told a few of those closest to her, especially as police promised to update her before the case became public — which she says they did not.

At first, she said it felt scary to read what people thought online about the case. But with time, it began to feel validating.

A woman whose identity can't be revealed due to a publication ban says Yin Yeung Derek Chan filmed her without her knowledge, in a video later shown to her by police. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

"It kind of made me feel like I was able to then be like, you know what, this was really messed up, and this happened to me, and I am allowed to feel violated by this situation, and I should allow myself time and space to have those feelings," the woman said.

"It doesn't devalue who you are … you didn't do anything wrong to put yourself in this situation, and none of it was your fault."

World.title: Trump to ban import of Canadian booze, motorcycles, other goods into U.S.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump hit back at Canada's counter-tariffs with stiff new tariffs on billions of dollars in some products, and outright bans on others, including alcohol.

U.S. President Donald Trump is banning the import of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and various other products into the U.S.

Trump signed five proclamations on Tuesday night, which will ban those Canadian imports as of Sept. 29, and slap 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products starting next week.

Whey products and molasses are also included in the new ban, while certain dairy products, paper and wood products, aluminum products, furniture and mattresses will be subject to 50 per cent levies.

This is the latest move in an escalating trade war between Canada and the U.S. and comes after Canadian retaliatory tariffs, promised after trade talks fell apart last month, came into force on Tuesday.

A senior Trump administration official told reporters on background that Washington opted for outright bans instead of tariffs because some Canadian provinces banned the sale of American alcohol in provincially run stores.

"These are things that we are doing in order to level the playing field, defend American production and take action against one of the only countries on the planet to retaliate against the United States," the official said.

"Canada set this precedent of banning things."

The official said that they estimate the import ban would impact "single-digit billions" of dollars worth of Canadian goods.

WATCH | Former ambassador to U.S. Hillman 'struck' by untenability of deal: Former ambassador to U.S. Hillman was 'struck' by untenability of trade deal | Duration 12:50 Prime Minister Mark Carney is bracing the Canadian public for impact as counter-tariffs hit U.S. goods overnight. Former Canadian ambassador to the United States, Kirsten Hillman, who held the office under both Trump administrations, joins Power & Politics to discuss the latest retaliation.

Trump to bar Canada from purchasing contracts

Trump is using Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act, or the Smoot-Hawley Act, to implement the import bans. The same section was used to tariff a swath of Canadian imports last month, on top of sectoral tariffs that have been in place for over a year.

The proclamations say the U.S. will also remove tariffs from a series of products, including salt, toilet paper, refined lead and fishing rods.

Earlier, Trump moved to bar Canadian-made products from eligibility for certain U.S. government purchasing contracts.

In a post to his Truth Social platform on Tuesday afternoon, Trump said he is directing the General Services Administration — the independent agency that oversees federal government procurement — to remove Canadian-origin products from its "multiple award schedules."

While the General Services Administration's preferential purchase program accounts for roughly $50 billion US worth of procurement per year, only 58 Canadian companies were granted contracts through the program in 2024-25, the most recent fiscal year with details available, according to information extracted from a GSA database by CBC News.

WATCH | Can the U.S. and Canada still negotiate?: Are there still opportunities to negotiate after latest U.S. trade war move? | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 4:08 The Trump administration's new bans on Canadian imports, including booze and motorcycles, are set to take effect on Sept. 29. As the tit-for-tat trade war escalates, former U.S. trade official Ryan Majerus discusses if that deadline creates a window for potential negotiations between Canada and the U.S.

LeBlanc calls U.S. response 'unjustified'

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said in a statement on social media Tuesday night that the government is assessing the latest moves.

"Our first priority remains on protecting and supporting Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses from these unjustified actions," he wrote, adding that he is in contact with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

"When the U.S. is ready to engage, our government will work in good faith and constructively towards a more secure mutually beneficial trading relationship that fully respects Canadian sovereignty," LeBlanc said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney released a video Tuesday morning warning Canadians that the country's pivot away from the United States will come at a cost — but insists the alternative would be far worse.

The prime minister reiterated Canada's plan to respond to the U.S. trade war by striking new trade deals with other countries to become less reliant on the U.S.

"We have everything we need to pivot and prosper," Carney said. "That pivot will come at a cost. There's always a cost to action. But it doesn't come close to the cost of standing still."

Canadian and American negotiators were working toward a trade agreement that would have given Canada some tariff relief in key sectors. But the Carney government ultimately decided to walk away, with the prime minister calling what the U.S. was offering "uneconomic."

World.title: Vietnamese firm targets Canadians with fake AI news for profit, CBC/Rad-Can investigation reveals
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

During a corporate party with dancing mascots and pyrotechnics in early 2026, the CEO of HTV Network stood on stage holding a sign in Vietnamese that said "Doanh Thu Đột Phá." Translation: "Record Revenue."

The CEO, Ngo Anh Tan, had reason to celebrate that night. Since launching as an "international media company" that connects the "world with authoritative journalism" almost two years earlier, HTV now had at least 100 employees, according to a Vietnamese job listing.

But what the company purports to do contrasts vastly with its true nature, an investigation by CBC’s visual investigations unit and Radio-Canada’s Décrypteurs discovered.

WATCH | Investigating an AI slop content farm in Vietnam: Exposing a Vietnamese AI fake news empire targeting Canadians | Duration 6:51 A network of hundreds of websites and Facebook pages is pushing fake news to a global audience including Canadians. CBC’s visual investigations team and Radio-Canada’s Decrypteurs trace the network to a company in Vietnam that claims to have more than 100 employees to reveal how the global misinformation economy operates.

Ngo and his team secretly run an AI-slop empire out of Hanoi, Vietnam, polluting social media feeds around the world, targeting users with fake content and sensationalist stories that range from Elon Musk banning Teslas in Canada to clickbait-style posts exploiting the Tumbler Ridge shooting.

The team uncovered close to 200 Facebook pages — with more than 55 million followers — that shared links to about 50 HTV-connected websites that generate revenue by running ads, often next to inflammatory or misleading political and religious content.

Posts would target users around the world, including Canada. Some claimed Elon Musk was going to ban Teslas in Canada, others used clickbait-style headlines to exploit the Tumbler Ridge shooting. These pages connected back to HTV Network in Vietnam. (Illustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; Locker Room Talk/ Facebook; Milano Gaming/Facebook)

"It's quite staggering, the scope of what's being done here," said Fenwick McKelvey, a professor specializing in communications at Concordia University in Montreal. "[It’s] totally deceptive."

HTV Network shares a name with a legitimate, state-owned Vietnamese broadcaster, complicating efforts to trace its activities.

HTV owner Ngo Anh Tan holds a sign that translates to 'Record Revenue' during a corporate party. The party included fireworks and dancing frog mascots. (Illustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; Nhung Nhung/Facebook, Trang Dang/Facebook)

'Everyone wins except for Canadians'

The model was relatively simple: The company mass-produced AI-generated content — showing, for example, how the "U.S. lost its main city" in an attack by Russian President Vladimir Putin — posted it on one of the Facebook pages they ran and included a hyperlink.

That link would take users to one of HTV's many websites, where ads for things like fungus medication, Bank of Montreal or Nova Scotia tourism would be plastered across the articles. Ads on websites viewed by CBC were served through third-party platforms, not the companies themselves.

The pages, run out of an office in Hanoi, Vietnam, would post fake or misleading political or religious content to get people to click on a hyperlink to an external website. (Illustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; Life is Colorful/Facebook)

The CBC/Radio-Canada analysis revealed that in some cases, the Facebook pages were also monetized.

HTV CEO Ngo, through text messages, told CBC/Radio-Canada he didn’t have Facebook pages or websites. When asked why his phone number matched the one on the HTV website, he said "maybe someone has taken my information." Corporate records and domain registration documentation also matched Ngo’s personal information.

Once users clicked on the link, it would take them to websites full of ads. Ads ranged from the Bank of Montreal to Nova Scotia tourism to foot fungus medications. While some Facebook pages were monetized, this is how the company would generate much of its revenue. (Daniel Rofusz/CBC)

Ngo repeatedly denied knowledge of HTV sites or pages. In response to a written request for comment, Ngo replied, "I don’t understand what you mean."

CEO Ngo Anh Tan's phone number matched the HTV website, domain info and corporate records. (Illustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; HTV Network, DomainTools, Nguyen Thanh Tu)

The following day, the HTV company website was taken down. Ngo's Facebook profile was made private and many of the digital clues CBC/Radio-Canada used to connect the company to the accounts and websites disappeared.

On July 30, a day after CBC reached out to Ngo about his role in HTV network, the company's website was taken down. Many of the clues used to connect the company to the Facebook pages and websites disappeared. (Illustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; HTV Network)

Aengus Bridgman, director of the Media Ecosystem Observatory, a joint McGill-University of Toronto project, said that Facebook incentivizes this kind of low-quality, clickable content.

Meta, Facebook’s parent company, recently invited users to join its creator program , where money can be made from reels, photos and text posts.

"The way this gets resolved is that there is some cost to Meta for enabling this sort of scam, a real concrete cost … [a] financial penalty," said Bridgman. "They get engagement on their platform. They get money. Everyone wins except for Canadians, Canadian businesses and Canadian democracy."

Meta did not respond to CBC/Radio-Canada’s request for comment.

How we uncovered the network

Using a combination of corporate documents, on-the-ground reporting in Vietnam, and software including DomainTools, Darkside and OSINT Industries, the CBC/Radio-Canada team was able to expose how this network of Facebook pages and websites, which targeted audiences in the U.K., Europe, United States and Canada, is connected to HTV Network.

It started with a June 2026 report by the Media Ecosystem Observatory investigating "Facebook's News Slop Economy," which identified hundreds of Facebook pages and websites managed out of Vietnam.

CBC/Radio-Canada built off that report, discovering a unique email address — containing "kolax9843" — on one of the websites MEO identified.

That email was the primary contact email for dozens of low-quality, cookie-cutter sites, including one called Autulu. Ad-laden articles from that URL in particular were shared by more than 20 Facebook pages, including "Man City Daily News" or "Wonderful World News," with more than 50,000 followers combined.

Danny Fernandes, a Facebook page with more than a million followers, posted fake political content for engagement. It hyperlinked to a website that had the kolax9843 email, which CBC/Radio-Canada connected to HTV Network in Vietnam. (Illustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; Danny Fernandes/Facebook)

One verified Facebook page, "Danny Fernandes," named after the Canadian musician, has more than a million followers and has shared posts that included phrases like "how eight million Democrat votes just vanished" or "Kamala stepdaughter suddenly posted a bold message on Trump Inauguration day."

Fernandes did not respond to CBC.

"The deeper you dig, the more depressing it gets," said Bridgman. "At this scale of followers and number of accounts, this is likely a well-performing business."

CBC/Radio-Canada discovered another website featuring the "kolax9843" email: the company site for FG Media Corp., which contained a photo showing a group of people standing in front of a sign.

HTV Network posted jobs looking for content marketers, who would focus on American and European trends while managing English and Spanish Facebook pages. Salaries for jobs paid up to more than double the average salary in Vietnam. (Illustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; HTVONE1/TikTok)

The company: HTV Network

Images posted by HTV employees identified by CBC/Radio-Canada on Facebook and TikTok show a busy office, and the company frequently posted ads on Facebook for content marketing jobs paying up to more than double the average yearly salary in Vietnam.

One HTV Network employee, on their personal Facebook page, even posted a photo of them at work. On a computer in the background of the photo, a web browser shows the employee is logged in as a manager for a Facebook page called "I Love Rugby - Kelce." The hyperlinks on that Facebook page took users to the Autulu website.

The "kolax9843" email was also present on a website called Longbientruck, which was registered to Ngo Anh Tan. Domain info showed a phone number that matched the HTV Network website.

An HTV employee was seen running a Facebook page called 'I Love Rugby - Kelce' in the top left corner. The page would link to web site Autulu, which is connected to the HTV Network. (Illustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; I Love Rugby - Kelce/Facebook, Facebook)

Corporate records showed HTV Network Company Limited was created in 2024, with 7 billion Vietnamese dong (or about $350,000 Cdn) in seed money. The corporate records include the same phone number.

The CEO in those records: Ngo Anh Tan.

After CBC/Radio-Canada reached out, HTV added a disclaimer that declares the articles are "fictional and intended solely for entertainment purposes."

After CBC reached out to Ngo about his involvement in HTV Network, a disclaimer was added to the websites, saying the articles are 'fictional and intended solely for entertainment purposes.' (Btuatu)

Low-quality AI content

The advent of AI has led to an industry of creators who produce cheap, low-quality content at scale.

This, combined with changes to the monetization policies at Meta in 2025, has led to a proliferation of this type of content, said Craig Silverman, co-founder of the Indicator, a publication dedicated to exposing digital deception.

"This kind of AI-generated slop is very clearly not a priority for the company," said Silverman.

"For years, Meta was really focused on rolling out a variety of technical measures and human oversight to eradicate exactly this type of content. Now Meta, through its own action, has just decided to throw in the towel on it. To me, it’s just completely astounding."

Meta did not respond to queries about whether these pages violated their Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior policy.

In Vietnam, Facebook serves roughly 60 to 70 million people, generating $1 billion US in annual revenue for the company in 2018.

"What's interesting with Vietnam [is] you have a very sizable youth population that's highly entrepreneurial and well-educated," said Victoire Rio, executive director of What To Fix, a non-profit that focuses on policy changes and accountability for Big Tech.

"A lot of the actors … are operating very openly without any form of obvious accountability."

Do you have any tips on this story? Please contact VI@cbc.ca

World.title: Recent art thefts appear to be inspired by 2025 Louvre heist, art crime experts say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Art crime experts say last year's headline-grabbing Louvre heist appears to have inspired a rash of brazen art thefts, putting European museums that hold valuable works in a difficult position.

Thieves cut a hole in a fence and climbed through a window to steal four paintings from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera early Tuesday, local authorities said. They dropped two of the works as police gave chase.

Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir's most valuable works have sold for tens of millions of dollars.

Anthony Amore, an art theft expert and investigator based in Boston, Mass., says the Renoir theft is the latest in a string of high-profile incidents since thieves made off with $140 million Cdn worth of Napoleonic jewelry from the Louvre in Paris last October.

"In my twenty-odd years of doing this sort of work, I haven't seen anything on this scale," Amore said.

"My best guess is that perhaps the Louvre was a news hook, not just for the media, but for criminal gangs that saw the opportunity to steal valuables and get away with it."

Police arrested four suspects in the Louvre heist, but most of the jewels remain missing.

'Extraordinarily stupid'

Experts who spoke with CBC News noted similarities with other recent thefts, including the March theft of works by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse worth millions of dollars. Masked men broke into the Fondazione Magnani Rocca museum near Parma, Italy, but police recovered the paintings and arrested five suspects in August.

Four Renaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina, worth more than $100 million, were stolen from the Museo Regionale di Messina in Sicily in August in a crime that remains unsolved.

Other French museums have also been targeted in recent months.

Erin Thompson, a professor of art crime at City University of New York, calls the thefts "Louvre-inspired."

She says art heists tend to be carried out by "hired, low-level criminals," but added that stealing well-known artwork is "an extraordinarily stupid thing to do."

Thompson told CBC News that thieves rarely escape punishment and said the Renoir paintings would be very difficult to sell, given the high-profile nature of the theft and the works themselves.

"I think they read the headlines about the Louvre heist and not the rest of the story. Many people who steal art from display in museums, throughout history, have been good at stealing things and not good at thinking through the consequences," Thompson said.

"They spot the rather obvious security flaws of museums, they know that art is valuable, and they figure they'll take it and then come up with a plan afterwards."

Museums under pressure

Cagnes-sur-Mer mayor Bryan Masson said the Renoir theft should "serve as a warning about the protection of our museums."

The French government has come under pressure to address security failures at the country’s museums. A French parliamentary report ​this summer said museums lacked resources and were ill-prepared to safeguard valuable artworks and cultural artifacts.

A Culture Ministry survey in 2024 ⁠found that only one in four institutions had an emergency and risk prevention plan, while nearly half lacked ⁠any video surveillance.

The painting entitled Young Woman at the Well, by French painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, was stolen Tuesday. (Musée Renoir/Handout/Reuters)

Thompson says the situation poses a complicated problem. In some ways, she says, museum security is poor because of a "long history of poor funding" and assumptions that people "will behave in museums."

But, she says, there is only so much a museum can do.

"Many of them are in historical buildings that you can't exactly fortify. And the experience of going into a museum is supposed to be anybody can go buy a ticket and stick their nose a couple inches away from some priceless artifact," she said.

"You're not supposed to have searches and guard dogs interrupting your experience of contemplating art."

WATCH | Former FBI investigator on art heists: 89% of museum thefts have an 'insider-component,' former FBI investigator says | Duration 7:30 On Sunday, thieves slipped in and out of the Louvre, making off with eight pieces from France's crown jewels. Robert Wittman, former senior FBI investigator and founder of the FBI's art crimes team, discusses the complexity of the heist and whether it could have an 'insider-component.'

Sally Hickson, an associate professor of art history at the University of Guelph, says recent high-profile thefts have been carried out at smaller provincial museums that don't have sophisticated security.

But even better-known museums may not be as locked down as some people assume, she says.

"The kind of high-tech security that people tend to expect from the Oceans movies and stuff like that, that doesn't exist in even a lot of major museums."

Thieves will 'never, ever' stop: expert

Amore says France in particular has an "extraordinary" number of museums, all with differing levels of security.

But tightening security, he says, may only push thieves to move more toward more "smash-and-grab" style thefts — a trend that already appears to be happening.

An August report from pan-European police body Europol found that art thieves in Europe are resorting to more violent and forceful methods, and specialist gangs have increasingly been ⁠replaced ⁠by ad hoc opportunists recruited through social ​media.

"Even if all these museums do beef up their security, there will probably be people still trying to find ways to get around it," Amore said. "People will never, ever stop trying."

World.title: GlobalEye gamble: Ottawa chose surveillance plane without knowing it met military needs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ottawa had no guarantees that Saab's GlobalEye surveillance plane could meet military requirements when it began negotiations to acquire six of the Swedish manufacturer's early warning and control aircraft last spring, CBC News has learned.

Sources added that the most recent assessment of the GlobalEye came to the conclusion that the aircraft meets only a portion of the military's requirements and that modifications will be needed to achieve operational readiness.

Prime Minister Mark Carney surprised almost everyone in attendance at the country's premiere arms exposition last May in Ottawa, called CANSEC, when he announced plans to acquire the aircraft. He added the deal included a production line in the country for domestic and export markets.

Among those surprised was the commander of the Royal Canadian Air Force, who was in the room, say several defence industry sources.

CBC News is not identifying the contractors because they don't want to endanger their relationship with the federal government. Four of them spoke confidentially.

At the time of the announcement, the air force had yet to inform potential bidders of its exact technical and operational needs for a new fleet of airborne surveillance aircraft.

In an interview, Ottawa's point person on military procurement said that the government must also weigh factors such as cost, jobs and geopolitics in major military purchases.

"Are the requirements important? Of course they are," said Stephen Fuhr, secretary of state for defence procurement. "It's not the only thing that needs to be considered here.

"We need to leverage this money to stimulate our own economy. We need to become more independent. We need to think about supply chains and relationships."

Carney's announcement on the GlobalEye forced the Royal Canadian Air Force to scramble to try and match what the aircraft can do with what it needed in terms of a surveillance plane over the Arctic, said several confidential sources.

WATCH | More about the GlobalEye announcement: Canada negotiating to buy Saab's GlobalEye airborne early warning system | Duration 2:59 The Canadian government has entered into negotiations with Saab to buy its GlobalEye airborne early warning platform, to be built on a Bombardier 6500 executive jet at Saab’s plant in Toronto.

It was only in late June — more than three weeks after the announcement — that Canadian military officials met with Saab to go over the specific kinds of features the plane needs.

There was one follow-up session in August where the GlobalEye's shortcomings were confirmed.

Carney has made it a priority to increase the speed of military procurement, but critics say the desire to leverage the economy — through the Canadian jobs the GlobalEye could bring — is trampling on defence needs of the country.

For example, the military is concerned that the plane, under its current design and configuration, doesn't have 360-degree radar coverage. There are also concerns about the range and frequency of the radar.

Saab has proposed modifications, putting additional radar sets in the nose and tail.

There are also concerns about the number of crew stations and connectivity equipment to plug the plane into the NORAD network, which would limit the GlobalEye's ability to offer a "control" function during operations that involve a series of military assets.

The military is also seeking a radar plane that can be refuelled in flight to cover the vast expanses of the Arctic, a feature that is not currently included on the GlobalEye.

Saab says it's responsive to 'customer demands'

In an interview earlier this year, Saab deputy CEO Anders Carp said the company is well aware of the Canadian military's expectations and that the company is ready to meet them.

Overall, the GlobalEye's sensors offer 360-degree coverage, but the main radar on top of the fuselage offers coverage in the 300-degree range, he said.

"We do have a program in place where we can place in a forward-looking and an aft-looking radar, should that be something that the customer demands," said Carp. "And the same will go for air-to-air refuelling."

Also in an interview with CBC News last spring, Saab test pilot Jussi Halmetoja spoke about the flexibility of the company's engineering process.

"We have a spiralling development process on how to improve our systems across the board at Saab, and depending on customer requirements, of course," Halmetoja said.

WATCH | Defence minister on the GlobalEye deal: NATO GlobalEye surveillance aircraft acquisition a 'big step forward' for Canada: McGuinty | Duration 0:31 Defence Minister David McGuinty told reporters at the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, NATO's intention to purchase up to 10 GlobalEye early warning surveillance aircraft will be a 'very big step forward' for Canada's defence manufacturing industry. 11 countries, including Canada, are banding together in a joint procurement effort according to NATO's secretary general.

Fuhr added that sometimes, the government needs to opt for the "85 per cent solution," saying there is "nothing out there" that checks all possible boxes.

"There's gonna be trade-offs everywhere," he said. "So it's a function of balancing all those things to meet the moment."

Last spring, CBC News reported how Canada will have to ask the Trump administration to share a key piece of technology that allows fighter jets and early warning systems to communicate while maintaining stealth.

Experts doubt the United States will allow a high-tech data link used exclusively on F-35 fighters to be installed on either the early warning aircraft or the Gripen-E — if Canada chooses to buy that warplane.

None of Saab's U.S. competitors — L3 Harris and Boeing — were shown the air force's requirements, according to the confidential sources.

L3 Harris, headquartered in Melbourne, Fla., acknowledged in a recent interview with CBC News that it had not been privy to the Canadian surveillance plane requirements before the announcement.

Boeing, whose leadership is located in Arlington, Va., declined to say whether it has received an advance look, but a spokesperson added the company continues to stand ready to support the Canadian government.

The requirements form the basis of what the military needs to have in the aircraft — or any other piece of kit it is buying.

The process also helps the defence industry decide whether its product is the right fit. And if it is, the process sets the conditions to decide what kind of modifications might be required and eventually what the price will be.

The GlobalEye could end up being an extraordinary — but not unprecedented — end-run around decades-long procurement practice, says former senior defence procurement official Alan Williams.

The process, he said, is in place to prevent "governments making these decisions haphazardly."

Williams said it's important to distinguish between what the military says is absolutely essential in a capability and what is optional.

He also said he doesn't buy the argument that measures such as this are necessary to speed up procurement because there are existing authorities within existing legislation that allow the government to move swiftly.

"You don't have to go to these strange lengths in order to try to do things faster. Go through the front door, do things right and you can get the right result in a timely fashion," Williams said. "I think it really does undermine the process. And it makes us look, I think, very, very amateurish. It goes against the intent of the legislation."

Industrial policy vs. defence needs

Philippe Lagassé, a defence policy and procurement expert at Carleton University, said there is an obvious tension at play between Ottawa's focus on job creation and the military's long-standing alliance with the United States.

"It's important to recognize that military requirements are not handed down from on high in some platonic ideal. They are meant to reflect the government defence policy," he said.

"At the end of the day, the governments get to decide what they choose to prioritize and what they'd choose to emphasize."

Ideally, Lagassé said, Canada would have updated its defence policy and articulated "what the government believes the Canadian Armed Forces should be doing and with what kind of equipment."

That hasn't happened yet.

WATCH | Ottawa weighing another potential deal with Saab: What Canada’s fighter jet decision could mean for NORAD | Duration 5:13 As Canada weighs a choice between American F-35s and Swedish Gripens for its fighter jet fleet, CBC’s David Common goes to NORAD headquarters to ask top generals about the implications of operating a mixed generation fleet for North American airspace defence.

Lagasse also said, in an ideal world, there would be no "trade-offs between domestic industrial policy or defence policy."

Requirements don't give the military a veto over what the government intends to buy, he said.

"It means that the government has to come out and accept the operational risk that it's imposing" on the military, said Lagassé.

What happens if the trade-offs cost lives?

"I think that's the challenge, right? Who wears the operational risks that we're asking the Canadian Armed Forces to accept?" Lagassé said.

World.title: Montreal police allegedly cut locs from people's hair. Here's the anti-Black history behind that
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On June 12, Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher called a late-night news conference to announce that 16 police officers from the same station were under investigation for racist and hateful acts targeting Black and Arab people.

In a scandal that has intensified the spotlight on Montreal police, Dagher revealed that the allegations include officers cutting pieces of locs from people’s hair, collecting them and keeping them as trophies.

Charmaine Nelson, a p rovost professor of art history and the founding director of the Slavery North Initiative at University of Massachusetts Amherst, described the alleged acts as “a complete and utter horrific affront to us in terms of our bodily integrity.”

In interviews with CBC, Nelson and Aly Ndiaye, another historian, described the racist practice as rooted in the history of the transatlantic slave trade, including in Canada — and Quebec. They also broke down how that history has shaped present-day law enforcement practices.

Sixteen officers from the Montreal police station 39 in the borough of Montréal-Nord are under investigation. (Kwabena Oduro/CBC)

Ndiaye, also known by his stage name Webster, is a Quebec hip-hop artist and an independent historian. He is also the founder of Qc History X, a guided tour of Quebec City that looks into its history of people of African descent and slavery.

In addition to her roles at University of Massachusetts Amherst, Nelson is the founder and CEO of the Black Maple Magazine and a former Montrealer.

These interviews were conducted separately and have been edited for length and clarity.

Charmaine Nelson, the founding director of the Slavery North Initiative at University of Massachusetts Amherst, explains the history behind the allegations and discusses the significance of locs. "When you see someone with locs, we have committed to an aesthetic that celebrates the texture and plasticity of our hair. Pushing back against what? Western, Eurocentric ideas of beauty," she said. (Meghan Tansey Whitton)

WARNING: The following includes graphic descriptions of violence carried out during and after the era of the transatlantic slave trade.

What can wearing locs mean to Black people who choose to wear them?

Charmaine Nelson: Locs for Black people are not just hair. So, when you see someone with locs, we have committed to an aesthetic that celebrates the texture and plasticity of our hair. Pushing back against what? Western, Eurocentric ideas of beauty. So, for us to take this step to grow our hair, to groom it in this very specific manner, celebrate it in this way, is in defiance of white racism. We’re celebrating the beauty and specificity of us.

When you’re a Rasta too, you are dealing with scripture. There’s a covenant you made to never cut your locs. This is a covenant with God, this is a practice of spirituality for you as a Rasta. So, for these police to be attacking and assaulting Black people at the level of cutting and removing the locs, it is a complete and utter horrific affront to us in terms of our bodily integrity, and for many of us, our spirituality.

What is the history behind white people forcibly cutting Black people’s hair?

Charmaine Nelson: Under the law, [Black people were] chattel, they [were] movable personal property. "We're going to strip them of their status of human.” There was brutality, a systemic corporal assault against Black bodies as things.

And part of that, when we go back to the archives left by the white enslavers themselves, we can see that what became a normal form of punishment was head shaving, to cut enslaved Black people's hair against their will. And this happened often too between white women doing this to Black women who they perceived as beautiful to their white husbands.

" I will shave your head to the scalp so that you don't even have control over yourself in terms of how your body looks. That too, I possess as your enslaver. "

Aly Ndiaye: When you were caught abroad through the transatlantic slave trade and the Middle Passage, you were shaven as to strip you from your identity. When they would set foot on the boat, people were shaven, because African people had intricate designs in their hair because their hairstyle was a signifier of status, a signifier of your position in society or marital status. Were you a warrior going to war? For every step of life or society, you had a design in your hair.

Aly Ndiaye, an independent historian, spoke with CBC News to break down Montreal police's alleged actions and explain their connection to slavery and the history of racism in the province. (Philipe Ruel)

Then, you have the fact that because of racism, because of slavery, because of colonialism, Black people’s hair has been seen as something that wasn’t beautiful, that wasn’t up to the standards of the Eurocentric canons of beauty. So, people had their hair shaven, had their hair straightened, and would be judged upon their hair, their hairstyle, to this day, like an Afro being seen as not normal or not professional.

To get back your identity, let’s say in the 1950s and 1960s, people started to wear their Afro during the Black Power movement. There was this whole way to shape your identity closely linked to your hairstyle, so people would wear an Afro, would wear cornrows because it’s beautiful and it’s historical, also. People trying to get back their identity, their African identity that was stolen, that was dehumanized.

The iconic Afro hairstyle of American activist and thinker Angela Davis has become a visual symbol of the Black Power movement. (Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

Where does the racist practice of collecting Black people's hair as trophies come from?

Charmaine Nelson: On the heels of slavery, what started in places like the U.S. and other places in the Americas is a rise in lynching. A rise in white people, mobs getting together and saying: “This particular Black person – usually a man or a boy – we're going to kill him tonight as entertainment.” By the time photography came around, [white mobs] were taking pictures of this and they were turning the photos into postcards and they were putting a stamp on them and mailing them. When they would murder the Black person, they would usually then set him on fire and they would take mementos from his body, collectibles of his body, home with them.

Aly Ndiaye: It was a sign of body count, a way to humiliate the enemy or to post about your 'superiority.' When [Black people] were lynched, the lynchers with the lynch mob would afterward fight: " Who gets a finger? Who gets a finger bone? Who gets a toe? " People would cut off the genitalia and keep them. And to this day, people would open the drawers of their grandpas and find a human bone, which is a keepsake from that lynching.

WATCH | Residents protesting outside Montréal-Nord's Station 39 in June: Montréal-Nord residents rally outside local police station over racism allegations | Duration 1:32 Montreal’s police chief announced Friday that 16 officers from Station 39 in Montréal-Nord are under investigation for alleged racist and hateful acts committed against Black and Arab people. Residents gathered outside the station on Monday evening to demand justice and change.

Historically, what role has law enforcement played in policing, controlling and inflicting violence on Black people in Quebec?

Charmaine Nelson: The architecture of policing in the West, in the Americas comes out of slavery. The sheriffs [in Montreal and Quebec City] had their hands all over slavery because the sheriff was in charge of the jail. And when an enslaved person would escape, the sheriff had the duty to try to hunt down that enslaved person and return them to the white enslaver from whom they'd escaped. When someone went bankrupt, their estate was handed over to the sheriff, and if you were an enslaver, that meant the enslaved people literally went to the sheriff and the sheriff decided who they got sent to as payment for the debt you owed. Law enforcement’s hands were all over slavery. Law enforcement was embedded in protecting enslavers and securing their rights to continue to enslave people of African descent. So, Black people, from the inception, were the hunted, were the criminalized and the criminals.

What does this history reveal about these allegations?

Aly Ndiaye: Now, in the 21st century, when a cop decides to keep the loc of a Black person that has been harassed, this is linked to the lynching, this is linked to slavery. This is linked to racism and a way to assert your quote unquote superiority, to be able to boast about your racist acts. And also it's a way to maintain your body count. " So how many, how many locs do you have? " Instead of bridging the gap, they are widening the gap.

This act isn't in a vacuum. This is something that is tied to slavery, that is tied to colonialism, that is tied to racism, even though those cops, maybe they weren't like: " We'll bring it back to the days of slavery. " But still, the actions are tied to that long history of violence and the history of police, of policing Black lives. They will untie it from its history because this is always what is going on. They're always trivializing things. I'm eager to see what will be done with those people from the Poste 39. But I don't expect anything.

World.title: The biggest dinosaurs couldn't sit on their eggs. Scientists say they did this instead
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Fossil eggshells believed to be from some of the biggest dinosaurs that ever lived have been found in a surprisingly cool climate far from the equator.

But those massive titanosaurs couldn't keep their volleyball-sized eggs warm by sitting on them.

"They're too big," said University of Calgary paleontologist Darla Zelenitsky, who has been studying the problem. "The nest would be one big omelette."

A new study published on Wednesday by Zelenitsky and collaborators from Japan and Argentina has taken a microscopic look and figured out what they did to keep the eggs warm enough to hatch without sitting on their nests.

By looking at the microscopic pores on the eggshells, the researchers believe titanosaurs used the same incubation technique used by modern crocodiles — burying their eggs in warm piles of rotting vegetation, reports the study led by University of Tsukuba paleontologist Kohei Tanaka, Zelenitsky's former student, and published in Royal Society Open Science.

This is a scanning electron microscope image of one of the eggshell fragments in the study, along with with the relative size of a titanosaur and its eggs. Titanosaurs were too large to brood their eggs like birds. (Tanaka et al.)

The world of the giants

Titanosaurs were a group of gargantuan long-necked, long-tailed, plant-eating dinosaurs that lumbered on four legs and weighed up to 75 tonnes, or about half the mass of a blue whale.

WATCH | New titanosaur found in Australian outback: New titanosaur found in Australian outback | Duration 1:05 Paleontologists unveil one of largest dinosaurs that ever lived.

Volleyball-sized fossil eggs called Fusioolithus have been linked to titanosaurs, and previously found by the dozens in warmer climates.

Then in 2020 and 2024, fragments of Fusioolithus eggshells were found in the Chorillo Formation at the southern tip of Argentina. The rock formation dates back to the Late Cretaceous, 72 to 66 million years ago, just before the dinosaurs went extinct.

Paleontologists from Argentina and Japan uncovered titanosaur eggshells at the Chorrillo Formation near the southern tip of Argentina. (Tanaka et al.)

Its exact position has changed a little since then, but at the time, its latitude would have been as far from the equator as Red Deer, Alta., but with a climate similar to that of New York City today, Zelenitsky said.

Fossils found there reveal a lush coastal plain ecosystem where roaming dinosaurs included the titanosaur Nullotitan glaciaris, up to 25 metres long, along with the smaller, two-legged herbivore Isasicursor santacrucensis, tyrannosaur-like megaraptors and small birds. They would have lived among crocodiles, snakes, turtles, frogs, fish, mammals, snails and insects.

Still, Zelenitsky was surprised by the discovery of eggs of titanosaurs so far from the equator: "It's just a bit more tricky with larger animals because you need more resources to survive … and reproduce."

The outcrops of the Chorrillo Formation in Argentina. (© 2018 Armando Vega)

3 ways to incubate an egg

The problem is that dinosaurs needed to keep their eggs warm in order for their embryos to develop and hatch – for up to many months, Zelenitsky said.

Smaller, feathered dinosaurs were thought to sit on their eggs like most modern birds and use their body heat. That would have been impossible for huge titanosaurs to do without crushing their relatively tiny eggs.

An example of a whole, volleyball-sized titanosaur egg. They have been found by the dozens at sites closer to the equator. (Darla Zelenitsky)

But there are other options.

Sea turtles bury their eggs on sandy tropical beaches to be warmed by the sun – something that wouldn't work in cool, southern Argentina.

Modern crocodiles and birds called megapodes bury their eggs in decomposing plant matter. Microbes generate heat as they break it down.

Zelenitsky had previously found evidence that hadrosaurs in Alberta used this technique. So the researchers wondered if titanosaurs in Argentina did, too.

Eggshells have microscopic pores so the embryos can breathe. Those need to be bigger and denser to let enough oxygen through when eggs are buried. Eggs need to be less porous if exposed to open air to prevent the egg from drying out.

The researchers measured the porosity of the titanosaur eggshells from the Chorillo Formation using an electron microscope, and found they were very porous, suggesting they were buried.

Zelenitsky said the research shows just how adaptable dinosaurs were. "Even these absolute largest dinosaurs, you know, figured out a way to ... not only reproduce or nest in the lower latitude environments but also in these higher-latitude environments, which are usually more challenging."

The study was led by Kohei Tanaka, associate professor at the University of Tsukuba, left, and co-authored by his former PhD supervisor Darla Zelenitsky, an associate professor at the University of Calgary. (Riley Brandt)

Tsu-Ruei Yang, associate curator of vertebrate paleontology at Taiwan's National Museum of Natural Science, published a study earlier this year suggesting feathered dinosaurs called oviraptors used both sunlight and body heat to incubate their eggs.

In an email, he said he wasn't surprised that titanosaurs were nesting so far from the equator, as they were a very successful group of dinosaurs that spread around the world.

He noted that titanosaur eggs in places like Spain have been found with thinner, less porous eggshells, indicating more open nests.

"I would be curious if their nesting strategies were as diverse back [earlier] in the Cretaceous." He wondered if that kind of adaptation might be behind their ability to spread across the globe during the Late Cretaceous, and suggested a more comprehensive study of titanosaur nesting might provide the answer.

World.title: Ukraine has been trying to bring the war to Russia. More Russians are beginning to feel it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Kyiv reeled Tuesday from another night of deadly strikes by ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, Russia's state-controlled media didn't report on the damaged highrise buildings or the cars that were set ablaze.

Instead, Russian broadcasters reported that several military facilities in Ukraine had been successfully targeted, while at home, the country's air defences had intercepted more than 380 Ukrainian drones.

But Russia's own vulnerability has become harder to conceal.

Local officials reported that two civilians were killed in Russia during the overnight strikes. And there are reports in the country's media that Moscow plans to allow postal workers to arm themselves with anti-drone weapons.

The measures are another sign of how Ukraine's expanding drone campaign is bringing the war deeper into Russian territory — and increasingly into the lives of ordinary Russians.

WATCH | Huge Ukrainian drone strike hits targets deep inside Russia: Massive Ukrainian drone strike batters targets deep inside Russia | Duration 1:52 Ukraine hammered targets in Russia on Saturday, including Moscow, with hundreds of drones in one of its biggest attacks of the war so far, demonstrating its increasing ability to match Russia in long-range strikes.

A summer of strikes

For nearly five years, the Kremlin has tried to shield much of the population from the realities of its full-scale war against Ukraine, as well as its economic consequences.

But Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries, energy facilities and e-commerce warehouses this summer have been a blunt reminder that Russia is not impenetrable.

"After the active drone raids on Russia — on Moscow and the Moscow region in particular — anxiety has increased greatly," said Tatiana, 66, who wanted to be identified only by her first name. "We were driving to the dacha with the children and saw a huge column of smoke. Naturally, that also causes fear."

Tatiana, like others CBC News spoke with for this story, communicated through voice memos sent on a messaging app. No one wanted to give their last names for fear of being punished for speaking to foreign media about the war.

She said she sometimes lies to her grandchildren when they wake up at night because of the noise, telling them it is construction work because she does not want them to be afraid.

At her dacha, a country home, she said people talk about the fear caused by the buzzing of drones overhead.

Cars line up to refuel at a Lukoil gas station in Moscow on Aug. 17, amid fuel shortages following Ukrainian air attacks on oil refineries in Russia and gasoline production cuts. (Anastasia Barashkova/Reuters)

Ukrainian attacks on refineries and energy facilities have contributed to a fuel shortage in Russia, leading to long lines at gas stations, fuel rationing and public frustration. Videos posted on social media showed fights and arguments breaking out at some stations.

The government has taken steps to stabilize supplies, including importing fuel from countries such as India. It's a significant move given that Russia is one of the world's largest oil exporters.

The shortage has also helped fuel the popularity of GdeBENZ (Where is the Benzine), an app that directs motorists to gas stations with available fuel.

Measuring the mood

Denis Volkov, director of the Moscow-based research and polling organization Levada Center, said as the fuel crisis intensified earlier in the summer, surveys showed rising anxiety and a decline in approval of the Russian government.

But he said the mood has softened somewhat as fuel supplies have improved.

Levada’s August survey , published on Thursday, was conducted through video calls with 1,600 people across Russia. About one-quarter said they were experiencing tension and fear, while nearly 60 per cent described themselves as being in a normal mood.

About two-thirds said they had experienced problems with mobile internet access, messaging apps or fuel. One-third said the fuel shortage had seriously affected their lives.

A woman looks out of her apartment in St. Petersburg, Russia, on Aug. 25. A recent poll found that about one-quarter of Russians said they were experiencing tension and fear. (Dmitri Lovetsky/The Associated Press)

"The main concerns are, of course, economic, but also the overall continuation of hostilities," Volkov said in a phone interview with CBC News from Moscow.

Ksenia, 41, a single mother who works in the civil service in the Russian capital, said the drones do not frighten her terribly. But she is struggling with rising prices.

"It feels as though no salary or freelance work is enough to cover expenses anymore," she said in a message to CBC News.

"Is there any light at the end of the tunnel? Who knows."

Beleaguered economy

The Russian economy is expected to grow by just 0.4 per cent this year, while many non-military sectors are stagnating or shrinking. If Ukraine continues striking Russian targets, including its oil and grain export infrastructure, the country's economic growth could be pushed down further.

Last month, Andrei Klepach, chief economist at Russia’s state development bank, lost his job after giving a public speech about the economic problems created by the war.

Last week, the Kremlin envoy for international development, Boris Titov, was quoted as saying the Russian economy could go "berserk" if the country continues on a steadfast war footing.

In August, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree allowing the government to take control of infrastructure deemed critical if it is considered inadequately protected from drone attacks.

"The country is spiralling into a terrifying abyss. Especially when you look at the economic results of the last five years, it makes you want to cry," said Vitaliy, 40, a businessman from Noginsk, about 40 kilometres east of Moscow.

Vitaliy runs a business supplying spare parts to chemical plants. He said Western sanctions have made it difficult to obtain foreign-made parts, forcing the supply chain to shift toward what he described as the buying of "domestic crap."

"The business is going under. I am not down to my last piece of bread, but I am deeply worried about the future of myself, my family and my loved ones."

Vitaliy said he was also saddened by the attacks on e-commerce warehouses because of the losses they represent for other business owners.

People watch burning warehouses belonging to Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries, following a Ukrainian drone attack, in Koledino, a small village in the Moscow region, on Aug. 16. (Stringer/Reuters)

The one thing that gives him some solace, he said, is that his ID card says he is fit for military service "with restrictions." He hopes that will be enough to keep him from being swept up if the government launches another mobilization.

In recent weeks, rumours have circulated that Russia is preparing for another mobilization. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also speculated that it could happen after Russia's parliamentary elections scheduled for Sept. 18 to 20.

World.title: Interior design: The new crown jewel of the room
World.content:
Article content

When Lori Lievonen and her husband moved into their new condo in Stouffville, Ont., they wanted to make it their own. Yes, they could personalize the furniture, the cabinetry, the wall colour, the decor, but what about… the ceiling? The condo had a large open-concept kitchen, dining and living space that was mostly black and white. Lievonen began browsing the work of muralists online, when she was struck by a photo of a bathroom with elaborate painted flowers flowing from the ceiling down the walls.

World.title: The DEI tradeoff is worse than you think: Eric Kaufmann
World.content:
Article content

A new study is adding some important context to the debate around Diversity, Equity and Inclusion policies: specifically, the cost of these policies. The National Post’s Rob Breakenridge is joined by University of Buckingham professor and Macdonald-Laurier Institute senior fellow Eric Kaufmann to discuss his new study, “The Equity-Excellence Trade-Off: A Study of EDI in the Canada Research Chairs Program.” Kaufmann argues that the aggressive push within academia for DEI targets has come with significant and measurable costs to research. According to the study, groups that benefit from DEI policies tend to have the lowest research impact. Kaufmann says his research also points to a growing emphasis on “scholarly activism,” particularly in the social sciences and humanities. We’ll find out more about what the study found, and what sort of reform is necessary to address these problems. Watch the full video below.

World.title: De la Espriella lifts Colombia’s 10-year gun ban
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella lifted a gun ban that had been in place since 2015.

According to De la Espriella, the decision seeks to give “good citizens” a way to defend themselves against “criminals.”

“For years, law-abiding citizens were restricted, while criminals continued to arm themselves to the teeth illegally. That has to change,” said the president on social media platform X.

99.9% of crimes committed with weapons are committed with unlicensed, illegal weapons. Anything said beyond the mathematics is just opinion. Mathematics is an exact science. So I am pleased to sign this decree. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president said that those who want to carry guns legally must comply with strict regulations and can’t have criminal records.

The ban reactivates previously approved gun licenses and allows citizens older than 25 to purchase approved hand guns from Colombia’s State military industry.

In order to be given a license, a potential gun owner must undergo fitness tests and convince the military authority that his position in society merits a firearm.

The decision has long been awaited by conservative and far-right elements in society, who have claimed that the gun ban made them sitting ducks for extortionists, particularly in the countryside.

Experts consulted by newspaper El Colombiano warned that lifting the gun ban could increase deadly violence, particularly considering Colombia’s violent history and evidence obtained in countries where guns are legal.

“There is no evidence showing that these countries have seen a decrease in theft, extortion, and threats following these measures,” said the director of the Central University’s Security Observatory, Andres Nieto. “On the contrary, the evidence does show an increase in violence among citizens,” the scholar added.

The ban was initially imposed by former President Juan Manuel Santos in 2015 and has since been upheld by his successors.

World.title: Liberal Party joins Colombia’s far-right to form majority coalition
World.content:
The Liberal Party announced that it had joined the congressional coalition of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The party, which also supported De la Espriella’s presidential bid, said that it would join the coalition after “extensive deliberation and arduous debate among representatives, senators, and leadership” of Colombia’s oldest political party.

It is worth noting that the discussions between representatives and senators over the past several weeks have revealed disagreements among some members of our caucuses with the current administration, but they also acknowledge President Espriella’s ability to work toward stimulating economic growth, building a talent pool to provide real opportunities for Colombians, and restoring security and respect for institutions. Liberal Party

The liberals’ decision gives the government broad support in Congress and marginalizes the opposition led by the leftist Historic Pact Party.

In the senate, De la Espriella’s right-wing coalition can count on the support of 63 of 103 lawmakers. In the House of Representatives, the coalition consists of 123 of 183 lawmakers.

The Historic Pact, which won the elections and became the biggest party in Congress, was abandoned by the left-liberal Green Alliance party and can count of the support of 28 senators and 44 representatives.

The opposition party has been able to make temporary anti-government alliances with, for example, the far-right Democratic Center party of former President Alvaro Uribe.

World.title: Colombia’s president appoints controversial new spy chief
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella appointed retired army General Jorge Andres Zuluaga as director of the National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) despite pending criminal investigations.

Zuluaga, who spent 30 years with military intelligence, is best known for his participation in Operation Jaque, which liberated former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three American military contractors and 11 soldiers.

Throughout his career, the 61-year-old former general was deputy commander of the now-defunct Charry Solano intelligence school, commander of the Regional Intelligence #5 and the director of the National Army’s Technical Intelligence Center (CITEC).

Zuluaga received training in the United States and was a diplomatic aide at the Organization of American States.

He was removed as CITEC director in 2014 after prosecution investigators found out that he received intelligence illegally obtained from “Andromeda,” a clandestine intelligence unit that operated from a Bogota internet café.

In October 2024, war crimes tribunal JEP ordered the Prosecutor General’s Office to investigate Zuluaga for his alleged participation in the extermination of the leftist Patriotic Union party when he was the CITEC’s director between 2004 and 2005.

The prosecution has yet to decide whether or not to formally charge the retired general with the crimes he allegedly committed.

Zuluaga, who became a member of the far-right Democratic Center party after he was ejected from the army, has always sustained that he acted within the boundaries of the law.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with human rights office over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.
