World.title: Judge orders Colombia’s military to suspend air strikes on illegal armed groups
World.content:
A court ordered the government and the military to suspend air strikes on suspected members of illegal armed groups while studying the risk of harm to child forced recruitment victims.

In a preliminary sentence, the Bogota family court in response to a lawsuit that was filed by a civilian who claimed the State ignored its obligation to protect children when carrying out air strikes on illegal armed groups.

TO ORDER the PRESIDENCY OF THE REPUBLIC, the MINISTRY OF NATIONAL DEFENSE, the GENERAL COMMAND OF THE MILITARY FORCES, the NATIONAL ARMY, the COLOMBIAN AEROSPACE FORCE, and the NATIONAL NAVY, through the appropriate channels and within the scope of their respective authorities, that, pending a decision on the merits in this constitutional protection action, they refrain from conducting offensive air operations against targets regarding which there is certain, objective, or reasonably verifiable information regarding the presence of children or adolescents recruited or used by armed groups, until the necessary precautionary and protective measures have been adopted and verified, and it has been determined, based on the available information and applicable operational protocols, that there is no less harmful operational alternative that would allow the legitimate military objective being pursued to be achieved Bogota family court

According to Radio Caracol, at least 107 minors were killed in air strikes on illegal armed groups since they were resumed by former President Ivan Duque in 2018.

The sentence comes a day after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the military killed 23 “narcoterrorists” in the deadliest air strike during the peace process that started in 2016.

The president vowed to resume bombing campaigns that were all but suspended by former President Gustavo Petro as he sought peace and demobilization talks with multiple illegal armed groups, a strategy rejected by the new far-right government.

Following the killing of at least three children in an air strike carried out in August, Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora blamed guerrilla organizations for the deaths, claiming they were recruiting children for human shields and combatants.

World.title: Colombia’s education minister resigns after less than a month
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella replaced his education minister after she resigned, claiming “an unexpected family situation.”

De la Espriella announced on social media platform X that he had accepted the resignation of the evangelical Education Minister Viviane Morales, who took office on August 7, the first day of the administration.

I bid a nostalgic farewell to my dear friend Viviane Morales. God’s designs are inscrutable, and she must leave us early to take charge of a personal situation that I sincerely hope she can resolve very soon. President Viviana Morales

In the same post, De la Espriella said he had appointed Ilva Myriam Hoyos, stressing that “I am confident that she will be an outstanding minister and that she will serve Colombia with dedication, character, and conviction.”

While in office, Morales lead the government’s Culture War in education and vowed to remove “gender ideology” from Colombia’s classrooms, and proposed a law that would allow churches to provide public education services.

Hoyos, a catholic, warned in 2016 that a peace deal between the government of President Juan Manuel Santos and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC promoted gender ideology.

The new education minister used to work with Alejandro Ordoñez, Colombia’s notoriously far-right former Inspector General and the country’s current ambassador to the Organization of American States.

World.title: De la Espriella claims Colombia’s military killed 23, arrested 6 EMC guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella claimed Wednesday that Colombia’s armed forces killed at least 23 members of FARC dissident group EMC and captured another six.

In a video, De la Espriella said that “Operation Azarias,” targeted the EMC’s Carolina Ramirez Front and killed one of its commanders, a man called “Tigre” or “Pintado,” in the south of the Guaviare province.

A second guerrilla commander, “Victor,” was among the six alleged EMC members who were arrested during the operation, which included air strikes.

The president claimed that Victor carried out attacks against the military “during the elections, as part of the ‘gunpoint vote’ strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict.”

That narcoterrorist, whom we have now taken out of circulation, carried out attacks against members of the National Army and the Navy. During the elections, as part of the “gunpoint vote” strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict, this criminal ambushed a unit that was on the move precisely to protect citizens’ right to vote freely. President Abelardo de la Espriella

There is no evidence to suggest that De la Espriella’s predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro, employed illegal armed groups to coerce voters into voting against his would-be successor.

One minor allegedly survived the attack and was surrendered to family welfare agency ICBF. The Medical Examiner’s Office is expected to investigate how many minors were among the alleged “narcoterrorists.”

At least three minors were killed in a previous operation in Guaviare that killed at least nine alleged members of the EMC’s main rival, FARC dissident group EMBF, the Medical Examiner’s Office said earlier this week.

Air strikes against illegal armed groups are controversial as they could imply the blanket killing of victims of child recruitment, a war crime according to international humanitarian law.

The government has long insisted that those recruiting children and minors are responsible for the deaths of their victims.

World.title: Argentina probes 60 people and companies over Falklands oil without disclosing new names
World.content:
Argentina probes 60 people and companies over Falklands oil without disclosing new names

9th Wednesday, September 2026 - 10:14 UTC Full article

None of the 60 has been sanctioned: the proceedings are at an initial stage, and liability will be determined as each file concludes

Argentina's government has raised to 60 the number of individuals and companies subject to administrative proceedings over oil activity in waters near the Falklands, after opening case files against 15 more parties whose identities it did not disclose.

The measure was announced Tuesday by the Office of the President, in a statement signed by Javier Milei, and rests on Article 2 of Law 26,659, which bars carrying out, financing or providing services to hydrocarbon activity on the Argentine continental shelf without national authorization. The new files add to 45 opened days earlier. The statement did not identify those targeted or detail the conduct attributed to each. None of the 60 has been sanctioned: the proceedings are at an initial stage, and liability will be determined as each file concludes.

That approach contrasts with the first round. On September 4, when it announced the initial 45 proceedings, the government released the full list, which included Navitas Petroleum Development, Navitas Petroleum Atlantic, Rockhopper Exploration, Borders & Southern Falkland Islands, JHI Associates and supplier Noble Corporation, along with shareholders and investment funds such as AP Moller Holding, First Eagle Investment Management, Vanguard, Dimensional Fund Advisors and consultancy Netherland, Sewell & Associates. The list covered firms and individuals from at least eight countries.

The procedure was set out in Decree 868/2026, published on September 4, which designated the Foreign Ministry as the enforcement authority for the law. Where there are sufficient grounds, the ministry opens a case file and notifies the alleged infringer, who has ten business days to file a defense and submit evidence. A reasoned ruling can then close the proceedings or apply the penalties provided by law, ranging from fines equivalent to between 15,000 and 1.5 million barrels of oil to bans of five to 20 years, seizure of equipment and reversal of concessions held in Argentine territory. The framework also provides for excluding affected firms from the Large Investment Incentive Regime.

“The Argentine Republic does not and will not accept attacks on its sovereignty,” the statement said, reaffirming that the islands, South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands and the corresponding maritime areas “belong to all Argentines” and that “no one may dispose of their resources without our country's authorization.” The government added that it would exhaust every administrative, diplomatic and legal avenue available to it.

The universe under scrutiny is considerably larger. Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said on September 4, speaking to business leaders in Puerto Iguazú, that the government had notified some 180 companies from 29 countries. Quirno also indicated that the legal reform the executive plans to send to Congress would, alongside tougher penalties, include an exit route for companies that abandon operations in the archipelago and seek to work in Argentina again.

The administrative proceedings run parallel to a separate judicial track: the criminal complaint filed this week in federal court against five companies linked to the Sea Lion project. None of the allegations, on either track, has been proven. Navitas did not respond to the accusations and a Rockhopper spokesperson declined to comment; both companies have maintained that they operate under valid licenses issued by the self-governing Falkland Islands government, which Argentina does not recognize.

Sovereignty over the archipelago, a British overseas territory, remains disputed. In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of residents voted to retain that status. Foreign Office Minister Kirsty McNeill told the House of Commons on Tuesday that there could be no doubt about Britain's commitment to the islanders, and that hydrocarbon production is a commercial decision for the local government and the companies involved.

World.title: Colombia's human rights ombudsman challenges De la Espriella over display of bodies
World.content:
Colombia's human rights ombudsman challenges De la Espriella over display of bodies

9th Wednesday, September 2026 - 09:33 UTC Full article

“I do not recall seeing a president walking among the dead and feeling proud of those deaths,” Ombudsman Iris Marín said

Colombia's human rights ombudsman has challenged President Abelardo de la Espriella over the release of footage showing him walking among the bodies of suspected FARC dissident fighters killed in a military operation, in the first public disagreement between the rights body and the government that took office on August 7.

In a statement released Sunday, Ombudsman Iris Marín said the state and the government cannot enter into a competition to show which side is crueler, nor contend with armed groups over which instills more fear. She asked that the dead be “respected and treated with dignity” and said it should not become normal for bodies to form part of the staging of a public address. “I do not recall seeing a president walking among the dead and feeling proud of those deaths,” she added. She specified that confronting illegal armed groups militarily and protecting the population is a constitutional duty.

The footage came from Operation Azarías, carried out in late August in Miraflores, Guaviare department, against the Carolina Ramírez Front, a structure said to operate under the command of the man known as Iván Mordisco. The official tally reported 23 killed, six captured and two minors recovered alive and placed under the protection of the Colombian Family Welfare Institute, along with seized weapons and explosives. According to the forensic institute, two of the dead were minors.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara responded that same evening that the government considers the statement “a sad mistake” for equating the state with criminal organizations, and described the ombudsman's office as an institutional ally whose mandate the executive backs. Marín thanked him for the tone of the message and repeated her call for the government to reflect on how it communicates operational results, while noting that the office's early warnings have already flagged the use of drones, recruitment and the territorial expansion of armed groups. The president reiterated on social media that his responsibility is to fight those he considers terrorists and rejected the criticism.

It was not an isolated episode. The following Friday, De la Espriella presented four covered bodies to reporters, the result of a police operation in Riohacha against the Conquering Self-Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada, in which one of its leaders was killed.

Marín also warned about an unofficial website that keeps a tally of people captured or killed in operations ordered by the current government, and recalled the precedent of the so-called “false positives”: civilians murdered by soldiers and presented as combat deaths in order to obtain benefits from their superiors.

The debate comes amid a parallel judicial controversy. A court ordered the presidency, the defense ministry and the armed forces to refrain from air strikes where there is evidence that children recruited by those structures are present. The measure does not ban all bombings. The ombudsman's office recorded 1,173 cases of minors affected by forced recruitment between 2024 and July 31, 2026.

The president, elected in part on a promise of a hard line on security, has defended his security policy and released a performance tally that includes 14,914 arrests and 49,379 kilos of narcotics seized since he took office.

World.title: Argentine industry contracted 5% in July from June, its steepest monthly drop this year
World.content:
Argentine industry contracted 5% in July from June, its steepest monthly drop this year

9th Wednesday, September 2026 - 08:59 UTC Full article

Year-on-year, the manufacturing industrial production index fell 4.9% from July 2025, while the trend-cycle series was down 0.9% on the month

Argentina's manufacturing output fell 5% in July from June in seasonally adjusted terms, the sharpest monthly decline so far in 2026, the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INDEC) reported on Tuesday.

Year-on-year, the manufacturing industrial production index fell 4.9% from July 2025, while the trend-cycle series was down 0.9% on the month. The cumulative figure for the first seven months of the year shows a 2.6% contraction. The reading interrupts June's rebound, when activity had risen 2.1% year-on-year.

Twelve of the sixteen manufacturing divisions posted annual declines. The largest were in other equipment, appliances and instruments (-31.4%), machinery and equipment (-26.7%), clothing, leather and footwear (-15.9%), textile products (-13%) and non-metallic mineral products (-12.6%). In seasonally adjusted monthly terms, every category fell.

Within machinery and equipment, farm machinery production plunged 46.6% year-on-year, with lower output of tractors, harvesters, self-propelled sprayers and certain implement lines. In electronic equipment, production of computing, television and communications goods fell 49.8%, mainly on reduced manufacturing of mobile phones and televisions.

Economist María Castiglioni, director of C&T Asesores Económicos, said the scale of the monthly decline exceeded expectations and could lead to downward revisions of 2026 growth forecasts. She also noted that July tends to show greater volatility because of the winter holiday period.

The textile sector faces weaker domestic demand alongside stronger competition from imported goods, the statistics agency said. The Argentine Textile Industries Federation said 26,851 formal jobs had been lost in the sector since November 2023 and 750 establishments had closed, and described a shift in the sector's foreign trade: purchases of raw materials, yarn and fabric are falling while imports of finished garments are rising.

A survey by the Argentine Industrial Union found that 47.6% of companies in the sector had difficulty in July meeting at least one payment in full, among wages, suppliers, financial commitments, utilities and taxes. The body said 9.2% were behind on all those items simultaneously, the highest level on record and above the historical average of 4%.

Consultancy Industria y Desarrollo, led by former Industrial Union executive Diego Coatz, attributed the situation to a combination of weak demand, rising costs and adverse financing conditions, and estimated that the sector is seeing “nine closures a day.” The firm said arrears of more than 90 days among industrial companies rose from 0.7% to 3.8% over the past year and a half.

The head of the Association of Automotive Manufacturers, Rodrigo Pérez Graziano, described a period of readjustment in the sector, with production aligned to inventory levels and domestic demand, and called for competitiveness measures including a lower tax burden and new trade agreements.

Construction also declined in July, down 4.5% year-on-year and 4.6% on the month, though it retains a cumulative gain of 1.7% for the year.

World.title: Brent climbs back above US$100 to its highest level since late July
World.content:
Brent climbs back above US$100 to its highest level since late July

9th Wednesday, September 2026 - 08:51 UTC Full article

The market is also operating on thin margins

Brent crude for November delivery rose above US$100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since late July, in a session shaped by escalating attacks between the United States and Iran and by fears of further supply disruptions in the Middle East.

At 07:29 GMT, the European benchmark was trading at US$100.19 a barrel on the London futures market, up 2.20%. It was the fourth consecutive session of gains.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it had attacked two US warships overnight, along with Washington's bases in Jordan and around ten vessels attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz, in retaliation for earlier strikes on Iranian tankers. US Central Command, for its part, said it had destroyed five vessels it links to the Revolutionary Guard Corps, in response to attacks on one of its warships. Neither account has been independently verified; other coverage described those five vessels as oil tankers.

The rally is not driven solely by the Washington-Tehran exchange. Earlier this week, Houthi militias struck energy facilities in Saudi Arabia, including the Jazan area, wounding more than 70 people and halting operations at some sites, according to the Saudi energy ministry. Pulling the other way, Iran has said it is close to an agreement with Oman to manage vessel transit through Hormuz, a de-escalation track that eased prices last week.

Current levels remain below the highs reached earlier this year during the sharpest phase of the conflict. In March, Brent passed US$102, and weeks later futures topped US$109, with dated Brent above US$140, its highest since 2008.

The market is also operating on thin margins. The US strategic petroleum reserve fell below 290 million barrels, its lowest since 1982, after major economies drew on stockpiles and following a release coordinated by the International Energy Agency. Goldman Sachs this week raised its December 2026 forecasts by five dollars, to US$85 for Brent and US$80 for WTI, and warned that the barrel could exceed US$120 in 2027 if Gulf output remains four million barrels per day below prewar levels, a scenario the bank does not treat as its base case.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that crude prices would fall sharply.

Before the conflict, around 20% of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Argentina files criminal complaint against Navitas over Falklands; firm silent, shares slide
World.content:
Argentina files criminal complaint against Navitas over Falklands; firm silent, shares slide

9th Wednesday, September 2026 - 08:06 UTC Full article

Navitas did not respond to the complaint. Following President Milei's initial announcement, the company said it did not expect those remarks to have a material effect on the project's development

Argentina's government formally filed a criminal complaint on Tuesday against Israeli oil company Navitas Petroleum and four other firms over hydrocarbon exploration in waters near the Falklands, with the company yet to respond to the accusation and amid a slide in the share prices of those involved.

The filing, submitted to federal court by Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno with the backing of Treasury Attorney General Sebastián Amerio, targets Navitas Petroleum Development & Production Ltd., Navitas Petroleum Atlantic United, Navitas Petroleum LP, JHI Associates Inc. and Eco (Atlantic) Oil & Gas Ltd., along with their directors, managers, administrators and representatives. According to the statement from the Office of the President, three of those companies “allegedly” hold licenses granted by what it calls the “illegitimate government of the United Kingdom” to operate in the basin north of the archipelago. The government said the complaint amounts to an action to protect natural resources and Argentine sovereignty. The allegations remain unproven.

The complaint invokes Law 26,659, passed in 2011 under President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, which bars participating in, financing or providing services to unauthorized hydrocarbon activity on the Argentine continental shelf and allows bans of up to 20 years. The same statute was applied against Navitas in 2022 by Alberto Fernández's government, which barred the company for two decades alongside sanctions on other operators. Argentina had already declared activity in the area clandestine in 2012 and filed a similar complaint in 2015; neither measure halted the project.

Navitas did not respond to the complaint. Last week, following President Javier Milei's initial announcement, the company said it did not expect those remarks to have a material effect on the project's development or its timetable. A spokesperson for Rockhopper, the British partner holding 35%, declined to comment and referred questions to Navitas. Both companies have maintained that they operate under valid licenses issued by the self-governing Falkland Islands government, which Argentina does not recognize. Rockhopper is not among the companies named in the complaint.

Tel Aviv-listed Navitas operates and controls 65% of Sea Lion, a field roughly 220 kilometers north of the islands with estimated reserves of 1.7 billion barrels. The first phase, approved by both partners last year, is scheduled to begin extraction in 2028 at a rate of 50,000 barrels per day.

The most immediate impact was felt in financial markets and along the supply chain. Shares in Navitas and Rockhopper had fallen more than 14% since the presidential address, according to quotes circulated by Argentine media, while the oil services chamber CASEPE announced that its member companies would not take part in Sea Lion.

In his address last Thursday, Milei described oil extraction in the archipelago as a danger to Argentine sovereignty and dismissed the 2013 referendum, in which 99.8% of residents voted to retain their status as a British overseas territory. He argued that the islanders inhabit “usurped” territory and therefore lack any legitimate right to self-determination. That same day he announced the revival of plans for a naval base in Ushuaia, and on Monday he instructed Economy Minister Luis Caputo to prioritize it in the 2027 budget.

The United Kingdom responded on Tuesday in the House of Commons. Foreign Office Minister Kirsty McNeill said there could be no doubt about Britain's commitment to the islanders and described hydrocarbon production as “a commercial decision” for the Falkland Islands government and the companies involved, adding that the archipelago's future is for its own residents to determine.

Sovereignty over the islands remains disputed between London and Buenos Aires more than forty years after the 1982 war.

World.title: Latin America falls back in PISA 2025 as Argentina posts its worst score since 2006
World.content:
Latin America falls back in PISA 2025 as Argentina posts its worst score since 2006

9th Wednesday, September 2026 - 06:32 UTC Full article

OECD averages stood at 461 points in reading, 463 in mathematics and 482 in science, the lowest figures recorded since the test was first applied

All 13 Latin American countries assessed in the PISA 2025 report, released Tuesday, scored below the OECD averages in the three subjects measured, in an edition marked by broad declines and by Argentina's worst performance since it began taking part in the test.

The assessment, which the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development administers every three years to enrolled 15-year-olds, was the largest in the series: more than 760,000 students from 91 countries and economies took part. OECD averages stood at 461 points in reading, 463 in mathematics and 482 in science, the lowest figures recorded since the test was first applied. This round also added computational problem-solving as a fourth domain.

Argentina scored 367 points in mathematics, 389 in reading and 393 in science, down 11, 12 and 13 points respectively from 2022 and its weakest results since the series began in 2006. Only 24% of Argentine students reached level 2 in mathematics — the threshold the OECD considers basic — against 65% across the organization. The report also records a widening gap between the country's highest and lowest performing students in mathematics and science between 2022 and 2025. Regionally, Argentina placed behind Uruguay, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Brazil and Peru.

Uruguay posted the strongest performance in the region. According to the national report released by the National Public Education Administration (ANEP), the country reached 444.5 points in science — some nine more than in 2022 and its best result on record — 423.2 in reading, seven below the previous round, and 404.9 in mathematics, a statistically stable figure. Uruguay led the region in science and mathematics and ranked second in reading behind Chile. Even so, it remains below the OECD in all three areas: 58% of its students fail to reach the minimum level in mathematics and 43% fall short in reading.

Chile fell twelve points in reading, to 436, and nine in mathematics, to 403, while science held steady at 442. Since 2015, the share of students performing below the basic threshold has risen ten percentage points in both mathematics and reading. Brazil was essentially unchanged from 2022, with 408 points in reading, 377 in mathematics and 409 in science. Mexico dropped to 388 in mathematics, its lowest mark since 2006, and to 408 in reading, with a slight improvement in science to 414.

The OECD added a caveat for reading the declines in Colombia and Costa Rica, where secondary enrollment expanded over the past decade. The organization said the apparent setback in mathematics and reading is linked to the integration of students from previously marginalized populations into the system. PISA assesses only young people who are in school, so countries with higher dropout rates are measured on a smaller share of the age cohort.

Outside the region, the United States recorded 490 points in reading, fourteen fewer than in 2022 and its lowest level since the assessment began in 2000. Mathematics also hit a record low, while science remained stable. The test's organizers cautioned that the US student response rate and the volume of exclusions fell below required technical standards, meaning bias in the results cannot be ruled out.

World.title: Six in ten Argentines attribute Milei's shift on the Falklands to political convenience
World.content:
Six in ten Argentines attribute Milei's shift on the Falklands to political convenience

8th Tuesday, September 2026 - 10:02 UTC Full article

The sovereignty claim enjoys majority backing in Argentine society, but Milei's call for unity inspired confidence in 41% of those consulted and distrust in 56%

Some 61.1% of Argentines believe President Javier Milei adopted his current position on the Falklands out of political convenience, against 24.7% who attribute it to conviction, according to a survey by the consultancy Management & Fit of a thousand respondents with a margin of error of 3%.

The poll was released after the address the president gave to the nation on Thursday, in which he said the islands “are Argentine by history and by right, there is no discussion about it” and announced he would speed up sanctions against oil companies operating in the area without Argentine authorisation. Nine in ten respondents were aware of that address.

The figures distinguish between support for the position and the credibility of the shift. The sovereignty claim enjoys majority backing in Argentine society, but Milei's call for unity inspired confidence in 41% of those consulted and distrust in 56%. On the content of the speech, 44.6% considered he had announced concrete measures and 44.2% that he had confined himself to general statements, a tie within the margin of error.

The position marks a change from his earlier statements. Milei has repeatedly declared his admiration for Margaret Thatcher, British prime minister during the 1982 conflict, and had acknowledged the islanders' right to self-determination, arguing that Argentina should persuade them to prefer being Argentine. That possibility was ruled out in Thursday's message.

After the speech, the Office of the President circulated the results of an open poll run by the newspaper Clarín on its social media accounts, according to which 81.3% of those who responded supported the announced measures. Such polls are not representative samples and are not comparable with probability-based surveys.

The government is drafting a national sovereignty defence bill to send to Congress, along with the terms of the National Security Council the president announced. Officials calculate the opposition will find it difficult to reject legislation strengthening the defence of national interests.

The issue emerged at an adverse moment for the government's economic agenda, little more than a year before the 2027 presidential elections. Unemployment tops Argentines' concerns at 36%, ahead of corruption and inflation; arrears on credit to individuals reached 17.5% in June, and 60% of respondents in another survey expect their personal situation to worsen in coming months. Peronist lawmakers are preparing a session in the Chamber of Deputies on Wednesday on maintaining treatment for people with disabilities and relief measures for indebted households.

The United Kingdom has administered the archipelago since 1833 and Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed retaining British overseas territory status, with three votes against. Milei's speech followed remarks by Donald Trump, who said he reviews “every position” when asked about sovereignty over the islands, without committing to any decision.

World.title: Falklands: Lords confirm UK’s unwavering support for Islanders right to self-determination
World.content:
Falklands: Lords confirm UK’s unwavering support for Islanders right to self-determination

8th Tuesday, September 2026 - 10:00 UTC Full article

Baroness Winterton, “we have made clear to Argentina that the measures announced by president Milei will not change the UK’s unwavering commitment to the Islands”.

The issue of President Javier Milei’s speech last week with its threats to the Falkland Islands, Islanders right to self-determination and the Islands’ right to develop its resource, was addressed by the House of Lords on Monday.

Lord Callanan made a question on the matter to Baroness Winterton, who repeatedly replied on UK’s unwavering support for the Islanders and the Islands.

Lord Callanan, C, said, “my Lords I beg leave to ask a question of which I have given prior notice, the question is as follows, ‘To ask her Majesty’s government what recent discussions they have had, if any, with one, the government of Argentina and two, the government of the United States pertaining to the future of the Falkland Islands and what steps they are taking to ensure the security of those Islands.

Baroness Winterton of Doncaster, and Under Secretary of State for the Indo-Pacific, FCDO replied, My Lords, the UK remains steadfast in its support for the Islanders right to self-determination. This is not the first time Argentina has made economic threats against the Falklands.

These threats have not prevented the community’s remarkable economic development and we have made clear to Argentina that the measures announced by president Milei will not change the UK’s unwavering commitment to the Islands.

The United States is our closest ally, they can have no doubt about our unwavering support for the Islanders.

World.title: New 11-tower hotel and apartment complex proposed for Bahía de Banderas
World.content:
A major new 11-tower housing and hotel development in Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, has been proposed at a projected cost of 515 million pesos (US $30.5 million).

The proposal from BM/5096 Business Trust was published in the Environment Ministry’s Ecological Gazette on Aug. 20 for review, and the start of construction is contingent upon the development obtaining the necessary Environmental Impact Assessment (MIA).

The project, known as Ocean II, will cover 65,453 square meters of land, including private land, land reclaimed from the sea and a portion of the Federal Maritime-Terrestrial Zone. It is expected to consist of a hotel zone and a residential zone, accessible from Paseo de los Cocoteros Avenue.

A 187-room hotel will occupy the Palapar Lot within the Los Flamingos Master Condominium across five towers, ranging from five to 10 stories high, while six residential towers will contain 275 apartments. There are plans for basement parking for 784 vehicles.

Planned amenities include restaurants, a spa, a gym, a beach club, an event hall, retail spaces, swimming pools and over 25,000 square meters of green space.

The developers noted in their submission to the Environment Ministry that they expect the project to take around seven years to complete, with the first phase of construction slated to begin in March 2027 and completion expected in 2033.

The announcement is for a general area where beachside development has been controversial, as it is a nesting habitat for the olive ridley sea turtle.

In July, the Environment Ministry revoked a federal concession for a luxury development in Punta de Mita after finding unauthorized construction and environmental violations by developer Cantiles de Mita.

President Sheinbaum visited Nayarit over the weekend to deliver her second annual report, announcing the creation of a Master Plan to conserve beaches, guarantee free access and protect the entire state coastline’s biodiversity.

“I want to tell you that we’ve been working with the [state] governor for over a year on a master plan for tourism in Nayarit, because we don’t want the mangroves destroyed or all the beaches privatized,” said Sheinbaum in a speech.

With reports from El Sol de México and Tribuna de la Bahía

World.title: Mexico fails the 2025 PISA evaluation: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Just this morning, the 2025 PISA 2025 results were released and as feared, they are very concerning both on a global scale and for Mexico specifically.

As a reminder, PISA assessments test 760,000 15-year-old students in 91 countries in science, mathematics and reading. The results show a continued decline globally in all three areas with reading being the largest long-term weakness. Singapore students scored highest, followed closely by China, Japan and South Korea.

Mexico, which historically has done poorly, did even worse than in previous years. Some of the lowlights of Mexico’s performance:

Mexico performed below the OECD average in every 2025 PISA domain and placed 64th out of 91 participating countries/economies globally.

The last time the testing was done, in 2022, Mexico placed 51st out of 81 participating countries/economies.

Mexico declined in country rankings in math and reading, as well as compared to its previous performance.

Mexico ranks significantly below the OECD mean in math, science and reading.

This was Mexico’s fifth consecutive decline in reading since 2009. (The test is taken every 3 years.)

Half of Mexican 15-year-olds read below the minimum proficiency threshold. This is the threshold that one needs to be able to read in order to learn.

Other than the slight gain in science, the results are a disaster. Not only is Mexico getting worse in math and reading scores, but actually getting relatively much worse than other countries.

I often write about the potential of the Mexican economy, but these testing results are a significant red flag. I have written before about two concerns regarding the Mexican workforce:

1. The education barrier means companies have to make significant investments in workforce development and training to prepare workers. This is both a financial cost and a time loss, and puts Mexican operations at a disadvantage versus other countries.

2. The strengthening peso increases the cost of the Mexican workforce. A relatively lower-skilled, relatively expensive workforce means that many companies will instead invest in automation and robotics versus investing in workers.

World.title: Goods from Mexico now make up almost one-fifth of the US import market
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico captured almost one-fifth of the U.S. import market in July, well ahead of second-placed Canada, shipping a record US $60.55 billion worth of goods to its northern neighbor, according to official U.S. data.

Mexico’s share of the $332.92 billion U.S. import market in July was 18.2%, ahead of Canada (10.1%); China (8.1%); Vietnam (7.9%); and Taiwan (7.7%), according to data published last Thursday by the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

In other words, nearly one in every five dollars the United States spent on imports in July was spent on products from Mexico.

Compared to a year earlier, Mexico’s share of the U.S. import market increased 2.7 percentage points in July.

The difference between Mexico and Canada’s shares of the U.S. import market in July 2025 was 4.5 percentage points. In July of this year, the difference was 8.1 points. Similarly, the difference between Mexico and China’s shares of the U.S. import market increased significantly, rising to 10.1 points in July from 6.5 points in the same month of last year.

The increase in Mexico’s share of the U.S. import market coincides with a boom in Mexican exports. The boom is largely driven by a sharp increase in the export of computer equipment, including AI servers, and other electronics to the U.S.

While such products are helping to boost Mexico’s overall export revenue and share of the U.S. import market, their Mexican content is generally very low. That means that a significant share of the revenue Mexico receives from the export of tech products has already been spent on imported inputs, especially from Taiwan.

Mexico’s export revenue increased 33% annually in July

In July — for the first time in any month on record — Mexico’s revenue from selling goods to the United States exceeded $60 billion.

The year-over-year increase in revenue was 33.6% in July. The month-over-month increase was 9.6%.

Canada’s revenue from exports to the United States also increased on an annual basis in July, but only by 4%. Canada’s income declined on a month-over-month basis in July, falling 10%. Canada’s revenue from products shipped to the United States in July was $33.49 billion, equivalent to 55.3% of Mexico’s income in the same month.

China’s revenue from goods shipped to the United States in July was $27.07 billion, up 2.6% from the same month of last year.

Mexico’s exports to the United States reached a record level in July at a time when there was significant uncertainty in the bilateral trade relationship. On July 1, the U.S. government announced that it had declined to renew the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), the free trade pact that superseded NAFTA in 2020.

Despite that decision, the USMCA remains in effect, allowing most Mexican goods to enter the United States tariff-free and giving Mexico a significant comparative advantage over most of its competitors.

Mexico’s exports to the US increased 16% between January and July

The U.S. data also shows that the United States imported goods from Mexico worth $358.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026. That figure represents an increase of 16% compared to the same period of 2025.

Mexico’s share of the $2.08 trillion U.S. import market between January and July was 17.3%, up from 15% in the same period of last year.

Canada’s share of the U.S. import market remained virtually the same on a year-over-year basis, while China’s share fell almost two percentage points.

Canada’s income from goods shipped to the United States between January and July increased 1.8% to $233.66 billion. Its share of the U.S. import market was 11.24% in the first seven months of the year, an increase of just 0.08 percentage points compared to the same period of last year. Canada and the United States are currently engaged in a significant trade dispute.

China’s revenue from goods shipped to the United States between January and July was $156.39 billion, a 19.4% decrease compared to the same period of last year. Its share of the U.S. import market was 7.5%, down from 9.4% in the same period of last year. China and the United States are engaged in a long-running trade war.

Mexico is the top market for US exports

The U.S. data shows that the United States exported goods worth $34.24 billion to Mexico in July, an increase of 18.3% compared to the same month of 2025. In the first seven months of 2026, the United States’ revenue from goods exported to Mexico was $229.81 billion, a 16.8% year-over-year increase.

In July, and in the first seven months of 2026, Mexico was the top market for U.S. exports. In the first seven months of last year, Canada was the top foreign market for U.S. goods, just ahead of Mexico.

In the first seven months of 2026, U.S. exports generated total revenue of $1.43 trillion. Sixteen per cent of that revenue — or around one in every six dollars — was derived from goods sent to Mexico. After Mexico, the largest markets for U.S. exports between January and July were, in order, Canada, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and China.

Mexico’s trade surplus with US nears $130 billion

Mexico recorded a trade surplus of $26.31 billion with the United States in July. At the end of July, Mexico’s calendar trade surplus with the U.S. was $128.89 billion. At the end of July last year, it was $112.57 billion, 12.7% lower.

The only country that recorded a larger trade surplus with the United States than Mexico in the year to the end of July was Vietnam. The southeast Asian nation sent exports worth $149.61 billion to the United States in the first seven months of the year, while its outlay on imports from the U.S. was $10.75 billion. Vietnam thus recorded a trade surplus of $138.86 billion with the U.S. in the first seven months of the year.

Mexico’s large trade surplus with the United States has angered U.S. President Donald Trump, who takes the view that the U.S. is “losing money” if its imports from a certain country exceed its exports to the same country. On Friday, he threatened in a social media post to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT” if the U.S. Federal Reserve doesn’t lower its benchmark interest rate, which is currently set at 3.50%-3.75%.

Later on Friday, Trump asserted that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs, apart from “hot tamales” and “tomatoes,” a claim that collides with the reality that the U.S. and Mexican economies are highly integrated and that Mexico ships huge quantities of goods to its northern neighbor on a daily basis. The data on Mexico’s exports to the U.S. in July and in the first seven months of the year — and that on the United States’ exports to Mexico in the same periods — provide clear evidence of that economic interdependence.

World.title: 500 Chihuahua farmers are benefitting from a 20-year-old Tec student’s prize-winning filtration invention
World.content:
A 20-year-old engineering student from a farming family in Chihuahua has won a national award by developing an irrigation filter that could make water go further for drought-stricken farmers.

Luis Ángel Robles Morales, a mechatronics student at Tecnológico de Monterrey’s Chihuahua campus, leads OAKs Filtration, which last week received the 2026 Eugenio Garza Sada Award in the category of student social innovation.

The award — which includes a prize of 1 million pesos (US $59,121) for Robles — was one of three presented Sept. 2 by Tec de Monterrey and FEMSA, the Monterrey-based company that operates OXXO stores and controls Coca-Cola bottling operations in Mexico.

The two entities jointly established the award in 1993 in honor of the late Garza Sada, an industrialist who was among the university’s founders in 1943 and who helped lead a Monterrey business group that later became FEMSA.

Robles’ irrigation filter makes water use more efficient by preventing clogs that lead to wasted water, disrupted harvests and increased maintenance costs.

A persistent problem in drip and sprinkler systems is sand, mud and other particles clogging emitters.

So far, the system has benefited more than 500 farmers in the south-central region of Chihuahua, according to Tec de Monterrey.

Robles comes from a farming family: His grandfather grew corn, chiles and alfalfa, and his father branched off into making filters for irrigation systems.

In Chihuahua, the need for improved irrigation is acute.

From January through August this year, the state received 247.6 millimeters of rain — roughly 9.8 inches and 11.7% less than the same period last year, the newspaper El Diario de Chihuahua reported. By Aug. 15, drought was affecting 28.3% of the state, up from 11.2% in early May.

OAKs Filtration uses a carbon-steel outer casing and a PVC internal filtering element. Robles said the design provides two to three times the filtration area of commercial systems and channels debris toward the filter’s end, allowing it to clean itself through water flow.

In a test described by the digital news platform Expansion ESG, a competing filter clogged after 30 to 60 minutes, while the OAKs filter ran eight uninterrupted hours without pressure loss and was only about one-third full when inspected.

Robles said the price of the OAKs filter system runs from 30,000 to 100,000 pesos (US $1,773 to $5,910), while traditional commercial filters can cost 300,000 to 500,000 pesos (US $17,736 to $29,560).

OAKs was one of three 2026 Garza Sada Award honorees, with a total prize pool of 4.5 million pesos (US $266,000).

The others were pharmaceutical executive and conservationist Eric Hágsater Gartenberg, recognized for humanistic business leadership, and Formando Emprendedores, a nonprofit that provides education and youth-development programs in northern Mexico.

Since its founding in 1993, the award has recognized 81 winners.

Robles said he will devote half of his prize money to the project and half to an international entrepreneurial experience.

With reports from Expansión ESG, EJE Central, El Economista and El Diario de Chihuahua

World.title: Latest PISA survey reveals 4 in 10 Mexican students do not meet basic level in science, math and reading
World.content:
The latest edition of an OECD-conducted global education evaluation reveals a disturbing decline in the skills of Mexican students: four in 10 15-year-olds are scoring below the basic level in science, mathematics and reading.

The test, called the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), has been administered periodically since the turn of the century; this time to 7,843 students from 297 schools in Mexico. The 41.8% of students who scored below the basic level in the science/math/reading triad was more than double the 19.7% average of all countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Mexican 15-year-olds as a whole scored 388 points in mathematics, 408 in reading and 414 in science, all well below the OECD averages of 463, 461 and 482, respectively.

Mexican students aren’t just falling behind their global peers — their own results are slipping too. Since the 2022 PISA, Mexico has dropped seven points in both math and reading, even as it held steady in science.

Overall, the current test results are Mexico’s worst since 2009.

While it may be a small consolation to parents and the education community, Mexico is far from the only country experiencing a decline. “Globally, we have seen a dramatic drop, particularly in reading skills,” Andreas Schleicher, the OECD’s Director of Education and Skills, said in an interview with the newspaper El Financiero.

If the first step toward turning things around is a positive attitude, it may already be at hand. The OECD highlighted that 80% of 15-year-old Mexican students stated in the PISA test that they are curious about various topics, up by 7% compared to the global average. Another finding revealed that just 11% of respondents agreed that school is a waste of time, compared to the OECD average of 24%.

In another sense, the poor scores may be a case of Mexico being a victim of its own success. As pointed out in a report cited by Animal Politico, “Given the expansion of secondary education to previously marginalized populations, [Mexico’s] results appear somewhat more positive. ”

Meanwhile, Mexico is struggling, along with the rest of the world, with modern impediments to educational performance. According to Education International, the largest global federation of teachers, the decline in student performance can be attributed “to shorter attention spans, excessive use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the global teacher shortage.”

Despite that, the top-performing countries in all PISA areas were China, Singapore, South Korea, Estonia and Canada.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Authorities seize 300 computers from cryptomining farm siphoning power from Puebla grid
World.content:
Federal authorities dismantled a clandestine cryptocurrency mining farm in the state of Puebla where approximately 300 computers illegally connected to a hydroelectric complex were found to be mining digital assets.

The cryptomining farm was discovered in Tlaola, a municipality in the remote Sierra Norte region of Puebla, thanks to a joint investigation carried out by the Federal Attorney General’s Office, the Navy and state prosecutors.

En Tlaola, un inmueble presuntamente utilizado para minería de criptomonedas fue asegurado por @FGRMexico, @SEMAR_mx y Seguridad Pública Estatal del @Gob_Puebla. Se localizó infraestructura eléctrica, internet satelital y equipos especializados en generación de activos… pic.twitter.com/lfgKk3pY3s — Secretaría de Seguridad Pública (@SSPGobPue) September 6, 2026

During the operation, authorities uncovered a highly equipped digital operations center. Agents seized large-scale electrical and technological infrastructure that included transformers, medium-voltage terminals, 300 specialized computer units (GPUs) and operational satellite internet antennas.

The initial criminal charge being prepared is energy theft, but prosecutors say money laundering charges have not been ruled out. Forensic accountants are tracing the origin of the funds used to acquire the expensive technological hardware.

State authorities have confirmed that investigators have expanded their search to neighboring municipalities in anticipation of similar operations.

Puebla Security Minister Francisco Sánchez said the “farms” are part of a network that takes advantage of the proximity to hydroelectric facilities in the Sierra Norte to steal massive volumes of energy.

Cryptomining consumes a significant amount of energy and produces a lot of noise, Sánchez said, so remote and isolated locations away from communities are favored.

“We have been monitoring this … area of ​​the state, especially due to its proximity to the [Nuevo Necaxa] dam,” he said, adding that the discovery of a large-scale power line connection helped the authorities locate the clandestine farm.

Last year, officials busted a crypto farm in the small Puebla community near the dam where properties owned by the Electrical Workers Union were allegedly being used to operate mining facilities powered by illegal connections to the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) power grid.

Two other mining operations straddling the border between Puebla and Tlaxcala were also dismantled in 2025.

Cryptocurrency mining — which is not illegal in Mexico, although cryptocurrencies are not legal tender here — is a process that uses computers to solve complex mathematical operations in order to validate transactions and earn rewards in digital assets.

In its latest report on non-technical losses covering the period from January to July 2024, the CFE estimated that energy theft, meter tampering and illegal connections cost the company approximately 13.8 billion pesos (US $817 million).

Cryptocurrencies are increasingly being used to move funds between financial users and countries quickly, cheaply and discreetly, such that they have become a popular money-laundering tool for criminal groups.

With reports from El País, Xataka México, Debate and La Jornada de Oriente

World.title: MND Local: Pro tennis and golf face uncertainty in Los Cabos
World.content:
Money trumps tradition in professional sports, at least where the Association of Tennis Professionals (ATP) is concerned. That was the takeaway from the recent report by Spanish-language tennis journalist Iván Aguilar that the ATP 500 Series event in Acapulco (Abierto Mexicano Telcel) will go away in 2028 to make way for a new Masters 1000 Series event in Saudi Arabia.

Acapulco has been a mainstay on the ATP Tour since 2001, hosting the most consequential tennis tournament in Mexico and a marquee event in Latin America. The long-running competition has always drawn top-tier talent. Legendary Spanish player Rafael Nadal, for example, was a four-time champion at the Mexican Open in Acapulco. So its loss to the tour, if confirmed by the ATP, will be deeply felt.

🚨🚨🚨ACAPULCO Y LOS CABOS FUERA DEL CALENDARIO ATP🚨🚨🚨 ¡Mexico se quedará sin torneos ATP para 2028! Los árabes han comprado la licencia del Abierto Mexicano de Tenis. El Abierto de Los Cabos pasará a ser un Challenger 175 para jugarse en el primer trimestre del 2028 pic.twitter.com/TN8JLRAAPx — Iván Aguilar (@ivabianconero) September 2, 2026

Los Cabos will also be affected by the schedule changes, Aguilar noted, as the Los Cabos Tennis Open (Mifel Tennis Open by Telcel Oppo, in sponsor-speak), which recently celebrated its 10th anniversary, will be downgraded from an ATP 250 Series event to a Challenger 175 tournament in 2028, with a shift in its calendar placement also in the works.

This news, combined with recent announcements by the Professional Golfers’ Association (PGA) Tour, which is in the process of a major reworking of its own schedule, ensures that two of the three biggest annual sporting events in Los Cabos — Bisbee’s Black and Blue, the world’s biggest fishing tournament, is the other — will undergo significant changes in coming years.

The Saudi money driving ATP changes

The ATP’s calendar shakeup is being driven by Saudi Arabia’s US $900 billion Public Investment Fund (PIF), and by its dedicated sports arm, SURJ Sports Investment. According to The New York Times’ sports arm, The Athletic, SURJ has spent hundreds of millions of dollars buying back tournament licenses to clear a space on the calendar for a 10th Masters 1000 tournament, a 56-player draw likely to take place in Riyadh beginning in February 2028 with an estimated US $6 million prize pool. This is part of a massive overall investment by Saudi Arabia in the ATP Tour.

Among the licenses SURJ purchased to retire or relocate as part of the ATP’s “calendar optimization” program are those from the Chengdu Open, Hong Kong Open, Moselle Open, and the dormant Kremlin Cup. The Athletic reported in March that negotiations were also ongoing to acquire the licenses of tournaments in Acapulco and Buenos Aires. Aguilar’s subsequent reporting suggests the negotiations to acquire the license for the Mexican Open in Acapulco are complete.

Changes to the tennis tournament in Los Cabos

The loss of the Mexican Open and the demotion of the Los Cabos Tennis Open from an ATP-sponsored event to a second-tier Challenger 175 tournament amounts to a gutting of ATP events in Mexico. No top-tier ATP-sponsored events are expected to remain in the country by 2028. Los Cabos keeps its professional tournament, albeit with weaker fields — top-10 players have regularly appeared at the event during its decade-long history, but will likely become a thing of the past — and a fraction of the prize money.

The tournament will also move from its traditional late July calendar slot to sometime during the first few months of 2028. The 2027 editions of the Mexican Open and Los Cabos Tennis Open, meanwhile, have been confirmed, so there is at least one more opportunity for spectators to enjoy each of these events in their current form.

How the PGA’s new schedule affects Los Cabos

Just like in professional tennis, the other major North American individual sport, golf, is looking at major changes as it prepares to make its most significant structural overhaul in decades. Beginning in 2028, the PGA Tour will split into two tiers: a Championship Series and a Challenger Series. As a consequence of this update, the FedExCup Fall Series, of which the World Wide Technology Championship (WWTC) at Tiger Woods’ El Cardonal course at Diamante in Cabo San Lucas has been a part, will no longer exist.

Saudi investment has also played a role in the history of this tournament. For its first 16 editions, the WWTC was held at the Greg Norman-designed El Camaleón Mayakoba Golf Course on the Riviera Maya. However, when Norman became CEO of the Saudi Arabia-backed LIV Golf Tour, the PGA moved the tournament to Los Cabos in 2023. Diamante, the upscale resort and residential community that is home to several Tiger Woods-designed courses, became its new site, with the Woods-designed The Legacy Club talked about as the future location of the WWTC after its opening in 2027.

An uncertain future

But that future is now up in the air following the PGA Tour’s calendar shakeup. The WWTC, notably, only has a contract with the PGA Tour through 2027. Nor does it necessarily fit neatly into either of the new series tracks premiering in 2028. Although the WWTC has drawn top tour pros to compete for its distinctive El Arco-inspired trophy — Ben Griffin was in the world’s top 10 when he won the tournament last year — FedExCup Fall events are not high-profile enough to be slotted into the new Championship Series.

The Challenger Series is a possible landing spot — despite the international locale — and the Tiger Woods connection certainly helps, since the calendar restructuring was approved by the Woods-chaired Future Competition Committee.

But uncertainty remains … both for the WWTC and the only other PGA-sponsored event in Mexico, the VidantaWorld Mexico Open in Nuevo Nayarit. This year, the two are back-to-back on the schedule, with the VidantaWorld Mexico Open slated for Oct. 29 to Nov. 1, and the WWTC for Nov. 5 to 8.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: US, Mexico carry out ‘High Eagle’ operation to ground cartel drones along border
World.content:
Mexico and the United States are currently carrying out an anti-drone operation at the border between Baja California and California, according to the Mexican Ministry of National Defense (Defensa).

Criminal groups use drones near the Mexico-U.S. border to assist their illicit activities, including the smuggling of people and drugs into the United States.

In a statement issued on Monday, Defensa said that the Águila Alta (High Eagle) “binational anti-drone operation” is taking place in the border region between Tijuana, Baja California, and San Diego, California.

The ministry said that the Aug. 31-Sept. 21 operation is occurring “within the framework of the Mexico-United States Bilateral Implementation Group” — a security group established a year ago — and that it is related to “concurrent (mirror) operations that the Armed Forces of both countries and U.S. law enforcement agencies are carrying out through simultaneous reconnaissance along the common border.”

Defensa said that the aim of the operation is to have a “safer border through the detection and disablement of commercial drones that are used by criminals at the common border to watch authorities during the trafficking of people and drugs.”

It didn’t say how many drones had been detected and disabled during the ongoing operation.

The Defense Ministry, led by General Ricardo Trevilla Trejo, said that the operation — described as “similar” to one that took place at the border between Ciudad Juárez and El Paso in March — consists of two stages, the first of which has already been completed.

It said that stage 1 took place from Aug. 31 to Sept. 2 in Tijuana and San Diego. During the stage, “a coordination exercise addressing drone issues was conducted, culminating in simultaneous ground reconnaissance missions, with each force operating within its own territory,” Defensa said.

The ministry said that the second stage of the operation is taking place “as of this date” — i.e., Monday, Sept. 7 — and until Sept. 21. The stage involves “the deployment of forces in the border region of each country, supported by fixed and mobile anti-drone equipment,” Defensa said.

“Security cooperation between Mexico and the United States is carried out with full respect for national sovereignty and is governed by the principles of reciprocity, shared and differentiated responsibility, mutual trust and respect for sovereign decisions and territory, favoring at all times the interests of the Mexican state,” the ministry said.

The announcement of the bilateral anti-drone operation came three days after the United States Northern Command said in a statement that the Joint Task Force–Southern Border (JTF-SB) had taken down more than 300 unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), or drones, along the U.S.-Mexico border this year.

“JTF-SB defeated more than 300 UAS this calendar year employing kinetic and non-kinetic systems, with more than 100 defeats occurring in the month of August,” said USNORTHCOM, one of 11 unified combatant commands of the U.S. Department of Defense.

“… The UAS were assessed to be associated with illicit activity along the border. Transnational criminal organizations use UAS to support illegal cross-border activity, including smuggling operations and surveillance of law-enforcement and military personnel,” USNORTHCOM said.

It noted that JTF-SB personnel have conducted patrols along the border “in coordination with Mexican military personnel.”

Trevilla said Friday that U.S. authorities had informed the Mexican government that drones are mainly used in the border region by people who smuggle migrants into the United States

“They are commercial drones. They only capture images … and what they’re seeking to find are routes that are free, where there is no presence of [U.S.] authorities,” the defense minister said.

Last month, Mexico and the United States signed a defense agreement on new technologies that allows Defensa to acquire drones and counter-unmanned aerial systems in the U.S. Army’s online marketplace. However, the Defense Ministry said at the time that it hadn’t made any purchase commitment.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: BTV’s Sarstoon expedition discussed with Guatemalan officials, Foreign Affairs CEO says
World.content:
BTV’s Sarstoon expedition discussed with Guatemalan officials, Foreign Affairs CEO says

By Zoila Palma: CEO in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Oscar Arnold said during an interview with Love TV, that the Belize Territorial Volunteers (BTV)’s upcoming Sarstoon expedition has been discussed with Guatemalan counterparts.

“But the month of September seems to be that sweet spot where there is an uptick in the showing of patriotism. Some people show it in differing ways, but we are of the opinion that however that is done, that individuals should be responsible. We don’t expect anyone to be reckless, and we hope that no lives are put into jeopardy,” CEO Arnold said.

“We know and we understand, and so at the Ministry level, the level of the Belize Defence Force and the Coast Guard, discussions have already been made. I believe both foreign ministers spoke of this as well, and the commitment is there that if there is any small flare-up, to ensure that the communication lines are open-that the communication in place to ensure that we don’t have any escalation of whatever small disturbance may take place,” he added.

The Belize Territorial Volunteers is scheduled to visit the Sarstoon on St. George’s Caye Day, September 10, 2026.

World.title: Farmers trained in agroforestry for climate-resilient cattle production
World.content:
Farmers trained in agroforestry for climate-resilient cattle production

By Zoila Palma: Seventeen farmers from the Cayo District gathered on September 8, 2026, at Diamond R Farm in Esperanza for a training session focused on “Agroforestry in Cattle Production.”

The session was hosted by cattle farmer Raymond Harris and aimed to equip farmers with practical approaches for improving productivity and sustainability within their cattle operations.

The training was facilitated by Extension Officer Adelita Jones, with support from the Cayo Extension Service and funding from the CRESAP Project. CRESAP Officer Moh also provided farmers with information about the project and its support for climate-smart agricultural practices.

During the training, farmers explored how integrating trees, pasture and livestock can improve farm productivity while promoting biodiversity, soil health and climate resilience. Discussions also highlighted practical agroforestry techniques and climate-smart practices that can be incorporated into cattle production systems to help farmers adapt to changing environmental conditions.

A hands-on component allowed farmers to work in groups to develop and draw their own farm plans based on the knowledge gained during the training. The activity encouraged teamwork, critical thinking, creativity and farmer-to-farmer knowledge sharing, while helping participants identify ways to apply agroforestry practices on their own farms.

The training also included a farm walk at Diamond R Farm, where participants observed firsthand how agroforestry and climate-smart practices can be incorporated into a working cattle operation.

To encourage practical application, each farmer received a spade and an assortment of agroforestry tree seedlings to take home and establish on their farms, supporting efforts toward more productive, sustainable and climate-resilient cattle production in the Cayo District.
