World.title: Arlene Arnold denied bail in fatal pint bottle stabbing of common-law husband Clive Hendricks; Tells court she was punched several times to the head before attack
World.content:
Arlene Arnold denied bail in fatal pint bottle stabbing of common-law husband Clive Hendricks; Tells court she was punched several times to the head before attack

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City mother of six who claims she was being beaten by her common-law husband before she fatally wounded him with a broken pint bottle will have to seek bail from the High Court after a Senior Magistrate declined to release her on Tuesday.

Arlene Tanice Arnold, 50, is charged with manslaughter in the death of her common-law husband, 45-year-old Jeremy Gerald “Clive Tambran” Hendricks.

At Tuesday afternoon’s bail hearing, the Senior Magistrate said she had reviewed relevant precedents and found that bail had been granted at the Magistrate’s Court level in cases involving manslaughter by negligence, but not simply manslaughter. Arnold was therefore advised that her bail application would have to be made before the High Court.

She remains remanded at the Belize Central Prison until November 10 unless she is granted bail by the High Court.

Arnold was arraigned Monday, when no plea was taken. Her attorney, Ronell Gonzalez, told the court that she is the mother of six children, including two minors who depend on her, and argued that Hendricks’ death occurred during a domestic dispute in which Arnold had allegedly been subjected to violence.

The defence claims Hendricks had abused Arnold previously and that two reports had been made against him, with another matter involving the couple reportedly before the Family Court. Gonzalez further alleged that Hendricks punched Arnold around the head and temple during Saturday morning’s confrontation and that she reacted while fearing for her safety.

Police, however, offered a somewhat different account at Monday’s press briefing. ASP Stacy Smith said the Gender-Based Violence Response and Investigative Unit had advised investigators that there was no history of reported domestic violence cases between Arnold and Hendricks. Smith added, however, that people living in the area told police that physical altercations between the couple appeared to have been relatively common.

The fatal incident occurred at about 3:33 a.m. on Saturday, September 5, near the corner of New Road and Pickstock Street.

Police responding to the area found Hendricks lying in the street and bleeding profusely from his right arm. He was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital but was pronounced dead at 4:44 a.m. Investigators believe the wound to his arm may have severed a major artery.

Police allege that Hendricks and Arnold had been involved in a physical altercation when Arnold wounded him once in the right tricep with a broken pint bottle.

Arnold was later located at an address in the Holy Emmanuel area after her daughter reportedly contacted police. She was initially detained pending a murder investigation and later gave investigators a statement under caution.

After the case file was forwarded to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, police were directed to charge Arnold with manslaughter rather than murder.

Arnold’s attorney is now expected to pursue a bail application before the High Court.

World.title: 3 men, 17-year-old boy charged with stealing tractor belonging to Brian Mira
World.content:
3 men, 17-year-old boy charged with stealing tractor belonging to Brian Mira

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Four people, including a 17-year-old minor, have been charged with stealing a tractor belonging to businessman Brian Mira, brother of Belmopan Area Representative Oscar Mira and a figure linked to one of the family businesses at the centre of the ongoing “Mira Millions” controversy.

Tyrone Jordan, 27, of Hattieville; Dwayne Garbutt, 44, of Belize City; Estevan Humes, 51, of Santa Familia, Cayo; and the 17-year-old Hattieville resident appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, where they were jointly charged with theft.

All four pleaded not guilty and were granted bail of $3,000 each plus one surety in the same amount. They must report to the police station nearest their homes every Friday and are due back in court in November.

Police say the case unfolded shortly after 11 p.m. on September 5 when Hattieville officers, acting on information about a stolen tractor, went to an area near Mile 19.5 on the George Price Highway.

Officers reportedly encountered a red Massey Ferguson tractor being driven along a dirt road. A white International 10-wheeler truck was parked nearby, while a black Chevrolet Equinox was allegedly seen exiting the dirt road behind the tractor.

Police say the driver of the Equinox attempted to reverse after seeing the police mobile. Garbutt, who was allegedly driving the SUV, and the 17-year-old passenger were detained.

Humes was allegedly found driving the tractor, while two other men who were near the 10-wheeler truck were also initially detained as part of the investigation.

Police subsequently contacted Mira, 44, of Belmopan City, who visited the Hattieville Police Station and provided documents establishing his ownership of the tractor.

According to police, Humes later told investigators that he had been communicating with a man he knew as “Tyrone” and had arranged to pick up the Massey Ferguson tractor near Mile 19.5.

Police later detained Jordan in Hattieville on September 6. Investigators say Humes identified him as the man with whom he had allegedly been communicating regarding the tractor.

Jordan, Garbutt, Humes and the minor were subsequently charged with theft.

The identity of the tractor’s owner adds a political dimension to what would otherwise be a routine theft case.

Brian Mira is the brother of Oscar Mira, who stepped away from his Cabinet duties in June amid intense scrutiny over leaked SmartStream records showing millions of dollars in Government payments to businesses linked to members of the Mira family.

One of those businesses is MP Farms. Public reports identified Brian Mira as a contact for the company, while Stanley Mira was listed as its owner. 7News reported that leaked records showed 601 transactions totaling approximately $5.67 million to MP Farms between September 2024 and June 2026, with the overwhelming majority originating from the Ministry of Defence.

Earlier records also reportedly showed almost $390,000 in payments to MP Farms processed in a single day in September 2025, during the period when Oscar Mira held responsibility at the Ministry of Defence.

Oscar Mira has denied influencing procurement decisions or Government payments involving his relatives. The Auditor General is currently examining procurement processes at the Ministry of Defence, and no finding of wrongdoing against Mira has been made.

Garbutt was also separately arraigned on three traffic offences arising from the investigation. He pleaded guilty to driving without third-party insurance, driving an unlicensed motor vehicle and driving without a valid Belize driver’s licence.

He was fined $205 for the insurance offence, $55 for driving an unlicensed vehicle and $105 for driving without a valid Belize driver’s licence, with separate payment deadlines and default prison terms.

World.title: Police officer, licensed gun holder detained after 26-year-old shot during Belmopan dispute
World.content:
Police officer, licensed gun holder detained after 26-year-old shot during Belmopan dispute

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A police officer and a licensed firearm holder have both been detained as investigators try to determine who shot a 26-year-old man during a dispute in Las Flores, Belmopan on Monday night.

Police say officers responded to a residence at around 8:00 p.m. on Monday, September 7, following a report of a dispute. During the police response, the 26-year-old man was shot and injured.

He remains hospitalized in stable condition.

According to police, the investigation has so far established that both a licensed firearm holder who was involved in the original dispute and a responding police officer may have discharged their weapons.

Both firearms have been seized, packaged and will be submitted for comparative ballistic testing to determine which weapon fired the shot that struck the victim. Police say an expedited examination will be requested because the ballistic findings are expected to help determine how the investigation proceeds.

Both the licensed firearm holder and the police officer have been detained, and police have launched separate criminal and internal investigations into the incident.

During Tuesday’s press briefing, police were also questioned about allegations circulating on social media that the responding officer may have given the licensed gun holder permission to fire. Police said investigators were not aware of any information supporting that claim and stressed that there is presently no indication that the officer and firearm holder had any prior agreement or plan to act together.

Police urged anyone who witnessed the incident or has information supporting those allegations to make a formal report.

The identities of the detained men have not been released because neither has been charged at this time.

World.title: Truck rolled backwards on hill before fatal accident that killed Mauricio Solis, police say
World.content:
Truck rolled backwards on hill before fatal accident that killed Mauricio Solis, police say

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a fatal heavy-equipment accident near the Guacamayo Bridge that claimed the life of 49-year-old San Ignacio resident Mauricio Solis.

The incident occurred shortly before midday on Thursday, September 3, along the Chiquibul Road.

According to police, Solis was a passenger in a dump truck that was towing a trailer carrying heavy machinery. Investigators say the machinery was secured to the trailer and the driver was attempting to climb a hill when the truck reportedly developed mechanical difficulties and began rolling backwards.

The driver lost control and the vehicle overturned. Solis was thrown from the truck and became trapped beneath it, sustaining severe injuries. He was subsequently pronounced dead.

Police processed the scene and have opened an investigation. A file is being compiled and will be forwarded to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions for directives once the investigation is completed.

Solis was an employee of Bulridge Ltd. and was on duty at the time of the accident. However, Bulridge has since clarified that the dump truck, trailer and heavy equipment involved did not belong to the company and were not being operated by a Bulridge employee. According to the company, Solis had been assigned to accompany private contractor Bahadur Trucking & Backhoe Service to a designated worksite.

Bulridge said the equipment belonged to the private contractor and that, like Solis’s family, the company is awaiting the findings of the police investigation.

World.title: Belize Territorial Volunteers, BDF and Coast Guard coordinate security for annual Sarstoon expedition
World.content:
Belize Territorial Volunteers, BDF and Coast Guard coordinate security for annual Sarstoon expedition

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Belize Territorial Volunteers (BTV) met with senior officials of the Belize Defence Force (BDF) and Belize Coast Guard to coordinate security and operational arrangements for the group’s upcoming annual expedition to the Sarstoon River.

The meeting, held in Punta Gorda, brought together BTV leaders and Lieutenant Colonel Justo Veliz Jr., Commanding Officer of the BDF’s 1st Infantry Battalion, along with Lieutenant Juan Bulum, Sector South Commander of the Belize Coast Guard.

Discussions included measures aimed at ensuring the safety and orderly movement of participants during the September 10 expedition.

The BTV said that the meeting was productive and reflected a shared commitment to national safety and Belize’s sovereignty.

BTV said collaborative measures were established to prioritize the safety of both Belizean and international participants taking part in the excursion.

BTV Leader Wil Maheia expressed appreciation to the BDF and Coast Guard for their cooperation. “We extend our sincere gratitude to the leadership and personnel of both the Belize Defence Force and the Belize Coast Guard for their professional cooperation and dialogue today,” Maheia said.

“Working together ensures that our citizens can exercise their rights safely as we honor our nation’s sovereignty,” he added.

The BTV says the expedition will be peaceful and orderly, with participants travelling to the Sarstoon River on Thursday, September 10, as part of activities marking Belize’s 45th Independence.

World.title: Costly prisons
World.content:
In this August 2021 photo George Williams appears to be pondering his future while standing in the doorway of his house in Linstead, St Catherine. Williams who spent over 42 years in prison on murder charges despite being found unfit to plead from 1971, was released in 2020. He sued the State and was awarded $120 million in damages.

WITH the majority of lawsuits against the State filed by inmates seeking millions in compensation based on complaints about lack of bathroom facilities, overcrowding and general prison conditions, the Attorney General’s Chambers has recommended that the Department of Corrections “address the systematic deficiencies and the administrative shortcomings in order to cauterise the influx of these types of cases”.

“We have a lot of cases before the court that highlight these challenges,” director of state proceedings in the Attorney General’s Department Faith Hall said Tuesday on day two of the 14th annual Association of Caribbean Heads of Corrections and Prison Services (ACHCPS) Conference.

The confab is hosted by the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), Jamaica at the AC Hotel Kingston.

According to Hall, there are currently 10 claims before the Constitutional Court awaiting a ruling on these matters.

Addressing the issue of how the DCS can implement policies or amend systems to stem the influx of civil cases, Hall said chief among the Chambers’ recommendations is that the institution should “allow, where reasonable, liberal use of bathroom facilities; discourage the use of buckets for disposal of excrement; create a system of oversight for cleaning parties or manage it more closely or reimagine what is there; create a system of oversight to increase food standards and implement rehabilitation programmes focusing on hygiene and behaviour”.

Another area of concern is inmates’ lack of knowledge about the channels through which they can access legal help from outside the prison walls.

“The thinking is that when an inmate comes in they get an orientation package that informs about their release date, for example,” Hall suggested, adding that information about how to file appeals should also be included.

She said while the prison’s Bail and Appeal Section offers inmates help in filing appeals, it needs to do more in pointing them to the source of legal advice. According to Hall, a lot of the complaints by inmates is that when they go to that division they are discouraged from filing an appeal. She noted, however, that these claims have not been proven.

Hall also urged the DCS to make a strong push to address unsafe conditions within prisons as there is a serious possibility that DCS would be blamed if an inmate is injured by another using contraband.

“The responsibility is a multi-stakeholder one, in terms of preventing these kinds of claims that we are seeing at the Attorney General’s Chambers which are many times difficult for us to defend in court in this current climate where the society has become more aware of their rights and the society has become more litigious. Once it is [that] their rights are infringed — and there are attorneys there who are seeking out these persons — a claim will be filed,” Hall warned.

She noted that while many of the systematic failures which trigger lawsuits do not rest with the DCS alone, “the fact remains that the DCS plays an important role in advocating for the resources needed to carry out the functions given to it”.

Highlighting other claims being brought because of breach of constitutional rights or systematic deficiencies, Hall said these come from individuals “found unfit to plead and mental health patients” in addition to claims hinging on the inhumane and degrading conditions of prisons and unsafe custodial conditions.

She referenced the cases of Noel Chambers, an 81-year-old Jamaican man who died in custody on January 27, 2020, after being imprisoned for 40 years without ever standing trial, and George Williams who was released in 2020 after he spent over 42 years in prison on murder charges despite being found unfit to plead from 1971. She said these were cases of individuals being lost in the system, due to a multiplicity of errors on the part of various State actors, which have caused taxpayers dearly.

“What is important to note is that there were review mechanisms in place specifically to prevent a mentally ill person from being indefinitely detained without judicial oversight. However, regrettably those safeguards were not implemented in Mr Williams’ case,” Hall said.

“The responsibility of bringing him back before the court is not the DCS’s, so to speak. He was being housed by the DCS; there should have been some alert to say this was the situation and this was happening,” she added, pointing out that those shortfalls led to approximately $120 million in damages being awarded to Williams following the ruling by the court.

She said the department has appealed the ruling but only in respect of the quantum.

“The issues in relation to the failings and the breach of his constitutional rights were clear and we really wouldn’t have any defence for that. But we do believe the judge was a little heavy-handed, in terms of the award. But what the decision reinforced is that there are consequences that the State faces when it fails to address deficiencies in the prison’s administration, especially where vulnerable persons with mental illness are concerned,” she said and mooted electronic systems for tracking inmates among the methods to prevent them from being lost in the system.

In the meantime, she said while the ruling in relation to Williams’ payout is being appealed, $35 million of the $120 million was paid over to him in August this year “as a portion of what we think the claim is worth… as a show of good faith”.

The three-day conference, which began on Monday, is being convened under the theme ‘One Caribbean, One Vision’ and brings together senior correctional leaders, policymakers, and technical experts from across the Caribbean to discuss innovations, legal governance, and rehabilitation.

World.title: More school mergers coming
World.content:
Education Minster Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon and Hydel Cumberland Principal Carlon Pitt unveil the newly merged school’s name, crest, and motto on Monday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has signalled that more underpopulated schools could be consolidated or left off the Government’s reconstruction list, arguing that Jamaica cannot continue maintaining costly education facilities with too few students to fill them.

Speaking during Tuesday’s official launch of the Jamaica Reconstruction and Resilience Oversight Committee (JAMRROC) at Jamaica House in Kingston, Holness stressed the rebuilding of Jamaica after Hurricane Melissa would not simply mean restoring every damaged asset to its previous form.

He said some infrastructure would be rebuilt differently, some would be relocated, and some assets would not be rebuilt at all — a position he linked directly to the Government’s plans to consolidate parts of the education system.

“Please note they will not necessarily be rebuilt in the same place or in the same way, and there are some assets that will not be rebuilt. I think the public should become aware of that… We are in the process of consolidating our education infrastructure. There are… many schools that are underpopulated. And I know there is a great attachment to the schools because they signal the life of the community, but it is highly inefficient,” he said.

Holness argued that maintaining underpopulated schools places an unnecessary burden on taxpayers, as Government still has to cover fixed costs regardless of enrolment.

He said it was inefficient to maintain facilities designed for 1,000 students when only about 300 are using them, with taxpayers effectively footing the bill for space that remains unused because of sentimental attachment to the school.

Holness did not identify specific additional schools for closure or merger, nor did he announce a list of institutions that would be excluded from reconstruction. Instead, he described consolidation as part of a broader rethink of the country’s education infrastructure, against the backdrop of the massive rebuilding exercise triggered by Hurricane Melissa which ravaged sections of the country last year on October 28.

The prime minister’s comments come as Government has already begun restructuring schools where existing facilities and enrolment levels make consolidation a practical option.

On Monday, Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon officially unveiled the newly merged Hydel Cumberland High School in Portmore, St Catherine, bringing the two school communities together at the former Cumberland campus.

The move followed concerns about infrastructure at Hydel and the underutilisation of Cumberland, which had capacity for 1,200 students but was operating with just over 300 when Morris Dixon visited about a year earlier.

Morris Dixon said the merger was intended to make better use of existing resources and form part of a strategic restructuring of the education system.

“One of the things we had thought about was potentially moving the children in little groups to different schools, putting them all around St Catherine. But I think this is the best option. I think this was quite strategic in nature, and that’s how we’re going to continue to do this restructuring of education in Jamaica — be strategic — because now that we have one institution instead of two, it means we can direct more resources to one… that is our plan,” she said.

However on Tuesday, the prime minister acknowledged that schools are not simply buildings and that closing or consolidating one can have consequences for the communities around it.

He said the Government therefore intends to consult before making such decisions, while maintaining that public money must be used responsibly.

World.content:
King of Soca Machel Montano (left) shares the stage with dancehall artiste Ayetian during last year’s CMAs in New York.

AFTER three years of celebrating Caribbean excellence in New York City, the Caribbean Music Awards (CMAs) is coming home. For the first time since its inception, the awards ceremony will be staged on Caribbean soil, with Trinidad and Tobago selected to welcome artistes, industry stakeholders and music lovers for what is expected to be a landmark celebration of regional sound and culture.

The move will also usher in a new era for the CMAs as the event will move from a single celebratory evening to an immersive weekend featuring networking, industry discussions, cultural showcases and opportunities for fans to engage more closely with the people behind the music.

For Paige de Leon, regional public relations strategist for the CMAs, the expansion reflects the steady growth of an event that has increasingly established itself as a credible platform for Caribbean talent.

“I think that when you’re building a movement like this, you are going to find that if the quality of the offering and your product is really solid, and there is authenticity in your intention, you are going to see growth,” she said. “The growth is all positive. One of the things that I most appreciate about the Caribbean Music Awards, as a Caribbean woman, is that it is an intuitive entity that seeks to respond to the needs of its audience — the Caribbean Diaspora. That speaks very highly of its founders, and now to the fact that it will be held in Trinidad and Tobago.”

Since its launch, the CMAs has sought to provide a dedicated stage on which the breadth and diversity of Caribbean music can be recognised. Its growing reach was underscored last year when the awards were broadcast on BET, introducing the ceremony and its honourees to an even wider audience. Having strengthened its footing internationally, de Leon said the time had come to ensure that the people who live within the region and continue to fuel its musical movements could experience the ceremony for themselves.

“We’re bringing it to Trinidad because we want to make sure that the people of the Caribbean have the opportunity to experience the ceremonial splendour of their music in this way,” she explained. “We have spent the last three years or so building the event, and last year the CMAs were shown on a major network, BET, and that was a very significant moment for us. Now we want to connect our people with the music. We want the people who fuel this music to have access to this and how it is evolving.”

That connection will stretch beyond the awards stage. The weekend will begin with a Friday-night networking experience, allowing guests to engage with artistes, participants and other members of the entertainment industry. A celebration of the steelpan will also form part of the programme, paying tribute to an instrument born in Trinidad and Tobago that has become an enduring symbol of Caribbean creativity and identity. The weekend will also include a discussion forum bringing together various industry professionals to explore the Caribbean music industry’s place within the global entertainment landscape.

According to de Leon, the forum will provide space for serious conversations about the business, development and international integration of the region’s music.

“There is an intellectual side to the music that we must not forget,” she said. “That will make for a very robust and rounded weekend of activities.”

While several Caribbean destinations could have provided an appropriate backdrop for the historic occasion, de Leon said Trinidad and Tobago emerged as the most natural fit. Beyond its globally recognised Carnival and rich musical traditions, she explained that the twin-island republic possesses the infrastructure and expertise required to successfully stage large-scale entertainment events. Its reputation for celebration is also expected to bring a distinctive energy to the CMAs’ first Caribbean staging.

“We could have picked anywhere in the region to host the awards because, really and truly, the music is everywhere,” de Leon said. “However, we felt Trinidad and Tobago was a natural fit because we have the physical and human-resource infrastructure that routinely churns out shows of this nature. Trinidad is party central, so there will be a lot of activity that will make for a very interesting and vibrant weekend in the capital, Port of Spain. We’re all excited to have a successful weekend.”

The decision to bring the awards into the region also signals that the CMAs is no longer simply an ambitious new undertaking. Though entering only its fourth year, the ceremony is already being positioned as an institution capable of preserving legacies while acknowledging the contemporary artistes carrying Caribbean music into new markets.

“I think, over time, people realised that this wasn’t something that was going to stop and start again or fade away,” de Leon said. “There is a lasting, legacy-type feel to the awards, even though we’re just four years in.”

That commitment to legacy will be reflected in the recognition of Jamaican dancehall trailblazer Patra, whose commanding image and unapologetic expression helped introduce a new representation of Caribbean womanhood to international audiences.

For de Leon, the honour is also deeply personal. “Patra is one of those artistes who has had a really transformational impact on the music. She had such a significant impact on me as a young Caribbean woman when I saw how she handled herself and how authentic she was about her sensuality as a woman and her experiences,” she shared. “She has been a significant influence in spreading Caribbean music across the world. She’s very special to us because of what she changed in how we see ourselves, and we just want to give her her flowers.”

Although Trinidad and Tobago will be the first Caribbean destination to host the ceremony, organisers do not intend for it to be the last. The long-term vision is to rotate the awards throughout the region, allowing the countries that have shaped Caribbean music to participate directly in its celebration while benefiting economically from the event.

“The intention is most certainly to have the awards move around and have all the countries that contribute to the success of music in the region be a part of the celebrations,” de Leon said. “When you have an awards ceremony like this, it means you’re stimulating the economy in the country where that ceremony is being held, and we want that for every country in the Caribbean. We want the CMAs to become an important element of the global tourism product.”

World.title: $5-BILLION GROWTH DRIVE
World.content:
WISYNCO Group Limited is moving to spend up to $5 billion on its operations over the next three years to meet the growing demand for its manufacturing and distribution business lines.

That’s the update provided by Wisynco Group Chairman William Mahfood following the release of the company’s audited financials for the June 2026 financial year (FY). The next round of investments is focused on growing the company’s manufacturing capacity and warehouse space for its expanding proprietary and third-party product portfolio.

“If you were to lay it out on a map, over the next three years you’d see continued investment in capital in terms of buildings and equipment. We’re looking at even more factory and production [capacity] in the next year,” Mahfood told the Jamaica Observer during a recent phone call.

Wisynco spent $3.24 billion in capital expenditure (capex) on its property, plant and equipment for its 2026 FY, which saw $1.26 billion deployed on land and buildings and $1.13 billion for ongoing work.

Between the 2023 and 2025 FY, the company spent $14.65 billion in capex which supported its ability to meet domestic demand for its existing products, diversify into new packaging types and launch its alcohol portfolio, including its Legend beer. The company invested US$35 million ($5.47 billion) on its new brewery and manufacturing facility.

Mahfood revealed that the company recently acquired additional land at Lakes Pen, St Catherine, and is expected to complete a new 70,000 square foot warehouse by the end of the year which is near completion. This is on top of the new 60,000-square-foot distribution centre to be constructed in Lacovia, St Elizabeth.

“We acquired some land for further expansion across the road. So, we’re looking at building a new distribution centre. We’re going to submit the plans in probably six months,” Mahfood explained.

Wisynco’s expansion comes at a time when its revenue grew 14 per cent to $65.35 billion, underpinned by a diverse product mix and introduction of new products such as the manufactured alcohol and Stone’s Ginger Wine portfolios which contributed $397 million during the year.

However, the company also had to book $454 million related to the new special consumption tax on non-alcoholic sweetened beverages which it must book as revenue and deduct as an expense under cost of sales.

“We’re seeing steady growth every month on the new business, so that’s positive. Overall, we’re happy about the turnout. We’re excited about this year,” Mahfood explained on the new alcohol portfolio.

While the company is spending significant sums on marketing and promotions for its Legend and alcohol portfolio, it has not begun to significantly push this product in the export market.

Wisynco’s exports grew 26 per cent to $1.55 billion for the 2026 FY but represented 2.38 per cent of group revenue. Exports represented $628 million or 1.97 per cent of revenue in 2021, demonstrating how fast domestic sales continue to grow.

“Our main focus is still in Europe. We just started in Canada with a new partnership with GraceKennedy,” Mahfood noted while pointing to the USA and Eastern Caribbean as other focus markets.

The company’s operating profit climbed 12 per cent to $5.87 billion as it spent more on advertising, staff and property expenses following its recent expansion initiatives.

However, earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) improved 16 per cent to $8.62 billion for 2026. The EBITDA metric is used to remove certain non-cash expenses like depreciation which lowers the company’s operating profit and shows the business’ core profit capacity.

Although Wisynco generated $531.26 million in finance income from its cash and investment portfolio, the higher debt balance pushed up its finance costs by 2.5 times to $847.57 million. The company reported $87.16 million in share of profit from its 30 per cent stakes in Ringtail Holdings Limited and JP Snacks Caribbean Limited.

Ringtail, the parent company of Select Brands Limited, reported $8.07 billion in revenue and $711.46 million in net profit since the July 2025 acquisition. JP Snacks reported $2.19 billion in revenue and a net loss of $29.23 million for the reported period.

While Wisynco reported a two per cent rise in profit before tax to $5.64 billion, its net profit fell seven per cent to $4.12 billion due to the increase in deferred taxes. The earnings per share declined from $1.17 to $1.10.

Despite the slightly lower net profit, Mahfood is confident about the new year which will see the company ramping up initiatives to grow its manufacturing and distribution reach. This comes against the backdrop of the western Jamaica rebuild via the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority, which will see increased spending in the economy.

“As long as we have no more hurricanes, I think this is going to be a very vibrant winter season going into next year. We’re very excited,” the Wisynco chairman noted.

Wisynco’s asset base improved eight per cent to $47.30 billion as its PP&E stood at $18.37 billion, inventory at $8.53 billion, investments at $5.46 billion and cash at $5.34 billion. Wisynco’s sole stage two investment was restructured in December 2025 while the remaining $4.36 billion in investments are carried at stage one.

Total liabilities increased six per cent to $17.09 billion with total debt of $6.52 billion, while equity grew nine per cent to $30.21 billion.

Wisynco closed Tuesday at $20.14, leaving the stock up eight per cent in 2026 with a market capitalisation of $76.58 billion. That translates to a price to earnings ratio of 18.18 times.

Director Francois Chalifour sold 2,655,000 ordinary shares during the 2026 FY while Chairman William Mahfood and CEO Andrew Mahfood had reduced direct stakes in the business. Executive Lelani Hunt sold 412,937 ordinary shares, but Assistant Corporate Secretary Vanessa Young acquired 3,629 ordinary shares.

GraceKennedy Pension Fund Custodian Limited acquired an additional 15,556,346 shares to become the fifth largest shareholder with 48,478,631 ordinary shares or a 1.28 per cent stake. SJIML A/C 3119 and DOMHAD Investments Limited acquired an additional 2,038,856 ordinary shares and 806,949 ordinary shares, respectively. Sagicor Pooled Equity Fund is now the 10th largest shareholder with 26,913,562 ordinary shares or a 0.71 per cent stake.

World.title: GET BACK ONSIDE
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (centre) addresses a round table press briefing at the end of the FIFA Executive Summit at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James in January 2018. Also pictured are JFF President Michael Ricketts (left) and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani.

JAMAICA Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts is calling for unity between FIFA President Gianni Infantino and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani as tensions between the two reportedly continue to escalate.

The relationship between both men has come under scrutiny recently amid the fallout over Infantino’s scrapped proposal to sell stakes in FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cup.

Montagliani, who is a Canadian and Infantino’s vice-president at FIFA, is being touted as a potential challenger for the presidential elections next year. Infantino, who is Swiss, is seeking a fourth term as head of football’s world governing body, and is the only candidate who has publicly declared his intention to run on Sunday, with nominations closing in November.

UEFA, however, have called on Infantino to step down while reports from Europe suggest its member associations would strongly back Montagliani should he enter the race. Several European football associations have publicly withdrawn their support for Infantino, who has been in office since 2016.

Last month, Concacaf, which governs North America, Central America, and the Caribbean, released a joint statement with UEFA, and the Asian Football Confederation strongly criticising Infantino.

“When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned,” the statement said.

Montagliani and Infantino reportedly had awkward moments after Infantino’s impromptu visit to the Caribbean Football Union Presidents’ Meeting and Under-14 Challenger Series in Dominican Republic last month, which Ricketts attended. Montagliani had written to Infantino asking him not to attend.

During the tournament, Montagliani said he stood by the statement” and was coy when asked by

Sky News if Infantino should resign.

“That’s his decision, not my decision,” Montagliani told Sky. “My view is we have to follow proper governance processes and I have to respect my colleagues with that. Once we follow that then those decisions can be made my individuals.”

Reports from Europe also say that Concacaf members were “infuriated” by Infantino’s behaviour.

Ricketts, though, told the Jamaica Observer that both presidents were welcomed equally.

“No truth that Infantino was snubbed,” Ricketts said. “We did show him a lot of respect. In fact, both gentlemen — Montagliani and Infantino — were treated with utmost respect. We showed both of them love.”

However, Ricketts is hopeful that two can come together for football’s development.

“What we really want is for both gentlemen, Infantino and Montagliani, to come together and put the differences aside because obviously right now there’s a strained relationship,” he said.

“I would love for them to just put these issues aside, rekindle the love and warmth and the camaraderie and let’s move on with the growth of the football because both gentlemen in their own jurisdiction and their own portfolio responsibilities have done very well for football and I just hate to think that they are not now seeing eye to eye. The most important thing for me right now is for both of them to come together, put the past behind, get over this strained relationship and both of them continue to do what they’ve been doing for football.”

Ricketts says the JFF board will ultimately decide on supporting Infantino in the upcoming election in Morocco next March. Infantino needs the support of at least 106 of FIFA’s 211 member associations to secure re-election.

However, at least 14 FIFA member associations have publicly withdrawn support, including England and Italy.

Ricketts, though, says he won’t be influenced by the views and stance of some of the established nations.

“When Infantino tried to increase the numbers [for the FIFA World Cup], some of the bigger countries say that he was trying to bring in weak Caribbean teams into the World Cup,” he said.

“When he decided that he would increase our subvention, a number of big countries say that the Caribbean countries can’t manage from a fiscal perspective. So I am not even watching some of these countries because like I say, that’s how politics is. People will have different views and different opinions for different reasons.”

Infantino won a contested election in 2016 to replace Sepp Blatter, defeating Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa but has since been re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

World.title: WapiPay enters Jamaica through JN Money partnership
World.content:
WapiPay co-founder Paul Ndichu (second right) makes a point at the press event to formally announce the partnership agreement with JN Money to support payments to Jamaica through WapiPay’s global network. The signing was done at JN Group’s corporate office on September 3. JN Money will serve exclusively as the local payout conduit, using its established remittance infrastructure to deliver funds to recipients in Jamaica. Also photographed are (from left) Cedrica Reid, head of marketing and sales at JN Money; Horace Hines, general manager, JN Money; and Edward Ndichu, co-founder, WapiPay.

JN Money Services has added Africa-focused fintech WapiPay to its international remittance network, giving the cross-border payments company a foothold in Jamaica following regulatory approval to operate locally.

Under the arrangement, WapiPay customers will be able to send funds to Jamaica for collection at JN Money locations or have the money deposited directly into recipients’ local bank accounts.

Founded in Singapore in 2019, WapiPay operates from offices in Nairobi, Kenya; and Kampala, Uganda; and provides cross-border payment services to individuals, merchants and businesses. The company says it has established payment corridors across Africa, Asia, the United Kingdom and the United States.

WapiPay received approval from the Bank of Jamaica earlier this year to enter the local market, with JN Money serving as its local payout partner. The approval has also been independently reported as coming from the central bank.

The move comes as remittance providers continue to expand digital and cross-border payment options in a market that remains an important source of foreign exchange for Jamaica.

Total remittance inflows to Jamaica amounted to US$3.36 billion in 2024, equivalent to about 15.3 per cent of gross domestic product, according to Bank of Jamaica data. The United States remained by far the largest source market, accounting for roughly two-thirds of inflows.

JN Money General Manager Horace Hines said the WapiPay agreement forms part of the company’s efforts to widen the number of channels through which money can be sent to Jamaica.

“We are deliberate about building strategic partnerships that expand the ways customers can send money to Jamaica while making the remittance experience more convenient, accessible and reliable. As customer needs continue to evolve and demand for digital financial services grows, we remain focused on identifying innovative solutions and strengthening our network to better serve Jamaicans and their families, wherever they are in the world,” Hines said in a press statement.

JN Money currently has a presence in 18 countries, including Cayman Islands, Antigua, Guyana, and Turks and Caicos.

The company has also been adding international partners. Its portfolio includes Mastercard Transaction Services, which supports cross-border remittances from the United Kingdom, United States, Canada, and Cayman Islands.

Meanwhile, Jamaica marks WapiPay’s entry point into the Caribbean as it seeks to extend payment links between the region and markets where it already operates.

Josephat Nelson Mados, WapiPay country director for Jamaica, said the companies expect the partnership to improve connections between the Caribbean and markets in Africa, North America, the United Kingdom, and Asia.

He said customers are expected to benefit from competitive pricing, faster processing and greater visibility of fees, foreign exchange rates and transaction status. However, details around comparative pricing or processing-time data weren’t immediately clear.

WapiPay said its platform supports automated payment routing, real-time transaction tracking, reconciliation, settlement tracking, and partner reporting.

World.title: Rough start
World.content:
Grade two students at Holland Primary School in class under a bamboo structure on Monday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

THE education ministry on Monday reported a generally smooth reopening of schools across the island for the start of the 2026/27 academic year but principals, mostly in hurricane-ravaged western Jamaica, highlighted a raft of difficulties.

Among the complaints were incomplete repairs as well as classes held in heat-trapping tents that turn into sweltering ovens under the tropical sun.

“Based on preliminary data received from all seven educational regions covering approximately 1,000 schools, only three schools did not open today, meaning that approximately 99.7 per cent of the schools captured in the data were able to open on the first day of the new school year,” the ministry said in a news release.

While the ministry said late furniture delivery was among the most frequently reported challenges on Monday, Jamaica Observer journalists received first-hand reports of the rough start to the academic year in the sections of the island that suffered the brunt of Hurricane Melissa’s fury last October.

Stories on Pages 3 to 10.

World.title: Two traditions, one future
World.content:
Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon (centre), along with former Hydel High Principal Dr Walton Small (right), as well as teachers and students of the newly merged Hydel Cumberland High School, release balloons in celebration of the official opening of the merged institution on the first day of the new academic year, Monday. (Photos: Garfield Robinson)

EDUCATION Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon officially unveiled the newly merged Hydel Cumberland High School Monday, declaring that the unification wasn’t about erasing either school’s identity, but rather combining the best of their traditions to create a single learning environment better equipped to serve students and make fuller use of existing resources.

“I love to see the new motto: ‘On the wings of excellence, endeavour to soar.’ And that’s a merger of the two mottos of the two schools. So even starting with the name, we merged the two schools. With the motto, we have merged the two schools and their ethos,” Morris Dixon said Monday while delivering greetings at the name unveiling ceremony at the school’s campus in Portmore, St Catherine.

As she helped to officiate both the historic first day of the school and the start of the 2026-2027 academic year, Morris Dixon explained that Cumberland High School had a capacity for 1,200 students but had only been operating with just over 300 students when she visited about a year ago. She added that the infrastructural challenges at Hydel High, coupled with Cumberland’s available space, made the merger a practical option.

“One of the things we had thought about was potentially moving the children in little groups to different schools, putting them all around St Catherine. But I think this is the best option. I think this was quite strategic in nature, and that’s how we’re going to continue to do this restructuring of education in Jamaica — be strategic — because now that we have one institution instead of two, it means we can direct more resources to one… that is our plan,” said Morris Dixon.

Already, significant investment is being made in the new school. The minister announced that $70 million is being spent to improve its electrical system while work is also being done on the home economics laboratory.

She added that the school’s parking lot will be expanded to accommodate the increased number of staff, while upgrades to the sporting facilities are also planned.

“So there’s a lot that will happen here, and Principal [Carlon Pitt] can ask for everything he wants. Principal, we’ve already granted your first wish, which was more students, but your success, the success of this merged institution, is really important to the Ministry of Education. We are very much committed to it. We’re committed to seeing the traditions work together and to achieve so much more,” she said.

Morris Dixon acknowledged, however, that bringing together two established school communities would not be without challenges but promised that her ministry would be strongly supporting the school’s leadership to smoothly navigate any trials that may arise.

“There are understandable emotions when schools merge. I know there is sadness from some who are, you know, leaving a space that they’re used to. There are those who are seeing all these new children come and these new teachers come. There are a lot of emotions involved in this, and so I want to acknowledge those emotions. Change is never easy; it’s always hard. And us adults, we sometimes have a harder time than the children with change,” she said.

“So teachers, I know this is an emotional period for you… I know that you’re great, I know you’re wonderful, I have no doubt that we have the best teachers in this world in Jamaica, so I know we can get through this. The ministry is here to support, in whatever way we can, to the students who may be coming to this new environment. You have a good principal, you have a good team here; you’re going to be okay,” Morris Dixon assured.

Principal Pitt told the Jamaica Observer that as the former head of Cumberland High he was highly receptive to the idea of a school merger.

Welcoming this new chapter in his career, Pitt emphasised that his vision focuses heavily on academics while prioritising students’ holistic development.

Highlighting Cumberland’s status as a leading Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) institution in St Catherine, alongside Hydel’s strong culture of sports and academics, the principal noted that the merger offers the perfect opportunity to fulfill his goals.

“Whatever we do in school, it must result in student outcome, the students must be the biggest beneficiary of whatever we do. And so the primary focus is on adding value, value-added education, adding value to the students with respect to their starting point and where they exit. So far we have added more sciences to the curriculum. We have now the traditional sixth form… we have a sports programme to roll out that we are excited about, and so with all of these things it is about the holistic development of the child,” Pitt said.

World.title: Serbian leader calls snap elections after dissolving country’s parliament
World.content:
Demonstrations erupted after a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people. Protestors have demanded accountability over the disaster and called for early parliamentary elections.

On Monday, Prime Minister Đuro Macut asked Vučić to dissolve parliament and call fresh elections. “If we want to mitigate tensions in society there is no better way than to ask people,” Macut said.

Vučić, who has been in power as ‌president or prime minister for 12 years, has faced calls to step down since the 2023 parliamentary elections, amid allegations of electoral fraud. His second and final term as president is set to end in 2027 and his powers will not expire with the dissolution of parliament.

In June, Vučić said he would resign as president “within weeks,” but his ambitions to remain in power continue. His Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) has nominated him for prime minister if the party secures a majority in the upcoming snap election.

Serbia has been a candidate for EU membership since 2012, but its bid has stalled over concerns about democratic backsliding in Belgrade and its refusal to sanction Russia for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

World.title: Le Pen’s National Rally fires security volunteer over racist remarks caught on tape
World.content:
“Proceedings will be initiated, and the sanctions will match the seriousness of the facts,” the statement said.

The Carcassonne local police did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

The National Rally said in a statement that the volunteer was “immediately removed” from his role and “expelled” from the party after its leadership learned of the video. The prosecutor’s office in Carcassonne told the AFP news agency it had opened an investigation on the basis of the footage.

But the party’s opponents said the incident was evidence of the National Rally’s inability to fully extract itself from its racist, xenophobic and antisemitic roots. Le Pen’s father founded the party, then known as the National Front, alongside a ragtag group of political misfits and Nazi collaborators. The elder Le Pen was repeatedly convicted for hate speech, including downplaying the Holocaust.

Marine Le Pen kicked her father out of the party in 2015 as part of her years-long effort to clean up its image. The National Rally today enjoys unprecedented support, and most polls show Le Pen is the current favorite in the race to replace Macron in the spring of 2027.

Yet her party has frequently been forced to address offensive remarks made by lower-ranking officials and members, especially during election cycles.

“This is what France would look like if it were led by the National Rally,” Gabriel Attal, the candidate for French President Emmanuel Macron’s Renaissance party wrote on X.

Olivier Faure, the leader of the center-left Socialist Party who is vying for his party’s backing in the presidential race in a primary contest, said on X that voters should not give the National Rally “the keys to France.”

World.title: Ceux qui vont (vraiment) faire la campagne de Le Pen
World.content:
Depuis l’arrêt de la cour d’appel qui a permis à “la patronne”, comme la surnomment ses ouailles, d’être candidate, elle a réaffirmé ses vues tant sur la réforme des retraites que sur la question sensible de l’interdiction du voile musulman, faisant naître des interrogations sur le rôle du président du parti dans la campagne. La répartition des tâches entre les deux serait pourtant claire comme de l’eau de roche. A “MLP” la campagne pour l’Elysée, à Bardella celle pour les législatives et Matignon, comme futur Premier ministre.

En réalité, les missions des cadres du parti à la flamme ne sont pas encore toutes définies à sept mois du scrutin. Les fidèles de la quadruple candidate savent que des postes distribués en début de course évoluent toujours au fil de la campagne. Un cadre du RN, ayant demandé à rester anonyme pour parler plus librement, avertissait ainsi POLITICO fin août : “Ne rationalisez pas trop.” Si des interrogations, soupçons de déloyauté et équilibres à trouver demeurent, l’organigramme se met en place.

Les lieutenants

Ceux-là étaient déjà des “pièces maîtresses”, dixit Philippe Olivier, conseiller spécial de MLP, de la campagne de 2022. Le député de la Somme, Jean-Philippe Tanguy, et le bientôt ex-secrétaire général du groupe à l’Assemblée nationale, Renaud Labaye, restent des rouages clé de l’organisation de la candidate. Les deux hommes participent à l’essentiel des réunions stratégiques, sur son programme présidentiel ou pour la préparer aux rendez-vous médiatiques.

Ce qui ne les empêche pas de se faire parfois rabrouer sans ménagement par leur championne, quand ils abordent des sujets dont elle ne veut pas discuter, comme son procès, ou qu’elle ne goûte pas leurs sorties dans la presse.

Si Labaye s’apprête donc à rejoindre l’équipe de campagne, Tanguy, lui, peaufine les propositions économico-budgétaires, notamment le plan de redressement des finances publiques promettant 125 milliards d’euros d’économies (qui doit être détaillé cet automne devant la presse). Le numéro 2 du RN à l’Assemblée, qui portait les fiches de sa patronne avant le débat du Medef, a aussi plaidé en faveur de la “règle d’or budgétaire” qui figure désormais au programme maison et vise à rassurer les marchés. La proposition n’a pas encore été détaillée, mais pourrait être particulièrement ambitieuse : un cadre évoque carrément un objectif de déficit inférieur à 1% du PIB.

Tanguy, qui rêve toujours de devenir ministre de l’Economie, compte aussi parmi les émissaires de Le Pen auprès des patrons, “surtout sur les sujets de fiscalité”, précise une représentante de l’industrie qui l’a croisé plusieurs fois, sans entretenir de relations soutenues pour autant. “Plein de patrons ne sont pas d’accord avec lui, mais le trouvent câblé, commente un lobbyiste. Ça a une utilité auprès de ceux qui jugent Bardella sympa, mais limité, et restent gênés par le nom Le Pen.”

World.title: Jordan Bardella accuses EU Parliament of far-right ‘paranoia’ in court battle
World.content:
Bardella’s lawyer, David Dassa-Le Deist, told the court the decision was taken because of “prejudice” against far-right parties such as the National Rally. “There is a paranoia within the Parliament about the members who work for the far-right,” Dassa-Le Deist said.

Bardella had proposed that Paradol work every Monday to Thursday morning as a parliamentary assistant, with the rest of his time set aside for national party work. The Parliament said no, claiming it would be near-impossible for Paradol to separate his duties.

The Parliament’s lawyer, Lavinia Darie, backed up that decision Wednesday, saying Paradol’s National Rally job would mean him being available “around the clock.” She also disputed whether Paradol could decline to perform National Rally tasks for Bardella when he was supposed to be working as an MEP assistant.

She added that the case involving Le Pen showed there was a “high risk of abuse of funds” in Bardella’s case. The National Rally is on course to win next year’s French election. If Le Pen becomes president, Bardella could well be her prime minister.

Dassa-Le Deist said the rejection was unfair given hybrid working situations are “not prohibited,” adding that the “very competent” Paradol had been working with Bardella “for a very long time” and “knew how to carry out both of these roles.”

Judge Heikki Kanninen asked the Parliament’s lawyer whether they would have made the same decision if it involved an MEP from a different party.

World.title: EU seeks to transform procurement into €600B driver of industry
World.content:
“This is public money, which must also serve our collective goals,” the French commissioner said. “It’s the equivalent of a yearly recovery plan and about four to five times the EU budget in terms of spending.”

The Commission is also promising annual cost savings of €650 million for public authorities as three old directives and two dozen sectoral laws — spanning 900 pages — are boiled down into a single regulation running to just 200 pages. That ties in with von der Leyen’s broader second-term agenda of cutting red tape through a series of “omnibus” administrative reforms.

To harness public procurement to its strategic goal of strengthening European industry, the EU executive is betting on quality as the main driver in the awarding of public tenders. This would set a minimum quality weighting of 30 percent, rising to 50 percent for labor-intensive contracts. Environmental, social, innovation, security and resilience considerations would all count as quality.

Public authorities could still deviate from the rule if they can justify using price alone on the grounds that quality is guaranteed through technical specifications.

While public authorities can already put green or social criteria at the center of procurement, Commission research found that their use was neither optimal nor consistent across the bloc. Some contracting authorities, for example, fear litigation if they turn down the lowest-price offer.

European preference

The proposal also spells out how public authorities can favor EU goods and services — a power that they enjoy under existing rules but rarely use. Under the new rules, authorities could restrict participation, impose origin requirements, and reject tenders where EU or “covered” content accounts for less than 50 percent of the tender’s value.

World.title: Wie die AfD nun regieren will
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Ein historischer Wahlsieg in Sachsen-Anhalt wird für die AfD zur Zerreißprobe. Während Spitzenkandidat Ulrich Siegmund kompromisslos auf die absolute Mehrheit pocht, fordert Parteichef Tino Chrupalla die Bereitschaft zur Minderheitsregierung. Der offene Machtkampf zwischen Landesverband und Bundesspitze wirft die Frage auf, ob sich der gefeierte Wahlsieger mit seiner Alles-oder-nichts-Strategie am Ende selbst entzaubert.

Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler blicken hinter die Kulissen der neuen Magdeburger Fraktion, in der ein früherer Stasi-Offizier, ein verurteilter Betrüger und Akteure mit Neonazi-Verbindungen sitzen. Zudem beleuchten sie, warum auf der offiziellen Wahlparty KI-generierte SS-Lieder liefen und ob das BSW der AfD trotz aller Dementis doch noch zur Macht verhelfen könnte.

Den Artikel zur Wahlparty bei „AfD-TV“ von Frederik Schindler gibt’s hier zu lesen.

Abseits des Wahlerfolgs eskaliert in Nordrhein-Westfalen ein erbitterter parteiinterner Machtkampf. Schwere Vorwürfe über die systematische Zweckentfremdung von Mitarbeiterbudgets und mutmaßlichen Stimmenkauf setzen den Landesvorstand massiv unter Druck. Die Recherchen zeigen, wie tief das Misstrauen in den westlichen Verbänden sitzt und warum ähnliche Praktiken in Niedersachsen bereits die Staatsanwaltschaft beschäftigen.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.
