World.title: Séjourné says von der Leyen will decide his fate if romantic partner wins French presidency
World.content:
The pair were in a civil partnership from 2017 to 2022, while Attal held several ministerial positions and Séjourné was an adviser to Macron before becoming an MEP. They broke up for two years, before rekindling their relationship in 2024 .

Attal, who briefly served as prime minister in 2024, said last month that he and Séjourné would move into the Elysée Palace together if he wins the spring 2027 race to succeed Macron.

But Attal has been lagging in the polls behind far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen and Edouard Philippe, another former PM under Macron, since he declared his candidacy in May.

Séjourné also offered an indication as to how he would respond if Le Pen, a noted Euroskeptic who once wanted to bring France out of the EU, won the election.

He said he would “have to continue” in his position and defend EU interests.

“If I have to be more present in the media, or become more conflictual with France, to defend what I believe, then that’s what I will do,” he said.

World.title: German far right’s ‘remigration’ plans amount to ethnic cleansing, says Merz
World.content:
His comments come just days after the AfD won a landslide victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, in which the party just fell short of winning an absolute parliamentary majority.

“Remigration” is a far-right concept that can range from deporting people without legal status to the mass removal of immigrants and their descendants. The AfD had dedicated an entire chapter to “immigration and remigration” in its election program for Saxony-Anhalt.

Its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund — who is also the state’s potential next premier — attended a 2023 meeting at which party figures and far-right extremists discussed “remigration plans” that included the mass deportation of “non-assimilated” German citizens and sparked nationwide protests.

Merz’s comments constitute the harshest condemnation yet of the AfD’s policies and come as the chancellor himself is facing mounting questions over his ability to lead Germany’s weakened coalition government. His dismal approval ratings helped fuel the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday — and contributed to his party losing more than half of its support.

Following the election, Merz and his CDU are searching for a new narrative in their fight against the far right. The AfD, now the most popular party in national polls, has vowed to destroy Merz’s conservatives and seize power nationwide after the next national election, scheduled for 2029.

“You have failed to understand the message that voters in Saxony-Anhalt sent you last Sunday,” said AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel, who spoke before Merz in the Bundestag. “That doesn’t really matter anyway, because your time is up. The people want a change in policy, and they will get it. In the next election, the people will give the AfD — that is, us, the Alternative for Germany — a clear mandate to govern.”

World.title: One dead, several injured after train collides with truck in Poland
World.content:
A rescue operation is underway after a passenger train collided with a truck at a level crossing and derailed in Sokolniki Suche, near Warsaw, in Poland.

 

There were 120 passengers on board the train. Twenty people were injured, four of them seriously.

Karolina Jaworska, a press officer for the Warsaw State Fire Service, told Euronews that one person had died.

“We know of four people who were seriously injured, one of whom has died. The injured include the train driver, the truck driver and two passengers,” she told Euronews, adding that the person who died was a female passenger.

Jaworska said eight people with minor injuries were taken to hospital.

“A medical triage of the injured was carried out. Four people were handed over to emergency medical teams, including two who were transported by air ambulance helicopters,” the fire service said.

“Shortly before 12:00, a PKP Intercity train collided with a truck at a level crossing near Sokolniki Suche. The collision caused part of the train to derail and overturn,” Poland’s railway infrastructure operator PKP said in a statement.

Police said that "six carriages and the locomotive derailed as a result of the collision."

PKP said that “emergency services and railway representatives are working at the scene. Adam Wawrzyniak, a member of the PKP Intercity Management Board, has also travelled to the site. Replacement transport is being arranged for passengers, with three buses ordered.”

“PKP Intercity tickets will also be accepted on ŁKA and Polregio trains on designated routes. Emergency services are carrying out rescue operations and securing the scene. The causes and exact circumstances of the accident will be determined by the relevant authorities,” the statement said.

Train services on the line have been suspended.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reacted to the accident, saying: “We will begin work on tightening regulations for those who enter level crossings despite barriers and red lights. This has to stop.”

World.title: Would you let AI design your next tattoo? Tattoo artists say AI is changing the way they work
World.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how people decide what to permanently put on their bodies.

 

Many tattoo artists also rely on reference material as they work, particularly when making extremely detailed and realistic designs.

"This is also edited with AI. But this is my tattoo. It's not going to look like my reference exactly. Because I want that to look more realistic on the skin than on the photo itself,” said Brigi Fuzes, a Hungarian tattoo artist who has used AI to create reference images and believes AI can be an important tool for artists.

“That's something you do from your head. You can't do that with photos all the time."

Fuzes says around 70% of her customers now arrive with AI-generated images.

AI-generated images do not necessarily account for how light, shadow and fine details need to be adapted for tattooing, according to Fuzes, who has a background in fine art.

Extremely fine details that look convincing in a generated image may also fail to translate well into ink or remain clear as a tattoo ages.

"They think that's something possible on the skin. Like way too detailed. It might not stay in,” Fuzes said.

“Don't get me wrong, I do love details and my work is known for details, but at the same time, you want to make it right so it's going to last forever."

Related This manicure robot uses AI to paint your nails flawlessly in just 10 minutes

'AI as another design tool'

Edinburgh-based tattoo artist David Corden sees AI as the latest addition to tools artists were already using.

He previously used software such as Photoshop to build detailed reference images. AI can now help him improve old or blurry photographs, including pictures of deceased relatives that customers want tattooed.

However, he is frustrated by the growing assumption that highly detailed digital artwork must be AI-generated.

"You see videos come up on Instagram and somebody's zooming in on an iPad that an artist is working from going, 'Oh, AI image.' No it's not," he said.

"Some artists are better than you can possibly imagine."

Some tattoo artists still keep AI out of their creative process.

Tiago Miranda of Disturbia Ink creates his dark horror designs from his own imagination.

Unlike many tattoo artists, he does not use a reference photo to produce his work, and it all comes from the moment and the hundreds of pencil sketches he makes in his books.

Tattoo artist Ellie Diamond is also wary of AI, although she increasingly sees customers arrive with images they have generated themselves.

"If somebody brings us an idea and they're like, 'I've mocked this up,' I'm like, 'Okay, well, we can take that, but I'm going to draw you something much better than a computer can,'" she said.

"Most of the time the best tattoos come out of somebody just saying, 'Here's my idea, I love your work, you do your thing with this idea.'"

Can AI replace the tattoo artist?

The debate comes as tattooing has become increasingly mainstream in Europe.

A 2026 study found that 29% of adults in Sweden aged 20 to 68 have at least one tattoo, while a 2025 study involving more than 111,000 adults in France found that 11.5% were tattooed.

Veteran tattoo artist Dan Gold does not expect AI to take over his job. His bigger concern is how generative AI systems obtain the material used to train them.

"There ought to be some kind of AI tax or something like that," he said, "because they are using all of this data for free."

Diamond is also unconvinced that machines can replace the human appeal of tattooing.

"There's obviously something very innate and human about it," she said. "So I'm not worried that the machines are going to take over."

For more on this story, watch the video in the media player above.

World.title: Egypt, Greece and Cyprus back plans to bring Cypriot gas to Europe
World.content:
Egypt, Greece and Cyprus have renewed their backing for plans to send Cypriot gas to Europe through Egyptian export facilities, with Greece offering a possible onward route into southeastern and central Europe.

 

The plans come as disruption to Gulf liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies due to the ongoing Iran war and the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz continues to put pressure on European buyers to find alternatives.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides met in El Alamein on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast on Tuesday.

In a joint declaration, they called for work connecting Cyprus’ offshore gas fields to Egyptian infrastructure to be completed as soon as possible.

Cronos, Cyprus’ first gas development, is expected to start producing gas in 2028, according to Eni.

New contract for Cypriot gas project

On the same day as the summit, engineering company McDermott announced that Eni’s Cyprus subsidiary had awarded it a contract worth between $500m (€429.6m) and $750m (€644.4m) for work on Cronos.

McDermott said it would provide engineering and installation support and help manage the offshore development.

The contract follows Eni and TotalEnergies’ approval of the project on 28 July. The Italian and French companies each hold a 50% stake.

Cronos is to be developed through four offshore wells, with gas carried by an undersea pipeline to Egypt. It will use existing processing facilities linked to Egypt’s Zohr field before being sent to Damietta, where it will be liquefied and exported by ship.

Gas facilities in Egypt Eni

The Italian energy group said in July that using existing Egyptian facilities would reduce costs and speed up development. It also said the project would help restore regular LNG exports from Egypt.

At its planned production level, Cronos is expected to supply the equivalent of around 2.8 million tonnes of LNG a year. The field contains more than 3 trillion cubic feet of additional gas, according to Eni. The two companies will each market half of the output.

“This new gas route in the Mediterranean will contribute to Europe’s energy security by diversifying its LNG supply sources,” TotalEnergies chief executive Patrick Pouyanné said when the project was approved.

Where Greece fits in

Mitsotakis outlined a route through Greece’s Revithoussa and Alexandroupolis terminals, where LNG would be turned back into gas and sent to southeastern and central Europe through the Vertical Corridor.

He said the gas “could, in theory” enter Europe through Greek facilities.

Greece would therefore be one possible gateway rather than a compulsory stop. Eni said it would sell the gas primarily in Europe and other international markets, rather than send it exclusively to Greece.

The Vertical Corridor is not a single pipeline. It links existing gas networks running north from Greece through countries including Bulgaria and Romania towards Moldova and Ukraine, allowing LNG arriving at Greek terminals to reach markets further into Europe.

The proposed route would keep shipments from Egypt to Greece within the Mediterranean, avoiding Hormuz and the Red Sea. It would carry newly produced Cypriot gas rather than reroute existing Gulf cargoes.

In its July outlook, the International Energy Agency estimated total LNG supply losses of 140 billion cubic metres between 2026 and 2030, with the biggest impact on supply growth expected in 2026 and 2027.

Europe is also preparing to end its remaining Russian gas imports. EU rules provide for a full ban on Russian LNG from the beginning of 2027 and pipeline gas from autumn the same year, with Europe looking for alternative suppliers.

Wider energy ties and regional tensions

The cooperation extends beyond gas. El-Sisi and Mitsotakis discussed plans to connect their countries’ electricity systems during bilateral talks on Tuesday, according to the Egyptian presidency.

The proposed GREGY undersea power cable would carry renewable electricity from Egypt to Greece, with a planned capacity of 3,000 megawatts.

Developer Elica Interconnector said the electricity could supply Greek industry and be exported to other European markets.

All three leaders renewed their backing for the project in the summit declaration.

The trilateral partnership dates back to a first summit in Cairo in November 2014. The latest declaration also addressed maritime boundaries, saying agreements should comply with international law, including the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Greece and Egypt signed an agreement covering part of their maritime boundary in 2020. Turkey rejected it at the time, arguing that the area covered overlapped with Ankara’s claimed continental shelf.

Mitsotakis said on Tuesday that the partnership between Egypt, Greece and Cyprus was “not directed against any country”.

World.title: Russian hackers may have used fake CAPTCHA to hack Ukrainian government computers
World.content:
A suspicious cyberattack using fake CAPTCHA checks to target a Ukrainian government organisation has been linked to Moscow, according to a new report.

 

US tech giant Cisco said its cybersecurity researchers noticed unusual activity in the organisation's computer systems in April, asserting “with moderate confidence” that a Russian threat actor carried out the attack.

Cisco's researchers found malware known as Amatera running on the system, capable of stealing sensitive information.

It was also used to install software that could give an attacker access to the computer, including the ability to inspect files, transfer data and run commands, according to the company.

Cisco found that the software was configured to connect to a server with an IP address based in Russia.

The report could not verify whether any information was actually stolen from the Ukrainian organisation, whether hackers actively used that access or how the computer was initially infected.

Cisco researchers however assessed that it was part of a broader operation designed to steal cryptocurrency and credentials.

“It was not clear what started the execution chain,” the report said.

Related This AI is combating money laundering and keeping out Russian oligarchs

CAPTCHA checks as traps

In the Ukrainian system, Cisco researchers had seen a malicious file disguised with the name “verification.google” but could not trace what had caused it to run.

To understand how the Ukrainian infection might have been started, they searched for similar attacks and found another infection involving the same Amatera malware.

This time, they traced it back to compromised websites showing fake versions of Google’s CAPTCHA verification check, used to distinguish human visitors from automated bots.

But instead of simply asking users to tick a box or identify images, the fake check told them to open a window on their computer and paste in text that would run malware.

In that infection, Amatera was also used to install a program designed to steal cryptocurrency.

The program could monitor cryptocurrency wallet addresses victims copied and replace them with addresses controlled by the attackers, potentially redirecting payments.

Cisco says similarities between the infections suggest the attack against Ukraine may have started in the same way.

However, researchers could not confirm that the two infections began the same way or that the same group carried them out.

World.title: EU to give cities more power to curb Airbnb and short-term rentals
World.content:
European cities will have greater powers to restrict short-term rentals such as Airbnb under EU plans unveiled on Wednesday aimed at tackling rising housing costs in popular tourist destinations.

 

The European Commission set out conditions under which local authorities will be able to limit short-term lets as part of its affordable housing package, designed to address what Commission Vice-President Teresa Ribera described as a “terrible crisis”.

“When the market fails to deliver something as fundamental as an affordable home, public authorities have a responsibility to act”, Ribera said.

Short-term rentals are popular among tourists, but residents in cities such as Lisbon, Barcelona and Prague have blamed platforms like Airbnb for reducing the supply of homes available for long-term rent and driving up prices, sometimes forcing locals to move elsewhere.

EU data from 2024 shows that nearly 10% of people living in EU cities spend more than 40% of their disposable income on housing.

Related Brussels to open door to curbing Airbnb and second homes in bid to ease housing burden

However, the Commission's upcoming restrictions would be allowed only in areas with clear evidence of serious housing pressure.

For Airbnb-style rentals, the EU is particularly concerned about commercial operators running several properties as holiday lets, rather than people occasionally renting out their own home.

Under the proposal, cities would be able to target professional multi-property operators, but a person's ability to rent out their main residence would be protected.

However, the Commission acknowledges that short-term rental restrictions and limits on second homes can't solve Europe's structural housing shortage. Other challenges include high construction costs, expensive land, planning restrictions and lengthy permit processes.

"Europe's housing crisis needs structural solutions, and the implementation of this act should focus on increasing the supply of homes," said an Airbnb spokesperson.

World.title: Hungary takes one more step to normalise relations with Brussels over rule of law
World.content:
The Hungarian government has formally notified the European Commission of the reforms it has passed to address the EU's rule of law concerns, in a move that could unlock €4.2 billion in cohesion funding and restore access to EU programmes.

 

"The European Commission has received Hungary's written notification under the Rule of Law Conditionality Regulation. The notification sets out measures to remedy the situation that led to the adoption of protective measures," the European Commissioner for Budget, Anti-Fraud and Public Administration, Piotr Serafin, wrote on X on Wednesday.

The notification follows an agreement struck in May between Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, which included funding blocked over corruption and rule-of-law concerns.

At the end of 2022, the Council of the EU formally suspended €6.3 billion in cohesion funding to Hungary under the conditionality mechanism, citing shortcomings in the country's anti-corruption framework, conflicts of interest and systemic irregularities in public procurement.

That initial sum has since been reduced due to losses, meaning Budapest could now recover €4.2bn as part of a broader normalisation in relations with Brussels that began after Magyar ousted Viktor Orbán from power in April.

Resolving the issue goes beyond unlocking this amount: the conditionality mechanism also blocked funding to Hungarian public interest trusts and related entities, a legal structure the government uses to take control of public institutions such as universities.

As a result, Hungary-based students and researchers were locked out of EU programmes such as the Erasmus+ exchange scheme and Horizon Europe research grants.

In recent weeks, the Commission and the Hungarian government have worked closely together, meaning Brussels does not expect any surprises when assessing whether the reforms passed sufficiently address its concerns, Euronews understands.

Hungary remains eligible for €10bn under the Recovery and Resilience Facility, the EU's post-pandemic stimulus instrument, with a payment request expected later this month.

Just over €2bn in cohesion funding remains blocked due to concerns about the asylum system, child protection law and academic freedom.

The Commission now has one month to complete its assessment, after which it will refer the matter to the Council with a draft decision — only member states can terminate the conditionality mechanism.

"We will now carefully examine the notification," Serafin added.

World.title: When war takes away the classroom, can children ever catch up?
World.content:
For millions of children living through conflict, war can mean months or even years away from the classroom.

 

From Ukraine to Sudan and Gaza, schools have been damaged or closed and education systems disrupted.

As the world marks the International Day to Protect Education from Attack on 9 September, the latest Education Under Attack report says at least 8,566 attacks on education and incidents involving the military use of schools and universities were recorded in 2024 and 2025.

That represents an increase of more than 40% compared with the previous reporting period, with at least 10,600 students, teachers, professors and other education personnel harmed.

For Education Above All Foundation Executive Director Dr Maleiha Malik, the numbers point to consequences that can follow children long after the fighting stops.

“The impact of that is devastating,” Dr Malik told Euronews.

Dr Malik said the damage goes beyond school buildings, affecting entire education systems and potentially feeding “long-term poverty and cycles of violence”.

A school in the Zeleny Hai village in the Mykolaiv region of southern Ukraine, dated 13 March 2022. Education Above All Foundation

‘We can't compensate for the damage’

One of the biggest questions is what happens to children who have already missed months or years of education.

Dr Malik says accelerated learning programmes and technology can help close some of those gaps, but there are limits to what can be recovered.

“We can have some accelerated learning, they can catch up, but I don't want to give the impression that there is any way we can compensate for the damage that conflict causes. We can't.”

Dr Maleiha Malik says technology and accelerated learning can help children catch up, but cannot undo the damage caused by conflict. Euronews

According to her, the COVID-19 pandemic showed both the cost of disrupted education and how learning can continue when children cannot physically be in a classroom.

“During COVID we were able to look at new technologies, ways of delivering learning outside the traditional paradigm of a school building,” Dr Malik said.

But catching up academically is only part of the challenge.

“Even before we think about knowledge gaps, learning gaps, we have to think about that child as a whole,” she said, stressing the need to address trauma and the emotional impact of conflict.

Palestinian students survey the damage at a school in Gaza, dated 2015. Education Above All Foundation

‘An alarming red line’

Malik also pointed to the sharp rise in attacks on education.

“A 40% increase isn't just a small increase, it's a surge,” she said.

Citing a recent UN report on children and armed conflict, Malik pointed to the role of government forces in attacks on schools as one of the most concerning developments.

“I think the really alarming red line we've crossed this year is that government forces have crossed the line and are willing to use extreme state violence to attack schools, to attack education.”

“We haven't seen it to this level,” Dr Malik added, highlighting what she described as a greater willingness by states to risk attacking civilian targets and infrastructure.

Children crowd an overworked teacher at Unity primary school in the Kakuma refugee camp in North Western Kenya. Education Above All Foundation

Conflict closer to home

Dr Malik said the impact of regional conflict is also being felt by children in Qatar and other Gulf countries.

She said children have had to become familiar with rocket fire and interceptions, sudden school closures, airports shutting down, and flights being grounded.

“Clearly, that is a kind of constant interference, constant stress, anxiety for children,” she said, adding that it can have psychosocial and emotional effects on children, parents and teachers.

For parents trying to explain what is happening, Dr Malik recommended being honest without unnecessarily alarming children and using age-appropriate language.

A damaged school in Gaza, dated 2015. Education Above All Foundation

International law is meant to protect schools and civilians during war. But as attacks on education rise, Dr Malik said the international system is falling short.

“You can't help but reach that conclusion,” she said. “I think there's a huge failure in terms of the international community.”

She argued that the answer is not to abandon international institutions, but to strengthen them.

“I'm more determined than ever and would call for a strengthening of our commitment to multilateralism as a way of bringing about peace rather than war," Dr Malik concluded.

World.title: France co-hosts major space summit with Germany despite US firms' withdrawals and Merz absence
World.content:
Astronauts, heads of state, as well as major economic players in the space industry are set to unite on Wednesday and Thursday at the international space summit, co-hosted by France and Germany, at Paris’ Grand Palais.

 

Several US companies reportedly withdrew from the event, due to pressure from Washington over support for "EU policy positions."

Despite this, the summit comes at a strategic crossroads for the European space industry, described by President Emmanuel Macron as an opportunity to "bring Europeans together around a common ambition" and develop a "shared vision of Europe's place on the map of global space powers by 2035" when he announced the event in October 2025.

According to the Elysée, the summit will focus on international space cooperation and strengthening space security. In recent years, Europe has increasingly sought to challenge US dominance of the global space market: developing its own homegrown rockets and increasing funding for space at both a state and bloc-wide level.

Europe has historically invested 0.07% of GDP into space programmes, compared with 0.24% by the US.

But 2025 marked a turning point, as the European Space Agency (ESA) approved a record-breaking €22.3 billion budget for its three-year funding cycle (2026–2028) in November, with €35 billion for space for security and defence.

Lunar mining has also emerged as a potential avenue for securing clean-energy resources and critical raw materials, as Europe works to move away from Chinese and Russian dependencies.

Divergence between France and Germany

Nearly a year after Macron announced the summit, it encountered some bumps in the road before the event had even begun. Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz confirmed on Friday that he would not attend the summit due to domestic commitments, with defence minister Boris Pistorius and space minister Dorothee Bär set to go in his place.

Behind the scenes, France and Germany have faced a number of disagreements over space and defence projects, ditching the Future Combat Air System (FCAS) project in June 2026, after years of disagreements.

Macron has consistently stressed the importance of building up Europe's strategic autonomy, backing programs like Ariane 6, rather than relying on US providers such as Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

Meanwhile, Germany has expressed a greater willingness to rely on lower-cost US alternatives, such as SpaceX. On Saturday, German startup Isar Aerospace launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from mainland Europe, marking a major turning point in Europe's quest to secure independent access to space. Merz described the launch as “the beginning of a new era.”

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks during the general debate as part of the budget deliberations in the Bundestag in Berlin, 9 September, 2026 AP Photo

US companies withdraw from event

A number of US companies also withdrew from the event, after a White House official reportedly warned them that their attendance "could look like tacit support for EU policy positions," Politico reported.

A spokesperson for France's Ministry of Higher Education and Research, which oversees national space policy, told the AFP news agency that SpaceX, Blue Origin, Stoke Space, and Starcloud had withdrawn from the event, stating "it’s hard not to link it to the rumours of pressure in the press.”

Speaking to Euronews, Hermann Ludwig Moeller, Director of the European Space Policy Institute described France as a "driving force" in Europe's space sector, providing "strong political support" to the industry, stressing that the "relevance of space is only increasing."

A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket with the space observatory Roman Telescope lifts off from launch the Kennedy Space Centre, 30 August, 2026 AP Photo

"It is increasingly becoming a war fighting domain, while at the same time it has become evident also to the general public that conflict has become hybrid in nature, for instance through attacks on critical infrastructures in transport, energy, digital. This is where space can provide increased resilience."

Moeller stressed the role that space technologies such as satellite navigation have in terms of both civilian and military usage.

"While they are essential to everyday life, the war in Ukraine has also highlighted their strategic importance in modern warfare", he said.

Kyiv's reliance on Musk's Starlink following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has underlined the strategic importance of space services during wartime — that the satellite network provides resilient internet connectivity even when infrastructure is damaged or destroyed.

This reality also pushed Europe to develop its own independent satellite networks, notably the secure internet constellation known as IRIS².

World.title: Oil prices rise as Middle East conflict escalates
World.content:
The price of oil returned to triple digits in US dollars, as conflict in the Middle East threatens supply chains and puts a strain on global reserves.

Oil crude prices topped $100 ($86) a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July amid concerns over oil supplies due to the conflict in the Middle East.

"The move towards and back above $100 Brent is reflecting a market that increasingly must change its view on how long the Middle East crisis will continue to curb supply from the region," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at the Danish Saxo Bank.

The attacks on Saudi energy facilities by the Iranian-backed Houthisthreaten oil shipments on the Red Sea. This has been a key alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz path.

Meanwhile, the US attacked Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and in the Strait of Hormuz. "Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies," CENTCOM said in a statement.

Runing out of stock

Since the conflict in the Middle East started, oil exports have been reduced significantly, making some countries turn to their reserves.

The US has reported its lowest oil reserve since 1982, holding 289.7 million barrels. Former US President Joe Biden and President Donald Trump have used the reserve to cushion consumer prices amid the crisis.

The new price of the barrel is still below the peak reached early this year. In April, Brent jumped to $126 a barrel. Experts believe this is a big risk to a market with little room for capacity to absorb new disruptions occasioned by the war.

World.title: Syria arms depot explosion kills at least 14
World.content:
The explosion struck near the Syrian city of Sarmada in Idlib province in the northwest. The Defense Ministry said the weapons and remnants from the war were being stored temporarily at the site before being relocated.

Syrian authorities reported that at least 14 people were killed and another 11 wounded on Wednesday as a result of an explosion at a temporary site used to store weapons and remnants of the country's long-running civil war.

The explosion took place near the city of Sarmada in the northwestern Idlib province.

Emergency services and Red Cross workers rushed to locate and if possible rescue victims potentially trapped beneath the rubble Image: Moawia Atrash/dpa/picture alliance

What do we know about the explosion?

Syria's Defense Ministry said the weapons and war remnants were being stored termporarily at the site before being transported elsewhere. It said that some of its personnel were among those wounded.

The explosion in an area full of volatile materials led to secondary explosions and fires that hampered the emergency response. Smoke billowed from the blast site for some time on Wednesday.

"The toll from the explosion in a temporary storage for collecting weapons and war remnants near the city of Sarmada ... registered 14 killed and 11 injured in a preliminary count," the Idlib health department said.

Firefigthers battled to bring the primary and secondary fires under control Image: Kasim Yusuf/Anadolu/picture alliance

Authorities have not yet said what caused the explosion.

It was the second fatal incident of its kind in Idlib province this month. On September 1, five people were killed and others were wounded when a vehicle carrying ammunition exploded in Binnish.

Syria only recently emerged from more than a decade of civil war, when forces loyal to new President Ahmed al-Sharaa ousted Bashar Assad and took control of Damascus. Idlib was one of the hardest-hit regions in the country during the war.

Idlib province is still awash with ordnance after fierce fighting from 2011 until late 2024 Image: Kasim Yusuf/Anadolu/picture alliance

World.title: How Belarusians still find hope in a silenced country
World.content:
The documentary "Letters From the Silenced Country" depicts the ongoing repression under the authoritarian regime. Director Andrei Kutsila talked to DW ahead of the film's Venice premiere.

When Belarusians took to the streets in 2020 to protest against the disputed results of the presidential election, hopes were high that the regime of autocratic ruler Alexander Lukashenko would end, and that Belarusian society would find freedom.

But authorities responded with an unprecedented campaign of repression that continues to this day. All forms of dissent have essentially been silenced.

It's in this context that filmmaker Andrei Kutsila directed a new documentary that depicts the state's system of repression.

His film, "Letters from the Silenced Country," was co-produced by DW and premieres at the Venice Film Festival on September 9.

A silenced country

Like the 300,000 to 500,000 Belarusians who now live in exile, Kutsila realized that he had to leave his home country amid the state's crackdown on free speech.

While he was completing his previous film — the award-winning "When Flowers Are Not Silent" (2021), on the state's brutal suppression of demonstrations — different colleagues around him were arrested, he says.

Many of them have since been released, "but at the same time, new prisoners are found to keep filling the cells. The situation is not changing; it's even worse now," Kutsila tells DW.

As the film points out in a postscript card, the human rights organization Viasna has documented at least 65,000 politically motivated arrests and detentions in Belarus since the 2020 protests.

"From the outside, people live their normal lives, but the streets have become quiet and conversations are reduced to whispers," says Kutsila. Those who remained in the country can get arrested and sent to prison simply for posting Belarusian symbols of freedom and resistance online, notes the filmmaker.

That was one of the reasons that motivated him to make "Letters from the Silenced Country."

Returning to Belarus and to physically meet and film protagonists in his home country was not an option, so he searched for an alternative way to portray their situation after the protests.

Letters to prisoners served as a starting point to Kutsila's film project: "I read thousands of them," he says.

He then picked stories of individuals — political prisoners, exiles and underground activists — who embodied different aspects of the situation.

Footage from Belarusian prisons exposes harsh conditions for political detainees Image: DW/ZDF/Arte

Vitold Ashurak died in prison

Belarusian opposition activist and environmental campaigner Vitold Ashurak is one of the film's protagonists.

Sentenced to five years in prison for participating in the protests, Ashurak's fate is portrayed through his correspondence with friends and family during his imprisonment.

Letters from a friend include meticulously selected photographs. Ashurak finds brief moments of mental freedom in these pictures, while the same images are also poetically embedded in the film.

But CCTV footage showing prison guards beating inmates brings viewers back to the brutal reality: Vitold Ashurak died under suspicious circumstances while in custody. His name is remembered as a symbol of the state's repression.

Between resignation and hope

The film also includes animated sequences, based on drawings created by the young student Kasia Budzko, who was sentenced to 2 1/2 years in prison for participating in protests.

Another protagonist in the film is Andrei Ostapovich, a former criminal investigator. In August 2020, he left his position, writing a letter of resignation in which he denounced the police officers' brutality against protesters.

In the film, Ostapovich describes the sadistic tendencies he saw among the police force Image: DW/ZDF/Arte

As one of the first security officials who publicly and categorically opposed the Belarusian regime, Ostapovich fled the country — facing many perilous detours.

In one scene of "Letters from the Silenced Country," Ostapovich is asked if, after everything he's been through and witnessed, he still believes in a free Belarus. After much hesitation, his only response is a sigh of resignation.

Filmmaker Andrei Kutsila shares this ambivalence: "Of course, it's in a way my perspective too, as I tried to express my feelings through my protagonists." But, Kutsila focuses on long-term progress, as he adds, "history is the foundation on which we can build a free country."

"You know, 200 years ago Belarus didn't even exist on a map," he points out. There have been struggles to free the country ever since: "So from this long-term perspective, there is a lot of hope."

"No matter how awful the situation is, the only thing that can empower and give us hope is solidarity, connection between people and love. So these are the things giving us hope," notes Kutsila. "And the film, I think, shows this."

Edited by: Brenda Haas

World.title: Why we're still looking for dark matter
World.content:
When physicists said they may have spotted evidence of dark matter almost 100 years after it was proposed as a theory, the internet lit up. Here's why we're searching for the thing that holds everything else together.

On September 1, 2026, scientists at a dark matter detector called LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) reported they had observed an event, a particle interaction, that they were unable to explain.

The team, based in South Dakota in the US, said the event resembled what they think a dark matter particle should produce when it collides with liquid xenon, one of a range of materials used for detecting dark matter.

They stopped short of calling it the discovery, or proof of dark matter, that many in the field have been hunting for almost 100 years.

The term "dark matter" was coined by physicist Fritz Zwicky in 1933 as a means to describe unseen matter that would explain fast-moving galaxies.

The LUX-ZEPLIN observation came just days after the release of the second season of Dark Matter, a sci-fi thriller starring Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly. Both events pushed the term "dark matter" back into people's minds.

Here's what you need to know, with the science separated from the series.

What is dark matter in simple terms?

Dark matter is often described as an "invisible" substance. But it may be better described as "transparent" because it can be seen, or detected, by the gravitational attraction it exerts.

That said, it neither emits nor reflects light, and has never been observed directly. So, in that sense, it is invisible.

Is it true that 95% of the universe is invisible?

Yes, roughly.

Ordinary matter — everything that can be seen or touched — accounts for about 5% of the universe.

Dark matter accounts for about 27%, and dark energy, a separate force linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe, about 68%. Together they account for about 95%.

A different figure of 85% is dark matter's share of matter alone.

But does dark matter really exist?

The strongest evidence that dark matter exists comes from the so-called Bullet Cluster, which formed when two galaxy clusters collided. The collision produced hot gas clouds that interacted. This interaction showed revealed mass in the gas clouds that distributed differently from the gas. Researchers said that mass could be dark matter.

Earth spins at 1,670 km/h: Why don't we feel it? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How do scientists search for dark matter on Earth?

Scientists use detectors like the LUX-ZEPLIN that passively wait for interactions between naturally occurring particles and detect radiation.

They tend to be buried deep underground, where the surrounding rock blocks cosmic radiation that would otherwise distort signals.

They are built from materials chosen for their very low levels of trace radioactivity, so a genuine detection is not lost in background noise.

The LUX-ZEPLIN detector specifically works by watching for a faint flash of light and pulse of electric charge released when a passing particle strikes a liquid xenon particle. Liquid xenon, a noble gas, has good properties for detecting radiation.

What is dark matter made of?

The leading candidate particles are:

WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles, are the longest-standing theory. They are heavy and interact only rarely with ordinary matter.

Axions, which are lighter and behave more coherently than WIMPs. A team at Kyoto University, Japan, say data from Earth's magnetic field could be used to search for axions.

What does dark matter do to humans?

Dark matter passes through the body constantly, without measurable effect. Billions of candidate particles cross through a person every second, but only about ten strike a nucleus in the body over a year.

The resulting radiation exposure is far lower than what people receive from radon or cosmic rays.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

World.title: Cambodia's floating schools hit by rising fuel costs
World.content:
The Iran war has sent fuel prices higher in Cambodia, squeezing families who rely on fishing and boats for their livelihoods. For children living on Tonle Sap, rising fuel costs pose yet another barrier to education.

Every morning, 12-year-old Soksan Set faces a journey most children his age never have to think about. Outside his home, there is no road, only water.

Soksan lives in Prek Toal, a floating community on Tonle Sap, Southeast Asia's largest freshwater lake where boats are the main means of transport. A Grade 4 student at the local primary school, he travels several kilometers on water to attend class and sometimes helps younger children along the way.

But increasingly, the biggest obstacle between Soksan and his classroom is not distance. It is fuel. His family, like many others in the commune, depends on fishing for their livelihood. When fuel prices rise, they are forced to make difficult choices.

"When gasoline prices go up, we don't have enough money to take our children to school regularly," said Soksan's father, 41-year-old Set Soeum. "We don't catch enough fish, and we need around three liters (0.8 gallons) of gasoline a day to travel long distances for fishing. Because of this, Soksan often has to miss school."

For families living on the water, rising fuel costs can quickly become a barrier to education.

Remote schools also depend on boats to transport teachers, textbooks, classroom materials, food and maintenance supplies Image: Action Education/Education Above All Foundation

Why rising fuel costs hit Cambodia's poor the hardest

Cambodia relies heavily on imported fuel, leaving households exposed to global price shocks and regional supply disruptions. The 2026 Iran war has driven up energy costs, making transport to remote communities more expensive. Around Tonle Sap, this has hit students and their families.

Gasoline prices rose 45% and diesel prices more than 70% in March, the largest single-month increase since 2008, according to the World Bank.

Gasoline currently costs 5,700 riel ($1.41, €1.21) per liter, up 26.7% from 4,500 riel a year ago, according to Global Petrol Prices.

Although Cambodia does not depend directly on the Strait of Hormuz for most of its fuel imports, it is exposed to higher global oil prices and supply disruptions affecting regional suppliers. Cambodia imports all of its petroleum products and has no domestic refining capacity.

For Soksan's family, the pressure is felt both on the fishing boat and the school boat. Some days, they borrow money to buy gasoline. On other days, they cut back on food, clothing or school supplies.

"Five students collect money to buy gasoline, sometimes just one liter at a time," Soksan said. When they cannot afford even that, they row themselves. "We row the boat ourselves. It can take up to an hour, but we still try to go to school," he noted.

On the Tonle Sap, 12-year-old Siyien Ly walks more than 30 minutes to school during the dry season. When flooding makes the roads impassable, she relies on an aid-supported school boat. Some of her classmates have stopped attending, because their families cannot afford the cost of transport.

"Even though fuel prices are rising, we still keep trying to come to school because education is important for our future," Siyien said.

Siyien's family of six has four children in school. Her mother, Kunthea Chin, now sells sugarcane juice after Siyien's father developed serious hearing problems following a water-related accident.

Kunthea said that her daily income has fallen by around half from about $20 to around $10 while the cost of supplies has risen. The family spends around $150 a month on fuel, which they need for both the children's transport and her business.

Cambodia's floating schools face brunt of climate crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Taking risks to reach the classroom

Families also try to reduce costs by traveling together and sharing fuel expenses. Some have returned to traditional rowing boats. But saving money can come at the cost of safety.

When several children share a small boat, it can become crowded. During storms and heavy rain, parents worry about their children's safety on the water.

"My mother worries when too many students ride together," Siyien said.

Remote schools also depend on boats to transport teachers, textbooks, classroom materials, food and maintenance supplies. Higher fuel prices can therefore increase the cost of delivering education itself.

"For children living in floating and remote communities, access to education depends not only on having a school, but also on being able to reach it," said Samphors Vorn, country director of Action Education in Cambodia.

"When fuel prices rise, the cost of that journey rises with them. For families already living with very limited incomes, this can turn transportation into a barrier to attendance and, ultimately, to a child's right to education."

The Cambodian government has introduced measures to cushion consumers from international fuel-price increases, including fuel discounts, tax reductions and zero customs duties on fuel imports.

But subsidies at the pump cannot fully shield families whose incomes remain low and unpredictable.

Climate and economic shocks deepen education woes

In 2025, DW reported from the region on how climate change was disrupting children's education. Rising and falling water levels, extreme weather and the dangers of traveling by boat were making it harder for children in floating communities to reach school.

The challenges have since deepened.

Increasingly, the biggest obstacle between Soksan and his classroom is not distance, it is fuel. Image: Action Education/Education Above All Foundation

Today, 14-year-old Nary is no longer in the classroom. She has been unable to return because of persistent headaches following health complications linked to suspected long-term meningitis.

Her younger sister, 11-year-old Naren, continues to attend Grade 2. She relies on a school boat and pays around 12 cents for the return journey.

For their family, even small costs matter. Their father, Tit Sarin, earns around $7.50 a day from traditional fishing. But traveling farther across the lake to find fish can require about six liters of fuel, costing roughly $6.60.

"When we cannot afford fuel, we have to find other work," he said.

The family then works as day laborers, picking chilies for as little as 25 cents per kilogram. For families like Nary's, climate change and rising fuel costs are now a double burden.

Nary hopes to return to learning. Her father is saving to buy a boat dedicated to shuttling his children to school and back home.

This report was made possible by inputs from Education Above All foundation.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: EU proposes more restrictions for Airbnb, holiday rentals
World.content:
The European Union wants tighter rules on short-term rentals to tackle housing shortages in tourist hotspots.

Airbnb and other companies providing short-term home rentals could face tighter restrictions after the European Commission proposed new rules on Wednesday to help tackle housing shortages in tourist hotspots.

A surge in short-term holiday rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing and a spike in housing prices in many of Europe's most popular tourist destinations, prompting residents to protest in recent years .

What do we know about the EU's affordable housing proposal?

The EU's executive branch unveiled the measures as part of an "affordable housing" package, which will allow local authorities to limit short-term rentals to address what European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera described as a "terrible crisis."

"When the market fails to deliver something as fundamental as an affordable home, public authorities have a responsibility to act," the Spanish politician said.

The measures seek to harmonize rules across the bloc, after attempts to crack down on Airbnb-style rentals by authorities in cities such as Paris, Berlin and Barcelona, among others, were met with legal challenges by rental and tourism companies.

The European Commission's Affordable Housing Act — which still needs to be approved by EU legislators and EU member states — would provide cities with legal support by clarifying when local authorities can act against housing companies without breaking EU single market rules.

Under the proposal, city and local authorities would be allowed to limit short-term and holiday rentals as well as curb the purchase of property for short-term letting in areas considered to be "under housing stress," the European Commission said.

Spain: Tourism boom worsens housing crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For an area to be defined as "under stress," certain parameters — including the ratio between local housing prices and incomes — would have to be met.

Before restrictions can be introduced, cities would have to show that holiday rentals have had a major negative impact on the affordability or availability of housing for at least three years.

The proposed legislation will not impact landlords renting out their primary residence for short-term periods.

The Commission also recommended that authorities free up land for more housing and modernize planning and construction of new homes to address housing shortages.

How have rental companies reacted?

CCIA Europe, a lobbying group that represents Airbnb, among others, said the EU's measures fail to address the need for independent assessment of the restrictions.

"Europe will not solve its housing crisis by giving cities an EU framework to restrict short-term rentals and then letting them police their own ​compliance," CCIA's head of ⁠policy Alexandre Roure said in a statement.

"Without independent scrutiny or effective redress, this proposal will remain a paper tiger, leaving disproportionate restrictions ⁠in place and undermining ​the legal certainty the Affordable Housing Act is meant to provide," Roure added.

World.title: Syria: How  the 'house of sisters' threat split society
World.content:
Rumor has it that the 'house of sisters' is where kidnapped women from other Syrian sects are forced to convert to Islam. Nobody knows if it really exists, but it's being used to create communal tensions anyway.

A knock on the door, a muted threat and then they made the decision to leave the country, says Layla, a math teacher and mother-of-three in her 40s.

Until recently, Layla — who didn't want DW to use her full name for security reasons — was living in Damascus, Syria's capital. She and her family are Alawites, the same religious sect as former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad, who are often targeted because they're seen as Assad's allies.

"But we never supported him, his father killed members of my family. We hated him actually," she told DW. Still, she describes feeling fearful when rebel groups entered Damascus in 2024 for the first time after the fall of the Assad regime, calling them "extremists."

At first, she and her husband decided to stay in Syria. But then a stranger came to the door.

"He told me 'we know your daughter plays piano and has dance lessons. You should stop that. If you don't, maybe we will take her to the house of the sisters," Layla recounts.

In conservative Islamic circles, women playing music and dancing for an audience is frowned upon. And Layla had heard about the so-called "house of the sisters" — she had read online it was a place where Syrian women from other sects were forced to convert to Islam. A few days later, the family decided to leave the country. They are now in Lebanon.

"I just don't want my children to grow up that way," Layla explains.

What is the 'house of sisters'?

Headlines about the "house of sisters" first really made waves in Syria in May after an Alawite university student Batoul Alloush, 21, was reported missing by her family, possibly kidnapped, only to turn up later wearing religious clothing and saying she left her family in order to convert to Islam.

There were already other stories of missing women, including from the Alawite minority.

Reham Suleiman, a psychologist who works for the United Nations and with the Alawite community, told DW she has firsthand knowledge of several cases of kidnapping. "And it’s not just one incident or coincidence," she says. It is clear some of women were kidnapped for ransom money, revenge or forced marriage.

But other cases were apparently resolved when, for example, the women said they had been visiting friends, wanted to escape their families or had run away to a lover. Alloush herself said she wished to convert to Islam and leave her family. Her parents insist she's been drugged or coerced.

Organizations like Amnesty International and the UN's Commission of Inquiry on Syria say the cases — which number between 40 and 60 ­­— have not been fully investigated.

A political football

Syrian authorities did look into the "house of sisters." A spokesperson for Syria's Minister of Social Affairs, Hind Kabawat, told DW that the ministry has not licensed any facility with that name and that any unlicensed centers of this nature would be shut down.

Syrian fact-checking organizations like Verify-Sy found that pictures of the supposed "house of sisters" building were created with AI.

"A constant stream of unverified claims circulates on a daily basis concerning alleged kidnappings and killings, arrests and cases of torture in detention facilities," a spokesperson from Verify-Sy told DW.

"Verifying many of these is challenging when evidence available through open sources is scarce, contradictory or otherwise insufficient."

So whether the "house of sisters" exists in some form is unclear. But real or not, some groups appear to have instrumentalized it for their own agenda anyway, independent media outlet Shaam News Network, or SNN, wrote recently .

"Despite the absence of any physical evidence … social media platforms and pages began circulating 'the house' as an established fact," SNN wrote. "And it gradually became the focus of broader narratives about the 'organized kidnapping' of Alawite women."

International influencers

A private organization called the Syrian Investigation Mechanism, or SIM, founded in May 2026, links the "house of sisters" to a Muslim organization that proselytizes to gain new converts. SIM claimed the missing women were coerced into converting and held in "the house."

In an interview on YouTube , SIM director Yasser Shalati, who is based in Brandenburg, Germany, claims this is evidence of "demographic engineering." SIM did not reply to DW's requests for further comment.

Christian neighborhood in Damascus: There have been reports of more attempts to convert others to Islam since the fall of the Assad regime, which treated proselytizing as a threat to national security Image: Mohammad Bashir Aldaher/imageBROKER/picture alliance

A Berlin-based organization, the Union of Syrian Alawites in Europe, or USAE, has also repeatedly posted about the "house of sisters."

On his personal Facebook page, Muaiad Ibrahim, who is listed as USAE's deputy director in official court documents, regularly criticizes the new Syrian government and recently expressed support for Syria's highest religious scholar under the Assad regime, Ahmed Hassoun. In late August, Hassoun was sentenced to life in prison after being convicted of inciting civil war and complicity in intentional killing.

Other recently founded overseas organizations — including some that claim they have a network of millions of human rights advocates but link to incomplete websites — have also repeatedly disseminated stories about the "house of sisters."

Arab investigative journalism outfit DARAJ notes some of these organizations have been criticized for their apparent support of the Assad regime .

The damage done?

"This kind of information ebbs and flows, but it does have a real impact and its quite powerful," says Gregory Waters, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, who's traveled extensively in Syria and monitors events on his site, Syria Revisited.

"It has the political intent to isolate Alawites, to make them fearful and keep them from engaging with the government, with [Syrian] Sunnis, and maybe to some extent, pull them towards insurgent [anti-government] networks."

Online propaganda feeds on real events within minority communities, adding to their existing fears, he says.

Verify Sy conducts a monthly audit of online disinformation, and researchers there say incitement is the second most common objective. Waters says Syrian authorities have been trying to rein in local influencers who spread disinformation, although obviously they can't impact those based overseas.

Syrians are still finding mass graves after 14 years of a civil war that has resulted in polarized opinions among locals Image: Ugur Yildirim/DIA/IMAGO

Like anywhere else in the world, you'll get a wide spectrum of opinions within every Syrian community, Waters notes. "There are there those who will insist that there's a program of ethnic cleansing, and there are others who say life is fine, we are fully integrated into the state."

Although it depends which part of the country you're looking at, he doesn't think relations between different communities are getting worse.

"In Syria, everything is unique to its local environment," Waters explains. "So in some places, we could say that walls between communities have hardened over the past two years and little progress has been made in reducing that. But even so, the walls are not getting higher."

Stabilization first

"Right now, generally speaking, the government in Damascus is busy establishing institutions, taking control of the security situation and trying to stabilize the country," argues Naseef Naeem, research director at the Berlin-based Candid Foundation, which consults on Syrian affairs. But sooner or later, Syria is going to need more of a national dialogue between different community groups, he says.

In the meantime, both he and Waters believe the Syrian economy, devastated after years of war, could hold the key to better relations.

Every summer, Latakia's beaches in western Syria are a popular destination for thousands of Syrian holidaymakers Image: Elisa Gestri/Sipa USA/picture alliance

"As soon as the economic recovery really gets underway, many of these phenomena will gradually disappear," Naeem told DW.

For example, Waters says, over summer, a lot of domestic tourists, many of them Sunni, made their way to the Syrian coast, an area where many Alawites live.

"There was a massive tourism boom," Waters explains. "Everybody's interacting and I've heard from friends there that there wasn't harassment, no violence. The government and security authorities really emphasized supporting the tourism industry in coastal areas this year and it's had a really positive impact."

Those kinds of inter-community contacts in real life "help reduce the impact of disinformation campaigns and the level of fear," he concludes.

Edited by: K. Hairsine

World.title: LIV Golf in financial turmoil: what's next for the sport?
World.content:
Six months after Saudi Arabia pulled funding from the breakaway organization, LIV Golf have filed for bankruptcy protection. Several of the world's best players signed on to LIV, so where does that leave golf?

What has happened to LIV golf?

The breakaway golf tour, launched with much fanfare, billions of dollars of investment and a string of the world's best players, in 2021. But on Tuesday it filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States.

Bankruptcy protection is a way of keeping a company alive while it restructures its debts. In this case, LIV would be moving from being financed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), which pulled out in April, to being supported by BC Partners, a British investment firm.

"This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf," said the chief executive, Scott O'Neil.

According to documents related to the filing, LIV Golf has between $500m (€430 million) and $1 billion in estimated liabilities to at least 1,000 creditors. This includes an estimated $45 million to a group of top players like Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7 million), Jon Rahm ($7.5 million) and Dustin Johnson ($5.7million).

O'Neil added that LIV intends to move towards a "player-first ownership model," but detail is thin, and there is currently no schedule in place for 2027. Most of LIV's staff were laid off earlier this year.

What has caused LIV golf to go bankrupt?

The sudden withdrawal of the PIF, which had invested an estimated $5 billion in LIV Golf, is the over-riding reason. At the time, the PIF said that LIV Golf was "no longer consistent with the current phase of PIF's investment strategy."

This was considered evidence of the project's failure to overthrow the established PGA Tour or make much in the way of money or impact. While the huge prize money on offer lured away several big names, many more remained with the PGA Tour.

While Tuesday's legal move may buy LIV time, the withdrawal of Saudi funding, which was so key to its business model, gives O'Neil few options. To survive, it seems, it they must keep at least some of their big-name players while slimming down dramatically.

Why is Saudi Arabia investing billions in sports? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Is this further evidence of Saudi Arabia pulling out of sport?

It certainly seems that investment in golf is a thing of the past for the oil-rich, Gulf state. There have also been withdrawals of funding for tournaments, clubs or organizations in snooker, women's tennis, rugby and football. Saudi Arabia also backed away from its commitment to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games.

Sport was a key part of Vision 2030, a pet project of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that aimed to diversify the Saudi economy and, in the eyes of many, also help launder its reputation through sport and other cultural assets.

Saudi Arabia is scaling back many sporting plans, including for World Cup 2034 Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

The uncertainty caused by conflict in the Middle East has meant even the vast wealth of the Saudi ruling class has taken a hit while projects like the resort of Trojena, set to be a key resort in those Winter Games, have been scaled back.

The same is true of Neom, a proposed World Cup venue for 2034. Planned as an entirely new type of city — 500 meters high (1,640 foot), built in a straight line and powered by renewable energy, Neom's construction has been significantly scaled back. The Guardian reported in late 2025 that several proposed World Cup stadium architects have been asked to rethink their plans to cut costs.

What will happen to the LIV golf players now?

It is unclear what will happen to the LIV golf players. The PGA Tour and LIV Golf have always had a frosty relationship. Any player leaving to join LIV was immediately suspended from the PGA Tour, which runs all of golf's major championships.

The 'returning member program', used by US golfer Brooks Koepka earlier this year to return to the PGA, briefly offered a potential pathway. It was designed as a "route back to elite performers who no longer have contractual limitations preventing them from complying with PGA Tour rules and regulations."

However it is was only open to players who left the PGA Tour at least two years ago and have won the Players Championship or one of the four majors.

DeChambeau, Cam Smith and Rahm were, therefore, the only players that qualified. But with that door now seemingly closed even to them, a return looks complex.

"I'm not part of the discussions but I'm pretty sure they aren't going to be welcomed back straight away," said Rory McIlroy, a six-time major winner who has been consistently critical of LIV, in August.

"They were offered this returning member program back in February, the one Brooks [Koepka] took, but that has come and gone, and I think it was said at the time that the deal they get going forward if they decide to come back would not be as good at the one Brooks got. So I'd say it will be a tough road back."

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

World.title: Feijóo y Abascal acusan al presidente de no ser libre con Rabat y Sánchez replica: “Seré un perro, pero sin amo”
World.content:
Pedro Sánchez esperó hasta la última réplica al líder de Vox, Santiago Abascal, para soltar la frase que tenía más que estudiada: “A diferencia de usted, yo seré un perro, pero no tengo amo”. El presidente del Gobierno solventó así su primera sesión de control en el Congreso del nuevo curso político, que nace en pleno conflicto sin resolver en Ceuta y con la perspectiva omnipresente de unas elecciones generales aún sin fecha agendada. El PP y Vox siguieron un mismo guion en su acoso parlamentario a Sánchez: le acusaron de estar atado, condicionado, comprometido y de no ser libre con Marruecos. Abascal le quiere llevar a juicio por traición. El líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, metió esa imputación política en otro potaje con todos los problemas y escándalos que enfrentan Sánchez y su equipo. El presidente habló del Informe PISA y de que quedan retos por afrontar, y culminó sobre las exigidas elecciones: “Nos veremos en 2027 y les volveremos a ganar”.

En la estrategia de pintar la España de Sánchez como un territorio perdido ya en la “degradación” total, el líder de la oposición usó su primer duelo parlamentario de este periodo de sesiones en el Congreso para reseñarlo todo, desde los penosos resultados de PISA sobre la educación, “las aulas vacías en Ceuta pero llenas de espray pimienta”, las penurias económicas de las familias, el varapalo del Supremo a los intentos de nacionalización de descendientes de exiliados en la ley de nietos o los casos judiciales en marcha contra el PSOE en los tribunales. Con esos ingredientes como entrante, Feijóo llegó donde quería al subrayar que “el futuro político y personal” de Sánchez depende de otros, que pueden “cantar” en los juzgados o que pueden actuar como Marruecos.

02:17 Sánchez a Abascal: "A diferencia de usted, yo seré un perro, pero no tengo amo" El líder de Vox, Santiago Abascal durante la primera sesión de control del Congreso del curso político, este miércoles. Foto: EFE/ J.J. Guillén | Vídeo: EPV

Para Feijóo, el presidente de España “no es libre” y está condicionado, argumentando que “la agresión” sufrida en Ceuta fue “consentida e impulsada por Marruecos” y no ha tenido consecuencias. El dirigente popular formuló una pregunta a Sánchez que quedó sin respuesta directa: “Si mañana volvieran a entrar en Ceuta 80.000 personas, ¿usted qué haría?”.

Sánchez constató que Feijóo lo mezcla todo en sus intervenciones y optó por elegir solo una para centrarse en su primera respuesta. Habló de su “extraordinaria preocupación” por las consecuencias del Informe PISA, pero no lo hizo para mostrar autocrítica. El presidente ofreció datos para subrayar que durante su etapa al frente del Ejecutivo se han multiplicado por dos las inversiones en educación, de 3.200 millones de euros en los gobiernos de Mariano Rajoy a 6.000. A su vez, destacó que las autonomías son las que tienen más competencias educativas. Sánchez se agarró ahí a que aún queda legislatura y que el PP podría apoyar dos leyes relevantes en esa materia, como la de docentes que fija la ratio de alumnos en clase o la que plantea prohibir el uso descontrolado de las redes sociales a los menores de 16 años.

El líder popular presumió, por su parte, de que en la clasificación PISA las autonomías que salen mejor paradas, Madrid y Castilla y León ―aunque también Asturias (PSOE)―, son gobernadas por el PP, y las que peor, Ceuta y Melilla, dependen en esa cuestión del Gobierno central. También insistió en que Sánchez tiene su “lealtad comprometida” con Marruecos y acabó con un mensaje amenazante que más tarde repitieron casi todos los diputados del PP a los demás ministros y, en particular, al titular de Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska. Feijóo avisó a Sánchez: “Ha desprestigiado a su país y su país se lo hará pagar. Ponga fecha y nos vemos en las urnas”.

El presidente ratificó que efectivamente en 2027 habrá elecciones generales en España y vaticinó: “Nos veremos y les volveremos a ganar”. Pero también quiso reprochar al PP su cuestionamiento ahora de la llamada ley de nietos y las consecuencias de la paralización por parte del Tribunal Supremo del derecho a voto de los nacionalizados por esta vía. Sánchez recordó que con esa norma ya se celebraron los comicios de 2023 que ganó Feijóo, incluso en el voto exterior.

“Chantajeado” por Marruecos

El anticipo de Feijóo lo machacó en su intervención el líder de Vox, Santiago Abascal, que percutió aún más sobre los indemostrados compromisos del presidente con Marruecos. Abascal concluyó que Sánchez está siendo “chantajeado” por el país vecino con información sobre su familia; derivó de ahí que, por tanto, “el Gobierno de España está en Rabat, la presidencia en Marruecos” y avisó de que los objetivos de ese país, además de Ceuta, Melilla y Canarias, serán la islamización y convertir España en su “protectorado”. Sánchez casi miró para Feijóo para alertar de que Abascal “es una amenaza para España y Europa”. El presidente aseguró ahí que su Gobierno “no acepta el chantaje de ningún partido, país o poder” y, ante el retrato con que Abascal le presenta “con una correa al cuello”, le soltó que será “un perro”, pero sin amo. Abascal prescindió de los 12 segundos que le quedaban para formular la réplica a la que aún tenía derecho.

El portavoz de ERC en el Congreso, Gabriel Rufián, volvió con su monotema desde que empezó a advertir del tsunami que cree que se le viene encima a la izquierda en las próximas elecciones. Le preguntó otra vez a Sánchez por cómo afronta lo que queda de legislatura. Sánchez le mencionó como ejemplo las leyes educativas pendientes. Rufián le resumió el balance de las últimas 10 encuestas publicadas estas semanas por todo tipo de medios: el PP y Vox lograrían entre 194 y 213 escaños. Y alarmó de las regresiones en todo tipo de servicios públicos que podría provocar un ejecutivo de la derecha y la ultraderecha juntos. Sánchez compartió esa inquietud, pero no ofreció más receta que la de seguir avanzando.

02:16 Rufián: "¿Ha dicho que quiere ser presidente en el 27 y más allá? No me salen las cuentas" El portavoz de ERC en el Congreso, Gabriel Rufian, durante una sesión plenaria en el Congreso de los Diputados, a 9 de septiembre de 2026, en Madrid (España). Foto: Eduardo Parra | Vídeo: EPV

La sesión ya se adentró a partir de ahí en otros territorios. Todos los diputados restantes del PP, en preguntas al vicepresidente Carlos Cuerpo y a los ministros Félix Bolaños y Fernando Grande-Marlaska, les atizaron por Ceuta, hablaron de la invasión sufrida frente a la tesis de la crisis humanitaria y les previnieron, no quedó claro con qué información, de que acabarán pagando todo lo ocurrido en esa ciudad autónoma. A Marlaska, varios diputados del PP le afearon el informe interno de trabajo de su gabinete de comunicación en el que se retrata a decenas de periodistas, tertulianos y analistas sobre su definición ideológica. El ministro negó ese objetivo y esbozó un intento de pedir disculpas si las formas de ese documento no fueron las adecuadas.

World.title: Se intensifican las agresiones en Ceuta: “Me gritaron invasora y tuberculosa, me pidieron el DNI”
World.content:
Soraya Eguizábal tiene 13 años, un apellido vasco y la piel oscura. Es ceutí de nacimiento. “Vamos, que su abuela también nació aquí”, añade su madre, Fátima Taieb. Suena a justificación, porque lo es. La niña fue agredida verbalmente en una manifestación porque la confundieron con una migrante el pasado domingo. Lo cuenta pausada, un día después de que ocurriera y también la víspera de regresar al colegio: “Ahora tengo miedo de que me vuelvan a insultar o agredir, no sé qué va a pasar cuando vuelva”, dice. La madre explica que la niña ha salido poco a la calle desde la entrada masiva de migrantes.

“Yo estaba en mi casa, y vi por la ventana la manifestación. Como no tenía otra cosa mejor que hacer, le dije a mi prima que si bajábamos, y allí fuimos”, dice Soraya. Añade que su prima es “de piel más clara y casi pelirroja”. Las dos menores se unieron a los manifestantes, que comenzaron la protesta en la plaza de los Reyes frente a Delegación de Gobierno, para exigir la expulsión definitiva a Marruecos de todos los que cruzaron la frontera. “Y nos pusimos a cantar lo mismo que ellos, no sé, coreábamos, repetíamos Ceuta no se vende”, recuerda. Cuando la protesta alcanzó las inmediaciones de la frontera, una señora de unos sesenta años se acercó a ella y comenzó a increparla. “¿Tú qué haces aquí, invasora?’. ‘Fuera’, me decía. Y no paraba, ‘invasora’, ‘invasora”, explica Soraya. “Siguió así un rato, persiguiéndome, preguntándome que de dónde había salido. Yo le dije que de casa de mi madre”, añade.

Según su relato la señora comenzó a dirigirse al resto de manifestantes, señalándola, asegurando que “me había visto el día anterior en el hospital, porque yo tenía tuberculosis y otra cosa que no recuerdo”, y acusándola de ser una de las que había cruzado la frontera ilegalmente. Le tomaron fotografías y vídeos. La niña insistía en que era ceutí, y entre todos le exigieron que les mostrara la identificación. Llamó por teléfono a su madre. “Le dije que no le tenía que enseñar a nadie el documento si no era policía y salí corriendo para allá, pero cuando llegué ella ya se lo había mostrado”, cuenta su madre. La niña dice que una de las manifestantes se disculpó al verlo, pero que la mayoría la siguieron increpando a la voz de invasora. Fue a contárselo a los policías que vigilaban la concentración: “Me dijeron que si nos íbamos a poner así, nos fuéramos para atrás”, en referencia a ella y a su prima. Varios periodistas fueron también testigos de la escena. Además de su madre, su tía también fue en auxilio de la niña, y juntas tomaron fotografías y vídeos de los vecinos que la habían insultado.

Fueron a comisaría a denunciar los hechos, y aclaran que allí sí recibieron más comprensión. “Pero aunque insistimos, no nos dejaron enseñarles ni las fotos ni los vídeos para que les identificaran”, explica Fátima. Confía en que los agentes que lo presenciaron les tomaran los datos a los manifestantes, pero anuncia que no piensa parar si no lo hacen. “Esto no se puede consentir, tiene 13 años y tener la piel oscura no significa nada para que la traten así”, dice su madre. Aún así, quizá inconscientemente, empieza a buscar motivos: “La niña iba en chanclas y con sudadera, quizás por eso la confundieron también”, aventura.

De momento, la Policía Nacional no ha vuelto a ponerse en contacto con ellas, pero se aferran a la denuncia, a los vídeos y a las pruebas. No siempre las hay. Porque este tipo de incidentes, en los que ciudadanos son tomados por alguno de los migrantes del cruce masivo, son cada vez más habituales en Ceuta. La tensión de la ciudad, agotada de la falta de soluciones, cristaliza en incidentes de este tipo.

Al día siguiente de los insultos a Soraya, en el Paseo Sánchez Prados, en el centro de la ciudad, la policía tuvo dispersar a unos vecinos que se estaban enfrentando después de que un hombre agrediera a otro. Supuestamente le había confundido también con un inmigrante llegado en la entrada masiva: “Yo soy ciudadano español, tengo papeles desde hace más de 10 años”, cuenta Mohammed Charli, que denuncia la agresión.
