World.title: Letter from Brussels: Glorification of Mladic a Test for EU’s Position on ‘Dear Aleksandar’
World.content:
Aleksandar Vucic might have unintentionally found his campaign message, and it’s far from subtle: the European Union doesn’t want us. The Serbian president has been road-testing the claim for weeks now, but the death and funeral of Ratko Mladic have given it a stage no strategist could have built better.

Mladic died on August 27, aged 84, in The Hague, his final years spent serving a life sentence for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during the 1992-95 Bosnian war, atrocities the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia called “amongst the most heinous known to humankind”.

His body was flown home on a Serbian government plane. It lay in state at the Church of St Luke in Belgrade. On September 7, he was buried with military honours, his coffin wrapped in the Serbian flag, his officer’s cap and sabre resting on top, the Patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church presiding.

Vucic did not attend. His counterpart from Uzbekistan was visiting. It was a tidy piece of choreography: the coffin arrived in Belgrade on September 3, but the family “decided” the funeral would take place exactly on the day when Vucic couldn’t be there. But the president was represented anyway – by his son, and by cabinet ministers from Serbia’s ruling party.

World.title: Serbia’s Vucic Calls Early Parliamentary Elections for October 25
World.content:
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic on Tuesday set a date for early parliamentary elections on October 25, signing a decree dissolving parliament and the decision calling the elections – in which he is expected to run for prime minister, facing down a strong challenge from opponents.

“We need election results that will clearly demonstrate and determine the will of the citizens as to where, in what direction, and along which path Serbia is heading,” he said, adding that Serbia has been enduring “turbulence for more than a year and a half”.

Student-led protests have gripped the country since November 2024, sparked by the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that left 16 people dead, sparking nationwide outrage over alleged official corruption and negligence. The protests have posed the strongest challenge to Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party since it came to power in 2012.

Vucic claimed the “turbulence” in society was not merely the result of “conflicts between political parties or political actors here in Serbia” but also involved “significant interference by foreign powers”. He and his Progressive Party have often claimed that foreign states, including European countries, have been involved in supporting or inciting the student-led protests.

In his comments on Tuesday, however, he also insisted that Serbia, an EU candidate state, had chosen “a good European path, while [also] preserving traditional friendships, national pride, and dignity” – referencing Belgrade’s continued friendly relationship with Russia.

As one of the reasons for calling early elections, Vucic cited the organisation of the high-profile international EXPO 2027 exhibition, which will be held in Belgrade starting in May next year.

“If it were not for these tensions, if it were not for these political disagreements and conflicts, we certainly would not need [elections]. But any delay would jeopardise both EXPO and the survival of democracy as the best form of political system in our country,” he said.

On Monday, Prime Minister Djuro Macut proposed the dissolution of parliament, which was adopted by the government and sent to the President as part of the official procedure.

Many experts see the upcoming elections as the most challenging for Vucic and his party since 2012. The main opponent this time is Student List, made by the students who have been protesting. Its official candidates have been chosen by student groups whose names haven’t been published yet.

“The elections have been called after 492 days. It’s time for victory,” student organising group Students Blockade wrote on X on Tuesday. It was alluding to May 2025, when it first publicly demanded early elections.

Last Saturday, the Main Board of the Progressive Party named Vucic as their candidate for prime minister and as first on the electoral list “Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia” at the upcoming elections.

At the December 2023 elections, the Progressive Party won 46.75 per cent of the votes, while the largest opposition coalition, Serbia against Violence, won 23.66 per cent. The Progressive Party’s junior partner, the Socialist Party of Serbia, SPS, won 6.55 per cent.

World.title: Montenegro Opposition Moves to Oust Speaker for Mladic Condolences
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Montenegro’s main opposition party has moved to oust Speaker of Parliament Andrija Mandic over his public condolences following the death of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, media reported on Wednesday.

The initiative led by the Democratic Party of Socialists, DPS, was signed by 35 of the chamber’s 81 lawmakers, while 29 opposition MPs submitted a request for an extraordinary session on September 24 to debate Mandic’s dismissal.

The proposal says the speaker’s position carries “special political and institutional responsibility” and an obligation to safeguard the reputation and integrity of parliament, which represents all citizens.

Mandic publicly expressed condolences following the death on August 27 of Mladic, who was convicted by the UN war crimes tribunal in The Hague of genocide, crimes against humanity and other war crimes. He died serving his sentence.

The DPS said expressing sorrow for a convicted war criminal, particularly someone convicted of the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, is incompatible with the responsibilities of the speaker and Montenegro’s obligation to respect international court rulings and good neighbourly relations.

The proposal denies that Mandic expressed his condolences in a personal or party capacity, saying his institutional responsibility remains because he simultaneously holds the position of speaker.

The document cites critical reactions to the funeral from the European Commission and neighbouring Croatia, which condemned the glorification of war criminals and Mandic’s expression of condolences as incompatible with European Union values.

“When the actions of the speaker of parliament of a candidate country produce such reactions from EU institutions and a neighbouring member state, they can no longer be presented as a matter of his personal or party convictions,” the proposal says.

The DPS also argues that the episode is not isolated but forms part of a broader pattern in Mandic’s exercise of the speaker’s office.

The proposal also raises concerns about his alleged use of the speaker’s office to promote political and ideological positions.

The proposal recalls that Montenegro is entering a decisive phase of its EU integration process and that membership requires more than meeting technical conditions, including a clear commitment to European values, confronting the past, respecting international court judgments and maintaining good-neighbourly relations.

“We believe that the speaker’s latest action has crossed the line beyond which the question of his responsibility can no longer be relativised by the need to preserve the parliamentary majority or political stability,” the proposal says.

The ruling coalition’s three main groups, Prime Minister Milojko Spajic’s Europe Now Movement, the Democrats and the New Serb Democracy, which together hold 41 seats in the 81-member parliament, said they will not support the opposition initiative.

But parties representing Montenegro’s Bosniak and ethnic Albanian communities, which are also part of the governing coalition, have announced they will back the motion.

An absolute majority of all 81 lawmakers is not required to dismiss Mandic. The motion can pass with a majority of lawmakers present at the session, provided that at least half of all MPs are present.

Montenegro’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs this week also expressed concern about the glorification of Mladic during the recent commemorations of his death.

“It is our obligation to preserve the dignity and memory of the victims, to preserve the truth about crimes and individual responsibility for them, and to resolutely oppose any attempt to deny genocide, war crimes and other serious violations of international humanitarian law,” the Montenegrin ministry said in a statement on Tuesday.

World.title: Serbia, Bosnian Serbs Slate Sarajevo’s Expulsion of Diplomats over Mladic
World.content:
The Serbian embassy in Sarajevo. Photo: Serbian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Serbia’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday condemned the expulsion of two of its diplomats from Bosnia and Herzegovina as “yet another unconstructive move” that serves neither good-neighbourly relations, regional stability, nor the easing of political tensions.

It said Bosnia’s Foreign Minister, Elmedin Konakovic, “continues to resort to escalation and uses extremely difficult and painful issues from our shared past as an instrument of day-to-day politics and an election campaign”, adding that “such issues require responsibility and serious dialogue, rather than political instrumentalisation and unilateral moves that further deepen divisions.”

The ministry said Serbia will “examine all legal and political aspects of the announced decisions, including the issue of jurisdiction and the procedures for adopting them,” as well as their consequences for diplomatic relations.

On Tuesday, Konakovic announced the expulsion of two members of the Serbian embassy in Sarajevo after Serbia hosted the funeral with military honours of the convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic in Belgrade.

Konakovic said Serbian military attache Milan Dulanovic and Danko Maksimovic, an adviser to Serbia’s BIA intelligence service, were personae non grata and had 48 hours to leave Bosnia.

Officials in Bosnia’s mainly Serb Republika Srpska entity, also condemned the move and challenged its legality.

Republika Srpska Justice Minister Goran Selak insisted such foreign policy decisions fall under the authority of Bosnia’s tripartite state presidency, while the Foreign Ministry merely carries out adopted policy – which he said Konakovic “would have to know” before making moves that are “unconstitutional and illegal.”

He said the expulsion order “can hardly even be called a decision,” since such a decision must have grounding in the constitution and law. “This looks more like a pre-election pamphlet than a serious act of an institution,” Selak said, referring to upcoming national elections next month.

Selak said Konakovic has the right to his opinions, “including personal antipathy toward Serbia”, but not to present them as the country’s position or speak for Republika Srpska, adding that “Serbia is Republika Srpska’s most important partner”.

The Serb member of Bosnia’s three-member state presidency, Zeljka Cvijanovic, said Konakovic “cannot determine what Bosnia and Herzegovina is, or dictate to Serbia”. She claimed one of the two embassy staff had already left Bosnia after his mandate expired.

Konakovic based the decision on a 2004 rulebook of the state presidency, Under it, only the presidency can expel heads of diplomatic missions but the foreign minister can expel other embassy staff for cases including interference in internal affairs, espionage, or insulting statements.

World.title: Ex-Yugoslavia’s Queer Literary Heroes Tell Tales to Inspire
World.content:
After the Belgrade Pride march last weekend, Pride season in the former Yugoslavia – stretching from June to September – has drawn to a close. Whistles, rainbow flags and glitter (the queer community has a microplastics problem that we really need to discuss) are being stored away for the next time.

The intensified vitriol directed at those who believe their non-normative genders and sexualities are worth celebrating begins to wane. Familiar polemics within the LGBTQ+ community, however, continue: we keep asking ourselves, and those marching alongside us, whether Pride parades – organised by professional NGOs in coordination with the state and the police – are still worth showing up for.

As the season ends, and that question remains open, let’s keep Pride going through a Yugo Queer reading list.

World.title: ‘Disposable’ IP Firms in Serbia, Montenegro Obscure Origins of Russian Cyber Meddling
World.content:
Between late 2022 and February 2024, Azarov’s eServer said it was managing two IP ranges that subsequently came under the control of Stark Industries Solutions.

Following the EU sanctions, Stark Industries Solutions rebranded as PQ Hosting and transferred its IP resources under the umbrella of Dutch WorkTitans.

In May this year, Dutch police arrested the owners of WorkTitans and MIRhosting on suspicion of aiding Stark Industries Solution in circumventing sanctions.

Archived routing data show that at the end of 2024, Azarov was an upstream provider for PQ Hosting, i.e. the rebranded Stark Industries Solutions.

BIRN identified at least eight IP ranges that WorkTitans listed as being located in or used from Serbia and Belgrade, with Serbian Open Exchange, an internet traffic exchange point, serving as the internet gateway for all the ranges. These include two previously advertised by eServer.

Azarov said his company “had no direct business relations with Stark Industries”.

“Subnets roam between some providers and if we get request from any of our clients to announce network we just do so – that’s our part of hosting business,” he said in a response to BIRN, written in English.

“And you say it later came under control of Stark – then maybe they acquired it somehow.”

BIRN also identified three other IP ranges that have, over the past several years, moved between eServer, Stark Industries Solutions and Aeza Group.

An analysis of the RIPE NCC database shows that numerous IP ranges previously controlled by Azarov have since passed to two providers previously linked to the Russian bulletproof ecosystem and infrastructure used in cyberattacks: Cypriot-registered IT-Hostline and Russia-based Fortis.

IT-Hostline was previously a partner of Stark Industries Solutions and now provides infrastructure to Aeza Group, according to France-based cybersecurity firm Intrinsec, while Fortis’s infrastructure was used by FIN7 hacking group, responsible for mass financial theft and corporate extortion, Insikt Group reported last year.

Former eServer ranges are also now advertised by Global Connectivity Solutions and Global Internet Solutions, both linked to Aeza Group, Insikt Group said, and identified a number of ransomware groups that it said had used their infrastructure.

According to RIPE NCC data, among the current users of IP ranges previously held by eServer are: Russian provider Rost, whose infrastructure was also reportedly used in the Doppelganger campaign; Russian Timeweb, where researchers this year found more than 300 active C2 servers – systems used to send instructions to malware-infected devices and steal data; and US-based Baxet Group, whose infrastructure has been linked to cyberattacks by Russia’s military intelligence service, GRU, as reported by Arctic Wolf Networks, an American cybersecurity company, in November 2025.

Today, Azarov advertises an IP range belonging to Neterra Ltd, a Bulgarian provider previously used by the hacking-for-hire and corporate espionage group DeathStalker and whose infrastructure was also partly used to distribute Pegasus spyware, according to Amnesty International.

Azarov, however, insisted his eServer “has a strict anti cybercrime policy on all of our locations”.

“By targeting on B2B and B2C markets we always monitor our networks and try to keep environment safe and trustworthy,” he wrote to BIRN.

“You can see that our networks are not in SBL and other lists and if some IPs get into it we act immediately. So as I told you we did not work directly with Stark Industries but even if their networks were announced by some of our clients, they were applied the same strict rules and filters so I don’t think there was any malicious activity.”

Typically in cybercrime, when one network is shut down or sanctioned, attackers simply transfer IP addresses and other internet resources to linked providers and continue their operations. This is how sanctioned companies Aeza and Stark Industries have continued to operate.

“Today, it is no longer a single server, but an entire dynamic infrastructure that is constantly changing,” Radunovic told BIRN. “That makes it difficult to track because it operates across multiple jurisdictions and legal procedures, so investigators, alongside technical traces, also follow money flows, cryptocurrencies and other connections.”

World.title: Ratko Mladic’s Lavish Funeral was an Indictment of Serbia’s Govt: Experts
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Criticism has echoed across Europe over the high-profile funeral of Ratko Mladic on Monday in Belgrade, raising questions about the potential repercussions for Serbia of giving a convicted war criminal a hero’s farewell.

His funeral with military honours was attended by senior officials of Serbia and Bosnia’s mainly Serb entity, Republika Srpska.

Ministers from the Serbian government included Defence Minister Bratislav Gasic, Justice Minister Nenad Vujic and Culture Minister Nikola Selakovic.

World.title: Croatia: Glorifying Ratko Mladić is Contrary to EU Values – Suspend Serbia Talks
World.content:
September the 9th, 2026 – Through various political figures, Croatia has sent out the clear message that glorifying Ratko Mladić is contrary to EU values and that all talks with Serbia must be suspended.

Croatian politician Tonino Picula has warned that glorifying Ratko Mladić or relativising his crimes is “contrary to the values on which the European Union is founded.” “The burial of Ratko Mladić cannot be viewed solely as a private event because the participation of representatives of state institutions, members of the army and members of the authorities sends a clear political message.

Index reports that the disgraced war criminal Ratko Mladić was finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, crimes against humanity and war crimes. “Any glorification of him or relativisation of his crimes is directly contrary to the values on which the European Union is founded,” Picula stated.

serbia must confront its past

“Serbia’s desired EU path is not only a matter of opening negotiating chapters and fulfilling technical criteria, but above all a question of political choice and acceptance of European values. Serbia cannot at the same time claim that membership in the European Union is its strategic goal while tolerating or institutionally accompanying the glorification of people convicted of the most serious war crimes.

The European Union must not relativise such an event. The authorities in Belgrade must be required to make a clear break with the policy of historical revisionism and an unambiguous attitude towards the judgments of international courts. The European perspective also implies the ability of society and the state to confront the past, rather than glorify its darkest protagonists. Serbia chooses its own path, but the credibility of its European path will also depend on whether it is prepared to accept the truth about the crimes committed and stop glorifying their perpetrators,” Picula added.

a convicted war criminal for the world is apparently a man deserving of the highest honours in serbia

The former commander of the Bosnian Serb army, Ratko Mladić, who was finally sentenced to life imprisonment for the genocide in Srebrenica in July 1995, for the persecution and forced displacement of Bosniaks and Croats throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, sniper activity, shelling and terrorising of civilians during the siege of Sarajevo, and for taking members of UN peacekeeping forces hostage in retaliation for NATO bombings in 1995, died on 27 August in the prison hospital of the Hague Tribunal.

He was buried yesterday in the family tomb at Topčider Cemetery with church rites and military honours. Among the thousands of people in the procession and funeral cortège were individual ministers of the Serbian government and officials of Republika Srpska, while the service in the church was led by Patriarch Porfirije with bishops of the Serbian Orthodox Church.

World.title: Croatia Imports 870,000 Tonnes of Waste Each Year, But Why?
World.content:
September the 9th, 2026 – The hazardous waste scandal that has taken Lika and Croatia by storm shows no sign of dying down, but few realise Croatia actually imports 870,000 tonnes of waste each year. The question is: Why?

If Croatia has truly become Europe’s dumping ground, the 2024 statistics don’t really show it: about 90,000 more tonnes of waste actually left the country than entered it. However, that isn’t enough proof that there are no problems to speak of. The same system in which a Croatian factory legally imports scrap iron, paper or waste wood as raw material can be abused so that hazardous waste ends up buried in Lika.

Slobodan Mufic reports for Index that according to data from the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition, after Croatia’s entry into the European Union back in July 2013, an increase in waste imports was recorded, but exports also continuously grew. Since 2015, waste imports have only twice exceeded exports on an annual basis, and then by roughly five percent. As such, back in 2024, the last year for which official data exists, Croatia imported 871,255 tonnes of waste, of which about 7,100 tonnes of hazardous waste with prior approval. Five Croatian companies carried out the import of hazardous waste in 2024: C.I.A.K., Holcim, NEXE, Premifab and Spectra-Media. The largest part of the imported non-hazardous waste, more than half, consists of metal, paper, cardboard and wood that domestic companies process and use as secondary raw material in production.

During the same year, 961,442 tonnes of waste were exported from Croatia, of which hazardous waste accounted for 26,851 tonnes, or 2.8 percent of the total quantity. All exported hazardous waste ended up in other European Union member states, mostly in Austria, Germany, Poland and Hungary.

it isn’t possible for croatia to entirely ban waste imports

It should be emphasised that Croatia cannot simply ban the import of all types of waste from other EU member states, nor would that be good for Croatian industry. Cross-border waste shipments within the EU are regulated by European rules. Waste is considered goods and no EU Member State can prevent (by way of a general ban) what European Union regulations currently allow. As of the 21st of May 2026, the new EU Regulation 2024/1157 on waste shipments applies, which introduces different cross-border regimes depending on the type of waste and whether the waste is destined for disposal or recovery (reuse of waste as raw material or energy source). For waste intended for disposal, shipments are in principle prohibited, unless the competent authorities give consent. For waste going for recovery there is a prior consent procedure, depending on the degree of toxicity.

Recovery means that the waste is directed to some useful purpose such as recycling, composting or incineration and thereby replaces material or energy that would otherwise have to be obtained from other sources. Disposal means finally removing the waste at a landfill, storage facility or incinerator without energy recovery. Croatia, however, does not have to accept every waste that someone wants to send it. The law already prohibits some categories, for example the delivery of hazardous waste and mixed municipal waste for disposal, and gives the minister the possibility to additionally restrict certain flows if they endanger the domestic waste management system or public health.

why does croatia even need imported waste?

A ban on waste imports would also be harmful to Croatian industry. Existing energy recovery facilities alone have permitted capacities of almost 400,000 tonnes per year, and the largest consumers are cement plants. Našice’s NEXE energy-recovered 58,000 tonnes of waste in 2023 alone, Holcim in Koromačno today consumes tens of thousands of tonnes and plans to reach around 60,000 tonnes per year, while CEMEX in Kaštel Sućurac and Solin already obtains more than a third of the energy for cement from alternative fuels.

Cement plants do not need just any rubbish, but fuel from waste of precisely defined properties. Every shipment must meet quality and composition criteria, including calorific value and content of moisture, chlorine, sulphur and heavy metals, and facilities that incinerate waste are subject to special rules on combustion temperature, process monitoring and emission limit values.

In addition, low-quality or hazardous waste could damage the kilns. The estimate is that from the total municipal waste, of which Croatia collects around 1.9 million tonnes annually, only about 20 percent could become sufficiently high-quality fuel for existing facilities. This also explains the apparent paradox: Croatia can simultaneously have too much of its own waste and import the waste that industry needs. It does not matter to a factory where the scrap iron obtained waste status. What matters is how much it costs, what quality it is, whether it suits its process and whether it can obtain it in sufficient quantity.

the difference between legal trade and illegal disposal

That’s why the entire question of waste imports doesn’t really have a straightforward answer. The import of clean metal waste into a Croatian foundry and the illegal burial of hazardous waste are two completely different things. The first can reduce the consumption of primary raw materials and energy and represents a desirable part of the circular economy. The second is the opposite of the economy and constitutes a criminal offence. The grey area begins precisely between the word “recovery” on the document and what actually happened to the waste. A shipment can neatly and legally cross the border, arrive at a registered entity and still end up completely differently from what the documentation suggests. Exactly such an appearance of legality occurred in Gospić.

Regardless of the State Inspectorate’s data that from 2020 to 2025 the environmental protection inspection examined a total of 2,610 shipments and discovered as many as 1,611 illegal waste shipments, or almost 62 percent, the system was not entirely without supervision.

The problem was that supervision, permits and existing documentation did not ensure reliable tracking of the movement of waste to final treatment and did not prevent enormous quantities of waste from ending up where they should not have. Likewise, this does not mean that 62 percent of the total waste entering Croatia is illegal. Inspection controls are targeted, cover imports, exports and transit, and are also carried out subsequently at companies. An illegal shipment can refer to various offences, including incorrect classification or documentation. Not every such case is criminally similar to the current one in Gospić.

Europe and specifically Croatia are currently trying to close the space in which legitimate waste trade can turn into a cover for illegal disposal. New European rules strengthen digital tracking of cross-border shipments, and an important change is also coming in Croatia from tomorrow.

who took it first isn’t important, but who resolved it last is…

The Ordinance on amendments and supplements to the Ordinance on waste management was published on 31 August and enters into force tomorrow – 8 September. The waste recipient will have to provide the consignor with data on final treatment: the name and PIN of the final processor, their authorisation for treatment of the shipment, the date of completion of treatment and the final treatment procedure.

This goes straight to the heart of the problem exposed by the scandal in Gospić: it should no longer be enough to prove to whom the waste was handed over at the first step, but what happened to it at the last. But even the best electronic form will not help if the data are not checked, if capacities exist only on paper or if the inspection reacts only when tens of thousands of tonnes of hazardous waste are already underground. Tracking the movement of waste is not filing papers in a binder, but the state’s ability to determine for every disputed tonne where it ended up.

World.title: All Eyes are on the Dubrovnik-Montreal Connection in 2027
World.content:
September the 9th, 2026 – Many are looking forward to the upcoming Dubrovnik-Montreal connection set for May 2027 as Air Canada makes its return.

The new Dubrovnik-Montreal route coming in May 2027 will enable passengers from Dubrovnik to connect more easily with other destinations across not only Canada but all of North America via the Air Canada network, according to Viktor Šober, President of the Management Board of Dubrovnik Airport. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that flights between Dubrovnik and Montreal will operate three times a week from the 11th of May to the 24th of October 2027.

The new route will further strengthen the international connectivity of Dubrovnik Airport with the North American market and open new opportunities for the development of tourist traffic between Croatia and Canada. The introduction of the Dubrovnik–Montreal route is part of Air Canada’s largest intercontinental network expansion to date. For the 2027 summer season, the company is announcing more than 125 international routes and up to 169,000 seats per week from Canada to more than 85 international destinations. The new direct link with Montreal is of particular importance for Dubrovnik because it enables passengers from Canada to arrive more easily to the extreme south of Croatia without transfers at European airports.

major expansion

For the 2027 summer season, Air Canada is announcing more than 125 international routes and up to 169,000 seats per week from Canada to more than 85 international destinations. “Montreal is one of the largest Canadian transport and economic centres, and the new route will at the same time enable passengers from Dubrovnik to connect more easily with other destinations in Canada and North America via the Air Canada network,” briefly commented Viktor Šober, President of the Management Board of Ruđer Bošković Airport. For Dubrovnik tourism, it is particularly important that the route will operate for almost six months, from mid-May to the end of October.

The new route thus opens additional opportunities for the growth of tourist traffic from Canada in the pre-season and post-season, as well as for the further positioning of Dubrovnik in the segments of individual, premium and luxury travel. On the route to Dubrovnik, Air Canada will use the Boeing 787 Dreamliner, including a premium cabin with fully flat seats.

the return of air canada

Flights will be operated with an aircraft featuring Signature, Premium Economy and Economy cabins, offering passengers a high level of comfort and different travel options. The use of the wide-body Boeing 787 Dreamliner is additional confirmation of the potential that Air Canada sees in Dubrovnik and its tourist market, especially in the premium leisure travel segment. Canada is an important and promising market for Dubrovnik, and the establishment of a direct link with Montreal further confirms Dubrovnik’s international position and its attractiveness on the North American market. The flight to Dubrovnik marks Air Canada’s return to Croatia with its own aircraft after several years of absence.

The carrier first began flying to Zagreb in 1989 and discontinued flights in 1991, according to Ex-Yu Aviation News. Its subsidiary, Air Canada Rouge, resumed seasonal flights between Toronto and Zagreb in June 2018, initially with four weekly flights on a Boeing 767-300ER, marking the return of the Air Canada brand to the Croatian market after 27 years. The service was maintained during 2019 but was suspended back in 2020 due to the coronavirus pandemic.

World.title: Croatian National Theatre in Zagreb to Undergo Renovation
World.content:
September the 9th, 2026 – The beautiful buttermilk Croatian National Theatre in Zagreb is set to undergo renovation after over half a century of not being touched.

Since the Croatian National Theatre (HNK) building is individually protected as cultural heritage, all interventions will have to be designed in close accordance with the rules for the protection of cultural heritage. After almost 57 years since the last major renovation, the building of the Croatian National Theatre in Zagreb is once again undergoing a complete renovation. Poslovni reports that the last major construction renovation and reconstruction of the HNK took place from 1967 to 1969, and now the project has taken a new step — two bids have been received for the preparation of part of the conceptual design.

The renovation of the Croatian National Theatre building in Zagreb has taken a new step toward realisation after two bids arrived for the tender for the preparation of part of the conceptual design. Both are financially more favourable than the estimated procurement value of 1.2 million euros excluding VAT, as is currently understood. The most favourable bid, worth 762,400 euros excluding VAT, was submitted by a consortium of bidders led by the Faculty of Civil Engineering of the University of Zagreb, together with Studio Arhing and Toding. The second bid came from the company UPI-2M, which offered the job for 894,857 euros excluding VAT.

protected cultural heritage

The project concerns the structural, comprehensive and energy renovation of the existing building on Republic of Croatia Square, as well as two underground extensions. Under the stage, a reinforced concrete substructure is planned for the needs of new stage technology, while an underground floor would be built next to the existing building to ensure better working conditions for the three theatre ensembles. Since the Croatian National Theatre building in Zagreb is individually protected cultural heritage, all interventions will have to be designed in accordance with the rules for the protection of cultural heritage. The procurement includes projects for the structure, heating, cooling and ventilation, electrical installations, multimedia, water supply and drainage, traffic surfaces, fire extinguishing systems, and landscape architecture, including a green roof.

The architectural design is not included in this procurement because the client decided to organise it through a separate procedure. The conceptual design that will be prepared should serve as the basis for obtaining a location permit, as well as for defining individual phases of the renovation and estimating the costs of their implementation. The final decision on the selection of the contractor has not yet been made. After the opening of the bids, the public procurement procedure continues, and the deadline for filing an appeal against the bid opening procedure is ten days.

World.title: Former Croatian PM Seeks Suspension of Serbian EU Accession Talks
World.content:
September the 8th, 2026 – Former Croatian PM Jadranka Kosor is seeking total suspension of all Serbian EU accession talks, calling on Ursula von der Leyen to take action.

Former Croatian Prime Minister Jadranka Kosor has called on the European Commission to completely suspend Serbia’s EU accession negotiations following today’s mass farewell for Ratko Mladić in Belgrade, which was held with the highest state and military honours. “After today’s funeral, involving the anti-civilisational bowing of Serbia to a war criminal convicted of genocide, I expect the incompetent European Commission and its incompetent leader Ursula von der Leyen to fully suspend Serbia’s accession negotiations for entry into the EU. That is the minimum,” Kosor wrote on X.

a serbian state funeral for a genocidal maniac

Index reports that thousands of people gathered in Belgrade to bid a final farewell to the former commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. Disgraced Ratko Mladić was buried at Topčider Cemetery with state honours, in the presence of members of the Serbian Army and an honour guard. Numerous Serbian officials, the political leadership of Republika Srpska, and the Russian ambassador to Serbia attended the funeral. Before the burial, his coffin was displayed in the Church of St. Luke, where the service was led by Patriarch Porfirije. On the coffin were his officer’s cap and sabre, and members of the army and veterans of the former Army of Republika Srpska stood beside it. The Serbian Government had previously sent a state aircraft to collect Mladić’s remains from The Hague, and soldiers carried his coffin, covered with the Serbian flag, out of the plane. A commemoration was also held for him on Saturday in an official facility of the Serbian Army.

serbia honours one of the worst monsters of the 20th century

Mladić died on the 27th of August at the age of 84 in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence. He had suffered several quite serious strokes and his health had been declining rapidly for some time. He was finally convicted of committing genocide in Srebrenica, crimes against humanity, and war crimes during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. His forces were responsible, among other things, for the massacre of more than 8,000 innocent Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in July 1995, as well as for the multi-year, dreadful siege of Sarajevo.

the eu’s position is clear – no glorification of war crimes and war criminals

The European Union has already very clearly warned Serbia over the glorification of the vile Ratko Mladić. European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos cancelled a planned visit to Serbia after a state aircraft brought his body to Belgrade. The European External Action Service stated that the glorification of war criminals, denial of genocide, and revisionism have no place either in the European Union or in candidate countries. Serbia has otherwise held candidate status for EU membership and has been conducting accession negotiations since 2014.

World.title: Osijek Company to Develop Unmanned Systems & More in Vukovar
World.content:
September the 8th, 2026 – An Osijek company is set to develop unmanned systems in Vukovar and more as part of a five million euro project.

A new production facility is being built in the Vukovar Business Zone by the Osijek-based company GAUSS d.o.o., which focuses on the development of digital and high-tech solutions. Poslovni reports that last week, representatives of the investors, together with Deputy Speaker of the Croatian Parliament Ivan Penava, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries David Vlajčić, and State Secretary Dario Tišov, toured the investment worth slightly less than five million euros.

The new facility is expected to start operating during the second quarter of next year. It will develop and produce unmanned systems using artificial intelligence, smart software and other advanced tech. Hrvoje Sagrak, Director of Business Development and Sales at the Osijek company, emphasised that coming to Vukovar is an opportunity to transfer the experience gained through cooperation with international partners, especially in the United Arab Emirates.

“It is truly a great honour for us to be here in Vukovar because we have a unique opportunity to transfer the business experience and know-how that we have acquired through cooperation with partners abroad, primarily in the United Arab Emirates, to Croatia. Right here we want to build a point that will be a centre of excellence and a centre of knowledge about high technologies,” said Sagrak.

ai, unmanned systems and more

The future facility will not deal only with the production of aircraft. It will develop systems that include smart software, artificial intelligence and other devices, and the applications could range from surveillance and protection to fire prevention, protection of critical infrastructure and border monitoring. Special emphasis will be placed on the rapid development of new products and turning ideas into prototypes. Industry 4.0 technologies and 3D printers will be used so that new solutions can be designed, tested and verified more quickly and cheaply.

In the initial phase, around ten experts with multidisciplinary knowledge in electrical engineering and other modern fields are expected to work at the facility. “It isn’t about the number of employees itself, but about what will be developed through such a venture and spread throughout the entire ecosystem,” Sagrak said, adding that the facility has the possibility of further expansion.

the future has (finally) arrived in vukovar, a town scarred by the past

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister David Vlajčić recalled that the story of this investment has been ongoing since the time when he was assistant director of the Vukovar Business Zone. “The investor then took a plot and began developing something that combines hardware and software, i.e. solutions that we do not have in Croatia today. Such investments require a trained workforce, but at the same time they open up the potential for smart technologies from all over the world to come right here, to Croatia and Vukovar, and for us to have something special on the territory of the European Union,” said Vlajčić.

The importance of the investment was also highlighted by Deputy Speaker of the Croatian Parliament Ivan Penava, who believes that the project places Vukovar alongside modern technological environments. “The future has arrived in Vukovar,” Penava said, emphasising that artificial intelligence, 3D printers and unmanned aerial vehicles represent high-tech industry, and by connecting them integrated production is created.

“When we talk about artificial intelligence, 3D printers or unmanned aerial vehicles, each of these technologies on its own already represents high-tech industry. However, here we’re talking about integrated production and connecting all of that through one product. All of this has today, on a symbolic level, arrived in Vukovar,” said Penava. He added that talks with the investors lasted about two years and emphasised that their arrival is important because, despite economic logic, they are choosing Croatia and Vukovar also because of their connection with this area.

The investment worth slightly less than five million euros represents a new step in the development of the Vukovar Business Zone, as well as in the effort to position Vukovar as a place for the development and production of advanced technological solutions for the domestic and global market.

World.title: 3% More Vehicles on Croatian Motorways Than This Time in 2025
World.content:
September the 8th, 2026 – There have been 3% more vehicles recorded on Croatian motorways this year than back during this period in 2025.

From the beginning of the year until the end of August, 56.5 million cars passed along Croatian motorways, which is an increase of 1.6 million, or three percent, compared with the same period last year, HRT reports. “Croatia as a tourist country is recognised not only for its natural beauty, but above all for the safety it offers to all tourists, and this increase in traffic is a result of that,” said Ivan Ribičić, Director of the Toll Collection Sector.

Poslovni reports that the busiest periods, according to Ribičić, are the end of July and the beginning of August. “All three summer months were very successful. Compared with last year, that is 300,000 more vehicles. These are excellent results, he said. In the last three to four years, large traffic jams on Mondays have become increasingly frequent. This weekend also exceeded expectations. On Sunday by 18:00, 100,000 vehicles were recorded at the Lučko entrance alone, which is more than last year.

In the autumn, works on the Zagreb bypass are finally due to begin, which should make passage between Zagreb East and Zagreb West easier, as well as access to the Lučko toll booth.

World.title: New Poll Lays Bare Worst Result for HDZ in the Last Two Years
World.content:
September the 8th, 2026 – A brand new poll has showcased the absolute worst result for HDZ in the last two years, with Prime Minister Andrej Plenković personally scoring very poorly.

Public dissatisfaction over the hazardous waste affair in Lika has been reflected on the political scene, as shown by the latest monthly CRO Demoskop survey. Index reports that according to the poll conducted for RTL this month, both HDZ and SDP recorded a significant drop in support, with the ruling party, being HDZ, falling to its lowest level in the past two years.

If parliamentary elections had been held at the beginning of the month, HDZ would still have been the relative winner. Index reports that the CRO Demoskop survey was conducted by the agency Promocija plus from 1 to 3 September using a telephone survey (CATI) on a representative sample of 1,000 respondents. The sample was stratified by counties and settlement size, with control of socio-demographic characteristics. The standard sampling error is ±3.04% at a 95% confidence level.

most and Možemo! outperform hdz and sdp

According to the latest poll, HDZ has the support of 25.3% of voters, a drop from 27% seen in July. This is also the party’s weakest result since April 2024. SDP is in second place with 20.5% support, also recording a decline from 21.5% in July and its lowest rating in the current term. Možemo! ranked third with 12.9% support, a slight increase from 12.2% in July. The biggest rise was recorded by Most, which jumped from 7.7% to 9.5%. It is followed by the party Drito with 1.8% and Domovinski pokret with 1.6%. Both parties have slightly lower support than in July. Most thus recorded a rise of 1.8 percentage points, and Možemo! of 0.7. HDZ is down by 1.7 percentage points, SDP by 1.0, and Drito and DP by 0.5 percentage points each.

Other parties have support below 1.5%. Above one percent are Domino (1.4%), Centar (1.1%), Pravo i pravda (1.1%), IDS (1.0%) and Nezavisna platforma Sjever (1.0%). Below that threshold are HNS (0.9%), Hrvatski suverenisti (0.8%), HSU (0.8%), HSS (0.7%), HSLS (0.4%) and Fokus (0.3%). All other parties together have two percent support, while undecided voters stand at 16.9%.

president milanović receives the most positive rating among politicians, while pm plenković receives the worst

The most positively perceived politicians are as follows:

Zoran Milanović – 23%

Andrej Plenković – 15.6%

Tomislav Tomašević – 4.1%

Marin Miletić – 3.8%

Ivana Kekin – 2.9%

Dalija Orešković – 2.7%

Nikola Grmoja – 2.5%

Ivan Anušić – 2.2%

Sandra Benčić – 1.6%

Biljana Borzan – 1.5%

The most negatively perceived politicians are as follows:

Andrej Plenković – 37.3%

Zoran Milanović – 12.3%

Tomislav Tomašević – 5.6%

Sandra Benčić – 2.5%

Ivan Penava – 2.3%

Milorad Pupovac – 2.1%

Dalija Orešković – 1.8%

Hrvoje Zekanović – 1.6%

Siniša Hajdaš Dončić – 1.4%

Andrija Mikulić – 1.4%

most believe the country is heading in the wrong direction

This September, only 17.5% of citizens believe that Croatia is moving in a good direction, a drop from 20.2% in July. At the same time, the share of those who think the direction is wrong rose from 70% to 74.6%. Undecided stand at 7.9%. Among HDZ voters optimism prevails and 55.4% of them consider the direction good. Voters of opposition parties are considerably more critical.

President Zoran Milanović received an average grade of 3.08 for his work. He received the highest grade from SDP voters (3.97) and the lowest from HDZ voters (2.32). The work of the Croatian Parliament was rated 2.16. It received the highest grade from HDZ voters (3.0) and the lowest from Možemo! platform voters (1.69). The Government received a grade of 2.23 for its work, the lowest grade in the past year. HDZ voters rated the Government’s work at 3.81, while voters of other parties were considerably stricter. Support for the Government’s policy fell to 25.7%, compared with 27.6% in July.

the appalling lika hazardous waste affair is the hot topic

The hazardous waste affair in Lika and other parts of the country was the most important topic of the past month for as many as 40.4% of respondents. This is one of the highest results for a single event since measurements began in 2004. In second place in importance is the fire in Omiš and the surrounding area, which 27.9% of citizens singled out as a key event. These are followed by the heatwave (5.4%), inflation (3.5%), the extraordinary session of Parliament (3.0%) and the rise in fuel prices (2.9%). Among the more important topics are also sporting successes, Thompson’s concert in Vukovar and arrests related to arson.

World.title: Number of higher education students receiving needs-based support up by a quarter
World.content:
The number of bachelor's students in Estonia receiving need‑based support has risen nearly a quarter in four years, while more students work to cover rising costs.

While the mean monthly student income stands at €1,078, expenses average at almost the same: €1,023, and more than 60 percent of students now work while studying to make ends meet as the new academic year gets underway.

According to a recently completed Praxis study, expenses have grown nearly twice as fast as income for wage earners has, and students' income has increased considerably more slowly than that.

University of Tartu political science student Marian Müürsepp told ERR she knows many students who have even been skipping meals due to a shortage of funds. Others wait for reduced food items to go on sale, or wait until pastries get sold at half price in the evening. "Without my parents' support, I wouldn't be able to study in Tartu at all," she said.

Needs-based study allowances range from €150 to €440 a month, depending on household income. Students can apply if household income is below €756 per family member per month. A student is considered part of their parents' household until age 24, unless they marry or have a child earlier.

Ronja Ansmann, vice president of the Federation of Estonian Student Unions (Üliõpilaskondade liit), said the system's main flaw is how support gets calculated. "If you read the Family Law Act, it states that a student must be supported until the age of 21, which means that in practice the young person is left completely without protection, for three years," Ansmann said, adding that the system "simply isn't functioning at the moment."

However, Margus Haidak, senior adviser at the Ministry of Education and Research's higher education department, said boosting study allowances further would not be the rational thing to do at present. "The last time study allowances were increased, they were doubled. Today, spending on need‑based study allowances is around €15 million a year, and we see the primary priority as ensuring opportunities for tuition‑free study," he said.

Ansmann countered that while allowances were indeed raised in 2023, that was a one off: They had not increased at all from 2013 to 2023, and have not been raised again since.

Students can also apply for student loans of up to €6,000. Eneli Nairis, head of small‑scale financing at Swedbank, said demand has be rising every year since legislative changes in autumn 2022, with over 1,800 customers seen in 2024 — 4 percent of those eligible.

Müürsepp challenged the assumption that students are supposed to be poor. "I think that in the 21st century, getting a higher education should no longer mean that a person constantly has to worry about whether they have enough money for food or rent," she said. "That mentality should not be the norm."

World.title: Experiment: Pärnu County soil so 'alive' it devours pair of underpants in 3 months
World.content:
An unusual experiment at a horse farm near Pärnu revealed that underpants almost entirely degraded in the space of three months.

The purpose of the activity, at the Tori hobusekasvandus horse farm, was not to investigate the degenerative properties of underwear so much as to demonstrate that the soil is "alive."

The experiment's results will form part of an exhibition at the National Agricultural Museum in Tartu County.

On June 16, a pair of cotton underpants were buried to a shallow depth in the soil at the farm, around 30 kilometers from Pärnu. The Estonian Agricultural Museum (Eesti Põllumajandusmuuseum) aimed to assess soil activity.

The 'pants as they appeared on being buried in mid-June. Source: ERR

Twelve weeks later, the undergarments were dug up, revealing decomposition had been extensive – in fact, only the elasticated waistband remained intact, with the same being the case for another pair buried.

"They have decomposed unbelievably — there was almost nothing left of them. The control underpants had one very small piece left, while the actual underpants had only the waistband and a little bit of thread, that's all. We were not expecting that," said Kadri Valner, agricultural museum chief.

This was indication that the soil at the site was of good quality, with plenty of the microorganisms which speed up the decomposition process.

"Already while digging, it was clear that there were a great many earthworms and various microorganisms there," Valner said.

Kadri Valner holding what remained of the underpants. Source: Kristi Raidla/ERR

A similar experiment was conducted at the Jakobson Museum in Kurgja, also in Pärnu County, and at Ülenurme, near Tartu. These will be compared for decomposition rates, and at least one pair will be put on public display.

"If there is anything left at the other locations, we will first dry out the underpants, clean them, and on September 18 we will open an exhibition where they should also be on display," Valner added.

The exhibition "Milleks mulle muld" ("What Do I Need Soil For?") will be on display at the Estonian Agricultural Museum in Ülenurme, just south of Tartu.

World.title: Doctor: Pärnu methanol tragedy the first major touchstone for Covid
World.content:
Raido Paasma, then head of the intensive care unit at Pärnu Hospital and a clinical toxicologist and anesthesiologist, told ETV's "Ringvaade" that although a quarter of a century has passed since the tragedy, he still remembers many of the details.

At the time, Estonia was still a young country, having regained its independence just 10 years earlier, and incomes were limited. People bought alcohol on the black market where it was cheaper than in stores. To maximize their profits, illicit alcohol sellers mixed cheap methanol into vodka to increase the volume.

"People who knew where they could get their illicit vodka went there to buy it. If we look at the date, September 9 is right around the time pensions were paid. People had received their wages and pensions and it was also potato-harvesting season, so they went and stocked up. That's how it happened," Paasma said.

Paasma believes the people who mixed the drinks did not know how much harm they would cause. "To them, it was alcohol. The fact that it had one less H didn't bother them much."

The scale of the methanol poisoning was significant, but Paasma said the proportion of deaths was not exceptionally high compared with previous mass poisonings. "There have also been cases where 70 to 80 percent of those who consumed it died," he said.

Methanol is converted into a toxic metabolite in the body and ethanol is used as an antidote to treat methanol poisoning. During treatment, the concentration of ethanol in the blood must be kept sufficiently high; otherwise, the body begins to break down the methanol. This process produces toxic formic acid.

Drinking methanol does not cause the typical intoxication associated with ethanol. It also tastes different from regular vodka. "A couple of patients told me at the time, 'It was a damn strange drink. I drank it but didn't get drunk at all and it tasted strange too,'" Paasma recalled.

The mass poisoning was a major test for Pärnu Hospital. The hospital did not have sufficient capacity to treat all the patients, so some had to be transferred to other hospitals.

"We distributed the patients because we realized that our capacity to treat them on site was very limited. We could begin initial treatment, but then we needed somewhere with dialysis and greater intensive care capacity than Pärnu had at the time. Estonia's entire healthcare system responded to it and it responded as one. I think it was the first test ahead of the later Covid pandemic."

Paasma estimated that the most difficult period of the crisis lasted about a week and a half. Twenty-five patients died in the hospital, while 43 people were found dead outside the hospital. "When the poisoning has progressed so far that the heart is still working but the brain has already been damaged and the person develops what is known as brain death, unfortunately there is nothing that can be done."

Methanol poisonings still occur in Estonia today, but they are rare. "A month ago, there was a patient who had drunk methanol," Paasma said. "I don't know whether he is still alive. He did not regain consciousness, but his heart was working and he was able to breathe."

Paasma said methanol poisoning nevertheless remains widespread around the world, particularly in Asian countries. He cited three reasons: people seeking cheaper alcohol, poor availability of alcohol and religious restrictions on alcohol.

World.title: Minister: Estonia will have to shelve some investments in tight fiscal situation
World.content:
Budget talks are continuing within the government. On the one hand, the government is seeking to keep the deficit below 4.5 percent, but ministers acknowledge there is little room for spending cuts.

According to Minister of Economic Affairs and Industry Erkki Keldo (Reform Party), the government is drawing up the budget on the assumption that defense spending must remain at no less than 5 percent of GDP, meaning other areas will have to cut costs.

"We have promised to reduce the shortfall, or deficit, to below 4.5 percent. We are trying to do that. It simply means spending has to be reined in. Operating costs, technical costs. We will also have to forgo investments that might be possible in better times — buildings and other construction projects. We cannot afford those when a large share is going toward defense investments," Keldo said.

Making cuts within the Ministry of Interior's area of responsibility is difficult, Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said. Instead, additional funding would be needed to develop capabilities such as counter-drone defenses. Taro did not say Tuesday how much additional funding would be needed.

"I cannot imagine telling society right now that we are simply not going to deal with civil protection at all. We need shelters. Everyone agrees on that. Everyone is asking where those shelters are — where they are in schools, where they are in residential buildings. Or could we say, for example, that we are no longer going to build the national border infrastructure?" Taro said.

Social Democratic Party Vice Chair Riina Sikkut said the minority government needs opposition support to pass the state budget, but the government has not discussed its budget plans with the opposition.

"If everyone had the same information about the forecast and the use of foreign funding, it would be much easier to find support in the Riigikogu because otherwise questions inevitably arise about where a particular figure came from, why a particular choice was made and what the alternatives were," Sikkut said.

The government wants to make the major decisions on the 2027 state budget by the end of next week.

World.title: 3 cities submit bids to host Estonia's multisport arena by deadline
World.content:
Pärnu, Tallinn and Tartu submitted bids by the deadline to host the major arena planned by the Estonian Olympic Committee (EOK).

All three cities seeking to host the multifunctional arena submitted applications to the Estonian Olympic Committee (EOK) by the September 1 deadline.

More specifically, Pärnu, Tallinn and Tartu submitted proposed locations along with additional documentation, allowing the bids to now be compared, EOK multifunctional arena project manager Helen Veermäe told ERR.

"The aim is to ensure that all potential locations are assessed on a comparable basis and, above all, according to their substantive characteristics and potential," she said.

Tallinn proposed the Ülemiste freight terminal area as the location for the arena. Pärnu's preferred site is near the future Rail Baltica terminal, in Veterans Park next to Papiniidu Bridge on the banks of the Pärnu River. The City of Tartu has reserved a plot of land for the arena on Roosi tänav, near the Estonian National Museum.

The selection process will now begin. In May, the EOK and the Ministry of Culture formed an expert committee that will oversee the selection process and ultimately submit a recommendation, together with its reasoning, to the government.

Artist's rendition of the sports arena complex in Pärnu. Source: Pärnu CIty Council / +Arhitektid

As a first step, however, the expert committee will soon select an independent expert to conduct an economic impact analysis, Veermäe said.

"The independent expert selected will prepare a comparative economic impact analysis based on the materials submitted by the cities, gather additional data where necessary and conduct interviews with representatives of the cities and other key stakeholders," she said.

Once the expert committee has approved the expert who will conduct the analysis, the economic impact analysis will take approximately three months to complete. The expert committee will then prepare a summary and submit its recommendation on the most suitable location to the government, Veermäe said.

The government will make the final decision on which city the arena will ultimately be built in. Once that decision has been made, it will also become clear when construction could begin and when the arena could be completed.

The EOK began the arena project's preparatory phase last November. Among other things, representatives have visited Finland to study the business model of a multifunctional arena.

Plans for the arena began to be pursued more seriously after Estonia secured the right to host the 2029 European Basketball Championship. Estonia's largest indoor arena at present is Tallinn's Unibet Arena, which can accommodate up to 7,000 spectators.

A sketch of Arena Tartu proposed for the Roosi tänav 89 site in Tartu. Source: Tartu City Government / Kuu arhitektid

The government is currently discussing next year's state budget and the state budget strategy for the next four years. Economy Minister Erkki Keldo told "Aktuaalne kaamera" on Tuesday that some investments will have to be dropped in order to reduce the budget deficit.

"We will also have to drop investments that might have been possible in better times — buildings and other construction projects. We cannot afford them when such a large share is going toward defense investments," Keldo said. Estonia aims to spend at least 5 percent of its GDP on national defense in the coming years.

World.title: Estonian‑co‑produced film gets 7‑minute standing ovation in Venice
World.content:
The Estonian‑co‑produced feature "Woman Unknown" premiered Sunday at the ongoing Venice Film Festival's main competition, and got a seven‑and‑a‑half‑minute standing ovation.

"Woman Unknown" (Danish: Kvinde ukendt) is directed by Danish filmmaker May el‑Toukhy and is a psychological drama filmed primarily in Latvia. Of the 28 shooting days, 25 took place in Riga, with Estonia's Nafta Films among the co‑producers.

Esko Rips, CEO of Nafta Films and a co‑producer, said the film's selection among the 21 titles in the main competition is important recognition of the Estonian company's three years of work, which was a truly pan-Baltic states affair as it began in Lithuania and culminated in filming in Riga.

"For us, this confirms that operating in all three Baltic states gives us an advantage in producing international films. It allows us to find the best solution for each film in terms of financing, filming locations and creative needs," Rips said.

The Danish-Swedish-Latvian-Estonian co‑production was locally managed by Nafta Films' Latvian team, with co‑producers including Rips and Latvia's Madara Kalniņa.

"Woman Unknown" stands out in this year's competition also because el‑Toukhy is one of just two women directors from among the 21 competing films, ironically enough given women's invisibility and the limits imposed on them by society are central themes of the film itself.

"My film is about the invisibility of women. On the one hand, about objectification, and on the other, about how women are neither seen nor listened to," el‑Toukhy said at a film festival press conference.

"Woman Unknown" is set in Denmark at the end of World War Two. The story centers on Marie, a young nanny and housekeeper preparing to marry her wealthy employer, Christian, an older widower. A dark secret from her past — an intimate relationship with a German soldier during the Nazi occupation of Denmark — threatens her new life.

The film explores society's control over women's choices, their bodies and pasts, showing that the end of the war did not necessarily spell an end to all violence and condemnation.

Mathilde Arcel Fock ("Second victims," "Special Unit: The First Murder") stars in the lead role. The cast also includes Carsten Bjørnlun ("Barracuda Queens," "The Shooter").

The Venice Film Festival runs to Saturday.

World.title: Taking care of people with dementia left up to loved ones in Estonia
World.content:
A recent study finds that a unified system for helping people with dementia should be established so their loved ones do not have to seek assistance from multiple agencies.

Nearly 27,000 people with dementia currently live in Estonia and in an aging society, the issue is becoming increasingly acute. A dementia diagnosis affects not only the person with the condition but also their loved ones. Hanna-Stiina Heinmets, who counsels family members on a daily basis, said the loved ones of people with memory disorders most need services that give them a break.

"Their daily job is providing care and they may also be working at the same time. They essentially have two full-time jobs and for the most part, they cannot afford to take days off. They simply need someone to come in and take over the caregiving for a few days," said Hanna-Stiina Heinmets, a consultant at the Dementia Competence Center.

In many municipalities, home care is understood to mean little more than bringing firewood inside and delivering food to a person's home. But if a person with dementia needs help taking medication, for example, Heinmets said the recommendation is often to send them to a nursing home, even though they could still continue living at home. At the same time, nursing homes are reluctant to accept people with severe dementia and some have effectively been thrown out of five or six different nursing homes. A recent study found that access to assistance often depends on where a person lives.

"The situation is generally better in larger population centers. They have day centers and more services. There are more options and more resources. The most difficult situation is in sparsely populated, outlying areas," Praxis analyst Jane Ester said.

Ester said the first step should be to create a comprehensive support system for both people with dementia and their loved ones. Each family affected by dementia should have a designated person responsible for their case who would proactively contact family members, regularly assess what assistance the family needs and help them find it, rather than leaving people to navigate between different agencies on their own.

According to the Ministry of Social Affairs, the planned health and social care reform should improve the situation to some extent. In two years, the ministry hopes to begin testing, with the support of EU funding, solutions that will help people with dementia continue living at home for longer.

"I think these people's lives can be made easier. If we think about what can provide support right now, today, there is the Dementia Competence Center and its information line. That is somewhere people can turn for help today," said Kadri Mets, head of disability rights policy at the Ministry of Social Affairs.

World.title: Station Narva draws record 5,766 visitors for 10th edition
World.content:
The weekend's Station Narva festival attracted nearly 6,000 visitors, a record figure in the decade the event has been running.

The music and city festival, held from Thursday, September 3 to Sunday, September 6, brought 5,766 visitors, and founder and director Helen Sildna said attendance confirms that Station Narva has found a place in the hearts of its audience.

"The city of Narva and the people of Ida-Viru County have embraced us. It brings our team heartfelt joy to see such different people spending time together at the festival – from young people to seniors, from across Estonia and Europe. That is exactly our wish and aim: to create a cultural event that brings people together and unites, motivates and encourages them. We are already starting work today on the tenth Station Narva," Sildna said.

Culture Minister Heidy Purga (Reform), who opened the festival's music program, said Station Narva is evidence of how music brings people together and opens the city to new perspectives.

Narva's Hermann Castle during Station Narva 2026. Source: Kirill Jakušev

"You may leave here with a new favorite song, a new friendship or a reason to return to Narva. What moved me most this year was Skoone's concert and meeting local young people, whose energy and desire to connect their creativity with their hometown and Station Narva show that this festival has a future in Narva that is very much its own and very much needed," Purga said.

Musical headliners included British trip‑hop pioneer and Station Narva regular Tricky, Icelandic electronic pop act GusGus and Estonian artists spanning several generations and genres, among them folk‑pop band Sadu, veteran punk act Propeller and Narva native and 2023 Eurovision representative Alika, who was also celebrating her birthday.

Concerts mainly took place at the Narva Museum inside the historic Hermann Castle, and at the Ro‑Ro club.

Free daytime concerts featured actor and solo artist Mihkel Kuusk as well as other local and Estonian acts, art installations and more.

Next year's Station Narva is the 10th edition and is set to run over the same weekend, September 2‑5, 2027.
