World.title: Tiger sighted in Munnar tea plantation amid cattle attack concerns
World.content:
A tiger was spotted on the road connecting Goodarvila Estate in Nettikkudy Division to Silent Valley near Munnar. Upon noticing an approaching vehicle, the tiger retreated into nearby tea bushes.

Munnar Range Officer S. Biju confirmed the authenticity of a video showing the tiger and stated that the big cat’s presence has been reported in the area.

“Tiger sightings and cattle attacks have been reported in the Pampanmala, Thenmala, and Silent Valley areas. The tiger seen in the video is a healthy animal and is occasionally spotted in this region,” the official said.

Local residents said that the recurring loss of cows threatens workers and causes financial distress for plantation labourers reliant on dairy farming. Forest department officials confirmed that compensation is being provided for cattle lost to tiger attacks

Amid the recurring attacks across Devikulam and Munnar, the department plans to instruct plantation managements to ensure that livestock are sheltered in sheds by early afternoon.

World.title: SI attacked with weapon by habitual offender in Dindigul district; police open fire at him; both admitted in hospital
World.content:
In a shocking incident, a habitual offender, wanted in many grave crimes, allegedly attacked a sub-inspector of police with a sharp weapon and in retaliation, the officer opened fire from his service pistol in which the anti-social suffered injuries below his knee on Wednesday.

The habitual offender, Raja alias Chikkanampatti Raja (57), from Chinnalapatti in Dindigul district figured in 22 crimes, including waylaying, attempt to murder, robbery and murder.

In a murder case, a court had directed life sentence to Raja on April 5, 2025. Having appealed with the higher court on the order, Raja obtained a bail recently and was underground since then.

When the police came to know that Raja was reportedly threatening some of the witnesses, who had deposed in the murder case, they began to search for him, but in vain.

Dindigul SP S Jeyakumar formed a special team and were on the look out for the accused.

Batlagundu police team came to know that Raja was hiding in a place in N. Kovilpatti, which belonged to his sister.

A special team led by Sub Inspector (SI) of Police Arun Prasad zeroed-in at the location, but realising that police had come, Raja stepped out of the dwelling and assaulted the SI of Police with a sword. Taken aback, the police opened fire in the air and appealed to him to surrender. However, he rushed towards the SI and attacked him on his left hand. Immediately, the SI of Police fired at Raja’s knee.

Both the accused and the SI were rushed to Nilakottai Government Hospital. Subsequently, the accused was taken to Dindigul Government Medical College Hospital for treatment.

On information, Mr Jeyakumar visited the scene of crime and held inquiries in which Nilakottai DSP Illanchezhian, Batlagundu Inspector Gowtham and others were present.

A senior officer said that the SI of Police was stable and was recovering. Further investigation was on.

World.title: Devotees seek removal of Mathe Manikeshwari Ashram head
World.content:
Devotees of Mata Manikeshwari Ashram at Yanagundi in Sedam taluk staged a protest in Kalaburagi city on Wednesday, demanding the removal of Ashram president Shivayya Swami and an inquiry into alleged irregularities in the handling of donations and funds.

The protesters alleged that Mr. Shivayya had dissolved the existing trust and constituted a new one with his nominees without the consent of its members or following due procedure. They demanded an investigation into the constitution of the new trust and the restoration of the earlier management.

“We want a transparent inquiry into the funds and donations received by the ashram and the manner in which the new trust was formed without the consent of old trust members,” devotee Shivakumar Patil Telkur said.

Devotee Parvath Reddy sought a comprehensive audit of cash, gold and silver offerings, hundi collections and other donations received by the ashram. They also demanded details of collections and expenditure related to the proposed installation of a ‘Koti Linga’ on the ashram hill.

He said every donation received in the name of the ashram should be properly accounted for and its utilisation disclosed to devotees.

The protesters demanded that Mr. Shivayya be removed from the management pending an inquiry and that appropriate action be taken if the allegations were established. They also sought reconstitution of the management in accordance with the trust’s rules and the traditional practices of the ashram.

World.title: Forest Department withdraws case against farmer over tree felling on ‘patta’ land
World.content:
The Forest Department has withdrawn a case registered against a farmer for cutting trees on his ‘patta’ land in Pandippara, Idukki.

The case, registered at the Kattappana section office under the Ayyappancoil forest range, had attracted attention after forest officials booked Chackochan for cutting trees from his own land.

The farmer had cut two jackfruit trees, a mango tree and a ‘pathiri’ (yellow trumpet tree) from his property. The Forest Department assessed the alleged loss at ₹4,000. Timber valued at ₹15,607 and tools worth ₹2,200 were also seized during the proceedings.

Under the Kerala Land Assignment Special Rules, 1993, the department is legally empowered to initiate action for cutting only those specified tree species that are covered by the Kerala Preservation of Trees Act, 1986. The ten species covered by the provisions are sandalwood, teak, rosewood, irul, thempavu, kampakam, chempakam, dhaman (chadachi), red cedar (chandana vembu) and cheeni.

Following the intervention of Forest Minister Shibu Baby John, the department withdrew the case. The Minister also directed officials to return the seized timber and tools to the landowner.

World.title: Tejashwi writes to Bihar CM Samrat Choudhary over PDS dealers’ demands
World.content:
Leader of the Opposition in the Bihar Legislative Assembly Tejashwi Yadav on Wednesday (September 9, 2026) wrote a letter to Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary over the demands and “problems” faced by Public Distribution System (PDS) dealers in the State.

Mr. Yadav said PDS dealers play a vital role in the State’s public distribution network, ensuring delivery of foodgrains to millions of poor and needy families, even under challenging circumstances. He claimed that despite this, it is deeply unfortunate that their economic and administrative grievances have remained unaddressed for a long time.

Mr. Yadav alleged that dealers are facing a severe financial crisis due to “record-breaking inflation”, mounting administrative hurdles, delays in commission payments, and technical issues.

He demanded that PDS dealers be provided with a fixed monthly honorarium of at least ₹30,000, following the model adopted in Gujarat. He also sought provisions for the appointment of eligible dependents on compassionate grounds, with the time limit for such appointments removed, similar to the practice in Jharkhand.

Mr. Yadav wrote, “Commission payments pending for periods ranging from six months to a year must be cleared immediately as the delay in these payments has plunged thousands of PDS vendors and their families into a severe financial crisis.”

The RJD’s national working president added that an increase of ₹47 in the commission for PDS dealers had been announced before the Assembly elections. Despite a year having passed, if this increased amount has not yet been paid, it should be implemented with immediate effect and the arrears cleared, he said.

Strict action sought

“Strict action must be taken regarding complaints of alleged corruption, irregularities, and under-weighing at Bihar State Food Corporation (BSFC) warehouses, and the entire system should be made transparent. Real-time solutions must be ensured for issues related to weighing, under-weighing, e-PoS machines, servers, and other technical glitches, so that neither PDS vendors nor beneficiaries have to bear the brunt of technical failures,” Mr. Yadav wrote.

He also demanded an effective grievance redressal mechanism at the district and block levels to address genuine problems faced by dealers, while curbing alleged unnecessary administrative pressure and punitive action associated with the PDS system.

Mr. Yadav urged the government to organise regular tripartite meetings involving departmental officials and representatives of the Fair Price Dealers Association to find permanent solutions to the issues faced by PDS dealers.

“It is requested that an immediate, positive, and time-bound decision be taken regarding the demands of the PDS vendors. I am confident that the Government of Bihar will consider the legitimate demands of the PDS vendors with sensitivity and seriousness, and take concrete steps towards a speedy resolution,” Mr. Yadav said in the two-page letter.

Reacting to the letter, the Fair Price Dealers Association posted a message on social media saying, “All PDS dealers express their gratitude to the Leader of the Opposition in the Bihar Legislative Assembly, Tejashwi Yadav, for vigorously raising our pending demands and issues on public platforms.”

Meanwhile, an RJD delegation met an Election Commission official to demand an extension of the voter registration deadline for the Tirhut Graduate Constituency, the removal of names of “bogus voters” from the electoral roll, and the unlocking of the Election Commission’s registration portal.

In the absence of the Chief Electoral Officer, the delegation submitted a memorandum to Additional Chief Electoral Officer Ashok Priyadarshi. The delegation included the party’s national general secretary Bhola Yadav, along with Chittaranjan Gagan, Madan Sharma, and Faiyaz Alam Kamal.

World.title: Gujarat team appreciates APCNF natural farming model in Andhra Pradesh
World.content:
A Gujarat delegation visiting Guntur district to study the Andhra Pradesh Community-managed Natural Farming (APCNF) model has appreciated the visible transformation in farmers’ fields, particularly the shift from chemical farming to natural farming, increased crop diversity and biodiversity, improved soil health and enhanced income opportunities.

The 10-member delegation visited several natural farming models implemented by Rythu Sadhikara Samstha (RySS) and interacted with farmers.

“The transformation we witnessed on the ground, from chemical farming to natural farming, reflected in healthier crops, greater biodiversity, diverse cropping systems and improved income opportunities, clearly demonstrates the strength of the APCNF approach,” the delegation said.

The team first visited Vijay Kumar’s POP model at Pidaparthi, where around 35 crop and plant varieties are cultivated on 30 cents of land, generating a monthly income of ₹13,000 to ₹15,000. The delegation appreciated the favourable microclimate and the presence of beneficial insects.

It also visited Ratnakumari’s A-Grade okra model, which had more than 10 intercrops and banana plantations along the borders. Compared with a neighbouring chemical-farming field, the natural farming plot had healthier plants and fewer visible symptoms of virus incidence and leaf curling.

At Munnangi, the delegation visited Mastan Bhi’s five-acre natural farming paddy compact block and observed low weed pressure. Officials explained the use of Azolla for weed suppression and soil enrichment. The team also examined sticky plates, pheromone traps and L-shaped bund plantations used for pest monitoring and promoting biodiversity.

At Atthota, the delegation interacted with farmer Bapayya and appreciated his efforts to conserve indigenous paddy varieties and traditional seeds.

World.title: Man arrested for stealing clothes from girls’ hostel
World.content:
The Bellare police have arrested K. Ramachandra, 35, a resident of Koltige in Puttur taluk of Dakshina Kannada, on the charge of stealing clothes from the Government Girls Hostel in Bellare.

In a statement, the police said students of the hostel had on September 2 complained to the warden that clothes left out to dry were stolen. The warden checked CCTV footage and noticed a person trespassing into the hostel and taking away clothes belonging to some girls.

Based on the complaint, the police zeroed in on Ramachandra and arrested him on September 7 for stealing the clothes. He was produced before the jurisdictional magistrate court, which remanded him in judicial custody till September 15, the police said.

Woman arrested

The Kavoor police have arrested 44-year-old Lata Mariya of Akash Bhavan in Mangaluru, who had failed to appear before the court for over five years in a theft case registered against her.

In a press note, the police said Mariya was arrested in connection with a theft at a house in the Kavoor police station limits in 2019. Following her failure to appear before the court on several dates after being released on bail, the court issued arrest warrants and classified the case as a long-pending one. The Kavoor police arrested Mariya from Jyoti Nagar and produced her before the court, which remanded her in judicial custody, the police said.

World.title: ‘Varuna Yagam’ performed at Vinayaka ghat ahead of Ganesh Chaturthi
World.content:
With Vinayaka Chaturthi fast approaching, ‘Varuna Yagam’ (a ritual to invoke rain) was performed at the Vinayaka ghat under the auspices of the Kurnool city Ganesha Utsava Samithi on Wednesday. The ritual was performed so that the Vinayaka ghat will have enough water for the immersion of Ganesh idols installed in the city.

The ritual included the worship and invocation of Lord Varuna, ‘Varuna Japa’ (chanting), recitation of the ‘Virata Parva’, ‘Varuna Homam’ (fire ritual), and ‘Purnahuti’.

According to the committee members, similar rituals were performed during adverse weather conditions in the past as well.

The event was attended by festival committee president Moksheshwarudu, secretaries Kasi Viswanath, Nagaraju, and Pratap Reddy, former MLA S.V. Mohan Reddy, and committee members.

World.title: Security forces kill 11 terrorists during IBOs in Balochistan's Kharan, Washuk districts: ISPR
World.content:
Security forces killed 11 terrorists and recovered 2.9 tonnes of explosives in separate intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan’s Kharan and Washuk districts, the military’s media affairs wing said on Wednesday.

According to a statement by Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the security forces conducted the IBOs in Kharan and Washuk on September 6 and 7, respectively, on the “reported presence of terrorists belonging to Indian proxy, Fitna al Hindustan and neutralised 11 Indian-sponsored terrorists”.

The state has designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna-al-Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan.

ISPR said terrorists attempted to establish a roadblock in Kharan and disrupted local traffic on Sunday. “The security forces promptly intercepted and engaged the terrorists, whereby, killing eight Indian-sponsored terrorists,” it added.

The forces conducted another “deliberately planned” IBO in Washuk district on Monday on reports of the presence of terrorists, the statement said.

“During the conduct of operation, own troops effectively busted terrorists’ hideout and after an intense fire exchange, three terrorists were sent to hell,” ISPR said, adding that security forces recovered 2.9 tonnes of explosives being used for preparing improvised explosive devices (IEDs).

It further said that sanitisation operations were being conducted to eliminate “any other Indian-sponsored terrorist” found in the area.

ISPR reaffirmed that the security forces and law enforcement agencies would continue the “relentless counterterrorism campaign” under Azm-i-Istehkam, approved by the Federal Apex Committee under the National Action Plan, to wipe out the “menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country”.

President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif paid tribute to the security forces for killing terrorists and recovering the explosives.

“The nefarious designs of terrorists who are active under Indian patronage will be thwarted at all costs,” the president was quoted as saying in a statement.

“Operations will continue until the complete eradication of terrorists belonging to Fitna al Hindustan network,” he added.

PM Shehbaz also commended the security forces for foiling the attempt to block a road and disrupt traffic in Kharan and praised the professional capabilities of the forces for destroying a terrorist hideout in Washuk.

He reiterated the government’s aim to eradicate “terrorism conducted under India’s patronage” and pledged that operations against terrorist elements would continue with full force.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi lauded the security forces’ professional skills for thwarting the “nefarious designs” of the terrorists, his ministry said.

He saluted the security forces for eliminating the terrorists and said they were determined to eradicate the Indian-sponsored terrorists, the interior ministry said in a post on X.

“The brave sons of the security forces are a source of pride for the nation and it stands with them in the fight against terrorism,” Naqvi was quoted as saying.

Terrorism surge

Balochistan has witnessed a surge in terrorist attacks in recent weeks, prompting security forces to intensify counter-terrorism operations.

On the night of Aug 31-Sept 1, Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) terrorists launched a coordinated attack on the Customs House, located at Ziarat Cross on the N-50 National Highway, in Pishin district.

While security forces responded effectively and killed 10 terrorists, two officers were among six martyred in the fire exchange, ISPR said.

Also on August 31, 11 terrorists belonging to Fitna al Hindustan, who had blocked the N-40 Quetta-Taftan highway by establishing an illegal checkpoint for extortion in Chagai’s Nokcha area, were eliminated following an intense exchange of fire.

On September 2, security forces killed 12 terrorists in the Kalat district during an IBO conducted on the reported presence of Fitna al Hindustan terrorists.

Another 36 terrorists were eliminated during multiple “high-tempo” operations conducted in Mastung, Quetta, Kalat and Sibi districts, the ISPR said on September 4. These included thwarting an attack on a police station in Sibi’s Bhag area.

World.title: Asif warns Makkah defence pact could become operational after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has cautioned that the tripartite Makkah Defence Alliance between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye could become operational if there was a “spillover” of the conflict in Yemen into Riyadh.

The development comes after Yemen’s Houthi rebels launched attacks on oil installations in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, injuring 73 people.

Meanwhile, the defence pact, signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.

On the Geo News show ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath’ on Tuesday night, host Shahzeb Khanzada mentioned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and asked Asif whether the strategic pact could be operationalised.

Asif answered in the affirmative, saying there was no “ambiguity” as the pact stipulated that aggression against one party was equivalent to aggression against all.

“This is a joint defence pact. And unprovoked aggression or spillover of whatever is happening in Yemen into Saudi Arabia, definitely, the pact will become operational; there should be no doubt in this,” he said.

“We are bound by the terms and conditions of this pact and we will honour them in case there is a need,” he said.

Asked if Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had been in contact following the attacks, Asif said he was not aware of any engagement. However, he reiterated that Pakistan “is bound to react under the pact because it is [aimed at] joint defence and collective help in case of aggression”.

Asif further stated that the pact was not “aggressive in nature”, adding: “If there is aggression against one member state, then all three member states will respond in kind.”

The defence czar went on to say, “This is a trilateral pact [..] but even if it were bilateral, we would have responded.”

At the same time, Asif expressed hope that the situation will “come under control and die down”.

He also hoped that “the Houthis will realise that if [..] they attempt to export their internal matters, then the clauses of this pact over confronting aggression will become operative”.

“They should keep this in mind,” he said. Asif also noted that the Houthis were “non-state actors” and that Yemen’s government had responded to their attacks.

“There is sympathy for Iran around the Muslim world. There is no doubt about that, but exploitation of a bilateral dispute by non-state actors, I believe they are doing it at their own peril,” he said.

Asif observed that the pact could serve as a deterrent and went on to say that three countries “did not need to respond to aggression with aggression”, but held that the member states had established their respective strengths.

The defence minister added that the conflict in Yemen had been ongoing since 2014, recalling a visit he made to the country at the time in his capacity as the defence minister.

“At that time too, we helped Saudi Arabia,” he recalled, adding that Pakistan and Saudi’s long-standing ties and the “sanctity” of the Gulf country’s land “warrant that whenever there are testing times, we help them”.

On the stalemate in negotiations between the United States and Iran, the defence minister voiced optimism that “all doors have not closed”.

“I will not abandon hope that the process has ended or that all doors have closed. There is a stalemate, but I will say the situation is better than that,” he said, adding there was “indirect engagement”.

He noted that Pakistan walked a tightrope given its “brotherly relations” with countries on both sides of the conflict. Hoping that peace would prevail, Asif warned: “Israel will want that the conflict should continue and (Gulf) countries should be drained.”

He said Israel was not incurring any expenses in the war, as the funding “was coming from overseas”.

“In fact, I believe they are profiting off of it,” he said. He noted that people in Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon were paying the price for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s “lust for power”. However, he went on to note that there was a “silver lining”.

“In the world over, especially Europe, North America, New Zealand, Latin America, there is a sea [of] change in the opinions of people and people want to get rid of the Zionist lobby,” he said.

On Tuesday, the rebel group claimed attacks on four cities in the south of Saudi Arabia, which wounded more than 70 people and set oil installations ablaze. The Houthis said they had fired dozens of ballistic missiles, hitting the southern cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan, and Najran, including Abha International Airport, King Khalid air base, and facilities belonging to state oil giant Aramco.

In response, Saudi Arabia retaliated with strikes on Taiz and Marib provinces, as well as the Jubah district, east of the capital Sanaa. At the time, the Saudi foreign ministry said Riyadh would “take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty”.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had condemned the Houthi attack and assured Saudi Arabia of Pakistan’s “unwavering solidarity”.

“Such dastardly attacks threaten innocent lives as well as regional peace and security. We reaffirm our steadfast support for the kingdom’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity, and pray for the swift recovery of all those injured,” he said in a post on X.

The Foreign Office also issued a statement condemning the “reprehensible” attacks.

World.title: Two navy personnel martyred while patrolling at sea: DGPR
World.content:
Two Pakistan Navy personnel were martyred while patrolling at sea to ensure security, the Navy’s Directorate-General of Public Relations (DGPR) said on Wednesday.

“Shoaibur Rehman (PMA-IV) and Ghufran Nasar (PMT-II) embraced martyrdom while performing patrolling duties at sea to ensure security,” it said in a statement on X.

As per the statement, Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf expressed deep sorrow over the loss of precious lives.

“Senior Pakistan Navy officials attended the funerals of martyred sailors and met their families,” it added.

In March this year, the Pakistan Navy had launched Operation Muhafizul Bahr to counter “multidimensional threats to national shipping and maritime trade”.

According to the Pakistan Navy, the decision — which followed the launch of the US-Iran war — was made in light of the “evolving regional maritime security environment and potential disruptions to critical sea lanes”.

The statement noted that with approximately 90 per cent of Pakistan’s trade conducted via sea, the operation aimed to ensure that vital sea routes remained safe, secure, and uninterrupted.

World.title: Islamabad admin announces 'complete ban' on sheesha cafes as IHC gives a month to formulate regulations
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Islamabad Deputy Commissioner (DC) Irfan Nawaz Memon on Wednesday announced a “complete” ban on running sheesha cafes in the federal capital.

“Immediately implementing the Islamabad High Court’s order, a complete ban has been imposed on running sheesha cafes in the federal capital until further orders,” the DC posted on X.

He added that the restriction also covered all kinds of sheesha cafes, including those that had no-objection certificates (NOCs) and outdoor and indoor cafes.

Cafes found in violation of the order would be sealed, and a case would be registered against the owner, he warned, adding that assistant commissioners would ensure inspections on a daily basis.

The DC’s announcement came after the Islamabad High Court (IHC) observed earlier in the day that sheesha cafes couldn’t be allowed to operate without a proper regulatory framework and gave the district administration one month to formulate comprehensive rules and regulations.

IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar issued the directive while hearing petitions pertaining to several sheesha cafes in Islamabad and the action taken against establishments that had been allegedly operating in violation of their NOCs, issued under an interim arrangement.

DC Memon and Islamabad Inspector General of Police (IG) Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi also appeared before the court in their personal capacities at the hearing. Islamabad Advocate General Naveed Hayat Malik and acting Prosecutor General Manzoor Ahmed Jajja were also present.

During the proceedings, the chief justice said that the court respected the business interests of cafe owners, but the entire city could not be allowed to be affected in the name of business.

“Tomorrow, your brother or someone from your family could become a victim,” the chief justice remarked, referring to health implications.

He questioned the manner in which sheesha was being served, observing that if hashish was mixed with tobacco, it would amount to smoking. He further remarked that such activities were taking place openly and warned that the younger generation was being pushed towards destruction.

The Islamabad police chief informed the court that strict action had been taken against sheesha cafes following the court’s earlier directives, and cases had been registered against some establishments.

The IG claimed that police teams had faced resistance from cafe owners during raids and that children aged 14 and 15 had also been found at some establishments.

He further stated that an awareness campaign regarding the harmful effects and regulation of sheesha cafes had also been launched.

Following that, CJ Dogar observed that sheesha cafes could not be allowed to operate as they were running presently, without rules and regulations.

“There are no rules and regulations,” the chief justice observed, adding that the existing arrangement was damaging the lives of people in Islamabad.

Acting Prosecutor General Jajja told the court that children aged 18 or below were among those involved in selling sheesha and suggested that directions be issued to the Ministry of Health and the federal government to formulate proper rules.

He said the issue was more serious than that of smog and required a comprehensive regulatory response.

When the CJ asked whether the cafe owners “shut their doors” when a police team conducted raids, the Islamabad IG replied in the affirmative, saying that it had been several times.

During the proceedings, the chief commissioner and district administration submitted their written response to the court.

According to the response, NOCs for sheesha cafes are currently being issued under an interim arrangement pending approval of regular legislation by the federal government. The district administration said all NOCs had been issued without any fee.

The response stated separate standard operating procedures (SOPs) were not considered necessary as the criteria for issuing NOCs were based on the high court’s directives and World Health Organisation’s guidelines (WHO).

Under the existing arrangement, sheesha could only be served in an open, unroofed area. A separate written “terrace permit” was required from the assistant commissioner concerned for serving sheesha at an open-air location, the response said.

The assistant commissioner concerned would be given the authority to inspect an establishment, impose additional conditions and take action according to law upon receiving complaints from the public, it added.

The administration said a crackdown against sheesha cafes in Islamabad had been launched in 2021 and that unsafe storage of coal and related equipment posed a significant fire hazard.

It added that fire prevention and safety measures had been made mandatory for restaurants, while inspection teams had also been directed to check the validity and safety of fire extinguishers.

The administration maintained that sheesha and other tobacco products could only be served to adults and that environmental standards were required to be maintained.

It further stressed the need to implement international and legal regulations to protect citizens from exposure to tobacco smoke.

For its part, the IHC said that the existing court-approved arrangement would remain in force until the federal government framed regular rules.

He directed the district administration to formulate the required rules within one month and adjourned the hearing.

World.title: Pakistan collapse to 133 all out against England in third Test
World.content:
Pakistan slumped to 133 all out on the opening day of the third Test at Edgbaston on Wednesday after the latest in a series of woeful batting displays that have marred their tour of England.

Pakistan, already 2-0 down in the three-match series, banished seven players and sacked both head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant Umar Gul after a heavy 194-run defeat in the second Test at Lord’s.

They fielded three debutants among four changes to their side in Birmingham but the reshuffle, unsurprisingly, made little difference, with Pakistan yet to make 200 in five innings.

Pakistan again had few answers to Ollie Robinson (3-15) and Jofra Archer (3-25) as the new-ball pair made the most of helpful, overcast conditions after England captain Joe Root won the toss.

Fellow paceman Josh Tongue then got in on the act with 4-42 in an innings wrapped up inside 34 overs.

Only Saud Shakeel, fresh from his 97 at Lord’s, offered any resistance by a specialist batsman with 43 before tailender Mohammad Abbas was last man out for 21.

Pakistan’s latest slump started when recalled opener Saim Ayub was out for a duck, lbw to a typical Robinson nip-backer as the 32-year-old took his 100th Test wicket.

Express quick Archer then undid Azan Awais with a short ball.

Abdullah Shafique nicked Robinson to gully and Pakistan were 26-4 inside 10 overs when the experienced Shan Masood holed out, tamely attempting to pull Archer.

Pakistan captain Babar Azam, without a Test century in nearly four years, was dismissed for just seven, clean bowled by an excellent Tongue delivery that jagged back off the seam.

And Pakistan were 64-6 when wicket-keeper Ghazi Ghori, one of the three Pakistan debutants, along with Mohammad Imran and Razaullah, was lbw to Tongue for four.

Pakistan, who have lost 15 of their past 20 Tests, were seven down before lunch when Tongue bowled Imran for five with a brilliant yorker that broke a stump.

But Razaullah flayed the last ball of the session, from Tongue, over cover for four to bring up the 100.

Razaullah, however, fell to his first ball after lunch when his edged drive off Robinson’s leg-cutter flew to Ben Duckett in the slips.

Saud’s impressive 47-ball innings, including seven fours, came to an end when he was bowled between bat and pad by a seaming Tongue delivery that knocked over his off stump, with Pakistan now 107-9.

Abbas batted gamely before edging Archer to second slip.

World.title: Yemen rebels report fresh Saudi strikes as conflict deepens
World.content:
Yemen’s Houthi rebels reported dozens of Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday as daily attacks continued in a conflict that has reignited during the Middle East war, with hundreds of people killed in fighting near the Red Sea.

More than 40 attacks targeted several regions, including the flashpoint areas of Taiz and Hodeida, the scene of fierce clashes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition government, the rebels said.

The latest salvos in Yemen’s previously dormant conflict come a day after the Houthis set oil sites ablaze and wounded 73 in their heaviest missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia in years.

The fighting in Yemen is taking place against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which erupted in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.

On Wednesday, Iran said it attacked 20 American vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and targeted a US military base in Jordan in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian oil tankers.

The Middle East war has sucked in Yemen, the energy-rich Gulf and others across the region while roiling the world economy, as oil prices returned to $100 a barrel on Wednesday.

More than 500 people have died since the Houthis launched a major offensive last week to seize territory around the Bab al-Mandab strait, gateway to the Red Sea shipping route.

This frame grab taken from AFPTV video footage on September 9, shows smoke billowing during clashes between Yemeni government forces and Houthi fighters in the Al-Kadha area, west of Taiz province, on September 8. — AFP

The rebels, who have been attacking Saudi oil tankers, are trying to tighten their squeeze on the shipments, which analysts say are a lifeline for exports after the blockade of Hormuz.

Saudi airstrikes targeted “various areas across the governorates of Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeida over the past few hours”, the rebels’ Almasirah TV said on Wednesday.

There was no official comment from Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi civil defence later issued a warning for the southern governorate of Khamis Mushait, near Yemen, but quickly lifted it.

On Tuesday, Saudi authorities vowed to respond to the Houthi attacks, saying they caused fires and temporary shutdowns at oil sites.

This frame grab taken on September 9, 2026, from video footage released by the Saudi Ministry of Media on September 8, 2026, shows damage following Houthi strikes at an undisclosed location in southern Saudi Arabia. — AFP

The Houthis triggered the return to hostilities in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.

The government retaliated by striking the airport, an attack the rebels blamed on Saudi Arabia.

The ongoing exchanges risk returning Yemen to a conflict that left hundreds of thousands of people dead and sparked one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

The Houthis, after seizing Yemen’s capital and forcing out the internationally recognised government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

On Tuesday, the European Union urged the Houthis to end their attacks, calling them a “dangerous escalation”.

“We call on the Houthis to immediately end all attacks inside and outside Yemen, including attacks against commercial shipping in the Red Sea,” said Anouar El Anouni, a spokesman for the bloc’s diplomatic service.

World.title: Timings for govt schools, colleges across Sindh reduced by an hour
World.content:
The Sindh government on Wednesday reduced the class timings for public schools and colleges by an hour until further orders.

In a circular, the Sindh School Education and Literacy Department said school timings prescribed in an earlier notification would “stand reduced by one hour during the prescribed five days’ school-observing week”.

“All other terms, conditions and directions contained in the aforesaid circular shall remain unchanged and continue to be applicable,” the circular read.

It directed all heads of educational institutions and the field officers concerned to ensure “strict implementation of the revised school timings in letter and spirit”.

Single-shift schools

The timings for primary, secondary and higher secondary schools operating a single shift are:

Until Oct 31 — 8am to 1:30pm from Monday to Thursday; 8am to 12pm on Friday

Nov 1-March 31 — 8:30am to 2:00pm from Monday to Thursday; 8:30am to 12:30pm on Friday

Double-shift primary schools

The timings for primary schools operating double shifts are:

Morning shift

Until Oct 31 — 7:30am to 12:30pm from Monday to Thursday; 8am to 12pm on Friday

Nov 1-March 31 — 8:30am to 2:30pm from Monday to Thursday; 8:30am to 10:30am on Friday

Evening shift

Until Oct 31 — 1pm to 5pm from Monday to Thursday; 10:45am to 1:15pm on Friday

Nov 1-March 31 — 12:45pm to 4:45pm from Monday to Thursday; 10:45am to 1:15pm on Friday

Double-shift secondary schools

The timings for elementary secondary and higher secondary schools operating a double shift are:

Morning shift

Until Oct 31 — 7:30am to 12:30pm from Monday to Thursday; 7:30am to 10:30am on Friday

Nov 1-March 31 — 8am to 12:45pm from Monday to Thursday; 8:00am to 10:30am on Friday

Evening shift

Until Oct 31 — 1pm to 5pm from Monday to Thursday; 10:45am to 12:15pm on Friday

Nov 1-March 31 — 12:45pm to 4:45pm from Monday to Thursday; 10:45am to 1:15pm on Friday

College timings

Separately, a notification issued by the College Education Department said the timings would be reduced by an hour with immediate effect.

The new timings for the morning shift in colleges are 8:30am to 1:30pm from Monday to Thursday, and 8:30am to 11:30am on Friday.

For the evening shift, classes will be held from 3pm to 7pm Monday through Thursday, and from 2:30pm to 5pm on Friday.

In late July, the Sindh government announced a six-day week for all public and private educational institutions under its administration.

However, the next day, it said private schools could decide their weekly teaching and working days according to their own schedules and convenience.

On August 5, the government restored the five-day working week for schools and colleges, reversing its earlier decision.

Schools in Sindh had observed a “spring vacation” from March 16 to 31, while colleges and universities switched to online classes as part of the austerity and fuel conservation measures adopted to deal with the economic impact of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

In line with the austerity drive, the provincial government said Saturday and Sunday would be “off” days following the resumption of classes on April 1.

World.title: Karachi police obtain Mir Raza's crypto trading records for last 4 years: official
World.content:
KARACHI: Karachi police on Wednesday said they have obtained the crypto trading records of 25-year-old businessman Mir Raza Ali, who was found dead with a gunshot wound in Gulistan-i-Jauhar in July.

A police official, wishing to remain anonymous, told Dawn that police obtained a four-year record through the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) of Ali’s involvement in “futures trading” of cryptocurrency on trading platform Binance.

“It showed that he had been doing futures trading for the last four years,” the official added.

On Monday, Ali’s friend Abdul Hasem, appearing before a judicial commission formed to probe the circumstances and possible negligence around Ali’s murder, had also said that he and Ali used to do crypto trading.

However, Hasem said he had left the trading after sustaining losses while Ali was doing well.

The single-member judicial commission, chaired by SHC’s Justice Omar Sial, has been holding regular hearings.

Last month, police had sought the NCCIA’s expertise to retrieve Ali’s “digital records/WhatsApp account details” to ascertain anything suspicious.

The case so far

Ali’s body was found a day after he went missing on July 28. Since then, the case has been mired in controversy, with the deceased’s family accusing the police of trying to bury the facts, as the police initially attempted to build the case around suicide.

However, days after the recovery of Ali’s body on July 29, Karachi Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed had told Geo News that the post-mortem findings in the case had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs.

On August 6, a Karachi court took up an application by Ali’s father, allowed the exhumation of his body, ordered the formation of a medico-legal board for the purpose and directed that a second autopsy of Ali’s body be conducted.

The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with police surgeon Dr Syed as the convener. However, in the early hours of August 7, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department.

While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed.

But Ali’s family rejected the new board, which also resulted in the deferment of the planned exhumation on Friday. Meanwhile, the counsel for Ali’s family, Nasir, accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts.

The Sindh government then restored the original medical board, following which Ali’s body was exhumed on August 8.

A day later, the Sindh inspector general of police’s (IG) office notified the reconstitution of the investigating team probing Ali’s death, while Karachi Additional IG Azad Khan transferred the investigation into Ali’s murder to Zaman Town police station from Ferozabad Police Station, where the case was registered under charges of kidnapping.

The order for the probe team’s reconstitution also showed that a murder charge had been added to the first information report.

The same day, the Sindh government decided to seek a judicial commission for the case’s investigation, only to defer the plan a day later after Ali’s family said they had made no such demand and had faith in the new investigation team.

On Aug 19, Ali’s parents, Mir Hussain and Mariam Hussain, wrote to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah, seeking his “direct supervision of the murder investigation”. They also urged the chief minister to order an investigation and departmental inquiry into the previous investigation team and immediately suspend the officers involved.

The provincial government acknowledged the letter and announced the decision on Aug 23 to form a judicial commission to determine whether the investigation in the case was being conducted impartially and to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ali’s death.

However, the counsel for Ali’s family approached the SHC, objecting to the provincial government’s decision to form a judicial commission and seeking the formation of an independent and multi-agency JIT “comprising officers who have had no previous involvement in the case”.

On Sept 2, the SHC dismissed that petition filed by Ali’s family, observing that constituting such a body was the “prerogative of the government”.

Meanwhile, the final report of Ali’s second post-mortem for the Mir Raza Ali murder case confirmed that his death was caused by a gunshot wound to the back.

“Death occurred due to cardiac rupture consequent to perforating firearm injury of the chest,” the report stated, adding that the entry wound was on the posterior thorax (back) and the exit wound on the anterior thorax (front of the chest).

“The findings are inconsistent with suicide as the manner of death,” it confirmed.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
