World.title: Alas embraces challenge as Ateneo honors Baterbonia, Adili in UAAP Season 89
World.content:
Louie Alas leads the Ateneo Blue Eagles in such delicate times, taking over as interim coach for the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament following the resignation of former head coach Tab Baldwin

MANILA, Philippines – Guiding an embattled Ateneo team still reeling from the tragic deaths of Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili is no easy task, but coach Louie Alas is up to the challenge.

Alas said he never shies away from pressure as he leads the Blue Eagles in such delicate times, taking over as interim coach for the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament following the resignation of former head coach Tab Baldwin.

It will be Alas’ first head coaching stint in college since he called the shots in 2012 for the Letran Knights, a team he steered to three NCAA championships.

“When the incident happened, I was ready to go because of command responsibility,” said Alas, who was hired in 2024 as a deputy. “But when one of the priests approached me and asked me if I was open to being a temporary coach, I said, ‘Father, it is not in my personality to back down from challenges.’ When I saw the players, how could I leave them?”

Alas, 62, did not join the team building in Dipaculao, Aurora, where Baterbonia and Adili drowned during a seawater activity on June 8, and in turn, did not get punished by the UAAP.

Those in attendance were penalized, with the UAAP slapping Baldwin with a lifetime ban and handing assistant coaches Dean Castaño, Sandro Soriano, and Jon Jacinto indefinite suspensions.

“I was ready to go and ready to retire, but with that situation, I think no coach would leave. I guess I’m destined to be here. I was fine with being an assistant, I no longer wanted to be a head coach. But this is what the Lord gave me and I’m ready to accept the challenge,” said Alas.

And the challenge includes keeping his wards locked in as the Blue Eagles deal with the backlash over their UAAP participation, with many fans believing Ateneo should have been suspended for at least one season given the gravity of the incident that claimed the lives of two student-athletes.

Jeers from the crowd during the games are also likely, but Alas trusts that there is enough security at the venues to keep things in order.

“Our concentration is on the UAAP itself. I hope nothing untoward happens,” said Alas.

The Blue Eagles are coming off a promising run in the Pinoyliga Cup, where they reached the semifinals before losing to eventual champion UST Growling Tigers.

Alas’ son, rookie guard Kieffer, showed the way for Ateneo in the preseason tournament where it beat Our Lady of Fatima University, St. Benilde, and Mapua with an average of 18.3 points, 5.3 rebounds, and 2.5 assists.

Travis Roberts backstopped the younger Alas with 12.3 points and 4.0 rebounds, while third-year guard Jared Bahay produced 6.5 points, 3.3 rebounds, and 3.3 assists.

Alas, though, knows the competition in the UAAP is on a whole ‘nother level.

“We have no expectations because we want to take care of our mental [fortitude] first. But we’ll make sure that we’re ready when we go into a game,” said Alas.

“Of course, this is part of our healing. And winning would make it easier for us to heal.”

Ultimately, the Blue Eagles are not just playing for victories or school pride as they offer the season to Baterbonia and Adili, with the men’s and women’s basketball teams wearing memorial patches with the initials “RB” and “DA” on their jerseys.

“Ever since the accident happened, the first thing on their mind is to dedicate this year to [Baterbonia and Adili.] They are in the players’ hearts,” said Alas. – Rappler.com

World.title: For GCash’s early private equity backers, record IPO will be ultimate payday
World.content:
GCash's blockbuster IPO could turn years of paper gains into billions for its early private equity backers. For the retail investors buying in now, the question is how much growth still remains.

GCash has become so ubiquitous that its blue QR codes are just as easy to find in sari-sari stores as they are in malls. Its upcoming initial public offering (IPO) now promises to give ordinary investors a chance to own a piece of that success.

And for some of GCash’s earliest financial backers, an IPO poised to become the largest in Philippine history also offers the kind of exit private equity (PE) investors spend years hoping for.

Bow Wave Capital, Warburg Pincus, Insight Partners, and LGVP invested in Mynt — the parent company of the e-wallet giant — long before it commanded anything close to the valuation it’s seeking today. They helped bankroll its rise from fast-growing fintech to profitable household name. Now, the IPO could allow them to turn what has so far been paper gains into cash.

And this is no small liquidity event.

Under the latest offer structure, Mynt will issue up to 1.61 billion new shares, while existing shareholders will sell up to 6.42 billion shares. Another 1.20 billion shares available under the overallotment option will also come from existing owners.

That means only 20% of the firm offer is primary, while 80% is secondary. In other words, most of the shares being sold will come from existing shareholders rather than from new shares issued to raise fresh capital for Mynt.

By the time the bell rings, the vast majority of the IPO proceeds will be going to shareholders selling down stakes accumulated years earlier, giving some of GCash’s earliest backers the ultimate payday.

Meet GCash’s big winners

The institutional sellers are mostly early financial investors. At the P10 ceiling and assuming the overallotment option is fully exercised, the prospectus shows:

Bow Wave Capital , through ASP Philippines – could sell about P27.04 billion worth of shares, cutting its stake from 6% to around 1.82%

, through ASP Philippines – could sell about P27.04 billion worth of shares, cutting its stake from 6% to around 1.82% Warburg Pincus , through Lion Fintech Investments – could sell around P12.18 billion, bringing its stake down from 2.70% to around 0.82%

, through Lion Fintech Investments – could sell around P12.18 billion, bringing its stake down from 2.70% to around 0.82% Insight Partners , through Insight PHP Holdings – could sell about P8.53 billion, reducing its stake from 1.89% to around 0.57%

, through Insight PHP Holdings – could sell about P8.53 billion, reducing its stake from 1.89% to around 0.57% Advanced New Technologies , an Ant International-linked company – could sell about P25.18 billion, reducing its stake from 6.22% to around 2.30%

, an Ant International-linked company – could sell about P25.18 billion, reducing its stake from 6.22% to around 2.30% LGVP, through its three investment vehicles – could sell around P2.66 billion combined, cutting their combined stake from about 0.59% to roughly 0.18%

These are investors deeply familiar with fintech.

Bow Wave is a relatively specialized private equity fund whose mandate centers on online and mobile payments. It first backed Mynt in 2020, when GCash’s pandemic-era growth was taking off and Mynt was valued at close to US$1 billion, meaning it has been invested for around six years. Bow Wave has also backed Ascend Money, the company behind Thailand’s TrueMoney Wallet, another Southeast Asian digital payments success story.

Warburg Pincus, meanwhile, is one of the world’s most prominent private equity firms and has plenty of experience betting on digital finance in emerging Asian markets. Its portfolio has included MoMo, Vietnam’s largest e-wallet, Indonesia’s GoTo Group, which combines Gojek, Tokopedia and GoTo Financial, and Advance Intelligence Group, whose businesses include buy-now-pay-later platform Atome. Warburg joined Mynt’s 2021 funding round, giving it roughly a five-year holding period by the time of the planned IPO.

Insight Partners came into Mynt in the same 2021 round. The New York growth investor has an extensive fintech portfolio that includes payments company Checkout.com, digital bank N26, Indonesian payments firm Xendit, Flutterwave, and financial infrastructure company Tink.

But the sell-down doesn’t mean GCash’s most important strategic owners are heading for the exits. Globe Capital Venture Holdings, Mynt’s single biggest shareholder at 33.84%, along with Ant International Technologies (21.44%), Ayala-Mitsubishi vehicle AM 50 Ventures (13.02%), and MUFG Bank (8.05%), are all staying put.

Nor should the PE (private equity) sell-down automatically be read as a vote of no confidence in GCash.

“It is fair to say that the IPO provides a liquidity or partial exit opportunity,” FirstMetroSec vice president and digital solutions and investor engagement division head Andoy Beltran told Rappler, adding, “but I would be careful about interpreting that as them losing confidence in GCash because those are two very different things.”

After all, exiting is part of the private equity playbook. Unlike strategic investors such as Globe or Ayala, PE and growth funds generally don’t buy stakes with the intention of holding them indefinitely. They invest, help a company scale and multiply in value, then eventually sell some or all of their stakes so they can return capital and profits to their own investors.

The timing is hardly unusual either. Recall Bow Wave first invested around 2020, while Warburg Pincus and Insight came in during 2021, putting them at roughly five to six years in Mynt by the time of the IPO. From my own experience consulting on private equity deals — including fintech investments — that’s the exit window that funds look for.

How much growth is left?

That may be the more important question for retail investors taking their place.

GCash is already operating at enormous scale. Mynt posted P79.7 billion in adjusted revenue and P17.25 billion in net income in 2025, while GCash reached 41.5 million monthly active users by June 2026, equivalent to nearly 56% of Filipino adults.

Growth, however, has cooled from its earlier breakneck pace. Adjusted revenue in H1 2026 only rose 9.8%, while net income grew 7.3%. DragonFi equity analyst Jarrod Tin argues that GCash has already deeply penetrated its core wallet market, with competition from Maya, MariBank, and other financial apps making the next leg harder.

However, Beltran still sees a growth story, with more runway in lending, savings, investments and other financial services, but cautions investors not to expect the old growth rates indefinitely.

“The question is how much of that future growth is already being priced into the IPO,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: The problem with replatforming Alfred ‘Krip’ Yuson
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Filipino literature and the classics that have come out of it always deserve to be known, and it’s often made possible by efforts like republishing and circulating physical copies to make them accessible to even more readers. But when the author behind one of these books has caused more harm than good, it becomes an entirely different story.

Case in point: Alfred “Krip” Yuson and his 1988 novel Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.

The book was supposed to have been given new life by Exploding Galaxies — with the publishing house even standing by its initial decision to republish the book despite drawing backlash from members of the literary community. Here’s what went down.

Yuson’s web of controversies

Yuson, a Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature Hall of Fame inductee, has been accused of sexual misconduct on several instances by different individuals. His latest published work was the 2022 book The Mountain That Grew.

“Why re-platform a man who’s responsible for the harassment and suicide of women? I do not care how brilliant you think his book is. I DO NOT CARE. And I will NEVER understand,” writer Katrina Stuart Santiago said in a Threads post on August 26.

Santiago further attested that she knows of young female writers who have had their own share of “horrid” experiences at the hands of Yuson.

“I remember when writers were being ‘cancelled’ left and right for everything from minor indiscretions to horrible mistakes to bad decisions, my question then was: when do we talk about the dirty old men of the literary establishment? Because THAT is a list. And it also has a list of victims. Re-platforming one of them by reprinting his book seems like [a] signal, doesn’t it. Of many things, including that people think we forget who these men are. We do not. We cannot. WE SHOULD NOT,” she said in another post on August 27.

Santiago added that literary workshops fuel Yuson’s predatory behavior, given the power dynamics that exist in these spaces between mentors and their mentees.

In response, Exploding Galaxies had initially attempted to discredit Santiago’s commentary, stating that while sexual harassment isn’t something they take lightly, the allegations that have been thrown at Yuson “have not been proven or independently corroborated.”

“We republished Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café for its well-established literary merit, and we stand by our decision to publish the book,” Exploding Galaxies wrote in its first public statement on September 5.

“We also stand firm against dishonest and unfair attempts to discredit this republication, especially as it is coming from a person who has expressed a longstanding personal grudge against the author, and who has, over the years, leveled serious public accusations against others,” it added.

Public response

Other figures in the literary community were quick to weigh in on the matter, with award-winning writer Jose “Butch” Dalisay Jr. pondering on the topic of art being created by questionable individuals.

“Does moral or political purity translate to some kind of elevated prose, or more honest and insightful poetry?” he wrote in a Facebook post. “Can someone please put together a library of vetted literature (or otherwise a new Index Librorum Prohibitorium) to spare us the process, and so we can keep to the straight and narrow, and enjoy reading without guilt or shame?”

Dalisay had followed it up with another post apologizing for appearing to trivialize the plight of sexual harassment victims — adding that the phenomenon of enabling a culture of harassment in workshops was something he would take up with the UP Institute of Creative Writing.

“There was a specific context to my remark that sexual misconduct and plagiarism were “low-hanging fruit.” It was not to dismiss them but to suggest that they were, among human evils, among the most visible and most common (which makes them no less painful to those concerned). I was talking about the possible crimes writers and artists have been accused of, which include murder and treason, and other offenses that injure not just one but many,” Dalisay said.

“I apologize to those victims of sexual harassment who may have seen my remarks as dismissive; they were not meant to be. It is a serious problem we are confronting not only in literature but in society at large.”

2011 plagiarism case

But sexual harassment isn’t the only serious issue that Yuson has found himself involved in. Writer Jaemark Tordecilla had accused him of plagiarism in 2011.

Tordecilla noticed that Yuson lifted several paragraphs from sportswriter Rey Joble’s piece about former PBA commissioner Rudy Salud. Joble’s story was published under GMA News Online, while Yuson had passed off his own version of it to Rogue Magazine.

Yuson was serving as GMA News Online’s editor-at-large then, and was in charge of copyediting Joble’s draft. He explained that since he had rewritten portions of Joble’s work, he thought he was considered to at least be part-author.

While he apologized for his actions, Yuson had merely attributed them to his old age, being overworked, and the pressure of having to meet deadlines. He still continued to write more after, and had even published several more works, like Islands of Words & Other Poems (2015), The Music Child & The Mahjong Queen (2016), and In the Footsteps of St. Ignatius of Loyola (2017), among others.

Withdrawing the republication of Yuson’s book

On September 7, Exploding Galaxies eventually announced that it would no longer push through with promoting or publishing Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.

“We hear you all. We are sorry for the hurt this has caused our community. We are no longer promoting or releasing this book. As a publisher, we will do better. Thank you for speaking up,” the publisher said.

Exploding Galaxies also promised to “do better” in its mission to put works of Philippine literature back into circulation. But this still begs the question: How can publishers and literary circles do their part in discerning whether or not it is appropriate to promote a piece of work when the individual behind it has caused hurt to many others in the past?

Yuson has yet to comment on the matter himself. – Rappler.com

World.title: Supreme Court acquits Imelda Marcos in 7 counts of graft
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) 1st Division acquitted Imelda Marcos, the mother of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., in her graft cases related to Swiss foundations.

In a decision made public on Wednesday, September 9, the SC division overturned the Sandiganbayan’s November 2018 decision that convicted the 97-year-old former first lady of seven counts of graft.

“Accordingly, the Appeal is granted. The November 9, 2018 Decision of the Sandiganbayan in Criminal Case Nos. 17287, 17288, 17289, 17290, 22867, 22868, and 22869 is reversed and set aside. Accused-appellant Imelda R. Marcos is acquitted for the prosecution’s failure to prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt for violation of Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019, in relation to Article IX, Section 8 of the 1973 Constitution,” said the 50-page ruling penned by Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda.

Associate justices Ramon Paul Hernando, Henri Jean Paul Inting, Ricardo Rosario, and Jose Midas Marquez all concurred in the ruling.

The Marcos matriarch is acquitted four years into the presidential term of her son, who won the presidency in 2022.

The ruling

In its decision, the SC division said the prosecution failed to prove Marcos’ guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Beyond reasonable doubt is the threshold needed to convict an accused in criminal cases.

Marcos was charged with alleged violation of Section 3(h), which has the following elements:

the accused is a public officer

they have direct or indirect financial or pecuniary interest in any business, contract, or transaction

they either intervened or took part in their official capacity or connection with such interest, or they are prohibited from having such interest by the Constitution or by any law

The SC said it’s undisputed that the first element is present, but the second and third elements are contested. The Office of the Ombudsman presented documentary and testimonial evidence that sought to prove Marcos’ financial interest, but the SC said they were “inadmissible and lack probative weight.”

In Marcos’ case, the Sandiganbayan found that she had a financial and pecuniary interest in the foundations based on the Swiss documents. The documents were retrieved from Swiss banks and had been authenticated in accordance with Swiss legal procedure.

However, the SC said the Sandiganbayan erred when it considered the Swiss documents duly authenticated.

“The Court has emphasized that the rule on authentication, more particularly as to private documents, is in place to prevent the inclusion of spurious documents in the body of evidence. Thus, it is settled that private documents are generally inadmissible in evidence unless they are properly authenticated,” said the ruling, adding that the prosecution was not able to present a credible witness who could have testified to the documents’ authenticity.

In addition, even if the SC would ignore the probative weight of the prosecution’s evidence, Marcos must still be acquitted, said the Court. The prosecution, according to the SC, failed to prove that the alleged pecuniary interest was “covered by Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019 and Article IX, Section 7 (then Section 8) of the 1973 Constitution.”

“All told, the prosecution failed to establish that the subject foundations are businesses as the term is ordinarily understood. Any financial or pecuniary interest in the subject foundations is not covered by Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019 and Article IX, Section 7 (then Section 8) of the 1973 Constitution. Doubts on the coverage of the term ‘business’ should be resolved against the State and in favor of the accused-appellant,” said the ruling.

2018 Sandiganbayan decision

In the 2018 decision, the Sandiganbayan sentenced Marcos to six years and one month, up to 11 years, for each count. It also meted the penalty of perpetual disqualification to hold public office.

According to the anti-graft court, Marcos participated in the management of foundations which was a violation of the country’s anti-graft law. The Office of the Ombudsman also found that the public money involved in the private organizations reached $200 million.



It involved seven Swiss foundations. When one foundation closes, the money will be transferred to another, then the foundation will be closed again.

“Pertinently, the [Sandiganbayan] noted that the documents and testimonies presented by the prosecution showed that she has a direct or indirect financial interest in the foundations and has participated in the management of the same,” said the 2018 ruling of the anti-graft court. – Rappler.com

World.title: P6.2 billion slated for fertilizer, fuel aid to ease El Niño impact
World.content:
MARKET. People buy different kinds of basic commodities at the Paco Market in Manila on March 11, 2026.

On top of this, the Department of Agriculture is asking Congress for an additional P10 billion in its 2027 budget in anticipation of severe El Niño impact

MANILA, Philippines – The government is set to distribute P6.2 billion worth of fertilizer and fuel assistance to help cushion the impacts of the global oil crisis and El Niño on farmers and fisherfolk.

The fund is under the Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport, or UPLIFT, a comprehensive response to energy security and livelihood needs amid the Middle East conflict.

There is no identified number yet of beneficiary farmers and fishers, according to Department of Agriculture spokesperson Arnel de Mesa. To ensure good yield, much of the fertilizer aid will be distributed to places less affected by El Niño.

“One of the things that DA is really going to do is to maximize yield in areas not affected by El Niño,” De Mesa said in a press briefing on Wednesday, September 9.

De Mesa said the full impact of El Niño on crops and prices will not be felt until the first semester of 2027, and that these measures are preparatory before El Niño develops into a more severe state by the end of 2026.

“If the fund is released in October, it works exactly as support during El Niño,” said De Mesa.

The Department of Agriculture is also requesting an additional P10 billion in 2027 to augment cash assistance for farmers and fishers, in anticipation of El Niño impacts.

No impact on rice production, prices yet

The agriculture sector was left reeling from the effects of the southwest monsoon or habagat and past tropical cyclones, incurring production losses worth P4.38 billion. The palay sector lost P2 billion.

“Again, we do not see impact on rice prices because, in terms of volume, this is within our estimated losses every year because of typhoons, flooding, and other calamities,” De Mesa explained.

Estimated losses in rice production ranged from 500,000 to 600,000 metric tons, said De Mesa. The P2 billion worth of damage in the palay sector is “about only 70,000 metric tons of losses.”

In a bid to curb prices and support local production, the DA said it will not allow imports of high-grade rice in the meantime. According to reports, Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. talked with the rice industry to import only 25% (and above) broken rice. – Rappler.com

World.title: No travel tax, no budget: Can TIEZA keep its tourism projects alive?
World.content:
The pesky travel tax is easy to hate, but abolishing it could leave multi-year tourism infrastructure projects in limbo, especially with TIEZA not getting anything in the proposed 2027 budget

Even as the government keeps pitching tourism as a growth priority and jobs engine, the agency tasked with building much of its infrastructure is heading into 2027 with billions’ worth of ongoing projects and a proposed budget of exactly zero.

On top of this, if Congress succeeds in abolishing the travel tax, the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA) could also lose the revenue stream that normally pays for almost everything it does.

A source familiar with TIEZA’s budget planning told Rappler that the agency initially sought around P5.2 billion in national government funding for 2027. That request covered infrastructure projects alone and did not yet include personnel services or maintenance and other operating expenses.

Budget Secretary Kim Robert de Leon informed TIEZA that the request could not be favorably considered because of the government’s limited fiscal space, the source said. Consequently, the proposed 2027 budget carries zero subsidy for the agency, compared with P248 million for general administration and support in 2026.

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) echoed this stance during the budget hearing of the Department of Tourism (DOT).

“TIEZA’s proposal for National Government Subsidy in FY2027 is in view of several legislative measures proposing the abolition of the travel tax. However, as these bills remain under deliberation in the Senate and have yet to be enacted into law, the TIEZA’s requested subsidy was not considered in the FY [2027] NEP,” DBM Assistant Director Lulu Vispo said.

A zero budget may come with consequences on the tourism infrastructure pipeline. TIEZA chief operating officer Mark Lapid told lawmakers during the tourism department’s budget hearing that almost all of its projects are multi-year, with around P5.2 billion needed in 2027 alone to keep them moving.

The DBM, however, pointed to P2.355 billion in supposedly available TIEZA funds: P810.25 million in unobligated allotments as of March 31 and another P1.545 billion in unreleased 2025 appropriations.

“TIEZA may continue to utilize its travel tax collections to fund tourism-related infrastructures or projects,” Vispo added on Monday, September 7.

Meanwhile, TIEZA says that money is not sitting idly. Lapid told lawmakers that the roughly P2 billion cited during the hearing could not simply be used to pay for its infrastructure commitments as it was being used to fund the agency’s payroll.

“The P2 billion is for our personnel services in our office operations. So technically, we wouldn’t have any funds for infrastructure from the amount mentioned,” Lapid told lawmakers in Filipino.

The travel tax problem

The problem is that the pesky P1,620 travel tax that travelers love to hate is also what keeps much of TIEZA running.

Congress is now moving to abolish it. The House has already approved House Bill 8464, while Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said in August that the Senate is targeting abolition within the year.

Under the current setup, 50% of tax collections go to TIEZA, 40% to the Commission on Higher Education, and 10% to the National Commission for Culture and the Arts. TIEZA’s share from those travel taxes makes up roughly 95% of its funding, an agency source told Rappler.

The House bill does anticipate the problem by requiring the national government to replace those funds through the annual budget. The tricky part is timing. TIEZA is being told to prepare for a future in which the travel tax disappears, but it has yet to receive approval for replacement funding.

Photo from a TIEZA presentation shown during the House budget hearing for the DOT.

The tax cut could also have a very human cost inside the agency that needs consideration. A TIEZA presentation showed that around 300 travel tax personnel may be displaced out of its 1,045-strong workforce. Of those, 115 may have difficulty finding new work because of their age, while some 270 families could be affected.

Lapid told lawmakers that TIEZA cannot simply absorb the workers elsewhere because they are spread across international gateways nationwide and the agency does not have enough plantilla positions at its main office. Some could be terminated, while others may receive separation incentives.

Five projects may get a lifeline

During Monday’s budget hearing, the DOT made its case for Congress to restore an allocation for at least P1.3 billion for five TIEZA projects.

The list obtained by Rappler from a source includes:

P328.9 million for improvements of the Banaue Hotel and Youth Hostel complex in Ifugao. The TIEZA-owned property sits on a 5.3-hectare site overlooking the Banaue Rice Terraces and has 81 hotel rooms plus a 15-room youth hostel. TIEZA has been rehabilitating the aging property for years, which has remained temporarily closed.

The TIEZA-owned property sits on a 5.3-hectare site overlooking the Banaue Rice Terraces and has 81 hotel rooms plus a 15-room youth hostel. TIEZA has been rehabilitating the aging property for years, which has remained temporarily closed. P301.07 million for the CBDC River Water System in San Vicente, Palawan. This is meant to provide a long-term potable water supply to tourism establishments and communities around Long Beach, one of the main clusters of TIEZA’s San Vicente Flagship Tourism Enterprise Zone.

This is meant to provide a long-term potable water supply to tourism establishments and communities around Long Beach, one of the main clusters of TIEZA’s San Vicente Flagship Tourism Enterprise Zone. P400 million for iLIPAD , TIEZA’s airport development program with DOTr. Launched in 2020, the program helps fund upgrades to provincial airports, particularly facilities needed for night operations and greater flight capacity.

Launched in 2020, the program helps fund upgrades to provincial airports, particularly facilities needed for night operations and greater flight capacity. P212.2 million for the construction of a waste water treatment facility in Coron. The project is aimed at addressing the environmental strain that tourism and development place on one of Palawan’s busiest destinations.

The project is aimed at addressing the environmental strain that tourism and development place on one of Palawan’s busiest destinations. P63.7 million for the construction of Sky Garden in Barangay Lucap, Alaminos City. The project, which Marcos himself broke ground for in May 2025, is envisioned as another attraction and gateway near Hundred Islands, with elevated gardens, viewing decks, walkways, parking, a commercial center, and a multipurpose hall.

The proposed allocations for the DOT and its attached agencies are not yet final, however, as Congress can still revise the 2027 budget before it is enacted. But so far, lawmakers have appeared receptive to calls for more tourism funding, repeatedly pointing to the country’s infrastructure gaps and the need for greater investment.

After all, one need only look at NAIA to see what years of underinvestment can do to a country’s main international gateway — and how quickly things can begin to turn once fresh capital finally starts pouring in. – Rappler.com

World.title: [DECODED] Why gamifying abuse impacts all of us
World.content:
Gamified abuse scales the way it does not only because of the bad actors that exploit them, but for the lack of accountability from the online platforms in which they thrive

In case you missed it, Rappler published a two-part investigative series over the weekend uncovering an online community that exploits women by sharing their intimate photos and videos without consent. The online forum called NSFWPH, which launched in April 2023, claims to have amassed 430,000 registered members and nearly 9 million posts and comments — all to share and consume voyeur content.

What’s more troubling, apart from the non-consensual sharing of intimate content featuring unwitting women, is that the members of this forum deliberately post and contribute to the forum as a point of pride.

Posts in the forum showed that many of the members of NSFWPH consider their participation a badge of honor, considering the lengths that they go to in order to obtain intimate photos and videos from women they know or interact with.

PART 1: How Filipinas’ intimate moments end up on a 430,000-member forum

Some even shared how they manipulated women into sharing nudes with them, which were in turn rewarded by the other forum members through congratulatory comments.

The forum treats these exploits, betrayals of trust, and, in some cases, content theft, as achievements that catapult a member’s “status” on the platform. The more a user shares and interacts on the platform, the more they get points that place them higher in NSFWPH’s ranking system.

This system has a name: it’s gamified abuse.

Because the higher a member ranks in the forum’s merit system, the more privileges they unlock, such as access to locked content or additional information about the victims, like their names or links to their Facebook and Instagram accounts.

Part 2: Gamified abuse: How a PH forum rewards submissions of non-consensual intimate content

In the case of NSFWPH, Filipinas were the victims. But the same business model is being used by bad actors across our current online ecosystem, targeting everyone vulnerable — including men.

Research and advocacy groups Reset Tech and Equimundo recently published a report called “The Grift Economy,” which examined how male loneliness is being monetized through membership schemes and so-called educational products. The report outlined how those in the “manosphere,” a collection of online communities focused on masculinity, are being pulled in with content that aligns with their ideologies, until they are drawn deeper into grievance-driven communities and, ultimately, monetized.

We see parallels in how the Grift Economy gamifies the exploitation of men’s need for connection to how the NSFWPH gamifies the exploitation of women’s intimate images and videos. Both employ these three mechanisms:

Points system turns participation into a game.

The NSFWPH forum gamifies its members’ participation by assigning them ranks. The Grift Economy explains how manosphere communities assign similar status systems in the “brotherhood” system. Such practice keeps members engaged, because they are rewarded through their participation.

Online platforms are active financial beneficiaries.

The Grift Economy points to online platforms as “usually the single largest financial beneficiary of any given operation.” This is because they share a portion of advertising income with the creators who run the ads that target vulnerable men.

In NSFWPH’s case, the result is a multi-layered monetization model. “The forum’s gamified system rewards users for uploading intimate content, while traffic and advertising turn exploitation into profit,” Rappler writers Gelo Gonzales and Lance Ariel Bustos said.

The problem is not limited to one platform.

Rappler’s investigation found that one of the most prominent members of NSFWPH is diverting the voyeur content he posts on the forum to a separate website where he set up pop-up ads that he can directly earn from, and to his own membership-based channel on Discord, a separate messaging and communication platform. By doing so, he is able to charge for more exclusive content.

The same is true for the Grift Economy. They thrive on different platforms, including YouTube, TikTok, X, Kick, Telegram, Instagram, and Spotify.

This practice makes the entire operation resilient: if one platform goes bust, other online communities will be able to absorb the operation, especially if they have lax policies against abuse and exploitation.

Gamified abuse is a business model, and it scales the way it does not only because of the bad actors that exploit them, but for the lack of accountability from the online platforms in which they thrive.

This makes all of us who spend time online vulnerable. – Rappler.com

World.title: Cendaña to Quiboloy camp: Better libelous than sex trafficker
World.content:
Akbayan party-list Rep. Percival Cendaña — Screengrab from an INQUIRER.net video

MANILA, Philippines — Akbayan party-list Rep. Percival Cendaña has made it clear that he would rather be labeled libelous than be described as a sex trafficker, in an apparent swipe at jailed televangelist Apollo Quiboloy whose camp had threatened to sue him and other lawmakers for cyber libel.

In a statement on Wednesday, Cendaña said that Quiboloy plans to file cyber libel complaints against him for claiming that the Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) founder was a child molester and human trafficker.

Aside from him, Cendaña said Quiboloy’s camp supposedly wants to include Sen. Risa Hontiveros and Mamamayang Liberal party-list Rep. Leila de Lima among the respondents for the planned cyber libel and libel raps.

Article continues after this 

READ: From DFA to court: How the US extradition request for Quiboloy will move

“I received news that the camp of Apollo Quiboloy is mulling the filing of libel raps against me, Sen. Risa Hontiveros, and Rep. Leila de Lima. I’d rather be libelous than be a sex trafficker. Thank God, I’m not any of them,” Cendaña said.

“I just want to clarify that Quiboloy has threatened to sue me for libel because I believed the statements of victims that he is a child molester, pedophile, and human trafficker. He really has to be extradited towards the US (United States) so that he can face the cases against him,” he added.

On Wednesday, Quiboloy’s legal counsel Ferdinand Topacio announced that they will be filing libel and cyber libel charges against the three lawmakers before the Pasig City prosecutor’s office.

But Cendaña believes Quiboloy and his team should focus their energy towards facing his alleged victims before a US court.

Article continues after this 

Early August, the US State Department sent through the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs a letter seeking Quiboloy’s extradition, so that he could face charges stemming from a 2021 indictment in California, due to sex trafficking of minors, visa fraud and bulk cash smuggling.

“If they are serious in their threat to charge me, Sen. Risa, and Rep. Leila, it does not come close to the fear and violence inflicted upon his victims and their families,” Cendaña said.

Article continues after this 

“My advice to Quiboloy is for him to devote his time and energy to face his victims in a US court. His time to face justice is nearing. I hope Quiboloy even has a tinge of regret for the brutality and evil he did,” he added.

The Department of Justice is still evaluating the extradition request, as Quiboloy also faces cases before the Philippine courts — a qualified human trafficking case before the Pasig City Regional Trial Court (RTC) and sexual abuse and maltreatment before the Quezon City RTC.

READ: DOJ to study US request for Quiboloy extradition

After the extradition request, Hontiveros said she was relieved that both Philippine and US authorities are seeking to hold Quiboloy accountable for his alleged crimes.

Hontiveros, chair of the Senate committee on women, children, family relations and gender equality, led the investigation into Quiboloy and his alleged involvement in large-scale human trafficking, sexual abuse of minors, forced labor and rights violations.

World.title: Palace names National Artists for 2025, 1st woman in visual arts
World.content:
Inquirer file photo.

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang has named 10 National Artists for 2025, including the first woman to be proclaimed a National Artist in the field of visual arts.

Through Proclamation No. 1414, s. 2026, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has declared 10 new National Artists:

Nicanor Tiongson and Gregorio Brillantes (Literature)

Imelda Cajipe-Endaya and Nunelucio Alvarado (Visual Arts)

Gabriel Formoso (Architecture)

Rafael “Nonoy” Froilan (Dance)

Maria Beatriz “Patis” Tesoro (Design)

Armando “Bing” Lao (Film and Broadcast Arts)

Teodoro Hilado (Theater)

Alfredo S. Buenaventura (Music)

READ: ‘Global Filipino Artists,’ not ‘National Artists’

Article continues after this 

Formoso, Lao, Brillantes, and Hilado received the recognition posthumously.

The latest batch of National Artists was announced four years after the previous honorees were named.

Tiongson

Tiongson is professor emeritus of the University of the Philippines (UP) Film Institute and a former dean of the UP College of Mass Communication in Diliman.

He is also an artistic director and vice president of the Cultural Center of the Philippines, as well as a founding member and former chair of the Manunuri ng Pelikulang Pilipino.

Article continues after this 

He authored The Cinema of Manuel Conde, The Urian Anthology, and The Women of Malolos, and edited the 10-volume CCP Encyclopedia of Philippine Art. His plays include Pilipinas Circa 1907, Basiila ng Malolos, Noli at Fili Dekada 2000, and Mabining Mandirigma.

Brillantes

Article continues after this 

He was a giant of contemporary Philippine literature whose canonical body of work, particularly his short stories in English, has been studied and celebrated by generations of literature and humanities students and practitioners.

Brillantes died at the age of 92 on the morning of Sept. 26, 2025.

Cajipe-Endaya

Cajipe-Endaya is one of the pioneers of feminist art in the Philippines. A printmaker, social realist painter, mixed-media and installation artist, curator, and art organizer, she is known for her advocacy for women and her focus on Philippine history and culture.

Marcos named her the first female National Artist in the field of visual arts. She is also the founding president of Kasibulan, a feminist arts organization active since 1987, and became the first editor of Pananaw: Philippine Journal of Visual Arts, the first publication of its kind on Philippine art.

Alvarado

Alvarado is celebrated for his progressive artworks depicting the plight and struggles of the Negros-based “sakadas,” or laborers hired from outside the region. He developed a distinctive style marked by bold colors, emotion, and strength.

Among his awards are the Thirteen Artists Award from the Cultural Center of the Philippines in 1992 and the Grand Prize in the Philip Morris Philippine Art Awards in 1997 and 1999.

His works have been acquired by notable museums, including the Metropolitan Museum of Manila, Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, and Singapore Art Museum.

Formoso

Formoso was an acclaimed architect known for designing the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Complex in Manila (1970), the Asian Institute of Management (1970), and the former Metropolitan Museum of Manila along Roxas Boulevard (1976).

He was among the first 100 architects in the Philippines and was included in the preliminary shortlist of National Artist nominees for Architecture in 2003.

Froilan

One of the pioneers of Ballet Philippines, Froilan was known as the country’s premier danseur. He partnered with leading ballerinas of his time and was best remembered for his roles in groundbreaking dance productions.

He was also regarded as one of the country’s most talented and prolific dancers and choreographers.

Tesoro

Tesoro is an artist, fashion designer, and lifestyle icon known as the Grand Dame of Philippine Fashion. She devoted more than 30 years to preserving ethnic Filipino clothing, reviving the piña fabric industry, and promoting Filipino craftsmanship and fashion on the world stage.

Lao

Lao was known for his award-winning screenplays for films such as Takaw-Tukso, Itanong Mo sa Buwan, and Kubrador, among others.

Recognized for his substantial body of work in Philippine cinema, Lao received several Gawad Urian awards, including Best Screenplay for Takaw-Tukso in 1987, Itanong Mo sa Buwan in 1989, Oras-Oras, Araw-Araw in 1990, and Tuhog in 2001.

His films with director Brillante Mendoza, Serbis (2008) and Kinatay (2009), also competed at the prestigious Cannes Film Festival.

Lao died on June 18, 2024, at the age of 75.

Hilado

Hilado served as technical director of the Cultural Center of the Philippines from 1969 to 1973 and as theater director of the Folk Arts Theater from 1973 to 1986.

A pioneering figure in Philippine theater, Hilado was widely recognized as the father of lighting design in Philippine theater.

He died of brain cancer at the age of 77 on Dec. 23, 2015.

Buenaventura

Buenaventura is admired for his compositions, which include operas, symphonic poems, vocal works, and chamber music.

He is known for masterpieces, compositions, and arrangements such as Lakambini and Mabuhay March.

The National Artist Award is the highest national recognition given to Filipinos who have made significant contributions to the development of Philippine arts and letters. It was created through Presidential Proclamation No. 1001 on April 27, 1972.

World.title: Antique seeks to preserve legacy of local heroes
World.content:
HEROES HALL. The Antique Provincial Development Council convenes for its third quarter meeting on Wednesday (Sept. 9, 2026). (Photo from Annabel Consuelo J. Petinglay / PNA)

SAN JOSE DE BUENAVISTA, Antique — The provincial government of Antique seeks to preserve the legacy of its local heroes by dedicating a hall at its old capitol building and publishing reading materials about their lives.

The Provincial Development Council, during its third quarter meeting on Wednesday, approved the inclusion of P3 million budget in the Supplemental Annual Investment Program No. 4 for the initiatives.

“We will be putting up a heroes hall and publication of reading materials to recognize and perpetuate the heroism of Antique’s local heroes,” said Board Member Vincent Piccio in an interview.

Article continues after this 

The reading materials will be distributed in schools, municipal and provincial libraries, he added.

The Heroes Hall will be placed beside the space reserved for the National Museum of the Philippines to house the memorabilia and artifacts of the local heroes.

“The Old Antique Capitol will then become a one-stop shop where the National Museum of the Philippines-Antique and the Heroes Hall would be located,” Piccio said.

Piccio said they are now coordinating with the National Historical Commission of the Philippines for the list of local heroes.

Meanwhile, he said the 127-year-old Philippine Revolutionary Flag will be installed at the heroes hall on Oct. 27, 2026, during the “Pagtugyan” (entrusting) ceremony.

Article continues after this 

The installation also marked the first year since it was turned over to the provincial government last year.

National Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro and Armed Forces of the Philippines chief of staff Gen. Antonio Nafarrete are among the dignitaries invited to grace the occasion. /apl

World.title: Chua: Sara Duterte contradicts anti-ICC stand by not trusting PH courts
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte. INQUIRER PHOTO / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte not having any trust for the Judiciary contradicts her previous stand that her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, must be tried in the country instead of the International Criminal Court (ICC), a lawmaker pointed out on Wednesday.

During a press briefing on Wednesday, Manila Rep. Joel Chua was asked whether Vice President Duterte’s actions — punching a sheriff enforcing a lawful order when she was still Davao City mayor and then claiming recently that she does not trust the court — already merits disciplinary actions meant for lawyers.

Before addressing the question, Chua said that this statement from the Vice President contradicts the stand of her family — that the older Duterte should be brought back to the Philippines’ jurisdiction.

Article continues after this 

READ: Surrendering Duterte to ICC doesn’t mean PH courts don’t work – experts

“Well, unang-una, hindi ko alam kung bakit niya sasabihin na wala siyang tiwala sa korte dito, samantalang no’ng kinukuha ‘yong kanyang ama, papunta sa, para litisin sa the Hague, eh sinasabi nila na gumagana naman ang korte dito, at kung meron mang dapat maglilitis sa kanyang ama, dapat dito nililitis,” Chua, a member of the prosecution team for Duterte’s impeachment trial, said.

(Well, first of all, I do not know why she would say that she doesn’t trust the court here, while when her father was being brought to the Hague for his trial, they said that the justice system in the Philippines is functioning, and that if her father has to be tried, it should be done here in the country.)

“So ito, makikita mo ‘yong mga conflicting statement na kanyang sinasabi, at bilang abugado, kaming lahat ay officers of the court, so kami dapat ay nagbibigay ng galang sa ating mga kagalang-galang na mahistrado,” he added.

(So you can see the conflicting statements she uttered, and as a lawyer, we are all officers of the court, so we should give respect to the Honorable judges.)

Article continues after this 

READ: Sara Duterte’s kill remark vs Marcos is ‘active threat’ – Palace

Last Friday, the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 98 issued an arrest order against Duterte over three counts of grave threats — one for each threat she made in November 2024, against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his wife First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and his cousin former House of Representatives Speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez.

Article continues after this 

On Saturday, Duterte showed up before the Quezon City RTC to post a bail worth P360,000, or P120,000 for each count.

At one point, Duterte appeared to be asking her lawyer for her impeachment trial, Atty. Michael Poa, as to how she will post her bail with several police officers around, saying that she does not feel safe as she might be gunned down like former Senator Ninoy Aquino was shot.

Duterte, a lawyer, said she does not trust the court.

“I do not feel safe, I really do not feel safe. I don’t trust the court, I don’t trust the police,” she told reporters and her lawyers.

READ: Sara Duterte posts bail: ‘I don’t trust the court’

Chua said Duterte can be a subject of a disciplinary action — possibly disbarment — if someone goes to the courts and complains about her attitude and demeanor.

“Well, pupwede siguro kung merong magsasampa sa kanya na mga disciplinary action sa kanyang pahayag na mga ganito, at saka very unbecoming para sa isang second-highest official ng ating bansa para magsalita ng ganitong sweeping statement laban sa ating mga kagalang-galang na korte,” he said.

(Well, someone can file a petition to have her subjected to disciplinary actions for such statements, as this is very unbecoming for a second-highest official of our country to make such sweeping statements against our Honorable courts.)

In a separate ambush interview after the briefing, Chua said that Duterte’s conduct deserves attention and consideration, and may be a subject of disbarment cases.

“Kaya dapat tingnan kung ito ay subject for disbarment,” he said. “Kung yung mga ordinaryong abogado nga na-didisbar, e yun pa kayang mga diretsang sinasabi o diretsang nambabastos sa ating mga korte?”

(This should be checked if it is subject for a disbarment case. If ordinary lawyers are disbarred, how about those who directly state things or disrespect our courts?)

Former president Duterte’s camp has questioned ICC’s jurisdiction several times, claiming that the ex-leader should be released immediately and unconditionally, despite the crime against humanity of mass murder charge against him for implementing a bloody war against illegal drugs.

According to the defense panel, the ICC only had jurisdiction over the Philippines when it was a state party to the Rome Statute, the agreement that created the international tribunal.

Duterte pulled the Philippines out of the ICC in 2018, an order that took effect in 2019.

However, the ICC maintained that it had jurisdiction of the crime against humanity raps against the former president, as the actions being pointed to by relatives of drug war victims happened before Duterte’s withdrawal.

The younger Duterte, meanwhile, is facing three counts of grave threats after the National Bureau of Investigation filed complaints for Duterte’s statements in a November 23, 2024 online press briefing.

As she criticized the House for detaining her chief-of-staff, Undersecretary Zuleika Lopez, Duterte went online for a briefing to berate the First Couple and Romualdez.

Duterte was then asked by a vlogger to take care as she may be in danger. The Vice President replied by urging people not to worry as she has talked to a person about killing the Marcos couple and Romualdez if she herself gets killed.

“Do not worry about my security because I already spoke to someone. I said, ‘If I am killed, kill BBM, Liza Araneta, and Martin Romualdez.’ No joke, no joke,” Duterte said in the November 2024 briefing.

The same matter has been the subject of the impeachment complaints against Duterte, which eventually was included in the Articles of Impeachment transmitted to the Senate last May 13.

World.title: Marcoleta asserts capacity to vote as judge in letter to impeach court
World.content:
Sen. Rodante Marcoleta — File photo

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Rodante Marcoleta has asserted his ability to vote as a senator-judge in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial despite his detention in a July 20, 2026, letter to Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero.

Marcoleta’s office released the letter Wednesday after senator-judges raised the possibility of revisiting Escudero’s ruling that 16 votes would be required to convict Duterte.

Escudero made the ruling with only 21 senator-judges able to participate in the trial following the arrest of Marcoleta and Sen. Jinggoy Estrada, both on plunder charges, and Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa’s hiding amid an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC).

Article continues after this 

“There is no impairment to my legal capacity to vote as a Senator-judge for I am not under preventive suspension,” Marcoleta wrote.

READ: Gatchalian: Up to court if Marcoleta, Estrada can join impeachment trial

He cited the Senate Rules on impeachment, which state: “The president of the Senate shall, in the event any senator cannot personally cast his/her vote due to any valid reasons, prescribe the manner and procedure on how the vote shall be cast and communicated to the chamber.”

Marcoleta said that, in his interpretation of the rule, senators “driven into hiding, detained, suspended, hospitalized but not permanently incapacitated or even temporarily abroad do not lose their seats in the Senate.”

He added that there should be no “constitutional obstacle” to his participation in the impeachment trial, and that the same should apply to Estrada and “others who may be subjected to political persecution and detention.”

Article continues after this 

“Limitations to my legal capacity to perform the functions of senator-judge are not insurmountable. Historically and realistically, there is no constitutional obstacle to the adoption by the Senate of means to overcome such limitations in order to ensure equality of arms between the prosecution and defense,” Marcoleta further said.

In the same letter, he voted in favor of Escudero’s ruling on the voting threshold.

Article continues after this 

Apart from the Constitution’s provision that “no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate,” Marcoleta noted that there was no objection to Escudero’s ruling when it was made.

“There were 21 senator-judges present. No one objected to the foregoing ruling. It is therefore the prevailing ruling of the impeachment court. I vote in favor of the foregoing ruling and reasoning,” he wrote.

READ: Senate impeachment court revisiting ‘2/3’ conviction rule

But Marcoleta opposed the designation of Escudero as presiding officer — a vote supported by 12 of the 24 senators.

To recall, on June 3, with the then-majority bloc — led by now Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano — absent from the plenary session, the 12 senators voted in favor of electing another senator to serve as presiding officer.

It was this vote that allowed the senator-judges to designate Escudero as the impeachment court’s presiding officer.

The same 12 senators contended that the number needed for a quorum should be based on the number of senators capable of being present during the session. At that time, dela Rosa and Estrada had been unable to participate because of their respective legal battles.

But the minority senators insisted that no quorum was formed that day, as the number should be based on all 24 senators.

“The Senate cannot distort the plain meaning of the Constitution by supplying additional exceptions, such as designating a senator other than the Senate president as presiding officer,” Marcoleta stressed. /das

World.title: Manila Water, Manila Water Foundation aid Montalban flood recovery
World.content:
The relief assistance provided by Manila Water and Manila Water Foundation reached 2,466 individuals from the flood-affected communities of Barangays San Isidro and San Jose in Montalban, Rizal. —Photo from Manila Water

MANILA, Philippines ‚ As recovery efforts continue in communities affected by recent jhabagat-induced flooding, Manila Water Foundation (MWF), together with the Manila Water Company’s Marikina Service Area, reinforced its support for residents of Montalban, Rizal, through the provision of safe drinking water and operational assistance to local government response efforts.

In coordination with the Municipal Government of Montalban, MWF handed over 350 units of 5-gallon potable drinking water to families displaced by the flooding in Kasiglahan 1K2 Phase 1 and Pag-asa Village. The relief assistance reached 2,466 individuals from the flood-affected communities of Barangays San Isidro and San Jose.

Manila Water’s Marikina Service Area also mobilized resources to assist local recovery operations. A total of five (5) water tankers were deployed to provide emergency water supply in affected areas, while four (4) trucks were dispatched to support clearing operations and help local authorities restore normalcy in impacted barangays.

Article continues after this 

READ: Manila Water Foundation boosts WASH support for schools

The turnover of the hydration assistance was led by Manila Water Foundation and Manila Water representatives alongside Montalban Municipal Mayor Ronnie Evangelista and barangay leaders from San Jose.

Recognizing the vital role of clean water during disaster recovery, Mayor Evangelista expressed his appreciation for the timely intervention.

“In times of disaster, access to clean and safe drinking water is essential. We are grateful to Manila Water and Manila Water Foundation for their immediate response and continued partnership in helping our communities recover and rebuild,” said Evangelista.

Manila Water Foundation handed over 350 units of 5-gallon potable drinking water to families displaced by the flooding in Kasiglahan 1K2 Phase 1 and Pag-asa Village. —Photo from Manila Water

READ: Manila Water Foundation gives WASH aid to flood-hit communities

Article continues after this 

The initiative forms part of Manila Water Foundation’s ongoing disaster response and resilience efforts under its Agapay: WASH in Emergencies program, which focuses on ensuring access to safe water for communities affected by natural calamities. Through close collaboration with local government units and partner organizations, MWF continues to support vulnerable communities as they recover from emergencies while promoting public health and well-being.

As families in Montalban work toward rebuilding their homes and livelihoods, Manila Water and Manila Water Foundation remain steadfast in their commitment to delivering timely and meaningful assistance, helping communities recover stronger and become more resilient in the face of future disasters.

World.title: Gatchalian: Collective action needed to build on PH gains in PISA
World.content:
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Wednesday called for a reassessment of the country’s education policies despite its improved performance in the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA).

Gatchalian said the latest PISA results underscore the need for collective effort and collaboration to address the country’s education crisis.

READ: PH improves rank in international education assessment

Article continues after this 

READ: Dy credits teachers for PH rise in global student performance

“This is an opportunity to build a system that will strengthen education for the benefit of millions of Filipinos in the years to come,” he said, emphasizing the importance of equipping Filipino children with the skills necessary to understand the world.

The Philippines recorded its highest PISA scores in science, mathematics, and reading in 2025, following its lowest point in 2018, its first year participating in the assessment, and minor shifts in 2022 after the pandemic.

The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development also recognized the Philippines as the fastest-improving country in reading over the past decade, with its score increasing from 24% to 31%. Science improved from 23% to 32%, while mathematics rose from 16% to 21%.

Sen. Joel Villanueva also recognized that the country’s improvement in PISA scores must encourage the government to remain focused on investing in teachers, particularly in teacher education and training, and on providing schools with further resources, even after achieving substantial results.

Article continues after this 

“The latest PISA results should give us hope, but they should also give us urgency. Let us use this improvement as a springboard for bigger and more meaningful reforms,” he said.

Villanueva then commended the Department of Education for its improved scores across its three domains, noting the hard work of teaching personnel and the people behind EDCOM II, or the Second Congressional Commission on Education, a reform aimed at addressing the country’s learning crisis.

Article continues after this 

“The results of PISA 2018 that exposed the learning crisis in the country were the main trigger for the establishment of EDCOM 2 in 2022… it is only fitting that we recognize and honor EDCOM II, especially the dedication and excellence of our Executive Director Dr. Karol Mark Yee. His leadership and unwavering hard work have exceeded our expectations and have been key to ensuring that reforms in our education sector have a clear, rapid, and meaningful direction,” he said.

Developed in 2022 in response to the learning crisis reflected in the 2018 PISA results, EDCOM II helped reform the country’s education sector rather than offer single solutions or isolated hearings within the system.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Government Meeting Puts Skilled Workers in Focus
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s first government meeting in its updated composition after the Kurultai elections focused on a topic that could determine the success of its economic transformation: whether the country will have enough skilled workers to support planned growth.

At the Sept. 8 meeting, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov called for an accelerated pace of work at a new stage of political and economic modernization. The decision to put workforce training at the center of the government’s first meeting highlights a growing concern: Kazakhstan has jobs, but increasingly needs people with the right skills to fill them.

By 2035, the economy is expected to require 2.9 million specialists, including 1.8 million workers in skilled trades. More than half of vacancies on the electronic labor exchange are already for working professions.

Political scientist Gaziz Abishev said the problem is therefore not a shortage of jobs, but a shortage of qualified workers.

He linked demand for technical specialists to existing industrial production, new projects under the country’s reindustrialization policy, municipal infrastructure modernization and rapidly growing cities.

Abishev cited Bektenov’s warning that Kazakhstan is “forced to attract thousands of specialists from abroad so that work does not stop,” underscoring the growing gap between demand for workers and the availability of qualified specialists.

Aligning training with economic needs

The government is seeking to make vocational education more responsive to these demands.

Education Minister Zhuldyz Suleimenova said Kazakhstan’s technical and vocational education system is being transformed according to labor-market needs. Some 480 colleges train working qualifications, while 57,000 students entered such programs this year.

Training programs are also being updated for a changing economy. New professions have been added to the national classifier, while micro-qualifications and AI-related skills are being introduced.

The Science and Higher Education Ministry estimates that more than half of labor demand is for technical and vocational specialists. Regional labor-market maps have identified more than 2,000 emerging professions and transformations of existing ones, including the use of digital twins and AI in production.

Employers are also becoming more directly involved. Nearly 50,000 students at 76 universities currently participate in dual education with 6,000 enterprises. Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund portfolio companies train more than 10,000 students annually through dual education and internships.

The need is particularly visible in energy and industry. Expansion of Kazakhstan’s three existing oil refineries is expected to increase refining capacity from 18 million to 29.2 million tons a year, while a planned new refinery would add another 10 million tons.

Such expansion will require a substantial increase in qualified workers.

Can training make these jobs more attractive?

The government’s challenge is not only to train workers, but to persuade people to choose these professions.

Abishev said many people remain reluctant to enter industrial and technical sectors because they consider wages insufficient. But he cautioned against viewing higher wages alone as the solution.

“Simple increases in wages without productivity growth lead to lower efficiency, higher costs and, ultimately, inflation,” he wrote on his Telegram channel on Sept. 9.

At the same time, he expects competition for qualified workers to push incomes higher. Experienced professionals in technical and skilled trades will always command higher incomes, he said. A shortage of skilled workers and competition for them will drive wages higher, while those who know their profession well, keep improving and have a strong work ethic will always be valued.

This could also alter the traditional perception of working professions. As AI transforms white-collar employment, technical occupations could become among the more attractive and better-paid positions in an economy still heavily dependent on physical infrastructure and industrial production.

The bigger test

The government is now developing a digital system to forecast labor demand, update qualifications and connect training with employment.

The priority professions list has already expanded from 51 to 174, covering engineering, construction, manufacturing, biotechnology, green and nuclear energy.

The first meeting of the updated government may therefore extend beyond education policy. Kazakhstan is preparing for an economy in which growth will depend not only on investment and new projects, but on whether it has enough people with the skills to build and operate them.

The question is no longer simply whether Kazakhstan can create jobs. It is whether it can prepare enough people to fill them.

World.title: Masdar’s 1 GW Wind Plant Highlights Kazakhstan’s Race to Build More Flexible Power System
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is moving ahead with a $1.4 billion renewable energy project with Masdar, a leading renewable energy company based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), as the country seeks to expand wind generation while addressing electricity shortages and building a more flexible power system. The development was discussed Sept. 8 during a meeting between Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov, Masdar’s Deputy Chairman for Business and Projects Abdullah Zayed and UAE Ambassador to Kazakhstan Mohamed Saeed Mohamed Al-Ariki.

The meeting focused on the implementation of a 1-gigawatt wind power plant with an integrated energy storage system in the Zhambyl Region, as well as prospects for expanding cooperation in renewable energy.

The project, being developed within the strategic partnership between Kazakhstan and Masdar, is expected to attract approximately $1.4 billion in investment. It will include a 1,000-megawatt wind farm and a 300-megawatt battery storage system with a capacity of 600 megawatt-hours. Full commissioning is scheduled for the third quarter of 2029.

From a wind project to a test of Kazakhstan’s energy transition

The Zhambyl project comes as Kazakhstan moves toward a more complex phase of renewable-energy development. Increasing installed capacity is only one part of the transition. The country also needs storage, modern transmission networks and regulatory mechanisms capable of balancing electricity generated from weather-dependent sources.

The storage component of the Masdar project is particularly important in this context. Wind generation can fluctuate with weather conditions, while electricity demand changes throughout the day. A large-scale storage system can help absorb excess generation and make electricity available when renewable output declines or demand rises.

The Energy Ministry has identified energy storage as a strategic priority. Speaking at the Go Net Zero – Central Asia and Caspian business summit, Turar Alimzhan, director of the ministry’s Department of Renewable Energy, said legislation on energy storage systems is currently under consideration, alongside a long-term concept for the development of green energy.

“We are moving toward this goal systematically. The law on energy storage systems is already under consideration, and this is one of our strategic priorities,” he said.

Under Kazakhstan’s electricity-sector development plan through 2035, the country intends to implement at least 8.4 GW of installed renewable-energy capacity. That target means that the next challenge will increasingly be not simply generating renewable electricity, but ensuring that it can be reliably delivered to consumers.

The Masdar project has already moved beyond the planning stage

The current construction phase also marks a significant progression for the Zhambyl project. When The Astana Times spoke with Masdar Chief Operating Officer Abdulaziz Alobaidli ahead of Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week 2026, the project was still undergoing wind-resource assessment. Alobaidli explained that developing a bankable wind project requires detailed on-site measurements rather than relying only on satellite or historical data.

“We have signed the Power Purchase Agreement, and we have moved into the development phase,” he said, noting that wind projects require specific on-site work, including at least one year of ground-based measurements to establish the project’s bankability.

Since then, the project has advanced to construction. On June 29, Kazakhstan and Masdar held a capsule-laying ceremony and officially launched work at the site in the Zhambyl Region. The progression illustrates the lengthy process behind utility-scale renewable investments, from resource assessment and power-purchase agreements to financing, construction and eventual grid integration.

Masdar sees Central Asia as a core growth market

The Zhambyl project is also part of Masdar’s broader expansion across Central Asia. “In Central Asia, we remain one of the largest renewable energy investors, with Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan, and Kazakhstan as core focus markets,” Alobaidli told The Astana Times. “We also continue dialogue with other Central Asian countries, supporting energy policy development and reform to improve bankability and attract investment.”

This regional approach reflects a broader transformation underway across Central Asia, where countries face similar pressures to increase electricity generation, modernize aging infrastructure and reduce the carbon intensity of their economies.

At the Go Net Zero summit, Alimzhan said Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan were increasingly coordinating their efforts to develop a new energy model in which renewable generation, energy storage and low-carbon technologies play a central role. The discussions also focused on the development of a green energy corridor linking Central Asia, Azerbaijan and Europe. The initiative has entered a practical implementation phase and is being considered as a potential area for deeper regional energy cooperation.

The grid will determine how far renewables can go

Kazakhstan’s renewable-energy ambitions ultimately depend on infrastructure beyond the power plants themselves. Large volumes of wind and solar generation require transmission networks capable of moving electricity from resource-rich areas to major consumption centers. This is particularly relevant for southern Kazakhstan, where additional generation capacity is being developed partly to address electricity shortages.

The transition therefore requires simultaneous progress in several areas: renewable generation, storage, transmission infrastructure, digitalization and regulation. The regional dimension adds another layer. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan already have interconnected energy interests, while the proposed Central Asia-Azerbaijan-Europe corridor could eventually create new opportunities for cross-border electricity trade.

Energy security and decarbonization are converging

For Kazakhstan, the renewable-energy transition is not only a climate-policy issue. The country needs to increase electricity supply while maintaining energy security and gradually reducing the carbon intensity of its economy. These objectives make renewable generation increasingly attractive, but they also expose the limitations of a power system designed around more predictable generation sources.

At the Sept. 8 meeting, Akkenzhenov said Kazakhstan was interested in expanding cooperation with international investors and technology partners in renewable energy.

“Partnership with Masdar contributes to the development of renewable energy and Kazakhstan’s progress toward carbon neutrality,” the minister said, adding that the project would support regional energy security, attract modern technologies and create new opportunities for energy infrastructure development.

World.title: Digital Customs Could Boost Kazakhstan’s Transit Potential, But Infrastructure Remains Key, Experts Say
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is stepping up its partnership with the World Customs Organization (WCO) as part of a broader strategy to strengthen the country’s position as a key Eurasian transit hub. But while digital customs reforms could significantly reduce trade costs and border delays, experts say their long-term economic payoff will ultimately depend on infrastructure, regional coordination and the changing geography of global trade.

The topic came into focus during a series of high-level meetings in Astana between President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and WCO Secretary General Ian Saunders on Sept. 8.

During the meeting, Tokayev said Kazakhstan is consistently developing a “smart border” model by introducing digital solutions to optimize customs procedures and improve freight transit across Eurasia. Saunders praised Kazakhstan’s progress in customs modernization and its growing role in developing the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor.

Customs modernization becomes part of a wider logistics strategy

Beyond the diplomatic symbolism, the meetings reflect a longer-term economic objective: transforming Kazakhstan from a transit country into an internationally competitive logistics platform.

Speaking in the meeting, Bektenov emphasized that resilient transcontinental trade has become one of the key drivers of Kazakhstan’s economic development. He noted that the WCO’s 2025–2028 strategic plan, Data-Driven Customs for a Connected World, closely aligns with Kazakhstan’s own digital reform agenda.

A central element of that strategy is the rollout of KEDEN, a unified customs system integrating declarations, transit procedures and border controls, alongside the Smart Cargo platform, which combines transport services, electronic permits and cargo tracking into a single digital ecosystem.

According to official data, 14.6 million tons of transit cargo passed through Kazakhstan during the first seven months of the year. Freight volumes along the Middle Corridor reached approximately 350,000 tons, with around 24,000 vehicles using the route.

Why digital borders matter

Farkhad Kassenov, head of the A+ Analytics research center, political scientist and international relations expert, notes that cooperation with the WCO should be viewed not as an isolated initiative but as one stage of Kazakhstan’s much broader transport and logistics strategy.

“Kazakhstan has been systematically synchronizing customs procedures, tariffs and border regulations with the countries participating in the Middle Corridor. This cooperation with the WCO is one of the stages of that much larger project,” Kassenov told The Astana Times.

The Middle Corridor has gained strategic importance as trade between China and Europe increasingly seeks alternatives to traditional northern routes passing through Russia. At the same time, Kazakhstan is also positioning itself within the developing North–South corridor, despite temporary disruptions caused by conflicts affecting the Middle East and maritime trade. According to Kassenov, removing bureaucratic barriers may prove almost as valuable as building new infrastructure.

“Digitalization can increase the speed of cargo movement by roughly 30% while simultaneously reducing logistics costs. When paperwork is synchronized and businesses use a single digital window, goods spend less time waiting at borders or in dry ports,” he said.

Digital gains cannot replace physical infrastructure

Yet customs reform alone will not solve every bottleneck. Kassenov notes that the Middle Corridor still faces structural constraints that digital systems cannot eliminate, including different railway gauges between China, Kazakhstan and Europe, as well as the natural limitations of crossing the Caspian Sea.
