World.title: Why Azerbaijan sees Talysh activism as security threat
World.content:
Persecution of Talysh activists in Azerbaijan

Talysh activists and researchers in Azerbaijan have over the years received lengthy prison sentences on charges of high treason, separatism and inciting ethnic hatred. Two of them, Novruzali Mammadov and Fakhraddin Abbasov, died while serving their sentences.

New cases have once again raised the question: where does the defence of national identity end and a threat to state security begin?

Jahid Kamal Isayev: jailed for 8.5 years

On 8 September, Baku Court on Grave Crimes sentenced Russian citizen Jahid Kamal Isayev, known on social media as Kamal Isayev, to eight years and six months in prison. He was found guilty of publicly calling for action against the state, disseminating attributes and symbols aimed at violating Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity, and inciting ethnic hatred involving violence or threats of violence.

Isayev was detained in November 2025 while travelling to Turkey and subsequently taken to Azerbaijan. The charges were based on his social media posts and statements. His defence argued that the videos contained no evidence of a criminal offence, that his remarks had been taken out of context, and that his activities were aimed at preserving the Talysh language and national cultural heritage.

In his final statement to the court, Isayev said he had never advocated the division of Azerbaijan. The prosecutor had sought a sentence of nine years and six months in prison.

Iqbal Abilov: 18-year prison sentence and worsening health in solitary confinement

The Committee for the Protection of Iqbal Abilov’s Rights said recently that the Talysh culture researcher had been placed in solitary confinement at Correctional Facility No 12, after which his health deteriorated.

According to the committee, Abilov arrived at the facility with a high fever and dizziness. He spent several days in the medical unit, but on 25 August, before he had fully recovered, he was returned to solitary confinement. He is reportedly due to remain there until 25 September. Abilov’s chronic bronchitis has worsened, while his breathing problems and attacks have become more frequent.

His supporters link the disciplinary measures against Abilov to his appearance in court wearing a T-shirt featuring a poem by Talysh poet Ali Nasir, as well as to media reports that physical force had been used against him while he was held in pre-trial detention.

Abilov, who lived in Belarus, was detained in July 2024 after travelling to Azerbaijan to visit relatives. On 20 May 2025, Lankaran Court on Grave Crimes sentenced him to 18 years in prison on charges of high treason, making calls against the state on the instructions of a foreign organisation, and inciting ethnic hatred.

Pro-government media accused Abilov of collaborating with Armenian intelligence services. Abilov and the committee campaigning for his rights reject the allegations, saying his activities were exclusively academic and cultural.

Amnesty International said Abilov’s trial was effectively held behind closed doors and that no compelling evidence of espionage was presented to the public. According to the organisation, correspondence used as the basis for the charges concerned academic cooperation on minority rights, linguistics and ethnography. No publicly available evidence that he had passed on classified information was presented.

Two Talysh intellectuals who died in prison

Novruzali Mammadov

Linguist Novruzali Mammadov, head of the Talysh Cultural Centre and editor-in-chief of the Tolyshi Sado newspaper, was arrested in 2007. In 2008, he was sentenced to 10 years in prison on charges of high treason and inciting ethnic, racial and religious hatred.

Prosecutors alleged that Mammadov had gathered information with the aim of establishing administrative autonomy in areas with large Talysh populations and had submitted appeals to international organisations concerning violations of Talysh rights. He pleaded not guilty and said he had been tortured. Human rights organisations at the time reported that the case was based on fabricated evidence and that his trial was unfair and held behind closed doors.

Following a prolonged deterioration in his health, Novruzali Mammadov died of a heart attack on 17 August 2009 in a hospital run by the Penitentiary Service.

In 2019, the European Court of Human Rights reached an important but nuanced conclusion: it did not establish that the state was directly responsible for his death, but found that the circumstances surrounding his death had not been effectively investigated.

The ECHR also found violations of the Convention in relation to Mammadov’s unrecorded detention in 2007, his ill-treatment and the denial of medical assistance during that period.

Fakhraddin Abbasov (Abboszoda)

Historian and political activist Fakhraddin Abbasov, known among the Talysh community by the surname Abboszoda, briefly served in 1993 as speaker of the parliament of the short-lived, self-proclaimed Talysh-Mughan Autonomous Republic.

Abbasov later lived in Russia and openly advocated political self-government and independence for the Talysh. In 2019, he was returned from Russia to Azerbaijan, and in February 2020 was sentenced to 16 years in prison on charges of high treason, making calls against the state and inciting ethnic hatred.

Amnesty International said it had examined Abbasov’s publications, interviews and appearances on internet television cited in the court ruling and found neither calls for violence nor acts that would constitute a criminal offence under international standards. The organisation concluded that Abbasov had been prosecuted for his political views.

Abbasov died on 9 November 2020 in Gobustan Prison. The Penitentiary Service said he had taken his own life in his cell and that, despite receiving medical assistance, he could not be saved. His death came around the time Azerbaijan announced that Shusha had been recaptured from Armenian forces. Reports at the time claimed that Abboszoda had taken his own life because he could not bear the news.

Amnesty International, however, said that the circumstances surrounding Abbasov’s death had not been effectively investigated.

Why does Talysh identity become a ‘security’ issue?

A comparison of these cases points to three factors.

The first is linked to the political legacy of the events of 1993. The attempt to establish the Talysh-Mughan Autonomous Republic created a historical backdrop against which the authorities subsequently came to view initiatives involving Talysh autonomy or political self-organisation through a security lens. Under this approach, the line between defending cultural rights, discussing autonomy and actions that the authorities may regard as threatening Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity can quickly become blurred.

The second factor is geopolitics. Talysh communities live not only in Azerbaijan but also in Iran. Activists’ residence in Russia and Belarus, their participation in conferences in Iran, or correspondence with scholars who are Armenian citizens have been interpreted in investigations as indications of foreign influence or espionage.

Espionage and incitement to violence are offences that states have a duty to investigate. However, treating academic contacts or political views as criminal requires specific and verifiable evidence, as well as justification that such interference is necessary.

The third factor concerns attitudes towards public expressions of a distinct Talysh identity. The Advisory Committee on the Council of Europe’s Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities has noted a discrepancy between the Azerbaijani authorities’ claims that “optimal conditions” had been created and assessments provided by representatives of the Talysh community.

The committee also noted that conferences on Talysh culture had attracted suspicions of separatism because of participants’ contacts with Iran and Armenia. It further reported allegations of pressure on some activists and observed that the use of minority languages remained largely confined to private and informal settings.

Key legal question

Azerbaijan’s constitution guarantees equality regardless of ethnic or linguistic background, as well as everyone’s right to preserve their national identity.

According to the official position, Isayev, Abilov, Mammadov and Abbasov were prosecuted not because they were Talysh, but for specific offences against state security.

At the heart of the dispute, however, is not ethnic identity itself but the evidence presented by the state: were allegations of incitement to violence, the disclosure of classified information or cooperation with a foreign intelligence service supported by clear and compelling evidence? Or were discussions of the Talysh language and culture, allegations of discrimination and even unpopular political ideas punished under legislation relating to state security?

The deaths of Novruzali Mammadov and Fakhraddin Abbasov in prison, as well as current reports about Iqbal Abilov’s health, take the issue beyond freedom of expression. It also concerns the state’s obligation to protect the lives and health of people in its custody and to conduct transparent investigations into deaths in detention.

In the absence of such transparency, the argument of “state security” appears less as a legal justification and more as a tool for suppressing independent voices associated with Talysh identity.

World.title: False claims that text of Armenia’s new Constitution has been published, and rebuttal
World.content:
Fake news about Armenia’s Constitution

Opposition politicians in Armenia and some local media reported that the new Constitution had been published on Sahmanadrutyun․com.

Artashes Ikonomov, co-founder of the Njhar constitutional movement, reported it on social media and described it as his “sensational discovery”. However, the Ministry of Justice quickly denied the report.

Armenia has been working on a new Constitution for a long time. However, the final version has not yet appeared on any official platform.

Fact-checking journalists analysed all the material claiming that the new Constitution had been published. They reported who spread the fake news and which media outlets carried it.

They also examined the website that published the text presented as the new Constitution. They identified errors in the fake document.

What Ikonomov claims

Artashes Ikonomov wrote on his Facebook page:

“The draft Constitution is available on Sahmanadrutyun.com. To understand what changes have been made, you need to read the entire draft.”

He urged people to read specific provisions of the draft and share the information so that “people know what awaits them in the future”.

Nina Karapetyants, who also co-founded the Njhar constitutional movement, published the same text on her Facebook page shortly afterwards. In the parliamentary elections, held in June, she ran first on the list of the political force “Against All”. This meant she would have become prime minister if the party had won the election.

Neither Karapetyants nor Ikonomov deleted their posts after the authorities officially denied the information they had published.

Moreover, Artashes Ikonomov published another social media post in which he described the Justice Ministry’s statement as a “disinformation denial”:

“The Ministry of Justice is spreading disinformation because it claims that disinformation is being spread on the Sahmanadrutyun.com website. I officially declare that this is the genuine draft of the new Constitution of the Republic of Armenia.”

Nina Karapetyants also stood by her position. Many social media users wrote in the comments under her post that the published information was an obvious fake. Karapetyants responded:

“What exactly is disinformation? That there is a website where the text of the Constitution has been published? That is an indisputable fact.”

Justice Ministry’s rebuttal

In response to information circulating on social media and on the pages of some media outlets claiming that the Constitution had been published, the Justice Ministry said:

“We would like to inform you that the published text is not a draft of the new Constitution, and the information being circulated is false.”

The ministry urged Armenian citizens and media representatives to refrain from sharing unverified information and wait for the official publication of the new Constitution.

Fact-checkers’ investigation

The fact-checking platform FIP.am conducted its own investigation. The fact-checkers said the website hosting the text raised suspicions.

According to Who.is, the domain name Sahmanadrutyun.com was registered just a few days ago, on 3 September:

“The domain was registered through GoDaddy for one year, until 3 September 2027.”

FIP.am could not establish who actually owns the website. The investigative journalists could not determine who created or published the document.

At the same time, they found it clear that this was a recently created website, not an official or professional platform that had operated alongside the process of drafting the new Constitution for a long time.

The journalists also concluded that the text being circulated was not a genuine draft of the new Constitution. They pointed in particular to:

internal contradictions between different articles,

unusual wording that resembles working notes,

typographical errors.

Moreover, key provisions of the published text closely resemble proposals put forward by Ikonomov and the Njhar constitutional movement he founded in 2025.

The fact-checkers specifically recalled that Artashes Ikonomov had said his proposed institutional system would include a State Council and a National Institute. He also proposed that the State Council should have nine members elected for nine-year terms:

“The document being circulated as a draft Constitution contains a similar structure. It also calls for the creation of an Institute of National Values and a State Council. The latter, again, consists of nine members with nine-year terms.”

FIP.am journalists also looked at which media outlets had published the disinformation. They included Mediamax and Armat Media, as well as the social media pages of Aysor.am and Politik.am.

“It is noteworthy that, according to the state registry, Ikonomov is one of the actual beneficiaries of Mediamax Media Company LLC, holding a 40 percent stake,” the publication says.

Fake news about Armenia’s Constitution

World.title: Council of Europe rights commissioner intervenes in Georgia FARA case
World.content:
Council of Europe on FARA

According to the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O’Flaherty has intervened as a third party in a case before the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) concerning Georgia‘s Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA).

The commissioner submitted written observations to the court which, according to GYLA, go beyond an assessment of the law itself and also address legislative changes adopted in Georgia over the past two years.

O’Flaherty called on the ruling Georgian Dream party to ensure a free and safe working environment for the country’s civil society sector in line with its international obligations.

The FARA law adopted by Georgian Dream came into force on 31 May 2025. The authorities say it was modelled on the equivalent US law. However, Georgia’s version of FARA targets civil society organisations and media outlets and restricts their activities, including their ability to work with foreign foundations and organisations.

According to GYLA, Michael O’Flaherty considers the adoption of the law to be part of a broader set of restrictions targeting civil society, which are having a negative impact on media outlets and non-governmental organisations working on human rights, democracy and the rule of law.

In his assessment, the law’s provisions do not meet the requirements of legality, legitimacy, necessity and proportionality established by the European Convention on Human Rights in relation to freedom of expression and freedom of association. The commissioner also pointed to the principle of non-discrimination.

The commissioner said the law contains vague wording and defines the concept of “political activity” too broadly. He argued that this makes it difficult to distinguish between legitimate international cooperation and foreign interference, while leaving it unclear who exactly is subject to the law’s requirements.

The commissioner also noted that the law establishes a strict system of administrative oversight which, in his assessment, approaches the severity of Russia’s “foreign agent” legislation. Deliberate violations of the law can result in criminal liability, including imprisonment for up to five years.

He also argued that the term “agent” carries negative connotations in public perception, meaning that the law’s entry into force contributes to the stigmatisation of civil society. The commissioner also pointed to what he described as a campaign by the authorities to portray non-governmental organisations and human rights defenders as “enemies of the state”.

The commissioner said the law targets specific individuals and legal entities on the basis of their foreign funding, resulting in unequal treatment. On this basis, he suggested that the European Court of Human Rights may find that the law forms part of broader restrictions aimed at intimidating organisations critical of the authorities and discrediting civil society activists.

The commissioner does not consider the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) in isolation, but assesses it alongside other legislative changes adopted in Georgia in recent years.

He noted that around a year before FARA came into force, the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence took effect, requiring organisations and media outlets receiving foreign funding to register as “organisations pursuing the interests of a foreign power”.

The commissioner stressed that both laws are currently in force at the same time.

He also noted that on 1 April 2025, the Georgian parliament amended 14 different laws, including by abolishing mandatory participation by civil society organisations in public decision-making processes.

On the same day, amendments to the Law on Broadcasting prohibited “foreign powers” from directly or indirectly funding audiovisual broadcasters or purchasing services from them. The powers of the National Communications Commission were also expanded, including its authority to issue warnings, impose fines, and suspend or revoke licences.

The commissioner also pointed to a series of amendments to the Law on Grants. Under changes adopted on 16 April 2025, foreign donors are required to obtain permission from the Georgian government before issuing a grant, while accepting an unauthorised grant is punishable by a fine equivalent to twice the value of the grant.

On 12 June 2025, the definition of a grant was broadened to include technical assistance, including the transfer of technology, knowledge and expertise.

Amendments adopted on 4 March 2026 further expanded the definition to include any financial or material assistance that could be used to influence the authorities or society. Government approval was also made mandatory for grants to legal entities registered abroad whose activities are related to Georgia.

The same amendments to the Criminal Code and the Code of Administrative Offences introduced administrative liability for commercial entities engaging in “political activity”, with repeat offences subject to criminal liability.

Violations of the Law on Grants are punishable by up to six years in prison, while money laundering for the purposes of “political activity” carries a prison sentence of up to 12 years.

The commissioner also highlighted amendments to the Organic Law on Political Associations of Citizens. Under the new rules, people employed by organisations that receive more than 20% of their annual income from foreign sources are prohibited from belonging to a political party. The ban remains in force for eight years after their employment ends.

Amendments adopted on 26 June 2025 also changed the definition of defamation in the Law on Freedom of Speech and Expression and shifted the burden of proof from the claimant to the defendant. The commissioner assesses that this change could encourage self-censorship.

The commissioner pointed to legislative changes affecting protests and freedom of assembly. He said parliament adopted several laws within a short period and without proper consultation with civil society or the Public Defender, significantly restricting freedom of assembly.

The commissioner says that effectively supporting the role and activities of civil society organisations is vital to a healthy democracy. He says the rights to freedom of association and freedom of expression must be protected in both the law and practice of Council of Europe member states.

The commissioner also notes that the commitment to creating and maintaining a safe and enabling environment in which civil society organisations and human rights defenders can carry out their work without hindrance was reaffirmed in the Reykjavik Declaration adopted in May 2023.

In his assessment, recent legislative changes in Georgia run counter to these principles and pose a threat to democracy.

The commissioner calls on Georgian Dream to ensure a free and safe working environment for the country’s civil society sector in line with its international obligations.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s SOCAR highlights progress in reducing methane emissions
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 9. SOCAR continues to implement its program to reduce methane emissions, the vice president of the State Oil Company of Azerbaijan (SOCAR), Afghan Isayev said during Baku Climate Action Week, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

According to him, with additional funding, it will be possible to implement further programs to reduce methane emissions and repair the relevant infrastructure.

“As part of SOCAR’s methane reduction program, measurement campaigns were conducted in collaboration with partners such as the Boston Consulting Group, Sniffers, and GHGSat. Over the past two years, the program has achieved progress amounting to approximately 1–2 million metric tons of CO₂ equivalent,” Isayev noted.

Speaking about the energy transition and the integration of renewable energy sources, he noted that solar and wind energy projects are supported by government programs, including investment certificates: "The goal for 2030 is for renewable energy sources to account for at least 30 % of the energy mix.

Partnerships with foreign developers, including Masdar, ACWA Power, BP, and Universal Energy, will enable us to exceed the 30 % target by 2030."

Isayev also noted the high potential of geothermal energy for both centralized heat supply and electricity generation.

He stated that, during discussions with the Minister of Energy, the development of geothermal energy was included in government programs that call for the drafting of new legislation and the creation of risk-mitigation tools.

Furthermore, Isayev reported that SOCAR, in collaboration with Schlumberger and Baker Hughes, conducted desk studies to identify areas in Azerbaijan with high geothermal energy potential: “SOCAR is currently seeking partners to participate in the capital of these projects in order to share project risks.”

World.title: Clean Energy Academy Programme launched in Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 9. The Economic Cooperation Organization Clean Energy Center (CECECO) and Germany-based Renewables Academy AG (RENAC) have launched the Clean Energy Academy Programme in Azerbaijan to strengthen professional and technical capacity in renewable energy and energy efficiency.

The programme is aimed at increasing the number of qualified professionals with the knowledge and skills needed to support Azerbaijan’s clean energy transition, according to CECECO.

The first phase will run from September to December 2026 and involve 20 representatives from Azerbaijan in a “Training of Trainers” programme. Participants will receive training in renewable energy, energy efficiency, clean energy technologies and renewable energy economics, while developing skills to deliver training in these areas.

The programme combines 50 hours of self-paced online learning with eight half-day live virtual training sessions. Participants who successfully complete the programme will receive trainer certification.

In the next phase, the trainers, in coordination with CECECO, will develop and deliver training programmes based on the needs of relevant institutions.

CECECO Executive Director Aysel Yagubova said the programme is designed to establish a sustainable national platform for professional education, technical training, institutional capacity building and knowledge exchange in Azerbaijan’s clean energy sector.

“Supporting the strengthening of local capacity and skills development remains one of the priorities of our social investment activities in Azerbaijan,” said Dr. Bakhtiyar Aslanbayli OBE, bp Vice President for the Caspian, Central Asia and Türkiye region. As Azerbaijan progresses towards its energy transition goals, the need for qualified local professionals who can contribute to expanding and transferring knowledge in renewable energy and energy efficiency is increasing further,” he added.

The project is being implemented as a social investment initiative funded by bp and its partners, with the aim of creating a sustainable pool of local trainers capable of independently delivering professional programmes in renewable energy and energy efficiency.

World.title: Iran appoints new consul general to mission in Kapan, Armenia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 9. Iran has appointed a new consul general to its consulate general in Kapan, Armenia.

The appointment was announced in a statement issued by the Iranian MFA following a meeting between Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi and the newly appointed Consul General in Kapan, Davud Yaychi. Prior to departing for Kapan, Yaychi briefed the minister on his program and priorities in his new position.

According to the ministry, during the meeting, Araghchi underscored the importance of Iran-Armenia relations within the framework of Iran’s good-neighborly policy and emphasized the need to further strengthen bilateral ties across various areas, particularly in the economic and consular spheres.

In 2022, Iran appointed Morteza Abedin Varamin as its consul general in Kapan.

In 2021, Iran decided to open a Consulate General in Kapan, Syunik Province, Armenia.

World.title: QazaqGaz, CNCEC discuss next stage of Kashagan gas plant project
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 9. Kazakhstan's QazaqGaz and China National Chemical Engineering Group Corporation (CNCEC) discussed further steps to implement a project to construct a gas processing plant at the Kashagan field, according to the Kazakh company.

This was announced in a statement by QazaqGaz’s press service following talks between Chairman Alibek Zhamauov and CNCEC Chairman Mo Ding’e during the QazaqGaz delegation’s visit to China.

According to the information, the parties discussed the current status of the project, completion of the Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) and preparations for the transition to the Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) stage.

"The 2.5 billion cubic meter per year plant will use advanced licensed technologies to process and purify highly sour associated petroleum gas. The project is expected to increase commercial gas production, address sour gas utilization and contribute to Kazakhstan's energy security, stable domestic gas supplies and export potential,", QazaqGaz said.

The parties also discussed the project's technical and commercial parameters and further coordination of work.

Following the talks, QazaqGaz and CNCEC agreed to synchronize work schedules and continue coordinating contractual documentation to move the project to the next stage.

According to the Kazakh company, CNCEC has experience in implementing large-scale chemical and oil and gas projects, including facilities involving complex technological processes.

According to NCOC, Kashagan is one of the largest oil discoveries made in recent decades, with estimated recoverable oil reserves of approximately 9–13 billion barrels (1–2 billion metric tons). The reservoir is located about 80 kilometers offshore from Atyrau in the North Caspian Sea, in waters 3–4 meters deep, with the reservoir lying at a depth of more than 4,200 meters below the seabed.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Alatau City, South Korea ink deal on digital twin pilot project
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 9. Kazakhstan's Alatau City Authority and South Korean technology companies AST Holdings Co., Ltd. and ILJOO GnS Co., Ltd. have signed a memorandum of understanding to develop a pilot project using digital twin and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies in Alatau City.

This was announced in a statement by the press service of the Alatau City Authority.

According to the information, the memorandum was signed in Busan on the sidelines of the World Smart City Expo.

'"Under the agreement, the parties will test technologies for collecting and synchronizing data on urban facilities, integrating utility infrastructure into a single system and using real-time data for city management. The pilot project will initially cover a limited area of Alatau City. Expert groups will determine the pilot site's location, the facilities to be connected, and the project's technical parameters," the statement says.

The digital twin will be developed alongside the construction of Alatau City, allowing its digital infrastructure to be integrated with the city's physical infrastructure from the early stages of development.

In the future, the system could be used for urban planning, traffic management, monitoring utility networks and assessing environmental conditions.

"For us, a Digital Twin is far more than a visual 3D simulation. We view it as the data-driven operating system for the long-term development of Alatau City. Building a smart city from the ground up gives us a rare institutional advantage: we can deploy modern digital architecture simultaneously with physical construction. Our key priority is transforming cutting-edge global expertise into applied solutions ready for effective scaling," Alatau City Authority CEO Alisher Abdykadyrov said.

AST Holdings specializes in three-dimensional digital models of cities and infrastructure by integrating geographic information system (GIS) and building information modeling (BIM) data with visualization, modeling and monitoring tools.

The company has participated in the development of South Korea's LX Digital Twin platform and the Digital Twin National Land pilot project. It also cooperates with Naver Cloud on a project to develop digital twins for five major Saudi Arabian cities - Riyadh, Jeddah, Mecca, Medina and Dammam.

ILJOO GnS specializes in digitalization solutions for industrial and urban infrastructure based on artificial intelligence, IoT and digital twin technologies. Its projects include digital solutions for Busan Eco Delta City and Busan Smart City Lab, as well as smart manufacturing and industrial management systems.

Following the pilot testing, the parties will consider expanding the functionality of the Alatau City digital twin to other parts of the city.

World.title: Three Lindsay Clancy jurors raise concerns after mistrial
World.content:
Three members of the Lindsay Clancy jury have spoken about failing to reach a consensus in an interview with US media.

Warning: This story contains details of a crime that may be distressing for some readers.

Foreperson Roni Carlson said all but one member of the jury were persuaded to find the defendant not guilty by reason of insanity, in an interview with NBC10 Boston.

After deliberating, Ms Carlson described being "excited" the jury had reached a consensus.

She began filling out the paperwork, but was interrupted by the lone juror.

"He had reasonable doubt, he admitted he had reasonable doubt," she said.

"But he said 'I'm still not gonna say she's not guilty by reason of insanity'."

Lindsay Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree murder over the deaths of her three children at their Boston home on January 24, 2023.

The Massachusetts mother's attorney said she had lost control of her mind due to postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors argued she knew what she was doing and acted deliberately.

After six-weeks of testimony, the judge ultimately declared a mistrial when the jury could not come to an agreement.

Loading Instagram content

Proof beyond a reasonable doubt?

The three jurors interviewed, Roni Carlson, Kellie Farina and Paula Devlin, raised concerns the lone juror's doubt did not match his verdict.

In the United States, the Due Process Clause in the constitution "requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt before a person may be convicted of a crime".

Judge William Sullivan addresses the jury during deliberations. (AP: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

Ms Devlin described the lone juror as "very arrogant".

"He really did not take on anything that anybody said," she said.

She continued to describe an interaction where he asked jury members who are nurses about Ms Clancy's medication and the toxicology report.

But then, Ms Devlin said, "he just completely disregarded the information that they gave".

'Did she know right from wrong?'

Ms Carlson explained that the majority found Ms Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity due to the evidence presented regarding her character and mental health.

"We weren't trying to figure out if she murdered the children, she did and she's admitting that," she said.

"We're trying to figure out did she know right from wrong at that time.

"Everything proved she loved her children — from her journals to her mother-in-law — everything proved that she loved her children so she had to have snapped and not know what she was doing."

The three women left the six-week trial as life-long friends, according to NBC10 Boston, saying they supported each other through the traumatic testimony.

Ms Farina described hearing Patrick Clancy's, Lindsay's husband, 911 call.

"It's something I will never not hear," Ms Farina said.

"When we heard it again in the jury room we were crying again, we were just like 'my god, the desperation, the despair in his voice'.

What happens next in Lindsay Clancy case The six-week criminal trial of Lindsay Clancy has collapsed without a verdict, with the judge declaring a mistrial.

"I felt that it was genuine."

Although the trial ended without a verdict, the case is not closed and prosecutors are free to start a new trial with a new jury.

Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz told reporters that no decision had been made on whether prosecutors would retry the case, but that his goal was always "getting justice for those three little babies".

World.title: Veterans headstone project fears funding promise falls short of need
World.content:
An organisation that helps to locate and name veterans in unmarked graves in South Australia is raising concerns about whether promised federal funding will be delivered.

The Headstone Project locates World War I veterans in unmarked graves and places a military service headstone there to recognise their service to Australia.

President of the SA branch, John Brownlie, said giving a veteran a headstone cost about $1,500 and that federal government grants contributed $620 toward that cost.

Getting a headstone for this veteran's grave will cost about $1,500. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Before the 2022 federal election, Labor committed $3.7 million in funding for the Headstone Project nationally.

Federal budget papers show $1.4 million over five years from 2025-2026 has been allocated for a range of memorial initiatives, including the Marking (First World War) Private Graves Grants program, which is the grant the Headstone Project applies for.

Those grant guidelines, as seen by the ABC, show only $58,000 is available nationally for this financial year.

The Headstone Project SA believes that number to be below what should be available.

These two nurses were given headstones that recognised their service. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Mr Brownlie queried the amount.

"Look at what you've [the federal government] promised, and look at what you've delivered, because there's a vast discrepancy," Mr Brownlie said.

"I think the behaviour of the government, quite frankly, is egregious."

The federal government did not provide an on-the-record response to the concerns raised by the Headstone Project SA, but the ABC understands all eligible applications have been awarded grant funding.

Deserve recognition

Ian Hopley is a former police officer who now investigates unmarked graves to provide military headstones. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Ian Hopley is a retired police officer who now assists with finding graves, determining that a veteran is buried in the grave and then researching and contacting living relatives.

The team searches cemetery records and picks out males of enlistment age born between 1870 and 1900; they then cross-check that with the national archives and find the graves of forgotten veterans.

Mr Hopley said the SA branch had provided headstones to nearly 200 servicemen and women and that about 500 were known around the state still to be waiting.

"Our work will go on for a very long time, provided we get the right funding and support," he said.

Mr Hopley said he came from a military family and believed the people in unmarked graves should be recognised for their service.

World.title: 'Wrong decision': New babies' hospital plans slammed by doctors
World.content:
Plans to manage high-risk births at WA's new Women and Babies Hospital represent the government doubling down on a "wrong decision", the doctors' lobby says.

The hospital is being built next to Fiona Stanley Hospital in Murdoch, about 20 kilometres from Perth Children's Hospital (PCH) where some infants will need to be transferred for specialist care.

Doctors and parents have long said the distance is unacceptable and called on the government to find a way of building the hospital on the QEII campus in Nedlands to make it easier for women and babies to be transferred to PCH and Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital.

Doctors say the new hospital, which is currently under construction, is too far from existing facilities. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

But the government maintains that is impossible without unacceptable disruption to other hospitals on the site, or intolerable delays.

Instead, the government has now outlined how it intends to allay the concerns of medical professionals and families by expanding existing services.

Neonate transfer upgrade

Paediatric services at Fiona Stanley Hospital will be upgraded, including extra specialist staff and services, and a second Newborn Emergency Transport Service (NETS) base established for babies who need to be transferred from the new hospital.

New $1.8b maternity hospital to be built at Fiona Stanley The WA premier announces plans to build a maternity hospital at the Queen Elizabeth II Medical Centre will no longer go ahead, instead committing almost $2b to a site in Perth's south.

"We've heard from clinicians that the time for the baby to reach the NETS team is a key consideration," Health Minister Meredith Hammat said.

"These are specialised staff, these are like mobile intensive care units and so they do provide that critical opportunity to stabilise a baby and transport them, so that is why we're making the decision about having a base here."

The government also believes locating a team at Murdoch will help with the timely transfer of babies from regional hospitals, because it is closer to Jandakot Airport where Royal Flying Doctor Service aircraft land.

Meredith Hammat says it is the right decision. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

More beds

Around $95 million has been set aside to add an extra 19 beds to PCH's neonatal intensive care unit.

Two adult beds will be added to handle a "very small number of cases" where women needed to birth at the children's hospital.

A new high-risk birthing unit is due to be built at Perth Children's Hospital. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

A consultation report, dated November 2025 but only tabled in parliament today, revealed clinicians rejected the idea of creating a smaller "satellite" facility to allow for births at PCH "due to clinical safety risks, limited workforce sustainability and fragmentation of services".

Doctors issue warning over maternity hospital move Doctors fear plans to move WA's main women's and babies' hospital 20 kilometres from its current location risk increased "mortality and morbidity" of critically unwell infants.

Ms Hammat said few women would give birth at PCH.

"It would only apply in those circumstances, a small number of circumstances, where a parent might also need to continue to receive treatment," Ms Hammat said.

Ongoing concerns

Australian Medical Association WA president Kyle Hoath said while the government's announcements were welcome, the profession still wanted the new hospital to be built at the QEII site.

Doctors want the new hospital to be built at the QEII site. (ABC News: Gregor Salmon)

"I appreciate that it's a full site that's difficult to make those allowances on, but this isn't good enough," he said. "We have a separation of services that need to be next to each other."

Opposition Health spokesperson Libby Mettam also wants a maternity hospital at the QEII site and said the government's plans were "flawed".

"It will still require a 20-kilometre journey for neonates requiring high-risk surgery at Perth Children's Hospital," she said.

Work begins on Perth's new $1.8b maternity hospital Perth's new Women and Babies Hospital will open on time, the state government insists, but it says the $1.8 billion budget may blow out.

Dr Hoath said his members believed between 100 and 200 babies a year would need to be moved to PCH.

The government's response to the November 2025 consultation report notes there is "no consensus on the size of the cohort needing 'time-critical neonatal transfer'".

The upgrades at PCH will require admin staff to be moved out of the building and the relocation of a surgical ward.

World.title: Hollands opens up on axing from Carlton AFL roster
World.content:
Elijah Hollands is at peace with the end of his Carlton career, saying he realises there are more important things in life that he needs to focus on.

Hollands was one of seven players delisted by the Blues on Wednesday, with former GWS star Zac Williams, Jordan Boyd, Lachie Fogarty, Lewis Young, Flynn Young and Harry Charleson also among the casualties.

But it was Hollands' axing just months after suffering an on-field mental health episode that represented the biggest story.

Carlton was fined $75,000 for its handling of Hollands during a round-six loss to Collingwood.

Hollands tallied just one disposal for the match, with his erratic behaviour catching the attention of fans even before the game started.

The 24-year-old was hospitalised days later before deciding to step away from football to concentrate on his mental health.

It meant Hollands wasn't able to add to his 47-game AFL career, 14 of which were played at Gold Coast.

His brother Oliver Hollands remains at Carlton.

Elijah took to Instagram to share his thoughts about the end of his time at the Blues, which could also spell an end to his AFL career.

Loading Instagram content

"Football means an extreme amount to me," Hollands wrote.

"My dad played professional footy, my great-grandfather played professional footy, my brother plays professional footy — it is everything I have lived and breathed for as long as I can remember.

"I have only ever wanted to do one thing my entire life: copy what was done before me and play AFL footy. It was something that I just knew I was going to do when I was a kid and it was all I ever cared about.

"And now, unfortunately, that purpose I had is no longer.

"I love this game, but I have come to realise that there are things in my life that are far more important than footy right now and they're the things I will now prioritise."

Hollands's father posts heartfelt message Elijah Hollands's father, former AFL player Ben Hollands, posts on social media pledging to help lift his son up and urging others to check on their friends if they are struggling.

Hollands thanked the greater AFL community for its support since his mental health challenges became public.

"As an extremely confident 18-year-old, I certainly envisioned my career going a whole lot differently, but I am OK with accepting that it just isn't in the plans set for me," Hollands said.

"I'll be moving into the next chapter of my life, leaving what will feel like a big hole to fill, but I am excited about what can come from having my health and mind in much greater shape."

Carlton's other big delisting was Williams, who joined the Blues from GWS at the end of 2020 on a six-year deal believed to be worth about $5 million.

The soon-to-be 32-year-old managed only nine games this year, with his time at Carlton plagued by injuries.

World.title: Anthropic researcher says some developers believe AI 'could kill us all'
World.content:
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon has quit the AI company, saying those building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade".

Mr Coxon said he had spent the past three years doing pre-training research at Anthropic and OpenAI.

"Neither company is acting responsibly," he posted on X.

"They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

Superintelligence is considered to be the stage of AI when machines surpass human performance in every field.

Anthropic Alignment Science lead Evan Hubinger posted a reply on X saying Mr Coxon was correct.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10 per cent within the next decade," he wrote.

"I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to."

Mr Coxon is one of a growing number of AI experts to call on the industry to slow down.

In July more than 1,300 employees of frontier AI companies signed a statement saying there was a "real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems".

The letter called on the US government to support an international effort to develop tools that can "deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development".

CEO and co-founder of Anthropic, Dario Amodei. (Reuters: Denis Balibouse)

Responding to the initiative in July, called Pacing the Frontier, Anthropic said in an X post: "Our own research on recursive self-improvement, published last month, points to the need for tools to deliberately pace the frontier of AI development ⁠so society can prepare".

OpenAI also responded to the letter, posting on X at the time: "We believe that, at some point in the future, AI acceleration ‌for ⁠frontier model development may be so high that the world will need to pace the rate of AI advancement."

AI could pose 'existential' risk, UN warns

The "alignment problem" for superintelligence is that an AI system may not share human values.

Autonomous drones and AI called out by UN human rights chief UN-rights chief has addressed a council in Geneva saying AI posed a threat to humanity.

On Monday, United Nations rights chief Volker Turk also warned that artificial intelligence could pose a threat to humanity and pledged to press AI firms to reduce risks that his office said included disruptions to services, communications and democratic systems.

He called for "cast-iron guarantees" to secure AI in a speech ahead of the start of his unprecedented second term.

"I share the concerns of industry insiders that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity," Mr Turk told the body in Geneva.

"I am calling here, today, for an all-out effort to put cast-iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI before it is too late."

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Man dies after shooting near community centre in Sydney's south-west
World.content:
A man has died following what police have described as a targeted shooting in Sydney's south-west.

Paramedics treated the man at the scene at a car park at a community centre in Punchbowl, but he could not be saved.

NSW Police were called to the site at about 5.50pm on Wednesday following reports of a shooting, with a crime scene now established.

Police say a silver Lexus sedan was spotted driving away from the area after the incident.

The man has not yet been formally identified, but Acting Superintendent Dean Johnstone said police believe him to be a 32-year-old man who was known to police.

Police say they are yet to identify the victim. (Supplied)

He said the incident was believed to be targeted, but would not confirm if the shooting was linked to organised crime.

Superintendent Johnstone said it was fortunate others were not injured in the incident.

"This is a callous act," he said.

"The implications of this act could have easily endangered other members of the community.

"Those actions cannot be tolerated."

A witness to the incident said he heard multiple gunshots and ran to provide first aid to the victim.

It comes after the state government on Monday announced a swathe of legislative reforms as part of a crackdown on organised crime.

It followed two suspected mistaken identity shootings in as many days last week.

Police and state government figures have repeatedly rejected suggestions underworld violence is out of control.

NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane acknowledged the shooting in a post on social media, noting it was the third incident of its kind in the city over the past week.

Police say no further information is available at this time, with investigations ongoing.

Anyone with information about the matter is being asked to come forward.

World.title: Police make arrests in long-running investigation of Bandidos bikie gang
World.content:
Seven alleged members of the Bandidos motorcycle gang's newly-formed Canberra chapter have been arrested as part of a long-running investigation into the group's activity.

It is alleged the group helped traffic more than 70 kilograms of cocaine with an estimated street value of over $10 million.

Over the past two weeks police said they seized quantities of cocaine, guns and drug trafficking equipment, precious gemstones, Pokémon cards and glass-sealed comic books from homes and cars connected to the accused.

Police say they began investigating the group in 2025.

Police said they would continue targeting organised crime gangs involved in the illicit drugs market. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

Spate of arrests in one week

At 1:30am on Wednesday August 26, police said officers executed a search warrant at a home in Taylor in Canberra's north, where they arrested a 36-year-old man.

In the home, they allege they discovered drugs believed to be cocaine, $500,000, a glock-style handgun and ammunition, along with drug trafficking items.

Later that day at 2:15pm, a home in Throsby was also searched, where police allegedly found and seized several vials of what is believed to be GHB and anabolic steroids.

A handgun that police allege was seized from one of the Canberra homes. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

Around three hours later, they then stopped a white Mitsubishi Triton in Belconnen, and arrested the driver, a 31-year-old man who was allegedly driving while disqualified.

A search of his vehicle returned a gel blaster firearm, suspected cocaine, and a mobile phone, police said.

The two men were charged with a range of offences including drug trafficking and firearms-related crimes.

Gems, Pokémon cards, seized from accused recruiter

That afternoon police also stopped another car in Lyneham, a white Toyota Landcruiser, and arrested a 36-year-old suspected gang member they allege has been recruiting people for criminal activity.

From his car they allegedly seized numerous Pokémon cards, diamonds, opals and other precious gems, and four vintage glass-sealed comic books.

The Bandidos recently formed a Canberra branch but have clubhouses across Australia. (ABC News: Henry Zwartz)

Police said they also found an accounts book detailing his assets and liabilities of more than $3.3 million.

ACT Policing later searched his home in Yarralumla, finding and seizing more vials of believed anabolic steroids, an extendable baton, and a white Volkswagen Golf.

Police say they charged one other person after he allegedly tried to smuggle evidence from a search warrant.

Over the following days, three more people were arrested in relation to the investigation.

Since the investigation began in early 2025, police say they have seized four vehicles as proceeds of crime and weapons including batons, tasers and knuckle dusters.

Detective Acting Inspector Mark Battye said the arrests were "positive" and "in the interests of community safety". (ABC News: Toby Hunt)

"Outlaw Motorcycle Gangs are not harmless groups riding motorcycles," ACT Policing Detective Acting Inspector Mark Battye said.

"They use greed, intimidation and violence to fuel the commercial trafficking of harmful drugs and weapons, making large amounts of money in the process that goes towards more offending.

World.title: Grief-stricken family recalls 'beautiful' mum killed in drunken crash
World.content:
A loving mother of four has been remembered as a selfless woman who has left an unimaginable void in the hearts of her children and family after she was killed in a head-on crash at Kaarimba in Victoria's north.

October 2, 2025, was a Thursday like any other for 45-year-old Nathalia mother Vilia Sutherland.

That afternoon, Ms Sutherland had just purchased groceries and was heading home in her Renault Captur SUV with the family's three dogs, two border collies and a labrador, when tragedy struck.

About 4:40pm while heading north on the Barmah-Shepparton Road at Kaarimba, about 25 kilometres north of Shepparton, a Toyota Corolla driven by 31-year-old Nathalia man Lance O'Brien veered into her lane, crashing into her car.

Ms Sutherland died at the scene and one of the border collies was later euthanased after sustaining critical injuries.

The then 30-year-old P2 driver O'Brien was hospitalised with serious injuries as a result of the crash.

Subsequent blood analysis found O'Brien had a blood alcohol content of at least 0.143 and the drugs methamphetamine, amphetamine and nordiazepam in his system.

According to prosecution documents presented to the Shepparton County Court, Jason Schreiber from the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine estimated O'Brien had a BAC more than three times the limit for fully licensed drivers, and possibly just below four times the limit.

The court heard after impact, O'Brien, who was trapped in his vehicle, asked a witness who had stopped to render assistance, "Did I kill someone?"

He then said, "I'm an idiot, I'm a f*****g idiot."

He was arrested on November 6, 2025, and charged with culpable driving causing death and contravening bail conditions.

On Wednesday he pleaded guilty to the charges.

Police charged Lance O'Brien with culpable driving causing death and contravening bail conditions. (ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf)

'A huge hole in my heart'

Ms Sutherland's eldest sister Annie Koopmans addressed the court, recalling how her sister's death had broken her heart.

"My life has never been the same since that October day," she said.

"There's a huge hole in my heart and it hurts so much, my family is broken.

"I'm her eldest sister; it's my job to protect her and I failed to keep her safe."

Ms Sutherland's elder daughter Tammy Woods told the court she recalled receiving a notification alerting her to a crash while over 3,000 kilometres away in Darwin.

She said despite contacting emergency services she could not find out anything else about what had happened.

"I'd never known hopelessness until this," she said.

Eventually, she heard from a brother that their mother was in a crash and did not survive.

Ms Woods said despite several months now passing since the crash, life had become harder and she missed being able to share special moments with her mum.

"Our lives will never return to the way they were, for my family and it will always be life before October 2 and life after," she said.

She said she kept wondering if her mum had time to react or was frightened in her final moments.

Addressing O'Brien in court, she said he had taken so much away from the family.

"You took [away] the opportunities for her to grow old surrounded by the people who loved her," she said.

" The greatest heartbreak of my life is I regret I will hate that I hate you because even I can hear my mum saying that's such a strong word and not to use it. "

Prosecutor Angela Liantzakis read out a statement from Tammy's younger sister Emily, who recalled turning 21 without her mum by her side.

"Every birthday I have after this one will be a reminder … every milestone I reach will have someone missing from it," she said.

She described her anger that her mother had been taken from her and said it impacted her sense of security and her outlook on life.

"I struggle to trust [that] people I love will be there tomorrow," she said.

"I feel guilty when I am happy, I have fear of phone calls after receiving a call from [my brother] … who said mum's been in an accident and didn't make it."

Speed a factor

The County Court heard O'Brien was on a P2 licence and was subject to a zero BAC condition.

He was also on bail at the time of offending with requirements not to drive a motor vehicle, consume alcohol or use a drug of dependence without lawful authorisation.

Prosecutor Angela Liantzakis told the court that analysis from the Collision Reconstruction Unit found O'Brien was driving at a minimum speed range of 115km/h -122km/h at the time of the crash.

During a Koori Court sentencing conversation, held in conjunction with Wednesday's hearing, O'Brien read from a statement saying how "deeply sorry" he was for the pain he had caused Ms Sutherland's family.

"I understand there's nothing I can do to undo the pain [from the] actions I have caused," he said.

The court heard he was "struggling" with drug and alcohol issues and recent trauma from losing two close relatives at the time of the crash.

"I know I can't change the past … I will carry away what has happened for the rest of my life," he said.

Judge Carolene Gwynn adjourned the matter for a further plea to appear in the Melbourne County Court later this month.

World.title: Boxing coach gunned down in latest Sydney gangland attack
World.content:
A boxing coach has been shot dead in an ambush in Sydney’s south-west, in what police believe is another targeted attack linked to organised crime. Louis Meehan, 32, was killed behind his boxing gym in the carpark of the Punchbowl Community Centre on Wednesday evening after being sprayed by gunfire by an assailant inside a silver Lexus sedan. Louis Meehan has been shot dead in the latest attack linked to Sydney’s gangland violence. Janie Barrett Police rushed to the carpark, administering urgent CPR to Meehan, while two onlookers knelt to pray for the man before he was pronounced dead. Meehan was walking alone when he was shot beside a white sedan at the entry of the carpark, which was full at the time of the attack.



Onlookers, including multiple school students, watched on from the edge of the carpark as paramedics worked to save him. Meehan has posed online wearing merchandise linked to the Alameddine crime gang. This includes clothing from Proper 60, a Merrylands-based group associated with the family, and Ready 4 War, the name of the Alameddine network’s drug-trafficking operation. Meehan was killed near the entry to the carpark. Janie Barrett Campsie Police Area Commander Dean Johnstone confirmed Meehan was known to police. “This is a callous act,” he said. “We do not believe that other persons were at risk. However, obviously, in a public place like this, those actions cannot be tolerated.”



Police had no information to suggest that Meehan’s life was in immediate danger, or an underworld contract had been taken out for his murder, according to Johnstone. Meehan, the son of former Australian boxing great Kali Meehan, played for the Sydney Roosters’ National Youth Competition side alongside brother Willis in 2013 before turning to full-time boxing coaching. Desperate paramedics attempted to save Meehan. SCN WorldStar He was a senior coach on the ‘Meehan Boxing Team’, a family-run business that conducted personal training sessions and boxing classes. His brothers are also involved in the business. The Punchbowl Community Centre carpark sits one block behind The Boulevarde, a busy high street adjacent to Punchbowl train station.



It is on the same road as St Jerome’s Catholic Primary School and St Jerome’s Catholic Church. The street has been roped off and blocked by marked and unmarked cars. Police have expanded the crime scene as they work to gather evidence. An expanded crime scene has been set up outside the community centre in Punchbowl. Janie Barrett The Punchbowl shooting comes two days after the Minns government announced a suite of measures targeting an outbreak of gangland violence on Sydney’s streets. The measures were flagged in response to last week’s mistaken identity killings of university student Marco Tapia, 23, and business owner Joshua Macdonald, 40, in the city’s west.



The reforms promised tighter targeting of offshore kingpins and local middle men orchestrating violent attacks and tougher penalties for teenagers carrying out gang-related shootings and firebombings. It marked the NSW government’s third significant crackdown on organised crime in two years and came days after the police minister denied authorities had lost control of escalating violence. Loading Conflict between the Alameddine crime family and Coconut Cartel has sparked an escalation in underworld violence in recent years, as the warring organised crime syndicates jostle for control of Sydney’s lucrative drug trade. Powerbrokers for both of the groups are living overseas, where they’re believed to be orchestrating criminal activities in Sydney while out of reach of Australian police.



Asked on Monday if community fears were justified following last week’s shootings, Premier Chris Minns said: “We do think there’s a problem.” “There [is] a disregard for human life I haven’t really seen before,” he said. “It’s been a regrettable and horrible part of life in Sydney.” It followed Police Minister Yasmin Catley’s insistence last week that the violence was not “out of control”. Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane referenced Catley’s comments following the Punchbowl shooting on Wednesday, writing on X: “Another deadly shooting in Sydney – the 3rd in a week. This time in front of a community centre. Do you still have things under control police minister Catley?”



Innocent men Marco Tapia, 23, and Joshua Macdonald were killed a day apart last week in what police say were cases of mistaken identity. Tapia was killed last Tuesday morning after a group of home invaders stormed his family’s Glen Alpine home before executing him in his bed. He was in his third year of a biomedical engineering degree at the University of Technology Sydney, and his only brush with the law was through a minor traffic offence. Macdonald was shot dead in the doorway of a Merrylands West duplex home the next day. CCTV footage outside the home showed a grey Audi sedan stopping outside the house before an assassin fires shots from the back passenger seat.



Macdonald, who didn’t live at the home, was arriving at the duplex with a resident and two children moments before he was shot. The owners of the Bruce Street residence are known to police and linked to organised crime. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: It was the most stressful thing she’s ever done, but the Traitors winner would do it all again
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Wednesday night, Kirby Bentley was named winner of the rebooted The Traitors Australia, claiming a prize pot of $200,600. The former Australian Survivor contestant and AFLW player was an OG Traitor who manoeuvred her way through the reality competition as her fellow Traitors – former Bachelor contestant Alex Nation, former MasterChef Australia contestant Alvin Quah and comedian Rhys Nicholson – were picked off by the Faithfuls. Called a “parlour game sociopath” in the final episode, Kirby had to convince The Real Housewives of Sydney’s Krissy Marsh and former Bachelor contestant Keira Maguire at the fire pit that she was a Faithful. Spoiler alert: She was not! Bentley talks to national TV editor Louise Rugendyke about her victory, what makes her such a good manipulator and which competition was harder: Australian Survivor or The Traitors? The Traitors Australia winner Kirby Bentley and host Gretel Killeen. Hello Kirby! How are you feeling now that it’s all over? It looked very stressful. It’s been an incredible experience. The show is just so complex that when you’re watching it, you’re like, “That’s that’s so simple, and it’s so obvious”, but it genuinely isn’t. I’m really relieved [it’s over] because it’s a stressful game. It was a wild ride, and they’ve done an incredible job [with the edit]. The show was filmed at an historic estate, Castle Claremont, in New Zealand’s South Island. How long did the shoot take? It was 12 days of filming, and I think 12 days is the maximum that I probably could have lasted because the moral dilemma of the human in you starts to play a part, and I was a Traitor the whole time. And it’s not a comfortable position to be in, when everyone’s their authentic self as faithfuls – and we’ve all got trust issues – so it’s just a really bizarre experience.



Related Article Spoliers

Reality TV What’s next for the winner of Alone Australia? He’s writing a cookbook, obviously What were you thinking on that first night, when host Gretel Killeen was choosing the Traitors, and you felt her hand on your shoulder? I genuinely wasn’t expecting it. I think I said to Gretel when she had asked if I wanted to be a Traitor, I was like, “If I’m a Traitor, I get to play the game and move the game the way that I need to as a Survivor person”, because there’s a reputation - “Survivor this, Survivor that” – that it has to be one of us [picked as a Traitor]. And I was like, “No, it doesn’t.” So when she selected me, I was so excited because if I wasn’t [picked], I would have been gone pretty early. How much did being a former Survivor player affect the way you played, especially when you had so much heat on you early on? The cast of Traitors Australia, which was made up of former reality stars. In an ideal circumstance, where you don’t wear clothes that Kween Kong can hear [Kween said she could hear the rustle of Kirby’s jacket when Gretel tapped her on the shoulder], I would have liked to have played a little bit lower. But I just ended up just adapting to what the game was giving. And when Kween heard it [the jacket rustle], and told people, I was like, “Well, let’s not let it ruminate any more. Let’s just bite the bullet and get Kween gone, and we’ll deal with the repercussions the next day.” There’s so much paranoia around Faithfuls, but it worked out a lot easier than I thought it was going to. I play a really aggressive game in Survivor, and it’s really cutthroat. If anyone ever says my name, it’s “Let’s just get them gone” and create that fear. And I did the same in this, and it worked. OK, Kirby, what is it about you that makes you so cutthroat? Why do you keep getting cast in these shows? I mean, you seem pretty nice to me.



Related Article Exit interview

Streaming Yes, Furious is a killer Epstein story but ‘it’s not just him’ … Well, there’s probably there’s another side of it. You don’t have people second-guessing themselves without the social aspect. So my biggest strength, it comes from my upbringing. I’m an Aboriginal girl. I grew up in a country town – white Australia, black Australia – I have learnt how to navigate those worlds, especially now as an adult in the corporate space. But when I’m playing these games, I want to connect on your level. I want to know who you are on your personal level, and make you feel safe to be around me, and it’s all genuine. That way, then I know how to navigate myself around you if you decide to turn on me. I think Claudia said it at one stage, and it didn’t make the cut, but she said, “I think you’re a Traitor” and I was like, “I actually think you are as well. And these are my reasonings”. I’m laying it all out. So if I can address the person directly in a respectful way, it doesn’t hit the same as manipulation. Because I’m not trying to manipulate. I’m just leaning into you as a human. Kirby Bentley hugs fellow contestant Keira Maguire after Bentley revealed she was a Traitor. Have you had people in your job or your family who are watching this and are now just going, “Kirby, can we trust anything you say or do?” A lot of the people who know who I genuinely am at my core, know that I was a prankster. I had to have a safe word, and it was “honest”. Like if I say “honest”, I would never lie. But in my real world, I don’t like liars. I like my space to be safe. I like to know who the people around me are as well. So, it’s a very different world that I walk in my real life. And these games, it’s just like football. You step over that white line, and your best friend can give you the biggest hit or tackle or whatever, and it’s not personal. We step back over that line, and we’re still mates. We’re just representing our jumpers under a set of rules. So it’s the same sort of concept. Gretel Killeen with Rhys Nicholson, who was eventually recruited by Kirby Bentley to be a Traitor.



You recruited Rhys as a Traitor, but in those last couple of episodes, things became quite tense between you – you wrote their name down twice! – what’s your relationship with Rhys like now? Nothing’s personal. Like in those moments, we are exhausted. I’ve been an OG Traitor from the start, and it hasn’t been easy. The heat’s been on me the entire game, so I’m trying to make decisions that – because I would have happily gone to the end with Rhys – and there were times where Keira and Krissy were off Rhys, so I was like, “OK, cool, we can make this happen.” But then when they [Keira and Krissy] were back on them [Rhys], I was like, “Well, I need to make this happen for me because that’s what the game is about.” So it was very conflicting. I would like to think that Rhys is in my life forever, and I think a lot of our cast, if not nearly all of our cast, feel the same about each other because it’s just such a unique experience. Related Article ★★★

Review Netflix’s Raygun documentary shows how she broke the internet – and herself How much research did you do? Because it seemed like some contestants knew how to play the game but others (looking at you, Dicko!) seemed to think they were playing Survivor. I made a point of watching them all [the international versions of The Traitors] just to be able to see if there are any patterns or styles of how to work your way through. And there is no formula. I think the complexities around it are personalities, experiences, exposure, pressure. All of those variables play a huge part in it. So you need to be adaptable, which is why your social game comes into play. So when you’re a safe person, when people freak out, they come back to you and they lean on you. I learnt that at a young age. But it works, and it’s worked really well for me in all the games that I’ve played. Kirby Bentley (second from right) with the Australian cast of Survivor: Australia v The World (from left) George Mladenov, Janine Allis, Luke Toki, Sarah Tilleke, David Genat and Shonee Bowtell. What was more difficult, Survivor or Traitors?



Traitors. But it’s different. I could easily sit on an island for 47 days, and there’s an element of trust and safety in your alliances, and you know what that looks like to a certain point. In this, as a Traitor, you don’t know if the Faithfuls are telling you the full truth, and they don’t even know what their full truth is. I don’t know if I could play as a Faithful in this game. It was hard enough as a Traitor, but they [Faithfuls] have no answers. There’s no such thing as evidence. It messes with your head on a different level. Related Article Review What to stream this week: Sharehouse comedy returns better than ever, plus five more picks You have to choose between Survivor All Stars and Traitors All Stars – what do you pick? Oh, I’ve always said I would do a Survivor All Stars. But I think I need a break from it because I don’t think anyone would trust me anyway, and I wouldn’t last. The only reason I would do Traitors is if we were all returning Traitor players, and if it was a world one, so or like UK, US, Oz, all came together with Gretel hosting. Well, I just hope everyone in your office is nice to you when you walk back in tomorrow morning... Yeah, we’ll have to regroup, do a team building and an honesty and trust game [laughing]. We will figure it out! The Traitors Australia is now streaming on 10Play.

World.title: Australian cars stolen for parts to sell to Iran and Russia, insurers say
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessConsumer affairsOrganised crime Australian cars stolen for parts to sell to Iran and Russia, insurers say Elias Visontay September 9, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Organised crime groups are stealing cars from Australian roads, shipping them overseas and stripping them down to sell the parts in Iran and Russia, insurers have warned, as sanctions make the black market for parts increasingly lucrative. The revelation from the Insurance Council of Australia comes amid fresh data showing Melbourne remains Australia’s vehicle theft epicentre. This is propelled by petty crime as well as organised syndicates packing stolen cars into shipping containers, sending them to intermediary ports to bypass detection before forwarding them to sanctioned nations. Stolen Australian cars are being shipped overseas, dismantled and sold to Iran and Russia where the black market for smuggled replacement components has become highly lucrative. Aresna Villanueva Victoria recorded over 12,300 car-theft claims in the 2025-26 financial year, costing insurers $244.3 million. While the number of theft claims remained stable, total costs grew by more than $21 million. More cars are stolen or broken into in Melbourne than in all other capital cities combined. Queensland motorists lodged 6200 theft claims costing $113 million, while there were roughly 5500 claims costing $98.7 million in NSW. In Western Australia, about 3500 claims cost $22 million. Nationally, the financial toll of car thefts exceeded half a billion dollars.



Insurance Council chief executive Andrew Hall said that while car theft includes joyriding and domestic re-selling, insurers believe a growing proportion of vehicles are stolen specifically for overseas export. Hall noted insurers report that two-thirds of vehicles stolen in Melbourne are never recovered locally and that detections of Australian-registered vehicle parts overseas have increased. Throughout the year, Victorian and Queensland police have raided shipping containers at Melbourne and Brisbane ports and at wrecking yards, uncovering hidden stolen vehicles. Authorities have also made a string of arrests linked to an international crime syndicate that has illegally shipped tens of millions of dollars worth of stolen cars to the United Arab Emirates. In an interview with this masthead, Hall revealed that insurers had since formed the belief that after arriving in the UAE on illegal shipments, the cars were being dismantled for parts to be sent primarily to Iran and Russia. A lucrative market for second-hand replacement components has emerged because sanctions prohibit manufacturers from selling legitimate parts to repairers in those countries.



Related Article Crime Hacked, stolen and shipped overseas: Police crack global car theft ring “Australia has become part of a global supply chain for sanctioned nations,” Hall said.
