Tech.title: We Tested 19 Portable Power Stations. These 4 Will Keep Your Fridge Running the Longest
Tech.content:
Portable power stations are lifesavers during a blackout, easily keeping your phones, laptops and routers fully charged. But what happens when you need to power something much larger, such as your fridge or washing machine? Many people assume they need to drop thousands of dollars on a whole-home battery system just to keep their food from spoiling.

To test that theory, we brought 19 large and extra-large portable power stations into the lab and hooked them up to a standard refrigerator. Our testing revealed a surprising truth: You don’t need nearly as much wattage as you might think. In fact, depending on your energy draw, a smaller, budget-friendly station is often more than capable of handling your heaviest home appliances.

Best Portable Power Stations for Emergencies See at CNET

Key takeaways The Fossibot 3600 Pro performed the best overall, keeping the test refrigerator running for an impressive 44.65 hours (1.86 days). The Oupes Mega 5 followed closely behind in second place at 43.72 hours (1.82 days).

The Oscal Power Max 2400 had the shortest runtime by far, lasting only 12.58 hours (0.52 days).

The Anker Solix F3800 Plus performed poorly for its size, lasting only 25.68 hours (1.07 days) despite its large 3,840Wh capacity.

The Bluetti AC200L unit is the efficiency king for large appliances, lasting 29.27 hours on a 2,048Wh battery.

The Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 is a standout performer, lasting 27.4 hours on a 2,048Wh battery.

Lab awards for power stations:

Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

CNET’s lab testing gives us reams and reams of data that let us determine the most efficient portable power stations across every size category. Our winners for round-trip efficiency, which measures how much energy you get back from the power station compared to how much power you need to draw from a wall outlet to charge it, are listed below.

Most Efficient Small Unit (<600 Wh): UDPower AC0600 (RTE: 72.92%)

Most Efficient Medium Unit (600-1299 Wh): Bluetti Elite 100 V2 Bio-Based (RTE: 83.44%)

Most Efficient Large Unit (1300-2199 Wh): Bluetti Elite 200 V2 (RTE: 81.08%)

Most Efficient X-Large Unit (>2200 Wh): Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus (RTE: 79.66%)

For charging speed, which measures how quickly a portable power station can charge to 100% from empty, we have only one winner.

Fastest charging: Oupes Mega 1 Lite 0.73 hours (about 44 minutes)

How CNET stress tests portable power stations for disasters

Each of the 19 portable power stations in our test batch was used to power a full-size refrigerator (Whirlpool, 60Hz, single-phase, 118V, full-load 7.2A) until the battery completely drained. We measured how long each unit kept the refrigerator running and reported the results measured in hours and days. Since this test reflects real-world use rather than a controlled laboratory measurement of battery capacity, efficiency ratings (round-trip efficiency) are only reported from our standard testing procedure.

While the results showed that larger units last longer for demanding appliances, they also revealed that slim, custom-designed models such as the Bluetti FridgePower prove you don’t need huge, bulky home backups. In fact, several of our better-performing models weren’t what we consider “extra-large,” ones with a capacity larger than 2,200 watt-hours, but rather fell in a more modest 1,300 to 2,199Wh range.

Unique measurements we use for our fridge stress testing

Measured watt-hours (Wh): The total usable capacity the battery has available to give.

Fridge watt-hours (Wh): The actual amount of energy the refrigerator consumed over the duration of the test.

Delta: The difference between the measured Wh and the fridge Wh. This represents the energy the power station consumed itself (idle draw) just to keep its inverter running for that amount of time.

Percentage reduction: The delta divided by the measured Wh. This gives us the exact percentage of the battery’s total usable energy that was wasted as internal overhead.

The best power stations for large appliances

Below is our list of power stations, ordered by how long they kept our test fridge running.

As seen in the combined list below, while the units with massive XL battery capacities generally sit near the top, highly efficient large units, including the Bluetti AC200L and the Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 can outrank several bigger systems (such as the Anker Solix F3800 Plus and Pecron E3600LFP) simply because they waste far less energy.

The extra-large models naturally dominated the absolute runtimes, but performance varied widely by efficiency, with the Fossibot 3600 Pro being our overall winner for both sheer runtime and efficiency at 44.65 hours (1.86 days). In the large category, while they have smaller batteries, the top large units proved incredibly power-efficient, with the Bluetti AC200L as the overall winner, delivering 29.27 hours of fridge runtime (1.22 days).

Fridge runtime in order from highest to lowest

Fossibot 3600 Pro: 44.65 hours (1.86 days) Oupes Mega 5: 43.72 hours (1.82 days) Jackery Home Power 3600 Plus: 38.58 hours (1.61 days) Jackery Home Power 3000: 32.05 hours (1.34 days) Bluetti Apex 300: 30.43 hours (1.27 days) Bluetti AC200L: 29.27 hours (1.22 days) Anker Solix F3000: 28.97 hours (1.21 days) Pecron E3600LFP: 28.15 hours (1.17 days) Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2: 27.40 hours (1.14 days) Bluetti Elite 200 V2: 26.32 hours (1.10 days) Anker Solix F3800 Plus: 25.68 hours (1.07 days) Bluetti FridgePower: 23.43 hours (0.98 days) ETAKER M2000: 22.48 hours (0.94 days) DJI Power 2000: 22.42 hours (0.93 days) BougeRV Rover 2000: 21.10 hours (0.88 days) Dabbsson 2000L: 21.00 hours (0.88 days) Grecell H2400: 17.75 hours (0.74 days) GoalZero Yeedi 1500: 16.50 hours (0.69 days) OSCAL Power Max 2400: 12.58 hours (0.52 days)

After testing eight, there’s only one extra-large portable power station we recommend for fridges

Extra-large (>2,200Wh)

Fossibot 3600 Pro: 44.65 hours (1.86 days) Oupes Mega 5: 43.72 hours (1.82 days) Jackery Home Power 3600 Plus: 38.58 hours (1.61 days) Jackery Home Power 3000: 32.05 hours (1.34 days) Bluetti Apex 300: 30.43 hours (1.27 days) Anker Solix F3000: 28.97 hours (1.21 days) Pecron E3600LFP: 28.15 hours (1.17 days) Anker Solix F3800 Plus: 25.68 hours (1.07 days)

The Fossibot 3600 Pro is our top choice for keeping your fridge running. Fossibot/CNET

The Fossibot 3600 Pro is the best power station for keeping your fridge running. It kept our test fridge running for 44.65 hours (1.86 days). That means you can get almost two days of cooling during a power outage if you own the 3600 Pro. It’s also remarkably power-efficient. Even though the Oupes Mega 5 had a much larger measured watt-hour (4,352.86Wh compared to the Fossibot’s 3,293.74Wh), the Oupes wasted an incredible 1,730.22Wh just to keep its inverter running.

This resulted in a 39.75% reduction in efficiency for the Oupes Mega 5. Meanwhile, the Fossibot only lost 860.03Wh to overhead (a 26.11% reduction), allowing it to power the fridge for almost an hour longer despite its smaller battery. This shows better power efficiency when handling the cycling loads of a refrigerator.

The Oupes Mega 5 has tons of power, letting you run a fridge for nearly two days. CNET

The Oupes Mega 5 comes a close second in the extra-large category, offering 43.72 hours (or 1.82 days) of power. On paper, while these models sound like they’re in a dead heat, it actually speaks poorly of the much larger Mega 5, which only has 4,352.86watt-hours, according to our measurements, despite what it claims on its box.

Contrast this with the 3,293.74Wh measured wattage of the Fossibot 3600 Pro. That means, despite having a massive 5,040Wh capacity on paper, the Oupes Mega 5 actually loses a huge chunk of it in real-world use, making it inefficient for running the cycling loads of a typical refrigerator.

After the Oupes Mega 5, our list starts to separate into more distinct winners. The Jackery Home Power 36000 Plus lasts 38.58 hours (1.61 days), while the Home Power 3000 lasts 32.05 hours (1.34 days). This is to be expected as a function of size and capacity, since each subsequent unit, such as the Bluetti Apex 300, had lower measured watt-hours and capacity than the preceding model.

The large portable power stations that punch above their weight

Large (1,300–2,199Wh

Bluetti AC200L: 29.27 hours (1.22 days) Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2: 27.40 hours (1.14 days) Bluetti Elite 200 V2: 26.32 hours (1.10 days) Bluetti FridgePower: 23.43 hours (0.98 days) ETAKER M2000: 22.48 hours (0.94 days) DJI Power 2000: 22.42 hours (0.93 days) BougeRV Rover2000: 21.10 hours (0.88 days) Dabbsson 2000L: 21.00 hours (0.88 days) Grecell H2400: 17.75 hours (0.74 days) GoalZero Yeedi 1500: 16.50 hours (0.69 days) OSCAL Power Max 2400: 12.58 hours (0.52 days)

If you’re looking for a smaller portable power station that can still keep your fridge and other key home appliances running, look no further than the Bluetti AC200L. With a capacity of just 2,048Wh, it ran the fridge for 29.27 hours.

It completely outclassed several XL units with significantly larger batteries, including the Anker Solix F3000 (3,072Wh), which lasted 28.97 hours, the Pecron E3600LFP (3,072Wh), which lasted 28.15 hours and the Anker Solix F3800 Plus (3,840Wh), which lasted 25.68 hours.

The Elite 200 can keep your fridge running for over 26 hours. Bluetti/CNET

It led the large category by a solid margin, beating out the Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 (27.40 hours) and the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 (26.32 hours).

However, the Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 is worth considering as well. Also offering a 2,048Wh capacity, it achieved 27.40 hours of runtime, comfortably outlasting the XL Anker Solix F3800 Plus despite having nearly half the battery size on paper.

How much power/wattage do you really need to run your key home appliances?

Our lab testing shows that you may not need as much power or wattage in your portable power stations as you might think. It all comes down to what you’re trying to power.

“In plain terms, 80% of users’ actual emergency power needs fall under 200W,” Sean Tan, PR manager at Anker Solix, said, referencing data from a survey of 759 Anker power station customers. “Fridges, Wi-Fi routers, lights, phone/laptop charging. Not air conditioners. Not power tools. The ‘wattage arms race’ has been optimizing for the 20% edge cases while the 80% majority pays a premium for capability they never use.”

For fridges specifically, you need to consider that they’re intermittent loads. That means they cycle on and off, drawing power heavily for short periods and then entering a low-power standby mode. Because of this, a power station’s inverter efficiency and self-consumption (idle draw) matter more than just battery size. That’s why a portable power station such as the Fossibot F3600 Pro can beat something like the Oupes Mega 5, which looks larger on paper in terms of capacity.

The Jackery HomePower 3600 has a huge amount of capacity for fridge backup. But despite winning a lab award, it surprisingly wasn’t our top performer. Jackery/CNET

“We generally recommend a 1kw or 2kw power station for common kitchen appliances such as refrigerators, microwaves and coffee makers,” said Brian Essenmacher, head of North American business development for EcoFlow. “These mid-sized units can typically power a fridge for a half day or full day.”

“A smaller 10- to 15-cubic foot refrigerator during a short four-hour outage may only require around a 1kWh power station,” said Marc Deng, R&D manager at Bluetti, concurring with the power estimate, though he pointed out that for US consumers, the requirement may be on the higher end. “But the reality for many American households is different. Larger French-door and side-by-side refrigerators are often in the 18- to 28-cubic-foot range, with typical power consumption around 80 to 190W. For families preparing for longer outages caused by hurricanes, winter storms or grid failures, around 2kWh becomes a much more practical starting point.”

What you need to know before buying a power station for a fridge

“The biggest trap is looking at capacity alone,” said Tan. “Capacity tells you how much energy is stored, not how much actually reaches the device.” He points to two things that matter more: light-load efficiency and idle consumption. “A home fridge runs at 100–200W, cycling on and off. Most of the time the power station is operating well below its rated output. Efficiency at these light loads varies dramatically between units.” As more idle consumption, “When the fridge compressor is off, the power station is essentially sitting idle, but still burning power. Industry typical idle draw is 15–20W. That adds up fast.”

Those looking for a reliable emergency fridge backup should prioritize low idle power consumption and high small-load efficiency over buying the largest, heaviest battery available. A well-optimized 2,000Wh unit can easily outlast a poorly optimized over 3,000Wh unit, as our data shows. By default, all portable power stations waste some energy; the key is to find the one that wastes the least, while also providing stable power.

Bluetti/CNET

Ideally, you also want one with an uninterruptible power supply (or UPS), which helps maintain stable, continuous power. “Modern refrigerators often rely on electronic controls and variable-frequency compressors, which are designed to operate continuously under stable power conditions,” said Marc Deng, R&D manager at Bluetti. “A good rule of thumb is that the UPS transition time should be below 20 milliseconds, with around 10 milliseconds being ideal. If the transfer is too slow, the refrigerator’s internal electronics may reset, causing the compressor and control system to restart unnecessarily. Over time, repeated interruptions can create additional stress on the appliance.”

It’s also important not to overlook the surge power stat that many portable power stations advertise. Deng pointed out that depending on the refrigerator model, the startup surge can range from around 600W to well over 1,200W. “Surge power matters a lot,” Tan said. “Compressor startup pulls several times the running wattage. A station needs 2,500–3,000W peak to reliably handle most residential fridges.”

The FridgeGuard is thin enough that it can sit on top of a fridge or in a tight corner. Jackery

You also need to consider the percentage of energy wasted as overhead. The Anker Solix F3800 Plus wasted 46.63% of its energy just keeping itself running, which explains its short runtime. The Pecron E3600LFP had the lowest overhead loss with a tiny 15.75% reduction, while other highly efficient units included the Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 (18.21% loss) and the Bluetti AC200L (22.16% loss). These low-loss units ensure that power actually reaches the refrigerator rather than being lost as internal heat.

In the XL category, our undisputed winner is the Fossibot F3600 Pro, which is $2,600 at full price, but frequently on sale for less. It lasted the longest and wasted the least energy in the XL category. For the large power stations, our winner is the Bluetti AC200L. It punched above its size and power capacity, offering excellent efficiency and the longest fridge runtime of any large portable power station.

Do you need a portable power station specially designed for fridges?

The FridgePower lets you pair multiple BlueCell batteries with it, giving you up to four days of runtime. Bluetti

It’s worth noting that there’s a new category of portable power stations, with slim models designed to sit on or be mounted behind a fridge. Examples include the new Bluetti FridgePower and the Jackery FridgeGuard, both of which I’m testing at home, while Anker’s Solix S2000 is a more traditional take on the capability.

Of these, we’ve only been able to run lab tests on the FridgePower, and the results are impressive. It falls into the upper tier of large portable power, keeping our test fridge running 23.43 hours (0.98 days), so it lasts nearly a full day. Of its 1,621.09Wh measured capacity, the FridgePower only lost 328.08Wh (a 20.24% reduction) to internal inverter overhead. This compares favorably with other, more efficient models.

While it won’t keep the fridge running for multiple days, even the bulky Fossibot 3600 Pro is hard-pressed to do that. The design is its biggest selling point: The FridgePower is slim, lightweight and can be out of sight and out of mind, unlike hooking up your fridge to a traditional power station. So while it’s not required to power a fridge, the FridgePower won’t look out of place in your kitchen and it provides sufficient power to get you through an outage.

Tech.title: Apple ‘Surprise and Shine’ Event Is Today: All the Rumors on a Folding iPhone, AirPods and Watch Series 12
Tech.content:
Wednesday’s “Surprise and shine” event is bound to be unlike most other fall Apple events. In addition to seeing the next-generation Apple Watch and AirPods, we could also get a first look at a much-anticipated, wholly new product: a foldable iPhone, rumored to be called the iPhone Duo.

This year’s event is a bit sentimental for the Cupertino company. Tim Cook announced in April that he is stepping down from his role as CEO, a job he has held for nearly 15 years after legendary Apple co-founder Steve Jobs stepped down in 2011. John Ternus, the company’s hardware engineering chief, stepped into the role just days before the event.

Apple is also heavily rumored to break with its usual routine by holding off on releasing a base iPhone 18 until next year, meaning only the more expensive Pro models will be revealed in September. That would give the foldable a center stage debut.

We’ll be keeping a close eye on the price tags. Apple raised prices across its computer and home devices this summer, attributing the cost increases to memory chip supply chain issues, largely driven by the AI race. Additional price hikes on Apple Music and Apple TV subscriptions aren’t helping cash-strapped consumers, either.



New iPhone 18 models, joining the foldable fun

Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup is likely going to look a little different this year. One of the biggest rumors is that Apple is going to do an extended rollout. This September, we expect to see the foldable iPhone Ultra, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, but we likely won’t get the base iPhone 18, iPhone 18E and a possible iPhone Air 2 until spring 2027.

The iPhone Ultra, as Apple’s much-rumored first foldable phone is tentatively named, has a book-style design, according to analyst leaks. Think more Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which opens like a book into a mini tablet — not like an OG ’90s flip phone.

But the possible $2,000 price tag means the Ultra likely won’t be a replacement for the base iPhone 18. More likely, it will be more of a luxury option. That may be one reason why a majority of US adults (75%) don’t care about foldable phones, a recent CNET survey found.

We had CNET’s creative director show us what we could expect from the new potential iPhone 18 colors. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max models are rumored to have bigger batteries, variable-aperture cameras and run on the new Apple A20 processor. More satellite connectivity, a smaller Dynamic Island and tweaked back camera islands are also possibilities. And these new phones could come in colors such as light blue, dark cherry and dark gray.

Running on all these devices is the already announced new family of operating systems. iOS 27, with the anticipated Siri AI revamp, is likely to be released this fall, along with MacOS Golden Gate, Apple TVOS 27 and more. Since we learned about these at WWDC in June, we’ve been playing around with the public betas to see what’s inside.

Apple Watch Series 12: Apple Health and Touch ID?

A Series 12 Watch is “all but guaranteed,” CNET wearables expert Vanessa Hand Orellana says. Less likely are a new Apple Watch SE and Ultra model since they were refreshed in 2025. But any new watches, the Series 12 and Ultra 4, are likely to come with a new processor, which should extend their life and usefulness for you.

The biggest design change expected is largely mechanical, not aesthetic. A more energy-efficient screen technology could be included to extend the watches’ battery life without sacrificing screen brightness. A new processor — probably named the S12 to match the line-up’s naming, despite “S11” being next in line — would also help with this.

The next Apple Watch Series 12 may bring back TouchID. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

Another potential addition could be biometric authentication — in other words, a Touch ID for Apple Watch. Some internal code leaks suggest Apple is working on integrating this tech into its wearables, but it’s unclear when it will be publicly available. Health features, like blood pressure monitoring, are also rumored to be in progress, but again, no guarantees. The Apple Health App’s AI overhaul has also reportedly run into issues.

Our early testing shows WatchOS 27 with Siri AI will bring a big boost to devices — at least, for the ones it’s compatible with, which isn’t all of them. Watches were excluded from Apple’s summer price hike, but similar raises from watches by Google and Samsung mean a higher starting price isn’t out of the realm of possibility.

AirPods with or without cameras

Possibly the biggest Apple rumor has been that the next generation of Apple AirPods will be equipped with a new, tiny infrared camera — not to take photos, but to scan its physical environment to power its visual intelligence, or AI, answers.

The AirPods 5 could look similar to the AirPods 4 (shown) but have performance upgrades. David Carnoy/CNET

These rumored “AirPods Ultra” sparked a lot of concern and outrage from tech enthusiasts, who have spent most of the summer criticizing other AI-and-camera-enabled wearables, like Meta’s smart glasses. Apple is known to tout its focus on privacy, so it will be interesting to see if Apple ultimately comes out with these earbuds and, if so, how it defends them.

AirPods are generally on a two-year refresh cycle, so we may get the AirPods 5 and AirPods 5 Pro this year. The previous model, the AirPods 4 with active noise canceling, is “something of a technological marvel,” CNET headphones expert David Carnoy said. Effective noise canceling is hard to achieve with an open-earbud design, but Apple’s previous success sets the foundation for even more progress here. The Apple-owned Beats 360 headphones could also get refreshed this fall.

For more, check out the best iPhones and best MacBooks for 2026.

Tech.title: This Is the Biggest 2D Map of the Universe. Here’s How to Use It
Tech.content:
Scientists have pointed telescopes at the sky and mapped the cosmos for centuries. That relentless pursuit is producing maps that are bigger and more detailed than ever. But there’s one map that stands out above the rest, and now it’s the largest 2D map of the night sky ever created.

The best part? Anyone can play with it.

The map, called Data Release 11 or DR11, comes courtesy of the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys team at NSF NOIRLab, headquartered in Tucson, Arizona, with contributions from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California and other agencies and organizations.

Covering 75% of the sky across 5.6 trillion pixels, DR11 is the team’s most comprehensive map to date, built upon prior versions of the same map . It expands on DR9 by 50% and brings back northern sky coverage missing from DR10. Based on 263,407 ground-based exposures by 160 scientists, the map catalogs 4 billion objects — including stars, galaxies, black holes and asteroids — in visible and near-infrared light.

Already cited in over 1,800 research papers, NOIRLab expects this to remain the premier 2D map of its kind for years. According to co-lead David Schlegel, it also laid the groundwork for identifying 60 million targets for the DESI project and for building a full 3D map, which was completed in 2026. With billions of targets still unstudied, Schlegel told CNET that “plenty of other discoveries” remain hidden in plain sight for public exploration.

Enough talk, let’s play

The map covers 75% of the night sky, with the black swath through the middle obscured by black holes, interstellar dust and other obstacles. Legacy Survey

The map doesn’t look like much at first. But if you pick a spot and start zooming in, you can get a pretty good idea of how vast it really is. What appears to be a cloud of pretty colors is actually billions of objects floating around in space.

You might notice that DR11, which is designed to see out into the universe, doesn’t contain any planets, moons or asteroids within our solar system. That may be a little bit of a bummer for some, but there are plenty of other objects to look for.

Though the user interface is a little overwhelming at first, you really only need four boxes to play around — and all four of them are right next to each other in the bottom-left corner.

Zoom: This indicates how zoomed in you are based on the +/- slider on the top left. It goes from degrees to arc minutes and then finally to arc seconds. I got most of my best results between 20 and 50 arc minutes.

Contrast and brightness: Below zoom, you’ll find the contrast slider, which reduces the background noise of the map. Under that, the brightness slider helps illuminate smaller objects. Adjust these settings as needed to get the best view, but start with the defaults.

Jump to object: This is the most important box, where you can type in the names of celestial bodies to find them on the map. I searched for a couple dozen celestial objects, and found them all pretty quickly. Online lists of named black holes, quasars and other cool celestial bodies can be a good starting point in exploring the universe — I have more tips for finding them if you keep reading.

Once you land on something, use the zoom slider in the top-left corner to zoom in and get a closer look. (Don’t use your mouse wheel for this because it zooms in wherever your pointer is, potentially taking you to a completely different part of the map.) You can also drag the cursor around the screen to view everything around the object you’re looking at.

A sky like you’ve never seen it

Arcturus is comparably huge in the night sky, and so it is also comparably huge on the map. Legacy Survey

My first visit on the map was to Arcturus, the fourth-largest star in the sky. Zoomed in, it’s much larger than every other object around it by a rather wide margin, which is why it’s so easy to find in the night sky.

Another search took me to LHS 1140b, the first star ever discovered that sits in another star’s habitable zone with an atmosphere. This one is much smaller than Arcturus and required me to zoom in to 30 arc seconds to see it. It’s quite close to its host star, which makes sense since the habitable zone is pretty close to the star itself. Earth would appear at a similar distance from the sun if viewed from this perspective.

The star that LHS 1140b orbits is also dimmer than many other stars. It’s about 20% the size of the sun, so it almost looks like a big planet rather than a small star.

This binary star system hosts planet HD 80606 b, a planet known to orbit so close to its star that it is scorched. It’s so close, in fact, that the light from the binary star system hides it completely. Legacy Survey

Some stuff is easier to find than others. For example, planet HD 80606 b is so close to its star that it is absolutely scorched, with temperature swings of 1,100 degrees Fahrenheit. Bright glare from its binary stars completely obscures HD 80606 b on the map. It’s still there, though, getting blasted by its star like a blowtorch caramelizing sugar on the top of a crème brûlée.

You’ll notice that the map has a large, sweeping blank spot running through it. These are the parts of the sky that haven’t been mapped yet. Researchers say that this is due to various obstacles, such as space dust, bright stars getting in the way of scans and black holes covering everything behind them.

For example, try searching for Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. The map shows you where it is — right inside one of those blank bands. The black hole prevents any telescope from seeing the stars and planets behind it, so that part of the map remains blank.

More advanced options

The planet LHS 1140b orbits a star about one-fifth the size of our sun, and is one of the better candidates for a planet hosting life. Legacy Viewer

You’ll also see a box with a ton of options in the top-right corner of the map. For basic viewing, you don’t have to interact with this box at all, but there are some fun things in there if you want to see them.

Images: This dropdown menu lets you select which set of images you want to use. Leave that on Legacy Surveys DR11 because that’s the most recent dataset.

Overlays: This menu is more complicated, as it includes a lot of different datasets you can overlay. Many of them just show which telescopes, instruments and surveys found each separate part of the map. You can leave them all off and still search around the universe for cool stuff.

However, there is one set of overlays that is worth your time: the Bright objects overlay, with options that actually help you navigate the map. For example, the Bright stars option will put blue circles around the brightest stars on the map with names, making them much easier to find. That’s how I learned that the designation for Arcturus is HR 5340.

Bright objects include star clusters, planetary nebulae and some more specific ones — but the most fun is the Constellations overlay, which shows off every constellation in the sky. If you toggle it on, pick a constellation and zoom into each corner and point, you can find the bright stars that humans used to construct these constellations ages ago.

Finding stuff to search for

Constellations such as Ursa Minor can be seen on the 2D map, letting you explore the bright stars that make up their shape. Legacy Survey

The real challenge in using the DR11 app is figuring out what to look up. There are all sorts of celestial bodies, and many of them have some pretty cool stories. However, there really isn’t much of a repository to find these things.

We know AI isn’t great at many things, but Schlegel suggested that a large language model may be pretty good for this application since it can scan the web quickly.

This isn’t without its caveats. Schlegel said that Google Gemini tends to “spit out sexagesimal coordinates” that don’t work in the map’s viewer website because they’re an archaic sky-mapping system. However, Anthropic’s Claude uses decimal-degree coordinates, which work. While the team is looking into supporting both, Schlegel said he prefers the newer decimal system over the archaic system originally invented by Hipparchus and Ptolemy.

The team also gave CNET a list of some pretty neat stuff to look up in the map viewer if you need more ideas. These are some of the most gorgeous pieces of imagery on the entire map:

NGC 5272 – The Globular Cluster

NGC 4826 – The Black Eye Galaxy

NGC 3351 – The Barred Spiral Galaxy

NGC 4486 – Virgo A

NGC 5457 – The Pinwheel Galaxy

NGC 4594 – Sombrero Galaxy

Schlegel also recommended visiting an FAQ web page for more granular guidance on using the search and overlay functions to improve your experience.

Tech.title: ‘Surprise and Shine!’ How to Watch Apple’s Event Today
Tech.content:
Apple

It’s almost time. Apple is holding its next event, which the company is calling “Surprise and shine,” later today. Historically, Apple has used its September event to announce new hardware, particularly the newest models of iPhones. That means we only have a few hours left see if Apple will unveil the rumored foldable iPhone.

You can catch the Apple event on Apple’s website, Apple TV, the Apple Developer app and the company’s YouTube channel today at 10 a.m. PT (1 p.m. ET, 6 p.m. BST). We expect to hear from Apple’s incoming CEO, John Ternus, for the first time in his role after he took up the mantle on Sept. 1.

Here are a few things Apple could announce at the event.

A foldable iPhone

Whether Apple calls it the iPhone Fold, iPhone Ultra or the iPhone Flip, the company could show off a foldable iPhone at its September event. Leaks and supply chain reports suggest the foldable iPhone will be a squat, book-style foldable, similar to the Samsung Galaxy Fold 8.

This is a mock-up of what a possible iPhone Fold might look like, according to CNET designer Jeffrey Hazelwood. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

Those same leaks also suggest the price of the iPhone foldable could be between $2,000 and $2,500, which could price many people out. According to a CNET survey, US adults are only willing to spend an average of $781 on a foldable iPhone, which is less than the price of the base model iPhone 17 ($799).

Patrick Holland, CNET’s director of content, said that foldable phones remain a niche interest among most shoppers, but that Apple is likely to price the device to reflect its expensive manufacturing costs.

New iPhone 18 Pro models

CNET’s Jeffrey Hazelwood created these custom renders of what an iPhone 18 Pro might look like. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

According to Bloomberg, Apple could unveil the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max at its September event, too. Those iPhones could also see a price hike, with prices starting at $1,200, up from the iPhone 17 Pro‘s starting price of $1,100.

You might notice that entry-level iPhone 18 models are missing from that lineup. That’s because Bloomberg suspects Apple will split the iPhone launch this year. That means we could see the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max in September before Apple rolls out the iPhone 18, iPhone 18E and potentially a refreshed iPhone Air in the spring.

New Apple Watches

The (from left to right) Apple Watch Ultra 3, Apple Watch Series 11 and Apple Watch SE 3. Apple could show new Apple Watches at its event in September. Carly Marsh/CNET

Apple is also reportedly preparing to announce an Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 at its September event. According to Bloomberg, the new watches could include faster chips and new health and fitness features. However, the new watches likely won’t receive a design change.

There’s no solid information about how much these watches will cost. However, Apple has raised a lot of hardware prices this year, so while the starting price of the Apple Watch 11 is $399, the Apple Watch 12 could cost more at launch.

The AirPods 5

The AirPods 4 (pictured) are a few years old now, so Apple could show AirPods 5 at the company’s September event. Apple/CNET

Bloomberg also reports that Apple could debut the AirPods 5 at the September event, releasing an updated version of the company’s entry-level headphones. Apple released the AirPods 4 almost two years ago, in 2024. Apple isn’t expected to show the rumored camera-equipped AirPods at the September event. We could see those later this year, or in 2027.

The AirPods 4 had a starting price of $129 at launch, but given Apple’s other price increases, the AirPods 5 could also see a higher starting price.

Apple did not immediately respond to CNET’s request to comment.

For more Apple news, here’s what to know about the new M6 Mac Mini and when you might be able to preorder an iPhone 18.

Tech.title: The Coolest Thing I Saw at IFA 2026: The Coolest, Quietest, Thinnest Laptop Concept
Tech.content:
Some concepts on display at trade shows are simply bald attempts at garnering attention on a noisy and crowded show floor. And then there are others that provide actual glimpses into the future. Lenovo’s Project Aero falls into the latter category. (I’d put all of its rollable display concepts into the former: fun to see in action, but not something I’d look for in my next purchase.)

There wasn’t much to the ThinkBook laptop used for Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade concept that would get you to stop and take notice. Other than being thinner and lighter than the typical laptop, it looked like a run-of-the-mill business ultraportable. And the Project AeroBlade demo wasn’t particularly compelling on the surface. The laptop’s screen didn’t magically expand at the press of a button to draw oohs and aahs. But under the hood, there was some tech that I hope moves from concept to reality before I need to buy my next laptop.

Active cooling without fans (and their noise)

The concept of Project AeroBlade is moving air in and out of the ThinkBook without the use of any traditional cooling fans. Lenovo calls it Active Flow, a solid-state active cooling system. Instead of fans, Active Flow uses small AirJet modules from Frore Systems. We’ve seen Frore’s AirJet modules before, but this is the first time we’ve seen them in an actual laptop.

AirJet modules use ultrasonic vibrations to pull cool air into the laptop and expel hot air out of it. These tiny modules are about the size of a mobile processor and are just 2.7 millimeters thick, and yet they are incredibly powerful. According to a Frore representative, an AirJet creates 10 times the back pressure, or suction, of a traditional laptop cooling fan.

With four AirJet modules inside instead of a pair of cooling fans, the ThinkBook that Lenovo used for its Project AeroBlade was impossibly thin and light. It was a 14-inch laptop that was only 11mm thick, or about 0.4 inches thick, and weighed just 1.8 pounds. When I picked it up, it felt like a movie prop — an empty shell of a laptop rather than an actual operating machine.

In addition to being very compact, the laptop looked extra polished with a bottom panel that was solid and smooth. Because the AirJets are more effective at moving air in and out of the laptop, the ThinkBook could be designed without any bottom intake vents. All of the air is pulled in and pushed out of a thin vent along the laptop’s back edge.

Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade laptop looks like a standard business laptop, albeit an extremely thin and light one. Matthew Elliott/CNET

Powerful and portable

The promise of Project AeroBlade is getting higher-powered CPUs in thinner and lighter designs. With fanless laptops, you must sacrifice some performance in the form of a low-voltage or throttled processor for the thinness and lightness.

The ThinkBook on display was running a mainstream Core Ultra 7 Lunar Lake 17-watt chip. I wonder if it’ll be able to accommodate a 25-watt Panther Lake or just a lower-wattage WildCat Lake that’s closer in thermal design power to Lunar Lake. And with the laptops we’ll soon see with Nvidia’s RTX Spark, can we look forward to a combination of a 38-watt RTX Spark and AirJet active cooling in the near future?



Another AirJet benefit is acoustics. Like a fanless laptop, the ThinkBook operates in silence but with active cooling that moves air in and out. I could not hear or feel the AirJet modules’ vibrations as they worked.

Further, without any moving parts, the laptop should last longer. Traditional cooling fans get gummed up with dirt and dust and, with their moving parts, are a common point of failure. I’d equate it to solid-state drives generally lasting longer than hard drives with spinning platters.

Lenovo’s concept fanless laptop cooling system uses two sets of four Frore AirJet modules. Josh Goldman/CNET

Lenovo wouldn’t comment on when this concept might turn into a final shipping laptop. And Frore didn’t say if it was working with other laptop manufacturers in addition to Lenovo. But given how much thinner and smaller the AirJet modules are in comparison to cooling fans, plus the fact that they can be located in different areas of the motherboard where heat dissipation is needed the most, implementing them will require a rethinking and reworking of laptop motherboard architecture. This reengineering will require some time, but I’m hoping we will see Lenovo release an AirJet-cooled ThinkBook next year. I also hope Frore’s AirJet tech will spread to other laptops beyond Lenovo’s.

I can envision a not-so-distant future where cooling fans inside laptops become as antiquated as traditional spinning hard drives.

Tech.title: The Best of IFA 2026, Where There’s No Such Thing as Too Many Robots
Tech.content:
After nearly a week roaming the halls of IFA 2026 in Berlin, CNET staffers have seen a lot of tech: some genuinely useful, some wonderfully strange. That includes a dishwasher and toothbrush equipped with cameras, a mom Roomba carrying a baby Roomba, and a variety of life- and voice-recording devices. Together, they offer a glimpse at how tech companies see the future.

Now that the show has come to a close, we’ve sorted through everything we saw to pick the standouts. Here’s the best tech we spotted at IFA 2026.

An all-seeing dishwasher

Miele’s Diamond G8 isn’t your average dishwasher. David Watsky/CNET

Miele’s new Diamond G8 dishwasher has an AI-powered internal camera that scans your dishes and decides how to wash them so it doesn’t miss a single spot. Though Home and Kitchen Managing Editor David Watsky, who saw the dishwasher in person, was skeptical about this feature, he was left impressed.

But the Diamond G8’s scrubbing smarts don’t stop there. If you want the Diamond G8 to run only when electricity is most affordable, it can do that, too, waiting for the hours when power costs less.

Note-taking earbuds

Plaud One: your AI note-taking assistant earbuds. Plaud/CNET

Going beyond its AI note-taking wearable pin and credit card-like device that you can attach to your phone, Plaud launched the Plaud One earbuds to capture and transcribe your conversations and calls. You can even talk to Plaud’s AI by saying, “Hey Plaud,” and then ask it your questions or give it directives.

“We’d always recommend informing people that you’re using a recording device, and it’s important to note that recording phone calls without permission from all participants can be illegal in some states,” principal writer Katie Collins wrote when covering the Plaud One announcement.

A robot vacuum that seals itself to carpet

The Roomba Max 875 Combo is all about clean carpet. iRobot

While robot vacuums are great for taking the effort out of keeping your floors clean, CNET’s testing has found that they don’t offer the same suction power as traditional vacuums. iRobot aims to improve on that with its new Roomba Max 875 Combo, which uses SealForce technology to seal itself to carpet and better suction up spots that need extra cleaning.

In a video call with Home and Robotics Editor Ajay Kumar prior to IFA 2026, Adam Pope, vice president and chief engineer at iRobot, said SealForce is like pressing harder with a traditional vacuum to thoroughly clean a specific patch of carpet, but in a robot vacuum format.

A smart ring puts contactless payments at your fingertips

Imagine how cool it will feel to use your ring for contactless payments. Circular

In addition to having the health-tracking capabilities we expect of smart rings, Circular has added contactless payments, a feature typically found on smartwatches and smartphones, to its new subscription-free Ring 3 Pro and Ring 3 Slim. When covering the launch, principal writer Vanessa Hand Orellana wrote that the company also gave both rings haptic vibration alerts, a feature previously available on its first Circular Ring, along with advanced sleep metrics, glucose trend estimates and access to its AI health coach.

A laptop built to be repaired

The Vero 16 comes with its own repair guide. Acer/CNET

With its new fourth-generation Vero 16, Acer brings the “right to repair” conversation into focus, as CNET writer Tyler Graham explained that the modular laptop is designed to let users easily upgrade its components themselves. There’s even a repair guide engraved on it to help with these swaps.

The Vero 16 didn’t come alone, as it was announced alongside Acer’s compact 14-inch Swift Blade 14 and sleek 16-inch Swift Air 16.

A speaker that lulls you to sleep

Sleep has never sounded so sweet. Katie Collins/CNET

Alongside its Sleep Earbuds 4 and Sleep Earbuds 4 Pro with a touchscreen case, Anker introduced the SleepLab Pro speaker, which uses radar to track your sleep, breathing and heart rate, then customizes its audio to help you drift off to dreamland and stay there. “It looks like a thoughtfully designed piece of kit that I know I’d be happy to have on my bedside table,” Collins wrote when describing the device. It also triples as a sunrise alarm clock and a nightlight that glows in a range of shades.

A non-Pro SleepLab has the same features, minus radar sleep tracking.

Dyson’s largest air purifier

Dyson’s new HushJet air purifiers are a total redesign. Tara Brown/CNET

The new Dyson HushJet Big+Quiet Cool Pure+Formaldehyde (try to say that five times fast) was designed to purify multiple rooms using the company’s most powerful processor. As Kumar put it, it looks like a Dune sandworm with its nozzle head that can be rotated and tilted. While operating quietly, the purifier can capture 99.99% of pollutants down to 0.01 microns for a breath of fresh air.

Lenovo’s first rollable work laptop

Lenovo is on a roll. Josh Goldman/CNET

Lenovo’s Project Swan concept is a laptop that expands horizontally at the touch of a button, transforming its display from 14 to 17 inches. But unlike the Legion Pro Rollable Graham spotted at CES 2026, this isn’t a gaming laptop – it’s for work. Perfect for work trips when you want a more compact 14-inch display for travel, but a 17-inch for getting the job done (or watching movies during your downtime).

Dyson’s first toothbrush

Plaque begone! Tara Brown/CNET

Dubbed the CameraJet, Dyson’s first toothbrush has a built-in, AI-powered camera that detects gaps between your teeth within 100 milliseconds so that it can floss while you brush. To do so, the brush has an anti-gravity tank that its charging dock fills with mouthrinse, which its jet uses to floss.

You can even use the CameraJet’s camera as an endoscope to see your teeth in the app, where brushing and flossing insights, coverage maps and guided cleaning are also available. However, this high-tech toothbrush comes at a cost: $500.

An Instant Pot-like feeder for cats

Get your cat to stop meowing at you for food, and let them meow at this machine instead. David Watsky/CNET

Pet care and home cleaning company Neakasa showed off its Riko smart wet food maker, which Watsky described as an Instant Pot for cats. All you have to do is add water to Riko’s reservoir and freeze-dried food, so refrigeration isn’t required. On demand or when feeding time is scheduled in the app, the device will prepare your feline’s feast by rehydrating and mixing the cat food. Bon appetit!

A smart radiator valve

Its high-res screen shows temperature, settings and device status in real time. Sonoff

Home Security and Smart Home Senior Editor Tyler Lacoma has been waiting for a smart thermostat that isn’t just for forced air heating and cooling, and smart home company Sonoff displayed exactly that at IFA. The TRV Smart Thermostatic Radiator Valve provides three temperature scheduling plans and frost protection and anti-calcification reminders. It even connects to window sensors to prevent energy waste. Just screw it onto your radiator’s valve pipe and let it take care of the rest.

A Roomba that carries another Roomba

A true dynamic duo. Ajay Kumar/CNET

Apparently, one Roomba is no longer enough. The Roomba Duo is a concept floor-cleaning system consisting of a large robot that vacuums and steam-mops open areas and a smaller Roomba that rides on top of it. When the Duo encounters furniture or another space it can’t squeeze beneath, a mechanical arm lowers the little robot to the floor and sends it in.

The two robots share a map and coordinate their cleaning through the Roomba app, while the larger unit also carries clean and dirty water tanks, a dust bag and enough hardware to function as its own mobile dock. It’s ambitious and ridiculous-looking, but honestly, it’s exactly the sort of thing we come to IFA to see. Because it remains a concept, iRobot hasn’t announced a price or release date.

An AI mic that writes your emails for you

Keyboards beware. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Collins got a first look at the Relay Q, which looks like a small lighter. Just hold down the top to whisper voice commands or whatever you want it to write. Then, double-press the top to send. You can even slide the top off the device, using its magnet to turn it into a wearable pin.

“What immediately impressed me about the Relay Q is its design and the tactile experience of holding the device,” Collins wrote. “I wasn’t surprised to learn the team members are Nothing alumni, responsible for helping design some of the coolest audio and mobile devices on the market.”

Home security with custom AI detection

Custom on-device AI with no extra costs? Say less. Reolink

At IFA, smart home security company Reolink showed off its AI engine, ReoNeura, which impressed Lacoma, who reviews home security tech for CNET, for several reasons. In addition to enabling users to customize its AI, ReoNeura doesn’t require a cloud or a cloud subscription. This would make it the only custom AI engine that doesn’t cost extra.

A wearable robot

You can have your robot and wear it, too. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

iKairos can be either a pendant on your necklace or a desktop robot. Currently being developed by Singaporean startup Lingverse and spotted by Collins, it tracks your conversations and environment to preserve memories and make helpful suggestions. Underneath its display with cartoon eyes, there’s also a camera you can use to take photos or videos.

Tech.title: Why Miele Put a Camera Inside Its Latest Dishwasher
Tech.content:
It seems the public wants fewer cameras, not more, but that hasn’t stopped the large appliance industry. While a fridge or oven camera almost certainly presents less of a privacy risk than a Flock surveillance unit — hey, it’s right there in the name — one could argue they’ve gone overboard.

Sensors and lenses have crept into nearly every other kitchen machine, met with a range of consumer sentiment. Smart ovens and connected refrigerators aren’t new, but a camera-equipped dishwasher? When I heard that Miele snuck one inside its latest model, the Diamond G8 unveiled at IFA 2026 in Berlin, I was suspicious. After a rep walked me through the new machine’s novel smart features, the reasoning came somewhat into focus.

A camera in Miele’s new dishwasher helps it choose the best cycle.

An AI-powered camera recognizes dish types to help pick a cycle

The small camera, fixed to the back of the dishwasher door, gets a clear shot of the dishwasher’s interior. It uses that view to take inventory of what’s inside, recognizing dozens of common kitchen items and tailoring the wash cycle and detergent volume accordingly.

The Diamond G8 is one of the smartest dishwashers we’ve encountered, and it’s easy on the eyes.

Got portable bottles or reusable straws in the dedicated slots? The dishwasher’s brain recognizes them and makes sure those items get the spritz they need. Load it up with pots and pans, and the camera identifies them, triggering a more intensive cycle so everything comes out clean. A smaller load prompts a lighter cycle, so you’re not wasting hot water or soap.

The G8 recognizes straws, flatware, silverware and cookware and adjusts its cycle for optimized cleaning.

The camera also determines how full the dishwasher is. Command the G8 to start when it reaches, say, 80% capacity, and it’ll monitor the load and automatically begin a cycle once it hits that threshold.

One of my favorite features has nothing to do with the camera

The G8 Diamond takes advantage of fluctuations in electricity prices throughout the day. Tell it to run when electricity is cheapest, and the dishwasher waits for those lower-cost hours before starting its cycle. It’s a small detail, but it points to where Miele – and kitchen appliances more broadly – seem to be headed: machines that don’t just perform a task, but figure out the best and most efficient way to do it.

The dishwasher can be programmed to run when energy costs are cheapest in your area.

Miele’s newly unveiled machine has other AI-powered features that encourage efficiency and performance. The G8 features careful water and energy monitoring, which you can track through Miele’s app. It also includes a smart detergent-dispensing system, first introduced by the brand in 2018, and a beefed-up hot-air drying system that Miele says gets dishes bone-dry every time.

The camera paired with a smart detergent dispenser doles out just the right amount of soap.

Miele plans to roll out the Diamond G8 in the European market later this year as it considers a North American strategy, according to a spokesperson.

A retail price is still under wraps, but I expect it to land in the super-premium zone. For a top-performing dishwasher you can buy today, see our list of the best models in 2026.

Editors’ note: David Watsky’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by IFA. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Meta’s New AI Agent Wants to Get Personal With You
Tech.content:
This seems to be the year of AI agents, and Meta is diving into the game. The company on Tuesday announced a new agent program called Muse, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg describes as a “personal agent” that understands your habits and goals. It’s available now in the US.

Introducing Muse, the personal agent that understands your goals and works 24/7 to get things done for you. — Mark Zuckerberg (@finkd) September 8, 2026

Agentic AI is a type of generative AI based on a large language model where agents, or bots, are meant to take actions autonomously on your behalf. Meta’s Muse, for example, can do online shopping (with your permission), create documents, fill out forms and respond to emails.

Meta says that Muse is a more general-purpose agent, not limited to specific tasks like coding. (If you want agentic coding help, you can use Muse Code, also recently released by the company.) You have to give Muse permission to access your apps and data, which you can revoke at any time. Like a lot of agentic AI tools, the more info you give it, the more personalized your results will be.

Muse runs “on its own dedicated computer in the cloud,” according to a Meta blog post, in what the company calls a “virtual machine.” The tool also has a separate Sentinel agent — you can think of it as a virtual traffic cop, giving Muse a red or green light before letting it out onto the internet to complete tasks.

Agentic AI can be risky. Over the summer, agents from Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic each slipped out of their testing environments and hacked outside websites, casting increased scrutiny on the potentially disastrous harm AI can do to our cybersecurity.

Meta’s vice president of Superintelligence Labs, Tarek Sheasha, said in a blog post: “The harness runs in its own isolated cell, it doesn’t see real credentials, and every interaction with the outside world runs through a Sentinel which the agent can’t override.”

Muse is available now on iOS and Android and on the muse.ai website. The company says it will be bringing the AI to its controversial smart glasses soon. According to Zuckerberg, it will be free for people to use “up to 100 million tokens per week” (one token is roughly equivalent to four characters). So unless you’re constantly running Muse on complex tasks, you should be able to use it for a while before running into a paywall.
